Justin Tang/Canadian Press[](https://www.thestar.com/news/popular-children-s-compression-swing-recalled-due-to-fall-hazard/article_1ae2a179-7483-40ce-ba81-e5046259d227.html)

ByMegan Mills Devoe Staff Reporter

Over 5,000 units of Harkla Compression Sensory swings have been recalled across Canada due to risk of injury caused by a fall.

According to Health Canada, some units of the swing, which is designed to hang from the ceiling, have faulty hardware which can result in the swing collapsing.

FREE ACCESS FOR 7 DAYS

No payment required

Email address Start My 7-Day Trial

Start My 7-Day Trial Cancel anytime

Secure transaction.Have an account? Log In)

“The swing’s ceiling hook can separate from its mounting plate, posing a risk of injury from a fall hazard,” wrote Health Canada in a recall notice published Oct. 29.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

The Zookeeper and The Tin Man: A Halloween Love Story

Image 10Image 11

As of Oct. 23, Harkla states that it has received one report of injury in Canada and 17 reports of injury in the United States.The company said it received four reports of the hook and plate separating in Canada, and 29 reports in the United States.

Compression swings are sometimes used by children with Autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and sensory processing disorder to help regulate their nervous system. Harkla’s swings are designed for children aged 3 and over.

Health Canada stated that this recall affect units of Harkla Children’s Compression Sensory Swings that have a blue fabric seat and come with a four-hole ceiling hook mounting plate for suspension, with a drop length of 18 to 24 inches. Affected units have either LS-COMP-1BLU or LS-COMP-1BLU-SW printed on the side of the product packaging.

According to Health Canada, the products were sold between March 2020 and April 2025.

The health organization has advised customers to stop using the product immediately and to contact Harkla in order to obtain a free repair kit.

Megan Mills Devoe is a staff reporter with the Star. Reach her via email:mmillsdevoe@thestar.ca

He says Port Coquitlam Mayor Brad West could be another “strong voice” to lead the provincial NDP.

The New Democrats have named former labour minister Jennifer Whiteside as their interim leader, and Kahlon says she will do a “fantastic” job.

Kahlon, who was first elected in 2017, says he doesn’t know what his future will look like beyond his immediate focus on his family, but he has told former caucus colleagues that he is around to help.

“There’s a lot of talent,” he told The Canadian Press.

stories.title: Police look for three men in violent Bridle Path home invasion
stories.summary: Father, two adult daughters were shot after masked suspects forced their way into the home before fleeing in an SUV
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Toronto police say they are looking for three young men following a violent home invasion and shooting in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood on Thursday.

They say all three suspects were wearing dark clothing, are estimated to be about 20 years old and are considered armed and dangerous.

Police first received reports of three people shot inside a residence in the Post Road and Hyde Park Circle at around 3:40 a.m. Thursday.

Investigators say a father and his two adult daughters were shot when the masked suspects forced their way into the home through the rear door, armed with guns and a hammer.

Police say the father and the mother were also struck with a hammer.

Police say the suspects fled in a dark-coloured SUV and anyone with information is asked to come forward.

stories.title: Canada needs a ‘good mix’ of new tech like drones, AI: Nato commander
stories.summary: Next week’s federal budget is expected to have more details about how Canada intends to meet ambitious defence spending targets by 2035.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
As Canada prepares to invest billions into national defence in the coming years, a senior Nato official is advising the alliance’s militaries to include a mix of cutting-edge technology like AI targeting and advanced drones into their plans.

Speaking to Global News from Riga, Latvia, ON Friday, Adm. Pierre Vandier said that it’s not a question of replacing “everything” with drones — but rather incorporating drones and other unmanned systems to protect and enhance existing military capabilities.

“A force that is not protected against drones and (drone) swarms is a force at risk,” Vandier, Nato’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, said in an interview.

Vandier was speaking after observing Nato exercises in Latvia that included a mix of electronic warfare and drones along with “boots on the ground” to simulate a cross-border invasion.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is top of mind for the alliance forces stationed in Latvia, including the roughly 3,000 Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) personnel stationed in the country as part of Operation Reassurance.

That conflict has seen dramatic developments in the use of drones in warfare, including to limit the effectiveness of more traditional military assets — such as tanks and ground forces.

But Vandier said that one of the lessons learned through the Nato exercises is that drone warfare doesn’t make those traditional military systems obsolete — but rather that drones and electronic warfare tactics, including in a “good mix” of other military capabilities, can make a force more effective.

“What we demonstrated was we can extend lethality and extend survivability of existing capabilities … if we bring them with a good mix of new technology,” Vandier said.

Vandier gave the example of an attack helicopter. With the use of both drones and anti-drone defences, the French admiral said that weapons system can execute missions “that were impossible before.”

“What robots are bringing is a risk management system, where you can open the tactical portfolio … and have better use of what you have,” Vandier said.

Since 2022, Nato has been running exercises with the Latvian Ministry of Defence to test electronic warfare, drone and AI technologies in “field-like conditions.” The exercises, known as the Digital Backbone eXperimentation (DIBaX), include the participation of defence companies and academics to test cutting-edge technology in a realistic setting.

According to a Nato official, this year’s exercise included testing of drone swarms, drone-to-drone combat and a cross-border incursion, along with electronic warfare tactics meant to jam or otherwise disable enemy drones.

These are themes that the CAF has been thinking about for years, including deploying anti-drone defences for personnel stationed in Latvia.

Earlier this year, the Department of National Defence launched the Defence Drone Initiative (DDI), an effort to both provide the CAF and the Canadian Coast Guard with new drone technology and to boost the domestic industry.

“Recent conflicts have underscored how rapidly drone technologies are transforming modern warfare and are central to modern military operations … Success increasingly depends on the ability to innovate, adapt and field new capabilities at speed,” the government said in July.

“Canada must be prepared to do the same.”

The push to develop Canada’s drone capabilities also comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to invest billions of new money into national defence, with Canada finally meeting its Nato target of spending two per cent of GDP on the defence this year.

The Carney government has released few details, however, about how it intends to reach the target of spending five per cent of GDP on defence by 2035. A recent analysis by the Parliamentary Budget Office suggested reaching that target would require “core” defence spending to increase from $95.7 billion in 2030 to $163.7 billion in 2035-36.

More details on how the Liberals intend to do that are expected in Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne’s 2026-27 budget, scheduled to be tabled next Thursday.

stories.title: Multiple fire departments respond to large dairy barn blaze near Listowel
stories.summary: Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night that affected dozens of cattle.

North Perth Fire Department crews from the Listowel, Atwood and Monkton stations were dispatched to a working structure fire at a dairy barn on Line 88 at about 9:05 p.m.

Mutual aid assistance was provided by fire departments from Minto, Mapleton and Howick as crews worked to contain the blaze.

Heavy equipment was brought to the scene at approximately 11:15 p.m. to assist firefighters.

Officials said 88 cattle were involved in the fire, although it remains unclear how many animals were possibly lost.

No injuries to firefighters or anyone else at the scene were reported.

While a cause has not been released, officials said the fire is not suspicious in nature.

stories.title: Bennett Jones, Borden Ladner Gervais hit in data breach targeting Bay Street law firms
stories.summary: McCarthy Tétrault and Davies Ward Phillips & Vineberg are also dealing with data breaches that have compromised thousands of files
stories.author: Alexandra Posadzki
stories.content:
Bennett Jones LLP and Borden Ladner Gervais LLP have confirmed that they were compromised by data breaches as part of a broader campaign that has successfully infiltrated at least four Bay Street law firms.

David Di Paolo, national managing partner and CEO of BLG, said an unauthorized third party accessed “a portion” of the firm’s Microsoft cloud environment, including files related to clients. The firm engaged Mandiant, a cybersecurity consulting firm and Google subsidiary, to investigate the incident, determine the scope of the breach and support remediation, Mr. Di Paolo said in a statement provided to The Globe and Mail.

Bennett Jones said two of its business services employees’ user accounts were compromised on Oct. 19 as part of what it called a “larger campaign targeting Canadian law firms.”

McCarthy Tétrault LLP and Davies Ward Phillips & Vineberg LLP are also dealing with data breaches that have compromised thousands of files in total, including client information, The Globe reported on Thursday.

All of the firms that were breached have notified law enforcement and are reaching out to affected clients.

“All the major law firms, and in particular, all the CIOs [chief information officers], are sharing intel and best practices,” Mr. Castiel said.

stories.title: Canada, EU lay out vision for closer ties in ‘dangerous and divided’ world
stories.summary: Canada and the EU are laying out their vision for what a closer relationship looks like in an increasingly “dangerous and divided” where trade has become “weaponized.”
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada and the EU are laying out their vision for what a closer relationship looks like as the world becomes increasingly “dangerous and divided” and where trade has become “weaponized.”

While the agreement, signed Friday, only refers to the United States once in reference to its sanctions imposed on the International Criminal Court, Prime Minister Mark Carney has made no secret of his plans to foster relationships with other foreign nations in the wake of increasing trade tensions.

“This is a positive alliance. It’s about creating opportunity, building prosperity, addressing sustainability, and reinforcing sovereignty,” Carney said. “It’s not against anything, it’s for. And those who choose to be for solutions will be pleased with the result.”

The prime minister said the agreement, in which Canada and the European Union agree to pursue “an even closer association” between their respective leaders, industries and people, vows to create opportunities for those on both sides of the ocean.

“Opportunity for our youth, for our artists, for our researchers, for our businesses. It’s about democracy, protecting against foreign interference and social media manipulation while supporting human rights, freedom, and the rule of law. This is about sustainability. Protect our oceans, our forests, and our Arctic, while developing practical, scalable solutions to climate change. And above all, it’s about sovereignty, about being able to live our lives as we wish,” Carney said.

The agreement sets out an alliance for trade, research, raw minerals, energy, security and preparedness, including vows to pursue easier digital money transfers between people in Canada and Europe as well as more opportunities for labour mobility and youth education abroad.

“This is based on partnership, balance, and mutual respect. And like any major bridge, each side has something to offer the other,” Carney said.

Both parties say they will collaborate to work toward connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, low-cost and more seamless border transactions, making it easier to conduct business across the Atlantic and transfer funds between the two economies.

Currently, large sums typically need to be handled by wire transfers which take days to process.

Canada and the EU will also launch negotiations to encourage deeper participation in Erasmus+, the EU flagship program for education, training youth and support to expand opportunities for students, researchers, educators and young people to gain international experience and promote training and lasting institutional partnerships.

Canada and the EU have also agreed to launch discussion on cooperating on skills development and enhancing labour and research mobility, with a focus on reducing barriers for young people and facilitating mobility for highly skilled workers.

“This alliance is built for people. The student in Edmonton who wants to study in Stockholm. The cancer researcher in Saskatoon who needs her answer today, not next spring. The Vancouver startup with new customers in Berlin,” Carney said. “We launch a new alliance for the future that will deliver now and in the future with like-minded nations. We’re just getting started.”

Canada has also signalled its intention to join the Ukraine Support Loan, affirming a commitment to support for Ukraine’s independence and sovereignty through political, financial, humanitarian, military and diplomatic aid.

“We see the world through the same eyes. What matters nowadays is not where a country is on the map, but what it is ready to build with us and what it stands for in the world of fierce geopolitical headwinds. These headwinds won’t stop blowing. This change is permanent and now it is time to act with confidence and with vision to build a new future,” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said Friday.

She said Canada’s priorities and visions align with the EU enough that “we can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we’ve done before.”

“In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty is no longer the freedom to act alone, but it is the capacity to act together.”

The two leaders have also laid out plans for participation on artificial intelligence, outer space, climate change, as well as European investment in critical raw minerals.

However, the agreement made no mention of whether Canada will align with European regulations on AI, which require the labelling content generated or assisted using AI.

stories.title: Trick-or-treating still popular among Canadians with children: poll
stories.summary: Toronto - A new poll suggests 80 per cent of parents with kids old enough to trick-or-treat will participate in the door-to-door ritual, but only half of respondents plan to dish out candy.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A new poll suggests 80 per cent of parents with kids old enough to trick-or-treat will participate in the door-to-door ritual, but only half of respondents plan to dish out candy.

The online survey from Leger asked 1,513 people aged 18 or older about their Halloween habits between Oct. 24 and 26. Of those, 419 were parents with kids of trick-or-treating age.

stories.title: Toronto police say three men wanted in violent Bridle Path home invasion
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto police say they are looking for three young men following a violent home invasion and shooting in the affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood on Thursday.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The head of a corporate real estate firm whose family was attacked during a violent home invasion in Toronto’s affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood says they experienced a “horrific” ordeal and are focused on recovery as police seek three suspects in the case.

In a statement released Friday afternoon, CEO of MAC Group David Morton said three members of his family were recovering in the hospital after being shot during the attack early on Thursday. He said all four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” Morton wrote in the statement.

“It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.”

Police first received reports of three people shot inside a residence on Hyde Park Circle at around 3:40 a.m. Thursday.

Investigators said a father, mother and their two adult daughters were in the home when masked suspects forced their way in through the rear door, armed with guns and a hammer. Police said the father and the two daughters were shot.

The male suspects then made their way to the second floor of the home and demanded valuables, police said. They got into an “altercation” with the family and shot their weapons multiple times, investigators said.

All three suspects in the violent attack were wearing dark clothing, are estimated to be about 20 years old and are considered armed and dangerous, police said in an update Friday. They fled in a dark-coloured SUV.

While his family is recovering from the attack, Morton said they are also “deeply concerned” about increasing home invasion violence across Toronto.

“No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives,” he wrote in his statement.

He urged anyone with information about the attack at his home to come forward. “We sincerely hope that the individuals responsible will be identified, apprehended and brought to justice.”

Toronto police Insp. Kristy Smith told a news conference Thursday that it was unclear if any belongings were stolen, or if the home was specifically targeted.

“Typically in an affluent neighbourhood come nice things,” she said. “There’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things.”

So far this year, 119 home invasions have been reported in Toronto, up more than 32 per cent from the same time last year, police said in an email.

At a Toronto police board meeting in April, Smith said the city saw a significant increase in home invasions in 2024, connected to the rise in violent car thefts.

This year, some neighbourhoods have become “hot spots” for these offences, she said. That includes areas in the police force’s 32 Division, which covers multiple neighbourhoods across North York, and 53 Division, covering midtown Toronto.

The Bridle Path neighbourhood is located in 33 Division, which also saw an increase in home invasion offences, according to police data.

Violent home invasions have been reported across the Greater Toronto Area in recent years.

In August of 2025, a man was fatally shot in his Vaughan home during a home invasion when he confronted the suspects. The man’s brother said one of the intruders allegedly pointed a gun at the man’s children before shooting him. His family witnessed the shooting.

Earlier that summer, Peel regional police laid 136 charges against 12 people after an investigation into violent home invasions and jewelry store robberies. They said 17 such incidents took place between May and December 2024.

As Toronto police continue to investigate the Bridle Path shooting, they say they will have an increased presence in the neighbourhood.

“We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is,” Smith said on Thursday. “People should be able to feel safe in their homes.”

Morton said many people have reached out with messages of concern and support. “The outpouring of kindness has meant a great deal to us during this incredibly difficult time.”

The family is focused on recovery and asks for privacy, Morton wrote. “Our priority is getting through this together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: London man sentenced to nine years for shooting outside downtown strip club
stories.summary: Kwabena Anhwere, 44, was sentenced Friday by Justice Kelly Tranquilli after pleading guilty to three firearm-related offences stemming from the April 2023 shooting
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London man who fired a handgun outside a downtown strip club more than three years ago has been sentenced to nine years in prison.

Kwabena Anhwere, 44, was sentenced Friday by Justice Kelly Tranquilli after pleading guilty to three firearm-related offences stemming from the April 2023 shooting outside the Solid Gold Club on Dundas Street.

During the sentencing hearing, the court heard how an argument inside the club led to Anhwere being removed by security guards. Surveillance video showed him getting up from the sidewalk with a handgun before running toward the entrance and firing a shot.

The bullet struck the door. No one was injured.

Justice Tranquilli described Anhwere’s actions as a “grave danger to public safety,” noting it was only by coincidence that the incident did not result in a tragedy.

The nine-year sentence reflects a joint submission from the Crown and defence.

Anhwere received credit for time spent in pre-sentence custody and has approximately four-and-a-half years left to serve.

He also received a lifetime firearms prohibition and is subject to mandatory DNA orders.

stories.title: Is permanent daylight savings time or standard time better? What to know
stories.summary: Transitioning to daylight saving time in the spring shifts daylight further into the evening, but in the winter it pushes sunrise later, especially in more northern latitudes.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
As we approach the end of Daylight Saving Time (DST), millions of Canadians will set their clocks back one hour this weekend, while millions of others will not.

The Maritime provinces as well as Quebec and most parts of Ontario and Nunavut, will adhere to the time old tradition of turning their clocks back, while B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Yukon and the Northwest Territories will remain on permanent DST.

Researchers have pushed for an end to time changes for years, citing concerns over sleep patterns, mental health, physical health and productivity. But now many are saying remaining on DST permanently May be the wrong choice.

“When you want to change to permanent time, it should be permanent standard time,” Kai-Florian Storch, a professor of psychiatry at McGill University, told Global News.

Transitioning to DST in the spring shifts daylight further into the evening making the day seem longer. But keeping that time into the winter months pushes sunrise later, especially in more northern latitudes.

“You don’t want to wake up too far away from sunrise, so you don’t want to wake up in the dark if possible. You want to wake up as close as possible to sunrise,” Storch said.

But on permanent DST, Vancouver, Calgary and Winnipeg will see the sun rise between 9 and 9:30 a.m. in the winter. In Edmonton, sunrise on the winter solstice will occur just before 10 a.m. In the territories the sun will rise after 11 a.m.

When the sun rises in the morning it resets our biological clock, Rebecca Robillard, a psychology professor at the University of Ottawa and co-chair of the Canadian Sleep Research Consortium, told Global News.

Having the sun rise later in the morning can cause mental and physical health issues , she said.

“Whether we talk about heart rate, metabolism, how we process sugar, insulin, all of our hormones are regulated by this biological clock,” she added.

These changes can result in an increase in heart attacks, complications related to immune disorders, digestive problems, kidney problems, pregnancy complications, anxiety, depression, substance use and suicide, she said.

“At the end of the day, I think this is not just a question of preference. This is really a question of public health that we should consider the well-being of all Canadians,” she said.

Some Canadian cities began changing their clocks in the early 1910s with the rest of the country standardizing the practice in the late 1960s. The original argument for the change was to increase productivity and facilitate economic interactions with the U.S. and other countries.

Now as Western Canada moves away from the practice, those provinces will be out of sync with their southern neighbours.

“It’s better to all make the same choice,” Patrick Baylis, a professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia, told Global News.

Aside from business interactions, Baylis said individual productivity could take a hit on permanent DST.

“You see this first and foremost in student performance, which matters for its own sake, but is also kind of an indicator for what might be happening in the economy,” he said, emphasizing that a lack of sleep can lead to poor performance.

He said shift workers and those with less flexible schedules will feel the hit the most.

“If you’re required to be at work at 8 a.m., this matters a lot because you’re now going from a few weeks where the sunrise was going to be after the time when you’re supposed to be at work, to a few months,” he said.

“The rule of thumb is the less flexible your work hours are and the closer that start is to when sunrise would have been, the more effective you’re gonna be.”

Baylis said the short term effects might be hard to track, but he expects the long term data to be telling.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced earlier this week on social media that his government would put an end to the time change s and will work to determine whether permanent DST or standard time will be the norm.

The province of Ontario previously said that it would get rid of the practice if its neighbours in Manitoba, Quebec and New York did the same.

Storch said he doesn’t think the change will last long.

“This waking up too early will make people upset and will maybe, in my prediction, convince people to again do away with it and switch back to permanent standard time.”

– With files from Global News’ Heather Yourex-West, Aaron McArthur and Tim Sargeant

stories.title: Family of First Nation woman who died amid lack of medical travel asks for OPP probe
stories.summary: The family of a northern Ontario First Nation woman who died after she couldn't get to crucial medical appointments following open-heart surgery has asked provincial police to investigate her death.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The family of a northern Ontario First Nation woman who died after she couldn’t get to crucial medical appointments following open-heart surgery has asked provincial police to investigate her death.

Eva Mamakwa said her 31-year-old daughter, Miranda Mamakwa, died in September after Indigenous Services Canada’s non-insured health benefits program did not arrange travel for her followup appointments after the April surgery.

Miranda Mamakwa lived in Fort Severn First Nation, a remote fly-in community on the mouth of the Severn River on Hudson Bay, with her three children and her parents.

The Nihb program for First Nations and Inuit people covers medical, dental and mental health care not available through private insurance or provincial health plans.

The family now wants Ontario Provincial Police to launch a criminal investigation into the individuals at Nihb who dealt with Mamakwa’s case. They allege the Sioux Lookout, Ont., branch of the program failed to arrange travel to medical appointments on four separate occasions from May through August, including appointments with cardiovascular specialists.

“This should never have happened to Miranda,” her parents, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, said in a statement.

“She should be alive today. We deserve to know how something like this happened, and we want the individual or individuals responsible for failing to respond to these urgent requests for transportation to be held accountable. They cost Miranda her life. They cost her children a future without their mother.”

The family sent a letter to police on Thursday with their request, their lawyer Julian Falconer said.

The OPP did not respond to a request for comment from The Canadian Press.

“We have created an apartheid system in this country as it relates to the delivery of medical services to Indigenous people. It must stop,” Falconer said in a statement.

Indigenous Services Canada has said it is working to improve the medical travel service and implemented a simplified travel submission process in early October. Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said her department is reviewing the circumstances of the case, and that Mamakwa’s community and family deserved answers.

Mamakwa’s doctors wanted followup care because she had blood clots and was taking blood thinners that required ongoing testing, her mother previously told The Canadian Press.

She tried to arrange travel through the First Nation’s nursing station, whose staff were trying to deal with the Nihb, but her family said they just never arranged travel. Her mother said the people in the program “didn’t care.”

In mid-August, Miranda Mamakwa became fed up with the program and wrote on Facebook: “If I die, pls go after em.”

She died of a brain hemorrhage on Sept. 8, her family said.

First Nation chiefs have for years sounded the alarm on the non-insured health benefits program. Several hundred First Nation leaders and community members held a sit in at the Nihb office in Sioux Lookout this summer as they demanded change.

Last month, more than a dozen First Nations and tribal councils filed a human rights complaint alleging widespread neglect of community health needs and seeking reform of the program. Collectively, they cite hundreds of missed medical appointments for those who live in northern Ontario’s remote fly-in communities.

Indigenous Services Canada has said the department takes seriously any complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that it would respond “through the appropriate process.”

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said her department is reviewing the circumstances of the case, and that Mamakwa’s community and family deserved answers.
Mamakwa’s doctors wanted followup care because she had blood clots and was taking blood thinners that required ongoing testing, her mother previously told The Canadian Press.

She tried to arrange travel through the First Nation’s nursing station, whose staff were trying to deal with the Nihb, but her family said they just never arranged travel. Her mother said the people in the program “didn’t care.”
In mid-August, Miranda Mamakwa became fed up with the program and wrote on Facebook: “If I die, pls go after em.”
She died of a brain hemorrhage on Sept. 8, her family said.

First Nation chiefs have for years sounded the alarm on the non-insured health benefits program. Several hundred First Nation leaders and community members held a sit in at the Nihb office in Sioux Lookout this summer as they demanded change.

Last month, more than a dozen First Nations and tribal councils filed a human rights complaint alleging widespread neglect of community health needs and seeking reform of the program. Collectively, they cite hundreds of missed medical appointments for those who live in northern Ontario’s remote fly-in communities.
Indigenous Services Canada has said the department takes seriously any complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that it would respond “through the appropriate process.”

stories.title: Maritime communities join movement to make Halloween accessible for all children
stories.summary: Treat Accessibly has been organizing events for children of all abilities and encouraging neighbourhoods to join in by thinking about how to make Halloween night fun for all.
stories.author: Ella Macdonald, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
A national movement is making trick-or-treating accessible for every child.

Now in its ninth year, Treat Accessibly has been organizing events for children of all abilities and encouraging neighbourhoods to join in by thinking about how to make Halloween night fun for all.

The organization’s founder, Rich Padulo, says it all began with an observation.

“My daughter was putting pumpkins on our stairs. It was 2017. She looked up and like any six-year-old, she thought about things nobody else does. And she said, how does that little boy that she saw using a wheelchair trick-or-treat at our home? And we immediately jumped into planning,” said Padulo.

“That Halloween, a week later, we (handed out treats) from the end of our driveway … And that is the movement that we’ve carried on.”

Padulo says the goal is to ensure children with mobility, sensory and neurological disabilities can easily join in the festivities.

“I had one dad race up to me to tell me that his daughter had never said anything to a stranger before saying trick-or-treat at one of our villages,” he said.

This year, 19 cities and towns in seven provinces are taking part with either a dedicated street or a special event.

In Moncton, N.B., there’s a whole village set up for little ghouls and goblins.

“We are New Brunswick’s only Treat Accessibly Halloween Village. So this Saturday, our event will demonstrate what an accessible Halloween can look like,” said organizer Amanda Martin.

“Instead of facing stairs, closed doors, children are going to visit decorated community stations inside the Resurgo Place museum.”

In Nova Scotia, Southampton Drive in Cole Harbour is Halifax’s official Treat Accessibly Halloween street.

Beginning at 4 p.m. on Halloween night, 22 homes on the loop street will bring their treats to the end of their driveways to make trick-or-treating more accessible for people with mobility challenges.

“Just the joy and delight that they experience mixed with the parents’ gratitude of not having to worry about their children’s happiness for a night — it makes it all worth it,” said street captain Calum Sencabaugh.

stories.title: OpenAI challenging B.C. privacy order for details of Tumbler Ridge shooting
stories.summary: Victoria - The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia says artificial intelligence company OpenAI is challenging an order to produce documents related to the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has filed a legal challenge against an order by British Columbia’s Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner to produce documents related to the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge.

A statement from the independent privacy watchdog said the California-based company had requested a judicial review in B.C. Supreme Court, challenging the request for certain documents as part of an ongoing investigation.

The office said it originally asked OpenAI in February to provide information, including the “specific interactions” its ChatGPT platform had with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar, following media reports linking the chatbot with the shootings.

Van Rootselaar killed eight people on Feb. 10, including five students and an educational assistant at a secondary school, before fatally shooting herself.

The privacy office said its probe is focused on the use of personal information in the chatbot’s responses, such as details in uploaded content or interactions with other ChatGPT users, and whether it would be considered appropriate under the circumstances, “including the potential for responses to influence behaviour.”

The office said OpenAI did not comply with its request and it launched an investigation in June, followed by an order in September compelling the production of the information, which the tech company was challenging.

“Due to the sensitive nature of the subject matter of this investigation, the (office) is limiting information disclosed publicly to what is strictly necessary,” it said.

“The (office) is providing key information about the investigation to the general public, now that it is in the public domain.”

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

The company shut down Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account in June 2025 after it was flagged for concerning behaviour, but it did not notify police.

The firm’s petition, stamped by B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver on Oct. 26, seeks an order quashing the investigation by the privacy office.

Alternatively, it asks the court to throw out the office’s order to produce information related to the mass shooting.

The petition says the order is an “unnecessary and impermissible demand for compelled production of personal information, and it would set a dangerous precedent.”

The statement from the privacy office, issued Tuesday, said it has jurisdiction over organizations that collect, use and disclose the personal information of B.C. residents under the Personal Information Protection Act.

But the OpenAI petition says “a tragedy, however grave, cannot give a privacy regulator expertise over online safety, nor does it expand the Oipc’s powers beyond their statutory and constitutional limits.”

The petition says the office had neither offered a “coherent rationale” for its investigation, nor identified reasonable grounds to believe OpenAI breached the provincial legislation in connection with the Tumbler Ridge shootings.

It argues the B.C. government’s lawsuit against OpenAI, filed in the United States, alleges the opposite — “that OpenAI should have made greater use of personal information by providing it to law enforcement eight months before the tragedy.”

The petition also says OpenAI had produced the shooter’s ChatGPT logs “subject to legal process from the RCMP” and subsequently provided the logs to the B.C. government as part of the province’s ongoing litigation against the company.

Several victims and their families have also filed lawsuits against the tech firm.

A 30-year-old resident of Bellingham, Wash., is meanwhile accused of conspiring with Van Rootselaar online, helping to set up a planned livestream of the shootings.

James Cody Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, pleaded not guilty in Seattle this month to the charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, with a trial set for December.

Bryant has been denied bail.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Montreal police officer could face charges after allegedly concealing evidence
stories.summary: City’s police chief to address the case and provide update on other misconduct allegations from earlier this year
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Montreal Police Chief Fady Dagher is promising to punish any officer who commits acts of misconduct that taints the uniform.

Dagher told reporters on Friday that he expects to give more details in November about ongoing investigations that have led to the suspension of six officers in recent months, and promised to take “unprecedented action” to address wrongdoing.

“I promise you two things: the truth, and the fact that unacceptable acts will never, never go unpunished,” he said.

“I’m not promising you that what we’re about to reveal is pretty. There’s more to come – I’ll tell you that right now. It’s not pretty, not at all, what you’ll see, what you’ll hear.”

Dagher addressed the ongoing controversy after the force announced in a news release that an officer could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a situation involving domestic violence in 2025.

Radio-Canada reported on Thursday that an officer responding to a call in connection with conjugal violence allegedly erased evidence provided by the victim.

The report suggested the officer knew the alleged perpetrator.

The news comes after a series of revelations that began in June, when Dagher announced that a 16-member patrol unit was disbanded and disarmed following allegations of racism, misconduct and criminal behaviour. Four officers from the patrol unit at the station, located in a multicultural neighbourhood, were suspended.

Dagher said five of the 16 members of the unit have since been cleared to return to regular duties, but three are on leave.

Police have previously said others from the patrol unit were reassigned to other duties or to administrative tasks.

The police chief also said the officer connected to the alleged domestic violence incident was placed on administrative duties in June as a result of information that emerged during that probe.

Dagher noted that the initial investigation into the officers began in March with an internal report, and that the probe was under way before the allegations surfaced in the media.

He suggested this shows that members within the force are breaking free of a code of silence that used to shield police officers who acted with impunity.

Dagher described the behaviour of police officers who disgrace the uniform as an embarrassment, while maintaining that 99 per cent of the force do an “admirable” job of serving the public.

“On one hand, I am very, very proud of my police officers who denounce,” he said. “And on the other hand, it’s so humiliating for my uniform, for the pride of my police officers, for their daily work,” he said.

Two officers from a downtown station were also suspended, ON Aug. 19 and Sept. 8.

The first officer was suspended for alleged “discriminatory acts,” police said on Friday. The second, who was suspended for “derogatory” acts, is under criminal investigation, the force said.

One of those officers allegedly urinated on homeless people, while the second officer allegedly posed for photos mocking suspects under arrest in humiliating positions. The allegations were first reported by Montreal daily news outlet La Presse.

Dagher said Friday that the alleged urination incident was being investigated by the province’s police watchdog, the Bureau des enquêtes independantes, and not his force.

“I have to let the BEI decide what they have on it, but it’s not a file that I have,” he said.

stories.title: What we know about the $40M lottery ticket validated hours before expiry in Ontario
stories.summary: Hours before a $40 million Lotto Max jackpot was set to expire, the winning ticket was validated at a lottery terminal.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Mere hours before a $40 million Lotto Max jackpot was set to expire, the winning ticket was validated at a lottery terminal, according to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG).

In a news release on Wednesday, OLG said the winning ticket for the Oct. 28, 2025 draw was “set to expire at midnight” if no one came to collect their prize.

Here’s what to know about the ticket and what would have happened if nobody came forward to claim it.

The winning ticket was originally purchased at a lottery retailer in Grey County, Ont., and the jackpot remained unclaimed for a whole year – until now.

“I am gobsmacked,” said Tony Bitonti, director of media relations at OLG.

Bitonti said the OLG typically isn’t concerned when a major jackpot goes unclaimed for the first few months, because winners often need time to process the news and consult financial advisers.

However, when the owner of the ticket failed to come forward after several months, the OLG launched an awareness campaign for the person with the winning ticket to come forward.

If the deadline for the prize were to have passed with no one claiming it, the $40 million prize would have been declared void and returned to players through future Lotto Max bonus games or promotions.

In an Oct. 5 news release , the OLG encouraged anyone who believed they May have won to “check places where they typically store their tickets,” such as their pockets, drawers, glove compartments and backpacks.

The OLG noted that Grey County is a popular vacation destination for cottagers and day trippers, so a visitor from elsewhere in the country could have purchased the ticket and forgotten to check it.

Bitonti said that as soon as a large winning ticket is validated at a lottery terminal, the computer on the lottery terminal and the lottery terminal itself trigger a notification to the OLG customer care center. The lottery terminal is then frozen in order to make sure all information about the ticket is preserved.

A customer care representative is then required to call the store immediately to talk to the retailer and the winner to begin the review process, which can include a proof of purchase, examining security footage and asking the redeemer questions about the purchase.

Bitonti claims the winner could be announced “within the next few days.”

“The next chapter is yet to be written, because we don’t know the full story yet,” he said.

It wouldn’t have been the first time a multi-million-dollar jackpot went unclaimed. In 2022, a $70 million Lotto Max jackpot was declared unclaimed after the winner of the prize failed to come forward a year after the original draw.

The winning ticket was originally purchased at an authorized retailer in Scarborough, Ont. It was declared the largest ever unclaimed prize in Canada.

stories.title: Montreal mayor backs police chief amid misconduct allegations against officers
stories.summary: Soraya Martinez Ferrada says Fady Dagher understands that the trust between the public and Service de police de la Ville de Montréal is paramount in Quebec’s largest city.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada says she trusts Police Chief Fady Dagher to change the service’s culture as he prepares to address a series of misconduct allegations involving officers .

Martinez Ferrada told reporters Friday that Dagher understands that the trust between the public and Service de police de la Ville de Montréal is paramount in Quebec’s largest city.

“It takes time to change a culture, and we see that resistance right now,” Martinez Ferrada said.

“We need to make sure that all police officers who see anything that doesn’t belong in the service of police should be denouncing it.”

Dagher will hold a news conference Friday afternoon to address the allegations, including a new one that surfaced this week.

Montreal police said in a news release an officer could face charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a 2025 domestic violence investigation.

Radio-Canada reported on Thursday that an officer responding to a call in connection with that case allegedly erased evidence provided by the victim. The report suggested the officer knew the alleged perpetrator.

The officer was stationed in the multicultural neighbourhood of Montreal-Nord, where four different officers were suspended over allegations of racist misconduct earlier this year.

Dagher will also provide an update on that investigation, as well as on the suspension of two officers from a downtown station .

One of those officers allegedly urinated on homeless people, while the second officer allegedly posed for photos mocking suspects under arrest in humiliating positions.

“Every event that happens has to be explained,” Martinez Ferrada said.

“We need to give the trust to citizens that we are on top of it and we’re changing the culture.”

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto CEO, daughters shot in Bridle Path home invasion identified: reports
stories.summary: Three masked suspects entered the residence with guns and a hammer just before 4 a.m. on Thursday.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Toronto CEO David Morton has released a statement about the traumatic attack on him, his wife and daughters in their Bridal Path home on Thursday morning, confirming the horrific details and condemning growing violence in the city.

“What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience,” he wrote.

Morton confirmed that three masked individuals forced their way into the family home, armed with handguns and a hammer. Three family members were shot and are recovering in hospital, he said, adding that all four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer, leaving all injured and requiring emergency medical attention.

“It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home,” he wrote, and expressed gratitude to the police, emergency responders, paramedics, doctors, nurses and hospital staff who acted quickly and have been providing care.

“We also want to thank our extended family, friends, neighbours and the many people who have reached out with messages of concern, prayers and support. The outpouring of kindness has meant a great deal to us during this incredibly difficult time.”

Meanwhile, Morton said that the family is “also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto. No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.”

He adds that the family hope the individuals responsible will be brought to justice and asked anyone with information that could assist the police investigation to come forward.

Bridle Path home invasion leaves Toronto dad and daughter fighting for their lives: police

Crown fails to get longer sentence for Ontario man who shot at intruders who shot his son

He also asked that the media and public respect the family’s need for privacy as they recover from the “traumatic experience. We are a family, and our priority is getting through this together.”

Morton is 75. The CEO is a graduate from Toronto Metropolitan University’s Hospitality and Tourism program. His wife, Doriana Zohil-Morton, 64, is the MAC Group’s president.Their daughter Maggie, who has a Bachelor of Arts in health studies from Queen’s University and a Master of Arts in health promotion from Dalhousie University, also works at the company in various fields, including sales, operations, and marketing.

Cristina is the founder of Zohil-Morton Law, focused on immigration. She attended university in England and was called to the Ontario Bar in 2024, according to the firm’s website.

On Friday afternoon, police released descriptions of three suspects and warned that they were considered armed and dangerous. All three were wearing dark clothing and face masks.

The first suspect is described as a Black man, around 20 years old, with a thin build. The second and third suspects were described as men, also around 20 years old.

Police have not revealed a motive, although Toronto Police Service Insp. Kristy Smith said at a news conference Thursday that the suspects demanded “valuables from within the home.” She said that she believes that the home was chosen due to its location in an affluent neighbourhood and no information at this time indicated that it was targeted.

The suspects drove away from the scene in a dark-coloured SUV before police arrived.

“We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is,” said Smith. She added that there would be an increased police presence in the area during the investigation.

“My thoughts are with the family and their loved ones, who are going through something no family should ever have to face. I am praying for their full recovery,” she wrote.

In May 2024, a person was arrested after trying to gain access to Canadian rapper Drake’s $100-million Bridle Path home. Earlier that week, a security guard was injured after a person shot at the house. The latter was believed to be fuelled by a feud between Drake and another rapper.

Here’s Morton’s full statement:

For immediate release

Toronto Family Speaks Out Following Violent Home Invasion in the Bridle Path

Toronto, Ontario – October 30, 2026

David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, issued the following statement on behalf of his family following the horrific and violent home invasion at their residence on Hyde Park Circle in Toronto’s prestigious Bridle Path neighbourhood during the early morning hours of October 29.

What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience.

Three masked individuals forcibly entered our residence, armed with handguns and a hammer. During the attack, three members of our family were shot and are currently recovering in hospital. All four members of our family were also attacked with a hammer, leaving everyone injured and requiring emergency medical attention.

It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home.

Our family is extremely grateful to the Toronto Police Service, emergency responders, paramedics, doctors, nurses and hospital staff who responded so quickly and have been instrumental in providing care and assistance.

While we are focused on recovery and supporting one another as a family, we are also deeply concerned about the increasing violence associated with home invasions and the safety of families throughout Toronto.

No family should ever have to experience this. People should be able to sleep peacefully in their homes without fear of armed individuals breaking in and threatening their lives.

We sincerely hope that the individuals responsible will be identified, apprehended and brought to justice. We encourage anyone with information that May assist the Toronto Police investigation to come forward.

At this time, we respectfully ask the media and public to allow our family the privacy and time needed to recover from this traumatic experience.

We are a family, and our priority is getting through this together.

stories.title: New Brunswick’s surplus power sales to U.S. could close Irving Paper, firm warns
stories.summary: New Brunswick's Crown-owned electric utility is being criticized for changing its policy on the sale of excess power.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s Crown-owned electric utility is being criticized for changing its policy on the sale of excess power.

Forestry giant J.D. Irving Ltd. executive Mark Mosher says his company and others used to purchase NB Power’s surplus electricity at discounted rates.

But earlier this year, the provincial regulator started allowing the utility to sell that surplus power to customers in the United States and other out-of-province customers at market prices.

Mosher says the policy change could drive up power costs for JDI Irving Ltd. subsidiary Irving Paper by an estimated $10 million annually and cause it to close.

He says that is because NB Power changed its priority rules to sell its cheaper surplus electricity to outside buyers first, forcing in-province industries to rely on more expensive excess power.

Meanwhile, Energy Minister Rene Legacy says the government can reverse the decision but won’t because it benefits other NB Power customers.

Legacy adds that the Liberal government won’t intervene in J.D. Irving Ltd.’s recent application to the regulator to reverse the request.

“We will see what the process is once the (Energy and Utilities Board) reviews what JDI has requested,” Legacy said in the provincial legislature earlier this week.

“We will not comment on the process until that is done.”

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada orders new trial for man acquitted of dangerous driving
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada has ordered a new trial for a motorist who was acquitted of dangerous driving charges after a fatal accident in British Columbia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada has ordered a new trial for a motorist who was acquitted of dangerous driving charges after a fatal accident in British Columbia.

Moshfeghi Zadeh drove into a busy Vancouver intersection on a red light in July 2021 and collided with another vehicle, causing Zadeh’s car to flip onto the sidewalk.

A man was seriously injured and his 18-month-old daughter was killed.

The trial judge found Zadeh’s manner of driving was not a marked departure from the standard of care expected of a reasonable person in the circumstances.

Zadeh was acquitted on charges of dangerous driving causing death and dangerous driving causing bodily harm.

A majority of British Columbia’s Court of Appeal dismissed the Crown’s appeal.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says seeing Earth during spacewalk 'changed' him
stories.summary: Longueuil - Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he was overwhelmed with emotion looking at the Earth during a seven-hour spacewalk on Thursday.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Longueuil - Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk said he was overwhelmed with emotion looking at the Earth during a seven-hour spacewalk on Thursday.

“I tried to focus really hard on not looking up at the high Earth,” he said. “Your mind doesn’t know what to do with that image,” he said.

“It’s exciting,” he added.

Kutryk and Nasa astronaut Anil Menon successfully installed seven of eight new solar panels on the International Space Station during the spacewalk. Kutryk became the fifth Canadian to perform such a feat.

Speaking to media as he floated inside the space station on Friday morning, Kutryk said the experience changed him. He said seeing the blue planet from the outside made him feel “very small” and “almost insignificant.”

”(I feel) like I want to make every decision I make in my life going forward, and just try to be a better person, the best person I can,” said Kutryk.

He described seeing the Earth while hovering in the vacuum of space as “very confusing” and “a sensory overload.”

He added that he was stunned by the beauty and fragility of the planet. He said that he could see his home province of Alberta from space, and he has posted several photos of what Canada looks like from the space station on social media.

“I do think that we come back to Earth with a changed perspective,” he said.

The astronaut described the experience as disorienting. He and Menon had to work in both the darkness of space and through blinding sunlight, ON top of the distracting view of the Earth. But he said the years of training paid off and the work went off without a hitch.

Kutryk is on his first mission in space and his trip outside the space station is expected to be his first of two spacewalks. Kutryk and Menon are scheduled to install the eighth solar panel during their next spacewalk.

Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.

Saint-Jacques led the news conference at the space agency’s headquarters in Longueuil, Que., with Eleanor Olszewski, the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada.

Saint-Jacques said Kutryk is “a real role model for Canadian youth.”

As an Albertan, Olszewski added that she felt “tremendous pride” seeing Kutryk make history with his spacewalk.

Kutryk and his crew’s mission is crucial, Saint-Jacques said, as the station is nearly 30 years old and its original solar panels have lost efficiency. According to the Canadian Space Agency, the new panels, paired with previously installed arrays, will help increase power generation capacity on the station by up to 30 per cent.

Mathieu Caron, director of the Canadian Space Agency’s astronauts, life sciences, and space medicine directorate, said the job couldn’t have been done without Canada’s decades-long contribution to space exploration.

Menon rode the Canadarm 2 robotic arm to perform the maintenance work. The spacewalkers also received support from the robotics team in Longueuil, and Canadian astronaut Jenni Gibbons gave the duo step-by-step instructions from Houston.

“We’re all incredibly proud,” said Caron.

While he tried to focus on the task at hand, Kutryk says he will make sure to take in the view during his second spacewalk next week.

paragraphs: Longueuil - Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk said he was overwhelmed with emotion looking at the Earth during a seven-hour spacewalk on Thursday.
“I tried to focus really hard on not looking up at the high Earth,” he said. “Your mind doesn’t know what to do with that image,” he said.
“It’s exciting,” he added.

Kutryk and Nasa astronaut Anil Menon successfully installed seven of eight new solar panels on the International Space Station during the spacewalk. Kutryk became the fifth Canadian to perform such a feat.

Speaking to media as he floated inside the space station on Friday morning, Kutryk said the experience changed him. He said seeing the blue planet from the outside made him feel “very small” and “almost insignificant.”
”(I feel) like I want to make every decision I make in my life going forward, and just try to be a better person, the best person I can,” said Kutryk.
He described seeing the Earth while hovering in the vacuum of space as “very confusing” and “a sensory overload.”

He added that he was stunned by the beauty and fragility of the planet. He said that he could see his home province of Alberta from space, and he has posted several photos of what Canada looks like from the space station on social media.
“I do think that we come back to Earth with a changed perspective,” he said.

The astronaut described the experience as disorienting. He and Menon had to work in both the darkness of space and through blinding sunlight, ON top of the distracting view of the Earth. But he said the years of training paid off and the work went off without a hitch.

Kutryk is on his first mission in space and his trip outside the space station is expected to be his first of two spacewalks. Kutryk and Menon are scheduled to install the eighth solar panel during their next spacewalk.
Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.
Saint-Jacques led the news conference at the space agency’s headquarters in Longueuil, Que., with Eleanor Olszewski, the minister responsible for Prairies Economic Development Canada.
Saint-Jacques said Kutryk is “a real role model for Canadian youth.”

stories.title: Harris, Riders eager to face Lions in CFL playoffs
stories.summary: Big games are where Trevor Harris believes he shines.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith
stories.content:
Big games are where Trevor Harris believes he shines.

The American quarterback is eager to show it when his Saskatchewan Roughriders take on the B.C. Lions in the CFL’s West Division semifinal on Saturday.

“It’s one of those things where you win or go home. And I feel like I’ve always thrived in those situations,” said Harris, who led Saskatchewan to a Grey Cup title last season. “When the moment gets big, some people can shrink a little bit. And I’m excited for that moment.”

The Lions and Riders come into the contest with identical 10-8 records in regular-season play.

B.C. earned hosting rights by taking the season series 2-1 with a 31-24 home victory over Saskatchewan on Sept. 25.

But the Riders have bounced the Lions from the playoffs two years in a row.

“Really, the last three years, I feel like we’ve played B.C. every other week,” said Riders head coach Corey Mace. “It’s going to be a great matchup.”

Saskatchewan will need to contain the Lions’ potent offence come Saturday.

B.C. was second in both overall net yards (416.7 per game) and rushing yards (118.7) across the regular season, and finished third in passing yards (314.9) as Canadian quarterback Nathan Rourke threw for 4,614 yards and 24 touchdowns.

“They’re a really good offence,” Mace said. “Obviously Nathan’s playing at a high clip, the receivers, I think they almost had four guys go for 1,000 (receiving yards), their running backs are really good, their O-line’s playing well, (head coach Buck Pierce is) a great play caller.

“So yeah, man, they’re a really good offence. They’re a really good team.”

Going up against a team for the fourth time in a calendar year can still bring surprises, said Harris, who threw for 5,370 yards during the regular season.

“There’s probably going to be some things that they do that they haven’t done yet,” he said. “That’s been par for the course. Every time we’ve played them, they’ve given me different looks and tried to fool me with certain things, people they put in positions.

“It’s going to be a lot about execution, but who can game plan and who can make those big-time plays in those big-time moments. And you never know when that moment comes. So you’ve always got to be on your toes, ready to rock.”

The winner will advance to face the Edmonton Elks (13-5) in the West Division final on Nov. 7 at Commonwealth Stadium in Edmonton.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Belleville cop who prevented a Jewish massacre released from the hospital and is recovering at home
stories.summary: Constable Jeff Smith was ambushed and gravely hurt when 29-year-old Sean Ward opened fire outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
“ Constable Smith and his family remain incredibly grateful for the overwhelming support shown by the community and beyond over the past several weeks. Every well wish and message of encouragement has been sincerely appreciated,” the police service said in a press release.

In an email to National Post, the police service added, “Regarding return to work question, right now, the priority is his recovery. We are encouraged by his progress and are pleased that he is able to recover surrounded by the support of family and loved ones.”

Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville police force, was stationed outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., during a Yom Kippur service on Sept. 20. He was ambushed and gravely hurt when 29-year-old Sean Ward opened fire. Ward yelled, “you are going to die for the Jews”, presumably at Smith and his colleague Const. Michael McCurdy, who was at the scene in less than three minutes. The two officers put their lives on the line to protect approximately 25 congregants gathered inside the synagogue , none of whom were hurt as the shooting ensued.

Smith sustained critical injuries after he was shot in the head and body. He has been in the hospital since then undergoing multiple surgeries until his release Thursday. Ward sustained injuries and succumbed to them at the hospital a day after the shooting. McCurdy was not injured during the shooting.

“Jeff, we wish you strength, healing and peace as you begin this next stage of your recovery. We hope you and your family can take some comfort in knowing that thousands of Canadians continue to stand beside you,” wrote campaign organizer Derek Kreindler on Thursday. As of Friday morning, the campaign had raised $969,110.

In a separate campaign for McCurdy, the Jewish community lauded the officer’s actions as he “prevented a deliberate, hate-motivated attack on the city’s Jewish community from becoming a mass-casualty event.” The campaign has, as of Friday morning, raised $58,400.

stories.title: London man charged in connection with three sexual assault investigations
stories.summary: A 49-year-old London man has been charged in connection with three sexual assault investigations, including one involving a weapon, according to London police.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 49-year-old London man has been charged in connection with three sexual assault investigations, including one involving a weapon, according to London police.

The charges stem from incidents that occurred between August and October in the city’s downtown core.

London police allege a woman was in an alleyway in the 200-block of Dundas Street on Aug. 17 when she was approached by an acquaintance and sexually assaulted.

Investigators allege the same victim met with the man again in early October in the 500-block of Richmond Street, where she was sexually assaulted a second time.

In a separate incident, police said a woman was outside a business in the 500-block of Dundas Street around 12:15 a.m. on Oct. 17 when she was approached by a man she did not know.

The pair spoke and walked together toward the 500-block of Queens Avenue, police said.

According to investigators, the man led the woman to an isolated area on Queens Avenue, produced a weapon and sexually assaulted her before leaving the area. The victim contacted police and officers searched the area but were unable to locate the suspect.

Police said investigators obtained surveillance video from nearby businesses and identified a suspect. Following his arrest, investigators determined the man was also responsible for the two earlier sexual assaults.

Matthew David Coveney, 49, of London, is charged with two counts of sexual assault, one count of sexual assault with a weapon and one count of obtaining sexual services for consideration.

Police believe there May be additional victims who have not yet come forward and have released photographs of the accused as part of the investigation.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the London Police Service.

stories.title: Snail mail art subscriptions let you be a modern art patron, at an affordable price point
stories.summary: The subscriptions are a more budget-friendly option for Canadians to collect art and for artists to foster community beyond the digital boundaries of social media
stories.author: Waheeda Harris
stories.content:
Tara Joy Andrews leads a double life. The Halifax-based designer spends her days online, creating digital assets for small businesses and book covers for self-published authors, but her passion project involves sending paper goods the old-fashioned way: through posted mail.

Andrews has always enjoyed all things analog. To marry her love of art, birds and snail mail, earlier this year she launched the Enchanted Postmark , a monthly paper goods subscription.

“I wanted to create something people could look forward to every month,” Andrews says. “It’s for people who miss the magic of real mail.”

Her $12 monthly package of bird-themed paper creations includes prints, postcards and mystery items. “I think we’ve lost a little of the anticipation and excitement with opening the mailbox and finding something that isn’t a bill or advertisement,” Andrews says.

Andrews is among a growing group of Canadian artists offering art at an accessible price point through monthly mail subscriptions. It’s a more budget-friendly option for Canadians to collect art and for artists to foster community beyond the digital boundaries of social media.

“These kinds of subscriptions are a modern, distributed version of patronage,” says Clayton Childress, a cultural sociologist and University of British Columbia associate professor of sociology. “In the early 2000s, smaller publishers like McSweeney’s did this too. It allows those in the creative arts to move from a super irregular income to having a port in the storm.”

For artist Solene Callioux in Lac La Biche, Alta., art subscriptions can provide some modest but consistent monthly support, at a price point that keeps her work within reach.

Callioux produces art in a variety of mediums including ceramics, wood carving, watercolours and pen drawing, typically sharing her work on Instagram. When she started seeing fellow artists launching subscription mail clubs, she decided to try it for herself.

Callioux’s Willow Art Post: Mail Club launched in September 2026 and now has subscribers in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, each paying $10 per month.

“I thought about what I’d like to receive, so each month a member will receive a small art print, calendar page, stickers and a bookmark, crossword or a paper treasure,” she says. Every element draws inspiration from Callioux’s personal sketchbook of illustrations reflecting her Métis heritage, the northern Alberta landscape and her faith.

“I can’t afford to buy art [myself], so I wanted to create something affordable and helps support me as an artist,” Callioux says.

For other artists, subscriber-focused art clubs are a way of creating and nurturing community among art lovers. That has been the case for architect and artist Jemma Chapman, who moved from the United Kingdom to Toronto in 2025.

A few months into her time in Canada, Chapman came up with the idea for Toonie Stamps, a series of illustrations featuring notable Toronto landmarks and characters, including St. Lawrence Market, the Raptors, Allan Gardens and raccoons, also known as “trash pandas”, that locals and tourists can purchase from one of her three Toonie Stamp vending machines installed around the city.

The stamp-sized illustrations are a way for Chapman to document her explorations of the city and pushed her to foster her artistic practice. “It came from a place of trying to find creative purpose while I was struggling to find employment after moving to Canada,” she says.

The monthly mail club was a natural extension of the project: Love Letters from Toronto delivers the art Chapman produces for Toonie Stamps to subscribers beyond the city and surprisingly she’s seen many locals sign up for the mail club too. Currently, 100 subscribers pay $16 a month.

In each delivery, mail club members receive an envelope themed to a particular Toronto neighbourhood that comes filled with a local postcard map, a mystery Toonie Stamp, stickers, a calendar page and a letter from Chapman featuring her latest local recommendations or funny personal anecdotes as a recent transplant to the city.

Chapman finds that for her subscribers, it’s not just about collecting art; it’s a way of connecting with the city they love. “The mail club focuses less on who I am as an artist or what I’m working on and more on the city itself,” Chapman says.
