stories.title: When Ontario falls back from daylight savings time, much of Canada will opt out. Sleep experts say it's a mistake
stories.summary: For the first time, B.C., Alberta and the Northwest Territories will not move their clocks back on Sunday.
stories.author: Kevin Jiang
stories.content:
On Nov. 1, clocks will fall back an hour for Toronto and much of Canada as we transition back to standard time. Not so for British Columbia, Alberta and the Northwest Territories: For the first time, these provinces and territories will be ditching the time change and sticking with daylight saving time year-round. We’re resurfacing this story, first published on April 30, 2026 , in which we asked sleep experts whether Ontario should follow suit .

Ontario sleep researcher Joseph De Koninck has spent the past two decades fighting to abolish the twice-yearly time change across Canada.

So when B.C., Alberta and Northwest Territories recently moved to adopt daylight saving time year-round , you’d think the 79-year-old professor emeritus would have been ecstatic. But all he felt was frustration.

That’s because from a health perspective, he feels the change is going the wrong way. “The worst situation by far is making daylight saving permanent,” said De Koninck, who researches sleep and dreams at the University of Ottawa. “The best is standard time year-round.”

While most Ontarians will turn their clocks back an hour this weekend, some communities in the province will no longer have to make the switch.

Most sleep experts, and Canada’s major sleep associations, recommend adopting permanent standard time instead of daylight saving time. But several provinces — including Ontario — favour daylight saving time regardless, despite urging from the Canadian Sleep Society , the Canadian Society for Chronobiology , the Canadian Sleep Research Consortium and more.

“It is a little bit frustrating,” said Rebecca Robillard, co-chair of the Canadian Sleep Research Consortium and an associate professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa. “There’s strong science out there to inform those decisions. We’ve been vocal about it, and we’ve been trying to reach out.”

Here’s why sleep experts are opposed to year-round daylight saving time — and what happened in other places that opted for it.

Daylight saving time is the practice of moving the clocks an hour forward from standard time in the spring, before returning back to standard time in the fall.

This bi-annual time change was adopted nationwide during the First World War to save on energy costs and has stuck around since — despite research showing the energy saved from the practice today is negligible .

Standard time is based on the position of the sun, meaning daylight is equally distributed before and after noon. So when we switch to daylight saving time, we’re shorting ourselves an hour of sunlight in the morning, especially during the winter. And that’s the crux of the issue.

Our sleep-wake cycles — as well as most biological rhythms in the body — are informed by sunlight. That’s why it’s crucial to get exposure to sunlight as soon as possible after we wake up; this sets our biological clocks, while elevating certain hormones that help keep us aware and alert throughout the day, explained Dr. Mark Boulos, a staff neurologist and medical lead at Sunnybrook Hospital’s sleep laboratories.

Meanwhile, an extra hour of sunlight in the evening “actually pushes our biological clocks back,” Robillard said, “so it makes it harder to fall asleep and harder to wake up.” These effects can be especially pronounced in Canada, where our winter days are already short on sunlight given our northern latitude.

“Springing forward in time is generally not good for you,” Boulos said. “It can certainly contribute towards health consequences like dementia, stroke, heart attack, diabetes, weight gain and depression.”

A study published last year found that adopting permanent daylight savings time would increase the prevalence of obesity, heart attacks and strokes compared to year-round standard time — although it found permanent daylight saving time to still be preferable over the bi-annual time change.

Historically, car accidents and even suicides tend to spike shortly after the transition to daylight saving time in spring. Research has also linked the time change to heart disease and mood issues .

Patricia Lakin-Thomas is a biology professor at York University who favours staying at standard time year-round because it is better for our

We appear to be moving that way.

In early March, B.C. announced it will make daylight saving time permanent year-round. In April, Alberta tabled legislation to do the same , and the Northwest Territories followed soon after . Meanwhile, Saskatchewan and the Yukon have adopted standard time year-round, which sleep experts strongly prefer.

A spokesperson for B.C.‘s Ministry of Attorney General defended its move, telling the Star that 93 per cent of residents were in favour of year-round daylight saving time, according to a 2019 survey, and that “people have different preferences regarding whether they want that potential extra hour of light in the morning or evening.”

“The extra evening daylight will provide more opportunities for family time, outdoor activity, and safer commutes,” they said over email.

Meanwhile, Dale Nally, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction, told the Star: “Our move to permanent daylight time keeps more daylight later in the day, when people can actually use it. We’re in daylight time for 8 months of the year already and if we went to standard time, the sun would rise as early as 4 a.m. in some communities during the summer.”

Ontario already has a bill, which received Royal Assent in 2020, that would make daylight saving time permanent year-round once enacted. But it requires neighbouring Quebec and New York to enact the same change before it can be proclaimed to come into force.

“Making daylight savings time permanent in Ontario without Quebec and New York State following suit would be disruptive for trade, stock markets and broadcasting,” said Hannah Jensen, spokesperson for Ontario Premier Doug Ford. She did not respond when asked why Ontario chose daylight saving time over standard time.

Toronto - Ontario is set to move parts of the province’s northwest region to permanent daylight time in order to align with Manitoba, Indigeno…

Robillard said Canada’s major sleep associations wrote to the leaders of every province and territory in Canada, offering to consult on the decision.

“My understanding is that the decision-makers are in a hard position to reconcile public opinion with the scientific facts,” she said. “That’s why I feel we need to do more education... and initiate more conversations about the hard science.”

The U.S. tried it in 1974 , to save costs amid an oil crisis, but the experiment didn’t last the year.

The missing hour of sunlight in the morning meant many students had to walk to school in pre-dawn darkness, sparking outrage after news articles recommended kids carry flashlights, employ a buddy system and wear reflective tape during their commutes.

Public support plummeted after a number of students were fatally struck by vehicles on their way to school, falling from 79 per cent in favour down to 42 per cent within two months of the change.

Four decades later, Russia adopted permanent daylight saving time in 2011. While it was initially popular, a survey two years in found less than a third of Russians approved. Lawmakers argued the change exacerbated stress and mental health issues, and cited medical reports showing an increase in morning road accidents in the year following the change.

Three years later, in 2014, President Vladimir Putin announced a permanent shift to standard time instead, which remains today.

Our sleep-wake cycles — as well as most biological rhythms in the body — are informed by sunlight. That’s why it’s crucial to get exposure to sunlight as soon as possible after we wake up; this sets our biological clocks, while elevating certain hormones that help keep us aware and alert throughout the day, explained Dr. Mark Boulos, a staff neurologist and medical lead at Sunnybrook Hospital’s sleep laboratories.

Meanwhile, an extra hour of sunlight in the evening “actually pushes our biological clocks back,” Robillard said, “so it makes it harder to fall asleep and harder to wake up.” These effects can be especially pronounced in Canada, where our winter days are already short on sunlight given our northern latitude.

“Springing forward in time is generally not good for you,” Boulos said. “It can certainly contribute towards health consequences like dementia, stroke, heart attack, diabetes, weight gain and depression.”

A study published last year found that adopting permanent daylight savings time would increase the prevalence of obesity, heart attacks and strokes compared to year-round standard time — although it found permanent daylight saving time to still be preferable over the bi-annual time change.
Historically, car accidents and even suicides tend to spike shortly after the transition to daylight saving time in spring. Research has also linked the time change to heart disease and mood issues .

We appear to be moving that way.

In early March, B.C. announced it will make daylight saving time permanent year-round. In April, Alberta tabled legislation to do the same , and the Northwest Territories followed soon after . Meanwhile, Saskatchewan and the Yukon have adopted standard time year-round, which sleep experts strongly prefer.

A spokesperson for B.C.‘s Ministry of Attorney General defended its move, telling the Star that 93 per cent of residents were in favour of year-round daylight saving time, according to a 2019 survey, and that “people have different preferences regarding whether they want that potential extra hour of light in the morning or evening.”
“The extra evening daylight will provide more opportunities for family time, outdoor activity, and safer commutes,” they said over email.

Meanwhile, Dale Nally, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction, told the Star: “Our move to permanent daylight time keeps more daylight later in the day, when people can actually use it. We’re in daylight time for 8 months of the year already and if we went to standard time, the sun would rise as early as 4 a.m. in some communities during the summer.”

Ontario already has a bill, which received Royal Assent in 2020, that would make daylight saving time permanent year-round once enacted. But it requires neighbouring Quebec and New York to enact the same change before it can be proclaimed to come into force.

“Making daylight savings time permanent in Ontario without Quebec and New York State following suit would be disruptive for trade, stock markets and broadcasting,” said Hannah Jensen, spokesperson for Ontario Premier Doug Ford. She did not respond when asked why Ontario chose daylight saving time over standard time.

Robillard said Canada’s major sleep associations wrote to the leaders of every province and territory in Canada, offering to consult on the decision.

“My understanding is that the decision-makers are in a hard position to reconcile public opinion with the scientific facts,” she said. “That’s why I feel we need to do more education... and initiate more conversations about the hard science.”
The U.S. tried it in 1974 , to save costs amid an oil crisis, but the experiment didn’t last the year.

The missing hour of sunlight in the morning meant many students had to walk to school in pre-dawn darkness, sparking outrage after news articles recommended kids carry flashlights, employ a buddy system and wear reflective tape during their commutes.
Public support plummeted after a number of students were fatally struck by vehicles on their way to school, falling from 79 per cent in favour down to 42 per cent within two months of the change.

Four decades later, Russia adopted permanent daylight saving time in 2011. While it was initially popular, a survey two years in found less than a third of Russians approved. Lawmakers argued the change exacerbated stress and mental health issues, and cited medical reports showing an increase in morning road accidents in the year following the change.
Three years later, in 2014, President Vladimir Putin announced a permanent shift to standard time instead, which remains today.

stories.title: Police and M.A.D.D. urges sober driving this Halloween
stories.summary: With Halloween around the corner, London Police, Provincial Police and Mothers Against Drunk Drivers London ar...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
With Halloween around the corner, London Police, Provincial Police and Mothers Against Drunk Drivers London are reminding drivers not to drive impaired but to find a safe drive home this weekend.

Police explain that with more kids out trick-or-treating in the dark and people heading home from a night out, impaired driver can become more of a risk then usual.

According to OPP, West Region recorded that impaired driver charges between Jan. to Sept. have been down six per cent compared to the same time frame last year.

Despite the decrease, Madd London and Area says impaired driving continues to put lives at risk, and those risks can be avoided.

“Because it’s not an accident, you know, getting behind the wheel impaired is completely 100% preventable. And so these aren’t accidents, these are tragedies and horrific crashes, collisions,” said Aaron Tennant, a volunteer and board member with Madd London and Area.

Impaired driving cases that happened recently have shown the dangers.

On Oct. 22, London Police charged a 22-year-old man after allegedly driving under the influence on Upper Queen Street causing a collison that resulted in the death of a woman.

Earlier on Oct. 4, another London man was charged with impaired driving after allegedly crashing with an ambulence and another car.

London Police Constable Gavin Dell, says Ride programs will be ran this weekend.

“But anytime around big events like Halloween, ride programs are conducted. And I’m sure individuals will see us out on the road throughout the weekend,” Dell said.

Impaired driving charges have also been down in the surronding area.

Middlesex dropped 24 per cent, Oxford went down 26 per cent and Elgin had a 19 per cent decrease.

Across the OPP West Region, there have been three fatal crashes where the main cause was impaired driving compared to 13 last year.

OPP Regional Media Relations Coordinator Derek Rogers, says Halloween causes more danger for children with darkness and costumes that make them harder to see.

“So, you know, we would ask anyone that’s going to drink to make other choices other than getting behind the wheel, because young lives depend upon it,” Rogers said.

Tennant says alcohol and drugs can affect a driver’s judgment and reaction time, making it harder to respond to hazards on the road.

He is also reminding families to stay alert while trick-or-treating.

“So it would be a message as well to the trick-or-treaters to keep an open eye and never assume that a driver can see you,” Tennant said.

Police are encouraging anyone attending Halloween parties to arrange a designated driver, taxi or rideshare before heading out.

“There’s no occasion worth risking a life,” Dell said.

stories.title: From homemade animatronics to carved pumpkins, here’s how Canadians are decorating this Halloween
stories.summary: Some readers spent months preparing for their latest spooky designs
stories.author: Jacob Dubé
stories.content:
Halloween is here, and Canadians everywhere are flexing their landscaping skills to create the spookiest displays for trick-or-treaters this weekend.

After the incredible displays we received last year, we asked Globe readers to share how they decorated their lawns this Halloween. From homemade animatronics to a return to low-tech pumpkin carving, here’s what you shared with us.

My wife and I have always loved Halloween and decided to start our haunt when we bought our home 20 years ago. The majority of our props and animatronics are handmade by myself, my wife, and son – we prefer to build our own rather than buying from retailers. This year we are also including an AI-powered animated skeleton that will have interactive discussions with our visitors. As I am in Quebec, I have bilingual audio for spoken words, and the controller plays each randomly. We receive over 400 children on Halloween night and hand out over 2,000 pieces of candy.

For us, Halloween is a passion, and we work year-round to make and repair props and then spend several weeks prepping the small space we have. It’s one of the best feelings to watch the kids try and figure out how something works and hear the older kids and adults comment on how much they enjoy the experience each year.

Kevin Thomson, St-Hubert, Que.

My Halloween decorations are deliberately old-fashioned and low tech – I love seeing real pumpkins carved and lit on Halloween. We usually have two or three pumpkins and we carve them with faces in a style the shape of the pumpkin suggests. I’ve been doing this for about 10 years. In our little mountain town, more and more people are decorating their lawns for Halloween.

Gayle Smith, Kimberley, B.C.

We have been busy adding to our yard to get it perfect for Halloween night. The house and yard have been taken over by skeletons. This year, we added a spider maze to the yard and the clowns have taken over my little baking shed. We grew a bigger corn patch and pumpkin field and decorated it with a scary burlap family – there are scarecrows that jump when you’re not expecting it.

My husband and I continue to do this every year when we see how happy the kids are when they show up on Halloween night. I’m keeping a childhood love going as long as I can – thank God I have a husband who will indulge all my crazy ideas.

Trish Dagley, Voglers Cove, N.S.

My parents graciously let me decorate their lawn year after year in a cemetery-style yard display. Unfortunately, living in a condo doesn’t afford me the space to sprawl out.

I’ve always been inspired by creating something that appears realistic, like theatrical stagecraft (which I was in school for before I became a registered nurse), and the magical imagineering behind many Disneyland attractions.

For me, it’s all about the dramatic lighting! It’s a labour of love and it brings me so much joy.

Thomas Urquhart, Surrey, B.C.

My family (wife and two girls) were inspired by the Wnba expansion team Toronto Tempo, so we put together a basketball display this season. The Scream selling popcorn was a new addition, since we had popcorn when we attended a Tempo game.

Since we only have two skeletons, we had to take a scene from the sport into more of a 1:1 format. We imagined dribbling or shooting at a net, which we repurposed from another family that had it on the curbside. We enjoy when others can smile, point and take pics.

Trent Melton, Toronto

We are doing a haunted garage walkthrough, offering an immersive experience with animatronics, lighting, fog, actors and more.

I change up the theme every year - while keeping some things consistent. For example, we always have clowns.

This year is a chance to visit the spirit world. Two actors will be spirit walkers, and my seven-year-old son will be a “soul stealer.”

We’ve been doing the garage for seven years, and reception has been great. Hopefully this is our best year!

Wesley Scott, Ottawa

stories.title: Downtown Vancouver condo finds buyer after two price cuts
stories.summary: With investors tapped out of the market, agents are working hard to find ‘that unicorn buyer’
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
68 Smithe St., No. 1509, Vancouver

Asking price: $1,599,000 (April, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $1,625,000 (January, 2026); $1,749,900 (September, 2025)

Selling price: $1,599,000 (June, 2026)

Taxes: $4,010.09 (2025)

Monthly maintenance fee: $767.54

Days on the market: 63

Property days on market: 286

Listing agent: Bronwyn Bertles, Engel & Völkers Vancouver

The sellers had to drop the price a couple of times to find that end-user who wanted the place for a long-term home, said listing agent Bronwyn Bertles. Investors have mostly lost interest in the condo market, so end users are the ones buying, she said. The sale took about two weeks of negotiation, she added.

“The buyers just fell in love with it. They already lived in the area and wanted more space. You really have to think of it as a long-term purchase because we’ve got anti-flipping taxes, and it can’t be vacant. So we really honed in on actual end users who want to live in the space for more than a couple of years. And these guys did.”

This fully furnished, upgraded unit was in mint condition when it hit the market, said Ms. Bertles.

The two-bedroom and den, two-bathroom, 1,034-square-foot unit had top-end finishings, with custom built-ins, a Murphy bed, wine fridge, wood veneer cabinets, air conditioning and floor-to-ceiling windows.

Located downtown near Yaletown, the 17-storey concrete building is eight years old and features a glass-bottom pool, hot tub, sky garden, electric vehicle charging and 24-hour concierge.

Agents are working hard to find buyers who recognize the value in properties that make for long-term homes, said Ms. Bertles.

“Vancouverites see the value and are still buying because it’s somewhere they want to call home; there’s an emotional attachment,” said Ms. Bertles. “It’s not just about investment, dollars, and those things.

“But if you don’t find that unicorn buyer,” she added, “it’s really hard.”

stories.title: Incoming Vancouver City Council expected to put renter concerns in focus
stories.summary: Overwhelmingly left-of-centre members have proposed tripling vacant home tax, creating landlord registry and a return to co-ops
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
The day after turning 21, Solomon Yi-Kieran became Vancouver’s youngest city councillor-elect.

The Coalition of Progressive Electors (Cope) member, who uses they and them pronouns, believes they are well positioned to represent residents who are struggling to find secure, affordable housing on a low-to-middle income.

They join a council comprising four Cope members, five Green Party members – including mayor-elect Pete Fry – one OneCity councillor and an incumbent ABC councillor. The council is now overwhelmingly left of centre, and renter protections and publicly developed housing are key goals for both Cope and the Greens. The members aim to broadly circumvent speculation and private development that places an emphasis on profits over housing rights. Both parties champion the return of co-ops as a model of affordable housing.

Yi-Kieran, a history major and transit activist, said their mandate is to secure housing “that regular people in Vancouver are able to afford, whether that’s for rental or for home ownership.”

They experienced the shortage of housing options firsthand while living in a newer building. Although its below-market units filled up right away, most of the market-rate rentals sat empty a year later because the $2,500 to $2,800 rents were unaffordable, they said.

To address the vacancies, Cope supports tripling Vancouver’s Empty Homes Tax to 9 per cent and closing loopholes that let new condos and multifamily buildings sit vacant.

“It just doesn’t make sense to me to see homes sit empty while regular people aren’t able to rent them,” Yi-Kieran said, arguing the tax hike will penalize major players who prefer to hold units vacant while waiting for demand to return.

“We want to make sure that we’re incentivizing the people who do own the buildings and the people who manage those properties to meet the public and the consumers in the middle … through something like an empty homes tax.”

Yi-Kieran said a top priority for Cope is establishing a landlord registry and relaunching a fully funded Renters Office with enhanced regulatory teeth, alongside implementing a formal tenant protection bylaw to block displacement.

“We want to be protecting people from eviction and from renoviction,” they said.

The Greens propose raising capital via a Vancouver Public Housing Bond to fund housing development on city-owned land. The members also plan to launch a rapid acquisition fund to purchase vulnerable older rental stock targeted for private redevelopment. Under their platform, major private developments would be required to deliver land or cash for non-profit or co-op housing, to be held by the public.

Newly elected Green Party councillor Stephanie Smith argues that city hall can no longer let the private development market dictate housing security. She said the Broadway Plan “overpromised and under-delivered,” failing to produce affordable housing while creating tenant insecurity and displacement.

“The city has approached development and redevelopment in a way that creates profound housing insecurity for thousands and thousands of Vancouver tenants, and has done so unnecessarily,” Ms. Smith said. “We’re tearing down some of the most affordable, accessible housing stock in the city and replacing it with housing that no one can afford. This is not progressive.”

The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

The Greens will let institutional investors buy into the Vancouver Public Housing Bond and earn a modest return. Ms. Smith said the Renters Office will monitor landlord compliance, implement staff-recommended “pace of change” caps that the previous council rejected, and protect vulnerable communities from displacement.

“Tenants shouldn’t be left to individually compel landlord compliance. That’s not equitable. It’s not successful,” Ms. Smith said. “There are way too many people looking over their shoulder waiting to be evicted. The lack of housing security is destructive to people. People can’t live like that, and they shouldn’t be expected to.”

David Woo is vice-president of development, Western Canada, for Starlight Investments, a global real estate investment and asset management firm based in Toronto. It has a reported $30-billion in assets under management. The company has about 3,500 apartment units in various stages of development in B.C.

In Burnaby, Starlight Investments manages Lougheed Village, which will comprise 1,728 units when built out. In Vancouver, the company secured rezoning approval for a 61-unit infill apartment project at 1755 Haro St., behind the Robson and Denman Safeway. The original 19-storey apartment tower will remain. At 1501 Haro St., it proposes a similar development: a 60-unit infill building behind an original 22-storey apartment tower. The zoning does not require below-market units. Because they add infill, the current tenants are not displaced, said Mr. Woo. The existing units, however, are upgraded to newer safety standards.

He said that because housing is top of mind for the newly formed council, he is hopeful they can work together, but he cautions against additional costs when returns on projects are often “razor thin and barely financeable.”

“If you go to the extreme on one end, then there’s no redevelopment opportunity. I believe there should be tenant protection, absolutely. But it needs to be done in such a way that projects can still be financeable; otherwise, it becomes extremely difficult to create net new housing. But that’s why we’re such big fans of infill because no tenants get displaced … it’s a win-win for everybody.”

The city has so far helped his industry deliver housing by reducing development cost charges and amending design guidelines, he said.

“We continue to feel optimistic about being able to deliver this housing under this new council,” said Mr. Woo. “Everybody recognized that not only is it a supply issue, but it’s a cost of delivery issue. And they started to recognize the pinch points and have granted a number of relaxations to help move projects that are sort of teetering on the verge of being financeable. And I think those efforts are great.

“As I understand it, the new council will try not to disrupt what staff has achieved and keep a lot of the senior staff in place. I think that continuity is important to keep the progress moving forward.”

paragraphs: The day after turning 21, Solomon Yi-Kieran became Vancouver’s youngest city councillor-elect.

The Coalition of Progressive Electors (Cope) member, who uses they and them pronouns, believes they are well positioned to represent residents who are struggling to find secure, affordable housing on a low-to-middle income.

They join a council comprising four Cope members, five Green Party members – including mayor-elect Pete Fry – one OneCity councillor and an incumbent ABC councillor. The council is now overwhelmingly left of centre, and renter protections and publicly developed housing are key goals for both Cope and the Greens. The members aim to broadly circumvent speculation and private development that places an emphasis on profits over housing rights. Both parties champion the return of co-ops as a model of affordable housing.
Yi-Kieran, a history major and transit activist, said their mandate is to secure housing “that regular people in Vancouver are able to afford, whether that’s for rental or for home ownership.”

They experienced the shortage of housing options firsthand while living in a newer building. Although its below-market units filled up right away, most of the market-rate rentals sat empty a year later because the $2,500 to $2,800 rents were unaffordable, they said.
To address the vacancies, Cope supports tripling Vancouver’s Empty Homes Tax to 9 per cent and closing loopholes that let new condos and multifamily buildings sit vacant.

“It just doesn’t make sense to me to see homes sit empty while regular people aren’t able to rent them,” Yi-Kieran said, arguing the tax hike will penalize major players who prefer to hold units vacant while waiting for demand to return.

“We want to make sure that we’re incentivizing the people who do own the buildings and the people who manage those properties to meet the public and the consumers in the middle … through something like an empty homes tax.”

Yi-Kieran said a top priority for Cope is establishing a landlord registry and relaunching a fully funded Renters Office with enhanced regulatory teeth, alongside implementing a formal tenant protection bylaw to block displacement.
“We want to be protecting people from eviction and from renoviction,” they said.

The Greens propose raising capital via a Vancouver Public Housing Bond to fund housing development on city-owned land. The members also plan to launch a rapid acquisition fund to purchase vulnerable older rental stock targeted for private redevelopment. Under their platform, major private developments would be required to deliver land or cash for non-profit or co-op housing, to be held by the public.

Newly elected Green Party councillor Stephanie Smith argues that city hall can no longer let the private development market dictate housing security. She said the Broadway Plan “overpromised and under-delivered,” failing to produce affordable housing while creating tenant insecurity and displacement.

“The city has approached development and redevelopment in a way that creates profound housing insecurity for thousands and thousands of Vancouver tenants, and has done so unnecessarily,” Ms. Smith said. “We’re tearing down some of the most affordable, accessible housing stock in the city and replacing it with housing that no one can afford. This is not progressive.”
The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

The Greens will let institutional investors buy into the Vancouver Public Housing Bond and earn a modest return. Ms. Smith said the Renters Office will monitor landlord compliance, implement staff-recommended “pace of change” caps that the previous council rejected, and protect vulnerable communities from displacement.

“Tenants shouldn’t be left to individually compel landlord compliance. That’s not equitable. It’s not successful,” Ms. Smith said. “There are way too many people looking over their shoulder waiting to be evicted. The lack of housing security is destructive to people. People can’t live like that, and they shouldn’t be expected to.”

David Woo is vice-president of development, Western Canada, for Starlight Investments, a global real estate investment and asset management firm based in Toronto. It has a reported $30-billion in assets under management. The company has about 3,500 apartment units in various stages of development in B.C.

In Burnaby, Starlight Investments manages Lougheed Village, which will comprise 1,728 units when built out. In Vancouver, the company secured rezoning approval for a 61-unit infill apartment project at 1755 Haro St., behind the Robson and Denman Safeway. The original 19-storey apartment tower will remain. At 1501 Haro St., it proposes a similar development: a 60-unit infill building behind an original 22-storey apartment tower. The zoning does not require below-market units. Because they add infill, the current tenants are not displaced, said Mr. Woo. The existing units, however, are upgraded to newer safety standards.

He said that because housing is top of mind for the newly formed council, he is hopeful they can work together, but he cautions against additional costs when returns on projects are often “razor thin and barely financeable.”

“If you go to the extreme on one end, then there’s no redevelopment opportunity. I believe there should be tenant protection, absolutely. But it needs to be done in such a way that projects can still be financeable; otherwise, it becomes extremely difficult to create net new housing. But that’s why we’re such big fans of infill because no tenants get displaced … it’s a win-win for everybody.”
The city has so far helped his industry deliver housing by reducing development cost charges and amending design guidelines, he said.

“We continue to feel optimistic about being able to deliver this housing under this new council,” said Mr. Woo. “Everybody recognized that not only is it a supply issue, but it’s a cost of delivery issue. And they started to recognize the pinch points and have granted a number of relaxations to help move projects that are sort of teetering on the verge of being financeable. And I think those efforts are great.

“As I understand it, the new council will try not to disrupt what staff has achieved and keep a lot of the senior staff in place. I think that continuity is important to keep the progress moving forward.”

stories.title: Over 36,000 space heaters sold in Canada recalled due to fire and burn risk
stories.summary: Certain units of Dreo space heaters have been recalled in Canada, United States.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
Dreo has recalled 36,288 portable space heaters because the devices May pose a fire risk to users.

“The recalled space heaters can overheat and ignite, posing fire and burn hazards,” the agency said in a national recall notice on Thursday.

Health Canada is advising anyone who owns the product to stop using it immediately. Affected space heaters have the model number DR-HSH015 printed on the bottom.

Article continues below

The heaters were sold in Canada between September 2025 to August 2026, the notice said. As of Oct. 22, Dreo had reported one incident in Canada, but no reports of injury.

The product was also recalled in the United States, where there were 16 incidents reported and one injury, according to the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission.

Customers who purchased an affected space heater can contact Dreo to receive a free replacement.

Megan Mills Devoe is a staff reporter with the Star. Reach her via email: mmillsdevoe@thestar.CA

stories.title: Bill Morneau named as next Cibc board chair
stories.summary: Former federal finance minister assumes role Jan. 1
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce CM-T is naming former federal finance minister Bill Morneau as the next chair of its board of directors.

Morneau will assume the role on Jan. 1, succeeding Katharine Stevenson, who is will retire from the board at the end of 2026.

Stevenson has been chair of the bank for six years and an independent director for 10 years.

Morneau has served as an independent director of Cibc since 2022.

Before entering politics, Morneau led human resources and pension services firm Morneau Shepell from 1990 to 2015.

Morneau currently serves as chair of NovaSource Power Services and as a director at Clairvest Group Inc.

stories.title: Magna’s third-quarter profit increases as revenue edges lower
stories.summary: Drop in revenue reflected lower light vehicle production and impact of divestitures, company says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Magna International Inc. MG-T posted higher profits in its third quarter as it dealt with rising commodity costs but also saw less of a hit from tariffs.

“As we have noted in prior quarters, we continue to experience inflation across several key commodities,” Philip Fracassa, Magna’s chief financial officer, said on the company’s earnings call.

“While this was a headwind in the quarter, we do expect to substantially mitigate or recover these increased costs over time.”

The auto parts maker, which keeps its books in U.S. dollars, says its net income attributable to the company amounted to US$383-million or US$1.44 per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of US$305-million or US$1.08 per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

Fracassa said that some input costs have become “incrementally worse” in the third and fourth quarter.

However, he added: “We actually are doing a little bit better on operational excellence, which is helping to mitigate that a little bit. We know when you take a step back, you look across key commodities; steel and aluminum were pretty well covered with resale programs with customers or index pass-throughs.”

The company also appears to be seeing some relief on the tariff front.

“Lower net tariff costs contributed approximately 30 basis points to margins,” Fracassa said on the call.

“Costs were slightly lower and we’re getting recoveries faster than we did last year. While the tariff situation continues to evolve, we currently expect that our full-year net tariff headwind will be similar to what we experienced last year.”

Speaking at the Ontario Auto Forum in May, Magna CEO Swamy Kotagiri said the auto industry can’t make it through heightened economic and geopolitical headwinds without clarity on the issues.

The auto industry has been facing uncertainty from trade tensions with the U.S., competition from Chinese automakers and shifting policies on electric vehicles. Canadian consumers are also watching their wallets and prioritizing value.

Magna’s sales for the quarter totalled US$10.06-billion, down from US$10.46 billion a year earlier. It says the decline reflected lower light vehicle production and the impact of divestitures as it also updated its outlook for 2026.

The company now expects total sales to come in between US$41.2-billion and US$42-billion, edging down from its previous forecast of between US$41.3-billion and US$42.5-billion.

“We lowered our sales expectations to reflect reduced vehicle production in China and unfavourable program mix,” Kotagiri said on the call.

Magna said it generated US$584-million in free cash flow during the quarter and raised its expectations for the full year, “reflecting our year-to-date momentum and confidence in our cash flow trajectory,” said Kotagiri.

The company said in its 2026 outlook that it expects free cash flow to come in between US$1.85-billion and US$1.9-billion, compared with its previous expectation of US$1.75-billion to US$1.85-billion.

On an adjusted basis, Magna says it earned US$1.83 per share in its latest quarter, up from an adjusted profit of US$1.33 per share a year earlier.

The auto industry has been facing uncertainty from trade tensions with the U.S., competition from Chinese automakers and shifting policies on electric vehicles. Canadian consumers are also watching their wallets and prioritizing value.

Magna’s sales for the quarter totalled US$10.06-billion, down from US$10.46 billion a year earlier. It says the decline reflected lower light vehicle production and the impact of divestitures as it also updated its outlook for 2026.
The company now expects total sales to come in between US$41.2-billion and US$42-billion, edging down from its previous forecast of between US$41.3-billion and US$42.5-billion.
“We lowered our sales expectations to reflect reduced vehicle production in China and unfavourable program mix,” Kotagiri said on the call.

Magna said it generated US$584-million in free cash flow during the quarter and raised its expectations for the full year, “reflecting our year-to-date momentum and confidence in our cash flow trajectory,” said Kotagiri.

The company said in its 2026 outlook that it expects free cash flow to come in between US$1.85-billion and US$1.9-billion, compared with its previous expectation of US$1.75-billion to US$1.85-billion.
On an adjusted basis, Magna says it earned US$1.83 per share in its latest quarter, up from an adjusted profit of US$1.33 per share a year earlier.

stories.title: Canada-European Union summit in Montreal concluding with digital trade on agenda
stories.summary: A major summit Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting with European Union leaders is set to conclude Friday with announcements on digital trade and academic exchanges.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
A major summit Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting with European Union leaders is set to conclude Friday with announcements on digital trade and academic exchanges.

Carney welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa to the Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Thursday.

While these meetings have been happening for years, this one sees Canada and the EU scaling up their efforts to deepen their commercial and diplomatic relationship.

Costa said he expects to see an agreement on digital trade finalized today, and news on programs for scientific research partnerships and university student exchanges.

Costa added Thursday he wants to see greater labour mobility between Canada and the Europe in addition to opening the door to easier student exchanges.

Culture Minister Marc Miller said Thursday any labour mobility talk in industries like film would need to include the provinces as many have their own tax credits that promote local talent.

Miller has been meeting with his European counterparts during the summit, talking about ways there could be similar regulations when it comes to promoting Canadian content on streaming services in Europe, and vice versa, alongside safeguards for children online.

“So two issues that are really important, and we’re not talking about the same exact rules potentially, but convergence and allyship with respect to large transnational companies that in some cases need to be regulated to protect kids or to promote our cultures in the face of overwhelming, monopolistic cultures, one of which is the United States, but others across the world,” Miller said in an interview.

While labour mobility in film and television production is an issue that requires further work, Miller said they are looking at ways to increase co-productions between Canada and Europe line the TV series Vikings, a Canadian-Irish co-production.

The minister said Canada already has co-production treaties with several European countries that allow joint pooling of tax credits to attract film and TV show productions.

Miller said he brought his EU counterparts to one of the promotional events for Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend, a documentary on Quebec Formula One drier Gilles Villeneuve that premièred at the Toronto International Film Festival. He said part of that visit was to look to get the film theatrical release in Europe.

Carney, Von der Leyen and Costa all said they would like to see Canada become an “associate member” of the European Union, despite countries like Germany rejecting that term and Canadian officials avoiding that phrasing.

Conservatives have criticized the summit, noting that nine of the 28 countries in the EU have yet to ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada.

stories.title: The Nine: Did Danielle Smith get her mandate?
stories.summary: The Big Story discuss where this leaves Danielle Smith's leverage against Ottawa and how the provincial NDP could get a seat at the table.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted October 30, 2026 7:24 am.

Now that question 10 has been put to rest, what about the other nine?

Albertans were asked a range of questions regarding the future of the economy, immigration system, and Canada’s constitution. Official results released on Thursday found that voters want changes to what programs and services non-citizens can access, while striking down any changes to the constitution including abolishing the Senate.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Jared Wesley, political science professor at the University of Alberta, to discuss where this leaves Danielle Smith’s leverage against Ottawa, how the urban-rural divide showed up in the results, and how the provincial NDP could pull up a seat at the table.

stories.title: Delving into the history of Canada's prime ministers
stories.summary: New institute aims to raise the profile of leaders who we don't talk enough about
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Standing beside the sunny final resting place Thursday for William Lyon Mackenzie King, in Toronto’s Mount Pleasant Cemetery, historian James Stewart couldn’t help but think about the service Canada’s 10th prime minister rendered to the country over a lengthy political career.

The legacy of King, a Liberal who spent more than two decades in office as the longest serving prime minister, gets scant attention, Stewart said.

“He’s not talked about in public discourse as much as someone like Mackenzie King should be, and like a lot of our prime ministers, they don’t take up a lot of space in the public square,” he said.

That’s why Stewart, a retired history teacher and the author of two books on Canadian prime ministers, along with one of his former students at Toronto’s Bishop Strachan School, Joanne Archibald — a historical consultant who wrote her Masters thesis at the London School of Economics on Pierre Trudeau, and earned her PhD from Queen’s University with a thesis on the leadership of prime minister Louis St. Laurent — decided to form a new organization with plans to change that.

“It’s important for us to understand who these people are,” Archibald said. “What makes them tick? Why did they get out of bed in the morning? How did they grow up? What’s their background? What influences them from a family structure point of view?”

The non-partisan Prime Ministers Institute will be committed to telling the stories of Canada through the lens of its prime ministers, from Sir John A. Macdonald to Mark Carney and those who succeed him. It aims to promote research, education and informed conversation about Canada’s political history, including the achievements, failures and legacies of those who led the country.

Part of protecting your sovereignty is knowing your history and knowing your culture

“None of them get talked about,” Stewart said.

“You might say there’s an exception with Pierre Trudeau because he still seems to loom large in the memories of the baby boomers and others, but the other prime ministers, we don’t really hear about them in the public conversation. And that could be anyone from Louis St. Laurent, to John Diefenbaker, even to a lesser extent Brian Mulroney, although he has been talked about a little bit because of his recent death. And then of course, John A. Macdonald gets talked about because of controversies about the removal of the statues and such, but we don’t have a good grasp of what kinds of legacies prime ministers left behind and what the consequences of their decisions have been, both for the good and the ill, and how they’ve managed the federation,” Stewart said.

“So, if we can bring more conversation to the public sphere, it’s going to be useful for us, particularly at this time where we’re trying to figure out what actually made Canada. What actually are we trying to defend when we say we want to protect our own sovereignty? And part of protecting your sovereignty is knowing your history and knowing your culture.”

Canadians in their 20s and 30s might not know what Lester Pearson, who was prime minister from 1963 to 1968, did “in terms of establishing national health care and establishing our own distinct Canadian flag,” Stewart said.

“If you look at somebody like Alexander Mackenzie, he was prime minister for one term after Sir. John A. Macdonald, but he established the Supreme Court in Canada and he also established the secret ballot,” Stewart said of the Liberal who was prime minister from 1873 to 1878.

“Everything that a prime minister does is laying a foundation for building the country and sometimes they’re a little bit minor but still have a role to play when you look at the grand scheme.”

When the rocky relationship between Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump creeps into conversation, Archibald notes there’s a lot we can learn by examining how other prime ministers have handled relations with their American counterparts.

Canada’s 12th prime minister, St. Laurent, had “quite close working relationships” with both Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower, she said.

“He played golf, for example, with Eisenhower at Augusta National Golf Club in 1956 and he came back to the House of Commons and talked about how the golf course was a great place for diplomacy because they were talking politics in between shots and in the golf cart on the way to the next hole,” Archibald said.

St. Laurent even attended a performance by Truman’s daughter, Margaret, a classical coloratura soprano, in Ottawa, she said.

“Harry Truman wrote a letter back to Louis St. Laurent saying how much he appreciated that Louis St. Laurent and his wife, Jeanne, went to support Margaret Truman in her performance in Ottawa. So, you can really see the personal connections between these leaders and the way in which that shapes their relationship.”

If we look at “previous examples of really nasty relationships,” those between John F. Kennedy and Diefenbaker stand out for their generational clash, as does the discord between Pierre Trudeau and Richard Nixon, Stewart said.

“If you look at Nixon’s speech to Parliament in 1972, he throws a lot of cold water on the relationship and says we need to get by the sentimental past and just look at both these countries that have different interests and different identities,” Stewart said. “He took all the sugar off and said we’re not always going to get along. So, he didn’t really push the rhetoric of the great relationship between the two countries.”

The new institute, to be known by its initials PMI, is a program of the Canadian Institute for Historical Education, a registered charity dedicated to promoting historical literacy through research, education, and engagement in the public square.

The PMI is supported by leading historians, journalists, and thinkers from across the country.

The institute is not located in a building but will be a virtual organization committed to in-person public engagement. It plans to partner with civic and academic institutions to engage with the public about political history and its relevance to today.

The institute will launch its first public event on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 6 p.m. at the Royal Canadian Military Institute in Toronto when it hosts a panel discussion on Prime Ministers and 24 Sussex Drive.

“He’s not talked about in public discourse as much as someone like Mackenzie King should be, and like a lot of our prime ministers, they don’t take up a lot of space in the public square,” he said.

That’s why Stewart, a retired history teacher and the author of two books on Canadian prime ministers, along with one of his former students at Toronto’s Bishop Strachan School, Joanne Archibald — a historical consultant who wrote her Masters thesis at the London School of Economics on Pierre Trudeau, and earned her PhD from Queen’s University with a thesis on the leadership of prime minister Louis St. Laurent — decided to form a new organization with plans to change that.

“It’s important for us to understand who these people are,” Archibald said. “What makes them tick? Why did they get out of bed in the morning? How did they grow up? What’s their background? What influences them from a family structure point of view?”

The non-partisan Prime Ministers Institute will be committed to telling the stories of Canada through the lens of its prime ministers, from Sir John A. Macdonald to Mark Carney and those who succeed him. It aims to promote research, education and informed conversation about Canada’s political history, including the achievements, failures and legacies of those who led the country.
Part of protecting your sovereignty is knowing your history and knowing your culture
“None of them get talked about,” Stewart said.

“You might say there’s an exception with Pierre Trudeau because he still seems to loom large in the memories of the baby boomers and others, but the other prime ministers, we don’t really hear about them in the public conversation. And that could be anyone from Louis St. Laurent, to John Diefenbaker, even to a lesser extent Brian Mulroney, although he has been talked about a little bit because of his recent death. And then of course, John A. Macdonald gets talked about because of controversies about the removal of the statues and such, but we don’t have a good grasp of what kinds of legacies prime ministers left behind and what the consequences of their decisions have been, both for the good and the ill, and how they’ve managed the federation,” Stewart said.

“So, if we can bring more conversation to the public sphere, it’s going to be useful for us, particularly at this time where we’re trying to figure out what actually made Canada. What actually are we trying to defend when we say we want to protect our own sovereignty? And part of protecting your sovereignty is knowing your history and knowing your culture.”

Canadians in their 20s and 30s might not know what Lester Pearson, who was prime minister from 1963 to 1968, did “in terms of establishing national health care and establishing our own distinct Canadian flag,” Stewart said.

“If you look at somebody like Alexander Mackenzie, he was prime minister for one term after Sir. John A. Macdonald, but he established the Supreme Court in Canada and he also established the secret ballot,” Stewart said of the Liberal who was prime minister from 1873 to 1878.
“Everything that a prime minister does is laying a foundation for building the country and sometimes they’re a little bit minor but still have a role to play when you look at the grand scheme.”

When the rocky relationship between Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump creeps into conversation, Archibald notes there’s a lot we can learn by examining how other prime ministers have handled relations with their American counterparts.
Canada’s 12th prime minister, St. Laurent, had “quite close working relationships” with both Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower, she said.

“He played golf, for example, with Eisenhower at Augusta National Golf Club in 1956 and he came back to the House of Commons and talked about how the golf course was a great place for diplomacy because they were talking politics in between shots and in the golf cart on the way to the next hole,” Archibald said.

content_blocks.text: St. Laurent even attended a performance by Truman’s daughter, Margaret, a classical coloratura soprano, in Ottawa, she said.

“Harry Truman wrote a letter back to Louis St. Laurent saying how much he appreciated that Louis St. Laurent and his wife, Jeanne, went to support Margaret Truman in her performance in Ottawa. So, you can really see the personal connections between these leaders and the way in which that shapes their relationship.”

If we look at “previous examples of really nasty relationships,” those between John F. Kennedy and Diefenbaker stand out for their generational clash, as does the discord between Pierre Trudeau and Richard Nixon, Stewart said.

“If you look at Nixon’s speech to Parliament in 1972, he throws a lot of cold water on the relationship and says we need to get by the sentimental past and just look at both these countries that have different interests and different identities,” Stewart said. “He took all the sugar off and said we’re not always going to get along. So, he didn’t really push the rhetoric of the great relationship between the two countries.”

The new institute, to be known by its initials PMI, is a program of the Canadian Institute for Historical Education, a registered charity dedicated to promoting historical literacy through research, education, and engagement in the public square.
The PMI is supported by leading historians, journalists, and thinkers from across the country.

The institute is not located in a building but will be a virtual organization committed to in-person public engagement. It plans to partner with civic and academic institutions to engage with the public about political history and its relevance to today.

The institute will launch its first public event on Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 6 p.m. at the Royal Canadian Military Institute in Toronto when it hosts a panel discussion on Prime Ministers and 24 Sussex Drive.

stories.title: The unexpected legacy of childhood adversity
stories.summary: Each child has a different history and reacts differently to harsh conditions, but they are all affected by them
stories.author: Thomas Verny
stories.content:
Thomas R. Verny is a clinical psychiatrist, academic, award-winning author, poet and public speaker. He is the author of eight books, including the global bestseller The Secret Life of the Unborn Child and The Embodied Mind: Understanding the Mysteries of Cellular Memory, Consciousness and Our Bodies .

No one comes through childhood entirely untouched or unscathed. One reason lies in the profound asymmetry of a child’s world.

The adult is big and strong; the child is small and vulnerable. One has power, the other has virtually none. One looks down, the other looks up, literally and metaphorically.

Love and dependence tend to become interwoven with frustration, resentment and envy, sometimes on both sides. We generally regard this imbalance as necessary, benign and caring. And usually, it is.

But what happens when the adults on whom a child depends are absent, overwhelmed, dangerous, or simply unable to provide for the child’s needs?

I was reminded of this recently when I attended the 35th anniversary celebrations of Smile as a Gift (Usmev ako dar), a charitable organization in Bratislava, Slovakia, that works with children in foster care and children’s homes, as well as families threatened by poverty, violence, imprisonment or illness.

Slovakia also has a Commissioner for Children (Komisar pre deti), charged with defending children’s rights under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. The current commissioner, Jozef Miklosko, is a man in his early 50s, with tousled blond hair beginning to turn silver, an infectious laugh, and enough energy and enthusiasm to power a small nuclear plant. He seems to regard his work less as a job than a calling.

He and I spent many hours talking about Slovak “social orphans.” He explained that these are children who have been separated from their parents because of a complicated mixture of neglect, poverty, parental incapacity, illness, imprisonment, abuse, family breakdown, separation from parents, violence, hunger, physical, sexual, and emotional abuse and, more recently, displacement by the war in Ukraine.

They are now under the care of the social-welfare system. Only a small proportion are orphans in the traditional sense of having lost both parents. Most live with relatives or foster families rather than in institutions.

Each child has a different history and reacts differently to harsh conditions. But they are all affected by them. At this very moment, hundreds of millions of children around the world are exposed to adversity. [1, 2, 3]

Many children and youth from disadvantaged communities do not eat, sleep, live, work or go to school in safe, stable places. Growing up under such stressful conditions undermines health, development and learning. [4, 5, 6]

It was less than three decades ago that researchers introduced the concept of Adverse Childhood Experiences, or ACEs, as a way of measuring the cumulative effects of childhood adversity. [7–9] What have we learned since then about their long-term consequences?

I don’t think you need a PhD or Dr. Google to figure out that hunger or ill-treatment will have a negative impact on the physical and mental health of any person, especially a young vulnerable child. Many studies have quantified such effects for individual ACEs. They appear to extend across the lifespan, increasing the likelihood of unhealthy behaviours, mental illness and a range of chronic physical diseases. And the risks tend to rise as adverse experiences accumulate. [10, 11, 12, 13]

A particularly thorough review was conducted by Professor Karen Hughes of Bangor University in the U.K. She and her colleagues reviewed 37 studies involving more than a quarter of a million people. What they found was that the more adversity people experienced in childhood, the greater their likelihood of encountering a remarkable range of difficulties later in life.

The links were relatively weak for obesity, physical inactivity, and diabetes; stronger for smoking, heavy drinking, cancer, heart disease and respiratory illness; and stronger still for mental health problems and risky sexual behaviour. But the most disturbing associations were with drug misuse, violence toward others and violence directed against oneself. [14]

Surprisingly, the commonly held belief that children who suffer physical abuse are at increased risk of becoming abusive parents themselves and children who have been sexually abused become adult sexual offenders is refuted by many academic studies. [15, 16, 17] Most abused children do not grow up to abuse others. That’s the good news.

The bad news is that drawing on very large population samples from Europe and North America, Professor Mark Bellis, a leading British public health researcher and expert on adverse childhood experiences, asked how much illness across entire populations might be associated with childhood adversity. He and his colleagues examined common ACEs such as physical, sexual and emotional abuse, domestic violence, parental separation, and living with household members affected by substance abuse, mental illness or criminality. [18]

What they found was that childhood adversity was common. In Europe, about 24 per cent of people had experienced one ACE, and 19 per cent had experienced two or more. In North America, about 23 per cent had experienced one ACE and a striking 35 per cent had experienced two or more, supporting the Hughes results.

Perhaps the most surprising finding was the sheer scale of the estimated financial burden. The researchers calculated that health problems associated with ACEs cost approximately $748-billion annually in North America and $581-billion in Europe. That is an incredible $1.3-trillion a year combined (all in U.S. dollars). More than three-quarters of those costs were associated with people who had experienced two or more ACEs.

Scientific research focused for a long time on the risks associated with adversity. The prevailing “deficit model” described children from high-stress backgrounds as being at risk for impairments in learning and behaviour.

The intervention goal was to prevent, reduce or repair the damage. Bruce J. Ellis and colleagues wrote in 2017 that missing from this deficit approach is an attempt to leverage the unique strengths and abilities that develop in response to high-stress environments. These were originally called “hidden talents” but are now referred to as “stress-adapted skills,” partly because “hidden talents” can sound as though adversity is somehow beneficial. [19]

Recent studies show that damage and adaptation can occur simultaneously. [20, 21] How do some individuals manage to flourish despite painful experiences that leave others struggling? I think the following brief biographies of three personalities throw some light on the subject that academic studies fail to do.

As you probably know, this year’s Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to 85-year-old South African jurist Navi Pillay. Born in 1941 in Clairwood, a poor Indian neighbourhood of Durban, Ms. Pillay was the fifth of eight children. Her grandparents had come to South Africa as indentured labourers. Her father drove a bus, supplementing his meagre wages by fishing. The family could afford neither newspapers nor a radio, and books were in short supply.

At 10, she boldly announced in class that she wanted to become a lawyer. Her teacher dampened her enthusiasm by pointing out that university tuition was expensive and her father could never afford to pay for it.

Ms. Pillay excelled at school, winning prizes for essays, including one examining racial discrimination in sentencing. This came to the attention of the local Indian community. Recognizing her abilities, members collectively helped finance her university education. At the University of Natal, she spent hours in the library. There she discovered the transcripts of the Nuremberg trials, which profoundly influenced her understanding of international justice.

She graduated in law in 1965. Subsequently, she served on international criminal tribunals and became United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.

We are all familiar with Charles Dickens. But most of us don’t know that his father was imprisoned for debt, and at 12 Dickens was sent to work in a shoe-blacking factory. The humiliation and insecurity of that experience haunted him and informed much of his writing. He made the suffering of impoverished children one of the great moral themes of his writing.

Abraham Lincoln is my last example. His childhood was marked by poverty, like the other two individuals mentioned, exhausting physical labour and limited schooling. When Lincoln was nine, his mother died. His father remarried a widow with three children.

Lucky for young Abe, his stepmother was not the folkloric evil stepmother but a significant positive influence. She encouraged his love of books, treated him affectionately, and maintained a close relationship with him for the rest of her life.

Although their childhoods differed considerably, Navi Pillay, Charles Dickens, and Abraham Lincoln appear to share several characteristics.

All three were intellectually curious despite environments that offered limited educational opportunities. They thirsted for knowledge, shared an awareness of the limitations of their present lives and would not accept them as permanent. They searched tirelessly for ways to escape them. They found people who encouraged them and helped them along the way to better themselves. Their childhood experiences shaped what they came to notice, care about, and fight for. And they developed verbal skills to adroitly combat injustice.

In some instances, having been powerless May make a person particularly aware of the powerlessness of others. Having been unfairly treated May motivate some individuals to a lifelong commitment to fair play and justice.

While there is no denying that adversity, especially early adversity, has a corrosive impact on a child, it is equally true that some people, like the three mentioned here and, of course, thousands of others who have the good luck of inheriting sterling genes, a pleasant temperament, persistence, ambition, intellectual curiosity, and who received encouragement from others, can overcome and grow from it.

What seems to be required is a kind of psychological alchemy: transforming one’s misfortunes to a reason to achieve something worthwhile with one’s life. And, of course, to repay society for saving them from living a blighted life.

The scientific study of ACEs shows us how experience becomes implanted in our biology and psyche and has such a long reach. In other words, how childhood becomes embodied. Even so, with the love and care of reliable adults, abused children do recover from their dark childhoods. Of course, because human nature is so complex, it is impossible to predict to what degree each child will recover. The important thing is that there are individuals and organizations that provide this type of help.

At the Smile as a Gift organization, I spoke to the professionals there and observed them interacting with the social orphans. They know that they cannot erase the past, that recovery from adversity is not about forgetting or papering over the hurts and wounds, and that childhood adversity leaves scars that never entirely heal.

But maintaining a safe place where truly dedicated and caring people provide many opportunities for reparenting, developing trust, good communication, education, counselling and a variety of workshops that help the children gain self-confidence and grow into the healthy adults they were meant to be. Individual resilience is not enough. Children need people and institutions that give them opportunities to recover.

Let us remember that adversity is not a witch’s curse, as in Sleeping Beauty, it is not destiny. It is also not necessarily ennobling. It is not one or the other.

The human mind is very complex. Someone May be highly successful professionally while battling constantly with their families. Another person May have significant psychological difficulties such as anxiety or depression yet possess remarkable generosity and compassion. You May ask yourself: Do I carry any scars from my childhood? And if so, how have they affected me?

In many cases adversity predates birth. I shall address that subject in my next column.

Of course, because human nature is so complex, it is impossible to predict to what degree each child will recover. The important thing is that there are individuals and organizations that provide this type of help.

At the Smile as a Gift organization, I spoke to the professionals there and observed them interacting with the social orphans. They know that they cannot erase the past, that recovery from adversity is not about forgetting or papering over the hurts and wounds, and that childhood adversity leaves scars that never entirely heal.

But maintaining a safe place where truly dedicated and caring people provide many opportunities for reparenting, developing trust, good communication, education, counselling and a variety of workshops that help the children gain self-confidence and grow into the healthy adults they were meant to be. Individual resilience is not enough. Children need people and institutions that give them opportunities to recover.
Let us remember that adversity is not a witch’s curse, as in Sleeping Beauty, it is not destiny. It is also not necessarily ennobling. It is not one or the other.

The human mind is very complex. Someone May be highly successful professionally while battling constantly with their families. Another person May have significant psychological difficulties such as anxiety or depression yet possess remarkable generosity and compassion. You May ask yourself: Do I carry any scars from my childhood? And if so, how have they affected me?
In many cases adversity predates birth. I shall address that subject in my next column.

content_blocks.text: No one comes through childhood entirely untouched or unscathed. One reason lies in the profound asymmetry of a child’s world.

content_blocks.text: The adult is big and strong; the child is small and vulnerable. One has power, the other has virtually none. One looks down, the other looks up, literally and metaphorically.

content_blocks.text: Love and dependence tend to become interwoven with frustration, resentment and envy, sometimes on both sides. We generally regard this imbalance as necessary, benign and caring. And usually, it is.

content_blocks.text: Slovakia also has a Commissioner for Children (Komisar pre deti), charged with defending children’s rights under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. The current commissioner, Jozef Miklosko, is a man in his early 50s, with tousled blond hair beginning to turn silver, an infectious laugh, and enough energy and enthusiasm to power a small nuclear plant. He seems to regard his work less as a job than a calling.

content_blocks.text: It was less than three decades ago that researchers introduced the concept of Adverse Childhood Experiences, or ACEs, as a way of measuring the cumulative effects of childhood adversity. [7–9] What have we learned since then about their long-term consequences?

content_blocks.text: I don’t think you need a PhD or Dr. Google to figure out that hunger or ill-treatment will have a negative impact on the physical and mental health of any person, especially a young vulnerable child. Many studies have quantified such effects for individual ACEs. They appear to extend across the lifespan, increasing the likelihood of unhealthy behaviours, mental illness and a range of chronic physical diseases. And the risks tend to rise as adverse experiences accumulate. [10, 11, 12, 13]

content_blocks.text: A particularly thorough review was conducted by Professor Karen Hughes of Bangor University in the U.K. She and her colleagues reviewed 37 studies involving more than a quarter of a million people. What they found was that the more adversity people experienced in childhood, the greater their likelihood of encountering a remarkable range of difficulties later in life.

content_blocks.text: The bad news is that drawing on very large population samples from Europe and North America, Professor Mark Bellis, a leading British public health researcher and expert on adverse childhood experiences, asked how much illness across entire populations might be associated with childhood adversity. He and his colleagues examined common ACEs such as physical, sexual and emotional abuse, domestic violence, parental separation, and living with household members affected by substance abuse, mental illness or criminality. content_blocks.text: What they found was that childhood adversity was common. In Europe, about 24 per cent of people had experienced one ACE, and 19 per cent had experienced two or more. In North America, about 23 per cent had experienced one ACE and a striking 35 per cent had experienced two or more, supporting the Hughes results.

content_blocks.text: Perhaps the most surprising finding was the sheer scale of the estimated financial burden. The researchers calculated that health problems associated with ACEs cost approximately $748-billion annually in North America and $581-billion in Europe. That is an incredible $1.3-trillion a year combined (all in U.S. dollars). More than three-quarters of those costs were associated with people who had experienced two or more ACEs.

I think the following brief biographies of three personalities throw some light on the subject that academic studies fail to do.

content_blocks.text: As you probably know, this year’s Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to 85-year-old South African jurist Navi Pillay. Born in 1941 in Clairwood, a poor Indian neighbourhood of Durban, Ms. Pillay was the fifth of eight children. Her grandparents had come to South Africa as indentured labourers. Her father drove a bus, supplementing his meagre wages by fishing. The family could afford neither newspapers nor a radio, and books were in short supply.

content_blocks.text: At 10, she boldly announced in class that she wanted to become a lawyer. Her teacher dampened her enthusiasm by pointing out that university tuition was expensive and her father could never afford to pay for it.

content_blocks.text: Ms. Pillay excelled at school, winning prizes for essays, including one examining racial discrimination in sentencing. This came to the attention of the local Indian community. Recognizing her abilities, members collectively helped finance her university education. At the University of Natal, she spent hours in the library. There she discovered the transcripts of the Nuremberg trials, which profoundly influenced her understanding of international justice.

The humiliation and insecurity of that experience haunted him and informed much of his writing. He made the suffering of impoverished children one of the great moral themes of his writing.

content_blocks.text: Abraham Lincoln is my last example. His childhood was marked by poverty, like the other two individuals mentioned, exhausting physical labour and limited schooling. When Lincoln was nine, his mother died. His father remarried a widow with three children.

content_blocks.text: Lucky for young Abe, his stepmother was not the folkloric evil stepmother but a significant positive influence. She encouraged his love of books, treated him affectionately, and maintained a close relationship with him for the rest of her life.

content_blocks.text: All three were intellectually curious despite environments that offered limited educational opportunities. They found people who encouraged them and helped them along the way to better themselves. Their childhood experiences shaped what they came to notice, care about, and fight for. And they developed verbal skills to adroitly combat injustice.

stories.title: London Knights survive comeback, start road trip with win
stories.summary: Jaxon Cover scored late in the third period, then again in overtime, helping the London Knights to a 5-4 win in North Bay Thursday night.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Jaxon Cover scored late in the third period, then again in overtime, helping the London Knights to a 5-4 win in North Bay Thursday night.

The Knights survived a comeback, having built a 3-0 lead in the second period, ON goals from Caleb Mitchel, Marcus Nordmark, and Kane Barch.

The Battalion scored three unanswered goals of their own though, tying the game midway through the third period.

Cover’s goal with a minute remaining in regulation was his fifth of the season, and seemed like it would end up the game-winner.

North Bay tied it with less than a second remaining in regulation time though, forcing the extra frame. Cover’s actual game-winner came 37 seconds into overtime.

This was the first of three straight road games for London, touring through Northern Ontario this weekend.

They play the Sudbury Wolves Friday night, before a Sunday afternoon tilt in Sault Ste. Marie.
