stories.title: Fredericton’s emergency shelter space shrinks ahead of winter
stories.summary: As colder weather approaches, those who operate homeless shelters in Fredericton are preparing to work with less this year.
stories.author: Johnny James, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
As colder weather approaches, those who operate homeless shelters in Fredericton are preparing to work with less this year.

Fredericton Homeless Shelters Inc. has run an emergency out-of-the-cold shelter in a building at the exhibition grounds for two winters now. The site allowed for around 33 beds.

However, the building is set to be demolished as part of a redevelopment project.

This week, Fredericton City Council approved another emergency shelter to operate this winter — but it’s at the Small Craft Aquatic Centre on the city’s south side, which is a smaller space.

“The Aquatic Center has been the appointed place right now and it will provide 10 emergency beds for overnight use during the winter months,” said Vanessa Foss, Fredericton Homeless Shelters Inc.’s director of business development.

Foss says the organization also has a men’s shelter with a 27-bed capacity and a women’s shelter with 10 beds “plus emergency couch.”

According to the latest numbers from the Human Development Council, as of September there were 353 people experiencing homelessness in Fredericton .

The data also showed 179 people were chronically homeless, which refers to people who have at least six months of homelessness over the past year or recurrent experiences of homelessness over the past three years.

“The numbers (of unhoused people) have increased quite a bit, so there’s a substantial need for individuals for housing and emergency shelters,” said Foss. “Between housing and shelter, there’s a significant need.”

Foss says work is ongoing to build a permanent shelter, but short-term measures are coming soon.

“We have started up our supported housing, so we have two houses now and then we’ll be opening a third in January. So that is increasing some supported housing elements, but that bigger project will be to come,” Foss said.

Council also approved a new courtyard lot for 12 Neighbours, a tiny home community, which will add 15 new units. The units offer a bridge between emergency out-of-the-cold services and permanent supportive housing.

“One of the things it does is helps us, of course, to deploy solutions more quickly but also house individuals that have some additional complexities that make it difficult for them to succeed even in a supportive, permanent housing context,” said Marcel LeBrun, president of 12 Neighbours, who spoke to council on Monday.

The Aquatic Centre emergency shelter will open in mid-December and is approved to stay open until the end of April.

stories.title: At Windsor’s film festival, a couple wise guys reveal how they uncovered Scorsese’s secrets
stories.summary: Documentary by Australian and British filmmakers is a true passion project, a testament to the immense cultural legacy of Martin Scorsese’s film
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
As far back as Lisa Downs and Ashley Pugh can remember, they wanted to make a documentary about Goodfellas .

Okay, that’s a bit of Scorsese-level hyperbole, but the pair of Australian (Downs) and British (Pugh) filmmakers – who are partners in work and in life – had been inching toward exploring the 1990 crime epic after previously making a series of docs chronicling the productions of more family-friendly big-screen classics: Flight of the Navigator , The NeverEnding Story and Flash Gordon , all of which were childhood favourites of Downs.

“I said to Lisa, ‘Well, you know if we’re going to keep making these kinds of movies, how about we do one about a movie that I love?’” recalls Pugh in an interview. “I first saw Goodfellas when I was 16, and like a lot of movie-obsessed teenagers, I fell in love with it. And we do have a history with the film as a couple. When we first started dating, as a surprise for my birthday, Lisa rented out a cinema so that we could watch the film together on the big screen. I thought after that, well, she’s a keeper.”

It would be fair to say, then, that the pair’s new documentary, As Far Back as I Can Remember ... The Story of Goodfellas is a true passion project, as much a testament to the directors’ romance as it is to the immense cultural legacy of Scorsese’s film, which is rightly considered one of the most influential films of all time. But producing the doc, which will make its Canadian premiere at the Windsor International Film Festival Nov. 2, wasn’t exactly as easy as, say, falling in love.

Determined to make a film that was more than just a standard behind-the-scenes doc that could have been included as a Blu-ray extra, Downs and Pugh spent years researching Goodfellas on a granular level. This involved going so far as to hunt down previously unreleased footage shot by a local film student featuring such cast members as Joe Pesci roaming the set and offering informal interviews – material that had been stored on VHS tapes locked away in an Alaskan safe for the past 35 years.

“We were very wary as to how to treat that footage – because it’s very old, we needed to gently upscale it because we wanted it to look archival without much sharpening – you don’t want it to seem like it’s AI or something,” Pugh says with a laugh.

The documentarians also spent untold hours trying to track down and gain access to as many cast and crew of Goodfellas as possible. Building upon a friendship that the pair had with Christopher Serrone, who played the young version of Ray Liotta’s mobster antihero Henry Hill, Downs and Pugh gradually accumulated a murderer’s row of talent. Eventually, they secured participation from dozens of key members of the Goodfellas team, everyone from actors Samuel L. Jackson and Illeana Douglas to mega-producer Irwin Winkler and screenwriter Nicholas Pileggi. (Alas, Scorsese, Robert De Niro and Pesci remained elusive, while Liotta died in 2022.)

“What we learned from making our previous films is that patience plays a huge part, especially when you have a film with so many people who you’d like to interview. With this movie, every character is iconic, even if they have one line,” says Downs. “Having an in with Chris was a wonderful start, but really we just scour IMDb and start reaching out to people.”

The doc’s biggest coup, though, came about through sheer luck. Learning that there was going to be a fan convention in Woodbridge, N.J., in 2025 called Paisan Con – a celebration of “Italian-American Pop Culture & Heritage” – Downs and Pugh hopped on a plane, brought their cameras along, and walked up cold to actress Lorraine Bracco, hoping that she’d simply say yes on the spot. Surprisingly, Bracco, a doyenne of mafia pop-culture thanks to her performance as Hill’s wife Karen in Goodfellas as well as her Emmy-nominated turn as Dr. Jennifer Melfi in The Sopranos – was all in.

“They were simply delightful, and they had such a love for Goodfellas that I instantly admired them. Their energy was contagious,” recalls Bracco in a separate interview. “Talking with people who love this movie, it’s the best part of being an actor. I’m still amazed that people of all generations, whether they’re my age or my father’s age or your age, come up to me and talk about how much they love this movie. It’s shocking, but it’s also not. Marty is a master filmmaker. So how lucky was I?”

Once Bracco was onboard the doc, an entire new world of Goodfellas was unlocked to Downs and Pugh – not only cast members who had been hard to reach, such as Debbie Mazar, but also crucial behind-the-scenes players such as casting director Ellen Lewis, who plucked everyday New Jersey residents to populate the film, ensuring Scorsese’s vision was that much more authentic.

“Sometimes you get surprised how welcoming people can be in this whole process,” says Downs. “For Nick Pileggi, I got a hold of his phone number through someone and just cold-called him. He was like, ‘Great, just come to the Hamptons and we’ll talk.’”

At the same time that the doc is making its way into the world one screening at a time – in Windsor, Downs and Pugh will be on hand as Bracco receives the festival’s Spotlight Award and participates in a postscreening Q&A – the filmmakers are making three other film-centric documentaries, including one focusing on the legacy of Goodfellas producer Winkler, who also developed such classics as Rocky , Raging Bull and The Right Stuff .

“It’s been a little like a travelling circus taking this movie around,” says Downs. “But the fact that Lorraine can be with us along the journey, we feel blessed.”

Also Playing at Wiff

Given its relatively small region and crowded spot on the fall-season calendar, the Windsor International Film Festival has been punching above its weight over the past few years. Now in its 22nd edition, Wiff will offer 232 features this year across 300 screenings, plus its annual $25,000 Canadian Film prize. Here are a few highlights of this year’s fest, running Oct. 29 through Nov. 8:

Paper Tiger: James Gray’s throwback crime drama starring Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson will open Wiff ahead of its release across the country later in November.

All of a Sudden: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s epic-length drama following the burgeoning relationship between two care workers, a hit at Cannes, plays Wiff before its gradual roll out across the country later this fall.

125, Rue des Malaises: The surprise Québécois hit of the summer, Louis Bélanger’s French-language dramedy following an elderly patriarch who chooses medical aid in dying hasn’t been available outside its home province.

Rose: The second big Sandra Hüller movie of the season – following this week’s release of Fatherland – stars the German actress as a mysterious soldier setting up shop in a 17th-century village.

The Debut: Wiff’s closing-night film was a breakout at Tiff in September, and features a standout performance from Julianne Moore as a suburban housewife who finds her creative side via her local community theatre troupe.

stories.title: Quebec plans to ban religious symbols in schools, Education Minister says
stories.summary: Parti Québécois promised to broaden provincial secularism laws during recent election campaign
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
The president of the National Council of Canadian Muslims is accusing the Quebec government of attempting to take away the rights of children by expanding secularism laws.

“We’re talking about going after the rights of children to have a spirituality and go to school,” said Stephen Brown in an interview.

Quebec’s new education minister, Joël Arseneau, told journalists on Wednesday that he plans to ban schoolchildren from wearing religious symbols. He added that doing so is “non-negotiable.”

The Parti Québécois had promised the ban during the election campaign that resulted in a PQ minority government. In its platform, the party wrote that secularism “embodies the desire of the vast majority of Quebeckers to live in a society where religion is practised in the private sphere.”

But Brown said the government is already breaking its promise to be the “the government of all Quebeckers.”

“What we’re seeing now is anything but that,” said Brown. “It’s ridiculous and a missed opportunity.”

Brown said the government had pledged to reach out to communities and find balanced policy solutions to difficult questions like secularism. He believes that believes preventing children from wearing religious symbols is “blatant discrimination against religious minorities.”

He said the rules would mainly apply to those who wish to wear the kippa, hijab, crucifix and turban.

“We should not live in a country where politicians are able to literally trade away the rights of Canadian citizens in an election or political game,” said Brown. “The Charter rights of Canadian citizens have to be worth more than the paper they’re written on.”

Québec solidaire’s education and secularism critic, Roxane Milot, said the leftist party will vote against the proposed ban.

“Leave the kids alone! The priorities for the education system are clear: address the staff shortage, repair our schools, put an end to the three-tiered school system and reduce the dropout rate,” she said in a news release.

In the same release, Québec solidaire said it is concerning to see the new administration get bogged down by “identity-driven one-upmanship.”

It is unclear when the PQ government intends to table a bill to this effect, though the legislature is scheduled to resume sitting on Nov. 17.

The Quebec government has been strongly criticized for its law banning employees of the public sector, including teachers, from wearing religious symbols.

A legal challenge of that law, known as Bill 21, has made it to the Supreme Court of Canada. Lawyers argued it raised serious concerns involving several Charter rights, including freedom of expression, conscience and religion.

Those legal proceedings are ongoing.

Brown said he is prepared to mount a legal challenge if the PQ’s proposal becomes law.

Jean-Christophe Jasmin, the Quebec director of Christian think tank Cardus, also opposes expanding secularism laws.

In an interview, he said the government’s rationale to ban religious symbols worn by government employees was “presented in the name of freedom of conscience.” The previous Coalition Avenir Québec administration had argued that children are subject to an authority figure, and that that figure must be religiously neutral as to not impose their beliefs on their students.

“I don’t see how that logic applies to children today. Children do not represent the state, they are part of civil society,” said Jasmin. “There is no duty of neutrality on the part of children. The argument doesn’t hold up.”

Brown agreed, saying the scope of secularism laws banning religious symbols has continued to expand since the CAQ took power in 2018.

At first, the government targeted those in positions of authority. It was extended to teachers, daycare workers, all school staff and parents who volunteer in schools.

The CAQ then expanded the scope of the law to the public sphere by banning praying outside, in universities and at workplaces.

“And now of course, we’re going after the rights of children. So where does this end?” said Brown.

Frédéric Bérard, a constitutional lawyer who took part in the legal challenge against Bill 21, did not want to comment on Arseneau’s comments but said it was to be expected.

He pointed out that former premier François Legault had openly said in a 2019 radio interview with Radio-Canada that Bill 21 was a concession to “people who are a little racist and don’t want to see religious symbols anywhere in public.”

“It’s never enough,” said Bérard. “It’s a slippery slope.”

stories.title: N.S. university teachers association says premier is using political intimidation
stories.summary: The Association of Nova Scotia University Teachers says it condemns the premier’s response, calling it a threat to academic freedom.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An association representing university teachers in Nova Scotia is accusing Premier Tim Houston of political intimidation after his office complained to a Toronto professor who had commented on a proposed artificial intelligence data centre.

Houston told reporters on Wednesday he’s glad a staffer in his office sent the complaint to the professor, saying his comments about the $10-billion data centre were wrong.

The Association of Nova Scotia University Teachers says it condemns the premier’s response, calling it a threat to academic freedom.

The premier’s office says it disagrees with the characterization and that it has a productive relationship with academic institutions in the province.

The complaint came after Sibo Chen, a communications professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, gave a media interview to CBC News saying that public concerns about the data centre project in Point Tupper, N.S., were valid.

A communications adviser with the premier’s office sent Chen an email describing his comments as slanted and irresponsible, and copied a CBC News reporter and the chair of Chen’s department.

The president of the association of university teachers says the premier’s response raises questions about what consequences Nova Scotia academics could face if they challenge provincial projects.

“Government influence over research grants, board appointments and institutional funding gives that concern real weight,” Mathew Reichertz said. “Faculty should never have to fear that sharing their findings could jeopardize their research support or bring pressure on their employer to discipline them.”

Everwind Fuels announced earlier this month that U.S. AI company Anthropic signed a 20-year lease for the data centre, sparking opposition from members of the public.

A petition to stop the development of AI data centres in Nova Scotia on Change.org had over 24,000 signatures as of Wednesday afternoon.

stories.title: Maya Gebala is being released from the hospital, father says: 'Never a day I stopped believing'
stories.summary: In an emotional post on social media, he called her an "inspiration" and said she was the "bravest person" he knows.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The father of Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor David Gebala says his daughter Maya, who was severely injured in February, is being released from the hospital.

In an emotional post on social media, he said it has been 262 days since she was airlifted to the BC Children’s Hospital. He recounted in the post on X Thursday that he was told at the time, presumably by doctors, that “we don’t think she’s going to make it through the night.”

He added, “Since then, I’ve watched you fight for every single one of those days.”

Maya has had several emergency surgeries, infections and other struggles during her hospital stay.

“179 days ago, your prosthetic skull was placed. Your fifth surgery, and the one that finally stuck. After that, things slowly began to feel possible again,” wrote David.

Eventually, he said he saw his daughter smile, was able to take her off the hospital grounds briefly, and was even able to celebrate when she turned 13 in September.

“There was never a day I stopped believing we would get here. The road ahead is still long, but this is a milestone no one thought we would reach,” he said.

He called Maya “the bravest person I know” and an inspiration.

“Look at you, my girl. You blew every expectation out of the water,” he concluded, adding that he was grateful for all of the medical professionals who helped her along the way and all of their supporters. “Now it’s time to leave these hospital walls behind and keep moving forward, Maya Bear.”

The post also included a video showing Maya, wearing sunglasses and smiling and gesturing happily, as she received the news that she would be released from the hospital.

In February, Jesse Van Rootselaar, a former Tumbler Ridge Secondary School student, killed eight people, including six children, and injured dozens before committing suicide.

stories.title: Poll suggests long wait times led half of Canadians to avoid going to the hospital
stories.summary: A new poll suggests long wait times lead half of Canadians to avoid seeing a doctor or going to the hospital.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A new poll suggests long wait times lead half of Canadians to avoid seeing a doctor or going to the hospital.

The poll was conducted by Léger and commissioned by right-leaning think-tanks the Montreal Economic Institute, SecondStreet.org and Canadian Constitution Foundation.

The percentage of respondents who said they avoided consulting doctors because of wait times was highest among women, people over 55 and Quebecers.

The poll ran from Oct. 16 to 19, 2026, among an online panel of 1,510 Canadians.

The survey numbers do not indicate whether the people who avoided seeing a doctor had seen a nurse or turned to other services like pharmacists.

It is also unclear whether respondents started avoiding hospitals because of wait times over the past year or at another point in their lives.

Just over a quarter of poll respondents said they have paid for private health care to avoid wait times or unsatisfactory service.

The survey also found that 61 per cent of respondents supported being able to pay out of pocket or use insurance to access private care if they could not get timely care in the public system. However, a quarter of respondents said they opposed the coexistence of public and private health-care systems.

Asked if they believed the health-care system in their area needed change, 84 per cent of respondents said yes.

The polling industry’s professional body, the Canadian Research Insights Council, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

stories.title: Police investigate arson attack on car outside home of Sikh independence activist
stories.summary: Surrey — Police in B.C. are investigating an apparent arson attack outside the home of a Sikh independence activist who was previously warned by officers that his life was under threat.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Surrey — Police in B.C. are investigating an apparent arson attack outside the home of a Sikh independence activist who was previously warned by officers that his life was under threat.

Surrey police say officers found a car engulfed in flames and a bus vandalized after the attack in the Surrey Central neighbourhood, where officers were called to the scene at 11:45 p.m. Wednesday.

Investigators say they believe a suspect fled on foot and no motive has been determined.

The Sikhs For Justice group says in a separate news release that the attack occurred at the home of Narinder Singh Randhawa, who was given a “duty to warn” notice by Surrey police in April and told there was an imminent threat to his life.

Randhawa has organized rallies for the Khalistan movement that seeks the formation of an independent Sikh state in the Punjab region within India.

A former leader of the group, Hardeep Singh Nijjar, was shot dead in Surrey in 2023, in an attack former prime minister Justin Trudeau said was linked to India by credible intelligence.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who visited India earlier this year, has refused to say if he believes the Indian government is involved in acts of foreign interference and transnational repression in Canada.

Randhawa previously told The Canadian Press that police said his activism and participation in protests May be behind threats against his life.

The Sikhs For Justice statement says protesters had rallied in Vancouver on the day of the arson attack.

The group urged police to investigate the attack as an act of terrorism.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published

Chuck Chiang, The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘What time is it?’ The answer May not be so simple after this weekend’s time change
stories.summary: Clocks are set to roll back one hour on Nov. 1, marking the official end of Daylight Saving Time and, giving us an extra hour of sleep. But for some it will be the last time they make the time change.
stories.author: Brandon Choghri; John Marchesan
stories.content:
By Brandon Choghri and John Marchesan

Posted October 29, 2026 3:13 pm.

When Canadians wake up on Sunday, the simple question of ‘what time is it’ may not have an easy answer.

Clocks are set to roll back one hour at 2 a.m. on Nov. 1, marking the official end of Daylight Saving Time (DST) and, giving us an extra hour of sleep. But for some it will be the last time they make the time change.

Despite growing calls to end the biannual time shift, most of Ontario will continue to turn back time this weekend. The province passed legislation in 2020 to permanently stay on Daylight Saving Time but it came with a caveat – both Quebec and New York State had to make the move at the same time.

While the U.S. Senate has yet to act on a House-passed bill to make DST permanent, Quebec’s new government signaled it intends to abolish the switch after this weekend .

If Quebec were to move forward with getting rid of the time change, it would follow in the footsteps of British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba, which ended the practice this year. These three provinces have chosen to keep daylight time year-round, as has the Northwest Territories.

Certain regions in the northwestern part of Ontario are also going to maintain daylight time year-round in order to align with Manitoba.

Time change hasn’t been an issue in Saskatchewan since it ended the practice back in 1966, while the Yukon stopped moving the clocks in 2020.

Confused yet?

“This coming winter is going to be very confusing for everybody, I can’t keep track of it,” said Dr. Patricia Lakin-Thomas, professor of biology at York University. “I’ve got a map on my computer I have to keep checking like, “What time zone are you in?'”

“What they’re going to find is next spring, these province’s are going to have buyer’s remorse after a winter of the sun coming up at 9 o’clock, 9:30, 9:45; people are going to switch their opinions and they’re really going to hate it.”

Daylight Saving Time was first introduced in Canada during the First World War as a way to conserve energy by maximizing daylight hours. The idea was that shifting the clock would reduce reliance on artificial lighting and heating.

While the original rationale for energy saving is less relevant today, the argument has been that the disruption to sleep schedules and the abrupt shift in daylight patterns outweigh any benefits.

“It’s very, very hard to get up in the dark in the winter mornings… and they’re going to feel jet-lagged, it’s like being jet-lagged all the time,” says Lakin-Thomas, explaining how our biological clock needs morning sunlight in order to reset.

“When we get late afternoon light, in Daylight Saving Time, it pushes our clocks late, we want to go to bed late, and then in the morning the alarm’s going off and we have lost sleep and we’ve thrown our body out of sync – our body thinks that its a different time zone. That’s what the problem is with late afternoon light and Daylight Saving Time.”

Analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

“When we’re on Standard Time, we’re going to be getting up closer to sunrise, which would be the natural time to get up, and our body can adjust, our body will be synchronized better and we’ll be ready to face the day.”

While the extra hour of sleep might be welcome, experts note that even a one-hour shift can affect circadian rhythms, contributing to higher rates of chronic diseases such as diabetes and weight gain, higher rates of cardiovascular disease, and even some kinds of cancer.

BUYERS REMORSE

“This has been sold by politicians as a feel-good factor, it’s very popular if you ask the population. Some of the politicians have claimed ‘We’re giving families another hour of light,’ but what they haven’t said is they’re stealing it from your morning to give it to your afternoon,” says Lakin-Thomas, who points out other places have gone down this road only to have buyers remorse; Russia tried year-round daylight time and ditched it after three years and the United Kingdom bailed after only two years.

During the 1974 energy crisis, the United States instituted year-round Daylight Saving Time, only to have the measure repealed after one year.

“Everyone seemed to like it before it took effect. However, once it took effect, a lot of people didn’t like the fact that they had to get up in the dark to go to work, and even more, they didn’t like sending their kids to school in the dark,” said Dr. David Prerau, one of the world’s foremost authorities on DST.

“People only think about the clock change, they don’t think about the negative of having Daylight Saving Time in the winter.”

Prerau noted that at one point after World War II, the United States actually allowed individual cities to decide if they wanted Daylight or Standard Time, and it was predictably chaotic.

“It got to the point where people didn’t know what time it was when they were calling somebody in another state. For a person who calls, not such a big deal but for business it was very bad,” he explained. “In Minnesota we have the twin cities of St. Paul and Minneapolis, and there was one time that one was on daylight time and one wasn’t.”

Scientists who study biological clocks and sleep experts are calling for a national strategy to rationalize the time zones and put them closer to “natural time” and do what would be best for the whole country.

stories.title: Labour unions set up 'war room' to fight Carney's Bill C-39
stories.summary: Union leaders announced they will set up a "war room" to coordinate their response to the federal government's latest major projects bill.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Canada’s labour union leaders announced on Thursday they will set up a “war room” to coordinate their response to the federal government’s latest major projects bill, which they argue undermines workers’ constitutional right to strike.

The unions warn the passing of Bill C-39’s changes on Section 107 of the Canadian Labour Code risks “triggering years of labour conflict and costly constitutional challenges.”

“Businesses want to get goods moving, reach new markets and build major projects” said Canada Labour Congress President Bea Bruske, in a statement Thursday. “Years spent fighting workers in court won’t accomplish any of that.”

Bruske made the announcement alongside David Chartrand, Canadian general vice-president of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, and Marty Warren, national director of the United Steelworkers.

Bill C-39 has been dubbed the most consequential economic legislation in this Parliament by the Liberal government. The nearly 240-page bill is intended to speed up the regulatory process for the approval of major projects and make changes to collective bargaining for federally regulated workers.

The bill has amassed critics, including unions, environmentalists and First Nations.

The legislation also clarifies Cabinet’s use of Section 107 of the labour code, by giving the labour minister “guardrails” on when they can intervene to end a lockout or strike, including a special mediator report and a national interest test.

Section 107 has been used by the Liberal government to end strikes and work stoppages at ports, railways, Canada Post and airlines. It is currently facing court challenges for its use.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said the bill protects and strengthens workers’ right to strike, rather than weakening it. She has also said the legislation ensures that Section 107 cannot be used pre-emptively.

However, union leaders’ testimonies in front of the Bill C-39 legislative committee, argue that the bill allows the government to legitimize its use of a section in the labour code it has no business using in the first place.

Meanwhile, business and industry groups have applauded the bill’s changes to Section 107 of the code and bargaining, which they believe will help curb the amount of work stoppages that have a significant impact on Canadian supply chains and the economy.

Bill C-39 was passed at second reading, with help from the Conservative Party. However, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has promised his party will make amendments “to protect the rights of workers.”

Opposition parties including the NDP and the Bloc Québécois voted against the bill.

On Wednesday, Conservatives voted in favour of NDP MP Leah Gazan’s private member’s bill which would repeal Section 107 from the labour code altogether. The bill was defeated by Liberal MPs.

Asked on Thursday to clarify his party’s position on Section 107, Conservative associate labour critic Colin Reynolds said “we need to look at it more thoroughly and ultimately that’s what we are looking forward to doing in committee.”

stories.title: Loonie hits six-week high as Canada-U.S. yield gap narrows
stories.summary: BoC decision sparks move
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar strengthened to a six-week ​high against its U.S, counterpart ‌on Thursday after the start of a Bank of Canada tightening cycle helped narrow the gap between Canadian and US bond yields.

The ⁠loonie ​was trading 0.1 per cent higher at 1.3982 per U.S. dollar, or 71.52 US cents, after touching its strongest intraday level since September 16 at 1.3966.

The gap between Canada’s ​2-year yield and the U.S. equivalent narrowed ‌by 4.7 basis points to about 128 basis points in favor of the U.S. note. It was as much as 160 basis points earlier this month, the widest gap since February 2025.

On Wednesday, ​the Bank of ‌Canada hiked its key interest rate by 25 basis points ​to 2.50 per cent and said further increases might ⁠be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from ⁠driving broader inflation, while the Federal Reserve left its policy rate on ​hold.

The yield spread move was “giving traders conviction to chase further gains for the loonie,” said Amo Sahota, director at Klarity FX in San Francisco.

“Oil prices are also remaining elevated, lending some support to the currency,” ⁠Sahota said.

U.S. crude oil futures settled 0.8 per cent lower on hopes for peace talks between the US and Iran but remained elevated at $102 a barrel. Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

The U.S. dollar fell against ⁠a basket of major currencies as ​US Treasury yields eased after the release of US inflation data ⁠that was mostly in line with expectations.

The Canadian 10-year yield was ‌down half a basis point at 3.853 per cent.

Ontario, one of the world’s ​largest sub-sovereign borrowers, forecast a wider budget deficit than previously expected and a delayed return to balance as it provides tax relief for businesses and support for sectors ​hit hard by US tariffs, a fiscal update showed.

stories.title: Hydro-Québec maintains plan to boost rates for data centres despite court ruling
stories.summary: Montreal - Hydro-Québec says it will continue seeking higher electricity rates for data centres and cryptocurrency miners after a court decision struck down governmental decrees that supported the plan.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Hydro-Québec will continue seeking higher electricity rates for data centres and cryptocurrency miners despite a court decision striking down governmental decrees that supported the plan.

Hydro-Québec is asking the province’s energy regulator to approve a new rate averaging 13 cents per kilowatt hour for data centres requiring more than five megawatts of power, which is nearly double their current rate.

The utility is also asking to raise the rate for cryptocurrency mining projects to an average of 19.5 cents per kilowatt hour.

In early 2026, the provincial government published two decrees expressing support for both increases. The government previously amended a law on energy resources to allow the province to express economic, social and environmental concerns to the regulator, which must consider them in its decision.

But Quebec Superior Court Justice Élif Oral ruled on Monday that the government had overstepped with these two decrees.

While the government can express concerns to the regulator — the Régie de l’énergie — it can’t impose an outcome as it did by directly supporting Hydro-Québec’s proposal, the judge wrote in her decision.

“The interpretation of the word ‘concern’ as proposed by the (government and Hydro-Québec) is so broad that it distorts its ordinary, grammatical meaning,” wrote Oral.

The provincial government’s justice department declined to comment on the decision and its energy department did not immediately respond.

The legal challenge was filed by Keel Infrastructure, Hive Digital Technologies and Flumen Energy. The companies, which are data centre and/or cryptocurrency developers, have opposed the rate hike in front of the energy regulator. The law firm representing the companies declined to comment on the decision.

Hydro-Québec spokesperson Cendrix Bouchard said the utility acknowledges the court’s decision.

“Hydro-Québec remains convinced of the value of its rate proposal, which was developed with the goal of protecting all of its customers in Quebec,” Bouchard told The Canadian Press in a statement.

At the first part of the hearing on the proposed hikes in early October, analysts for the utility argued that increasing the rates would ensure the potential growth of the data centre industry would not lead to higher energy prices for other clients.

At the time, two consultants hired by Hydro-Québec said they expect the demand from data centres to more than double between 2024 and 2030 — mostly because of the growing AI industry.

One of the actors opposing the rate hikes is Google, which announced in 2021 its intention to build a $735-million data centre in Beauharnois, Que. Google did not respond to a request for comment on Monday’s decision.

Jocelyn Allard, president of the Association of Industrial Electricity Users of Quebec, praised the judge’s ruling. The association acted as a third-party speaker in the case.

“It was our pretension that these decrees went further than the powers given to the government.… (The decision) couldn’t have been clearer,” he said.

The energy regulator should act independently, he said, adding that the provincial government already has the power to accept and refuse projects requiring more than five megawatts of power or to strike special contracts with individualized rates.

Allard said he hopes the newly elected Parti Québecois government will take the opportunity to clarify its energy plan and reaffirm the energy regulator’s independence.

“The new government could adopt a true road map to let us know where we’re heading,” he said.

Energy analyst Jean-Pierre Finet said he was not surprised by the decision.

“It’s not the first questionable decree that the government adopted,” he said.

Finet represents environmental groups in energy cases, including the one on rate hikes for data centres and cryptocurrency miners.

He sees the decrees as an example of the “politicization” of energy rates.

“That, I’m completely allergic to. Just remove the energy regulator if you want to just decide rates however you see fit,” said Finet.

While it struck down the decrees, Oral’s ruling also dismissed the argument by the data centre and cryptocurrency companies that the government acted in bad faith and to harm their industry.

“The evidence demonstrates that the contested decrees are consistent with the ongoing efforts by the government of Quebec to address the tightening of the province’s energy balance,” she wrote.

In drawing this nuance, the judge validated concerns motivating the rate hikes, said Allard.

paragraphs: Montreal - Hydro-Québec will continue seeking higher electricity rates for data centres and cryptocurrency miners despite a court decision striking down governmental decrees that supported the plan.

Hydro-Québec is asking the province’s energy regulator to approve a new rate averaging 13 cents per kilowatt hour for data centres requiring more than five megawatts of power, which is nearly double their current rate.
The utility is also asking to raise the rate for cryptocurrency mining projects to an average of 19.5 cents per kilowatt hour.

In early 2026, the provincial government published two decrees expressing support for both increases. The government previously amended a law on energy resources to allow the province to express economic, social and environmental concerns to the regulator, which must consider them in its decision.
But Quebec Superior Court Justice Élif Oral ruled on Monday that the government had overstepped with these two decrees.

While the government can express concerns to the regulator — the Régie de l’énergie — it can’t impose an outcome as it did by directly supporting Hydro-Québec’s proposal, the judge wrote in her decision.
“The interpretation of the word ‘concern’ as proposed by the (government and Hydro-Québec) is so broad that it distorts its ordinary, grammatical meaning,” wrote Oral.
The provincial government’s justice department declined to comment on the decision and its energy department did not immediately respond.

The legal challenge was filed by Keel Infrastructure, Hive Digital Technologies and Flumen Energy. The companies, which are data centre and/or cryptocurrency developers, have opposed the rate hike in front of the energy regulator. The law firm representing the companies declined to comment on the decision.
Hydro-Québec spokesperson Cendrix Bouchard said the utility acknowledges the court’s decision.
“Hydro-Québec remains convinced of the value of its rate proposal, which was developed with the goal of protecting all of its customers in Quebec,” Bouchard told The Canadian Press in a statement.

At the first part of the hearing on the proposed hikes in early October, analysts for the utility argued that increasing the rates would ensure the potential growth of the data centre industry would not lead to higher energy prices for other clients.
At the time, two consultants hired by Hydro-Québec said they expect the demand from data centres to more than double between 2024 and 2030 — mostly because of the growing AI industry.

One of the actors opposing the rate hikes is Google, which announced in 2021 its intention to build a $735-million data centre in Beauharnois, Que. Google did not respond to a request for comment on Monday’s decision.
Jocelyn Allard, president of the Association of Industrial Electricity Users of Quebec, praised the judge’s ruling. The association acted as a third-party speaker in the case.
“It was our pretension that these decrees went further than the powers given to the government.… (The decision) couldn’t have been clearer,” he said.

The energy regulator should act independently, he said, adding that the provincial government already has the power to accept and refuse projects requiring more than five megawatts of power or to strike special contracts with individualized rates.
Allard said he hopes the newly elected Parti Québecois government will take the opportunity to clarify its energy plan and reaffirm the energy regulator’s independence.
“The new government could adopt a true road map to let us know where we’re heading,” he said.
Energy analyst Jean-Pierre Finet said he was not surprised by the decision.
“It’s not the first questionable decree that the government adopted,” he said.
Finet represents environmental groups in energy cases, including the one on rate hikes for data centres and cryptocurrency miners.
He sees the decrees as an example of the “politicization” of energy rates.
“That, I’m completely allergic to. Just remove the energy regulator if you want to just decide rates however you see fit,” said Finet.
While it struck down the decrees, Oral’s ruling also dismissed the argument by the data centre and cryptocurrency companies that the government acted in bad faith and to harm their industry.
“The evidence demonstrates that the contested decrees are consistent with the ongoing efforts by the government of Quebec to address the tightening of the province’s energy balance,” she wrote.
In drawing this nuance, the judge validated concerns motivating the rate hikes, said Allard.
“These are not far-fetched considerations,” he said.
The energy regulator’s hearings on the proposed rate hikes are set to continue in December, at which time industry actors will present their perspective on Hydro-Québec’s proposal.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Maya Gebala released from hospital 262 days after Tumbler Ridge shooting
stories.summary: "262 days since we were told, “We did everything we could, but we don’t think she’s going to make it through the night'," David Gebala wrote on Thursday.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
Tumbler Ridge shooting victim Maya Gebala has been released from hospital.

In an update provided by her dad, David, he posted on X on Thursday morning that it has been 262 days since that fatal day in Tumbler Ridge.

“It’s been 262 days since you were airlifted to BC Children’s Hospital,” David wrote, adding “262 days since we were told, ‘We did everything we could, but we don’t think she’s going to make it through the night.'”

David said that since then he has watched his daughter fight for every single one of those days.

He said it was 251 days ago that Maya opened her eye, moved it and shifted her leg, only to be rushed into emergency surgery again for hydrocephalus.

It was 238 days ago when Maya was extubated and breathed on her own for the first time, David said, and 230 days when Maya was able to feel the sun on her face.

David chronicled the progress his daughter has made since she was shot inside Tumbler Ridge Secondary School on Feb. 10.

The small mining community of Tumbler Ridge was left reeling after the devastating mass shooting that killed eight people , as well as the shooter, and left dozens of others injured.

Maya and another victim, Paige Hoekstra, were airlifted to B.C. Children’s Hospital following the shooting.

David said it was 213 days ago that he wrapped his hands around Maya for the first time since the morning he left for work on Feb. 10.

He said 145 days ago, Maya intentionally smiled while they played thumb war and 140 days ago he wheeled Maya off hospital grounds for the very first time.

Forty days ago they celebrated Maya’s 13th birthday at the Foo Fighters concert.

“There was never a day I stopped believing we would get here,” David wrote.

“The road ahead is still long, but this is a milestone no one thought we would reach. Maya, you are the bravest person I know. You are an inspiration to so many people. Giving up was never an option for me, and it clearly never was for you either.”

David thanked the incredible nurses, doctors and therapists who helped their family reach this milestone.

“Now it’s time to leave these hospital walls behind and keep moving forward, Maya Bear,” David wrote.

“I love you forever and always.”

stories.title: Quebec education minister wants to ban schoolchildren from wearing religious symbols
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The president of the National Council of Canadian Muslims is accusing the Quebec government of attempting to take away the rights of children by expanding secularism laws.

“We’re talking about going after the rights of children to have a spirituality and go to school,” said Stephen Brown in an interview.

Quebec’s new education minister, Joël Arseneau, told journalists on Wednesday that he plans to ban schoolchildren from wearing religious symbols. He added that doing so is “non-negotiable.”

The Parti Québécois had promised the ban during the election campaign that resulted in a PQ minority government. In its platform, the party wrote that secularism “embodies the desire of the vast majority of Quebecers to live in a society where religion is practised in the private sphere.”

But Brown said the government is already breaking its promise to be the “the government of all Quebecers.”

“What we’re seeing now is anything but that,” said Brown. “It’s ridiculous and a missed opportunity.”

Brown said the government had pledged to reach out to communities and find balanced policy solutions to difficult questions like secularism. He believes that believes preventing children from wearing religious symbols is “blatant discrimination against religious minorities.”

He said the rules would mainly apply to those who wish to wear the kippa, hijab, crucifix and turban.

“We should not live in a country where politicians are able to literally trade away the rights of Canadian citizens in an election or political game,” said Brown. “The Charter rights of Canadian citizens have to be worth more than the paper they’re written on.”

Québec solidaire’s education and secularism critic, Roxane Milot, said the leftist party will vote against the proposed ban.

“Leave the kids alone! The priorities for the education system are clear: address the staff shortage, repair our schools, put an end to the three-tiered school system and reduce the dropout rate,” she said in a news release.

In the same release, Québec solidaire said it is concerning to see the new administration get bogged down by “identity-driven one-upmanship.”

It is unclear when the PQ government intends to table a bill to this effect, though the legislature is scheduled to resume sitting on Nov. 17.

The Quebec government has been strongly criticized for its law banning employees of the public sector, including teachers, from wearing religious symbols.

A legal challenge of that law, known as Bill 21, has made it to the Supreme Court of Canada. Lawyers argued it raised serious concerns involving several Charter rights, including freedom of expression, conscience and religion.

Those legal proceedings are ongoing.

Brown said he is prepared to mount a legal challenge if the PQ’s proposal becomes law.

Jean-Christophe Jasmin, the Quebec director of Christian think tank Cardus, also opposes expanding secularism laws.

In an interview, he said the government’s rationale to ban religious symbols worn by government employees was “presented in the name of freedom of conscience.” The previous Coalition Avenir Québec administration had argued that children are subject to an authority figure, and that that figure must be religiously neutral as to not impose their beliefs on their students.

“I don’t see how that logic applies to children today. Children do not represent the state, they are part of civil society,” said Jasmin. “There is no duty of neutrality on the part of children. The argument doesn’t hold up.”

Brown agreed, saying the scope of secularism laws banning religious symbols has continued to expand since the CAQ took power in 2018.

At first, the government targeted those in positions of authority. It was extended to teachers, daycare workers, all school staff and parents who volunteer in schools.

The CAQ then expanded the scope of the law to the public sphere by banning praying outside, in universities and at workplaces.

“And now of course, we’re going after the rights of children. So where does this end?” said Brown.

Frédéric Bérard, a constitutional lawyer who took part in the legal challenge against Bill 21, did not want to comment on Arseneau’s comments but said it was to be expected.

He pointed out that former premier François Legault had openly said in a 2019 radio interview with Radio-Canada that Bill 21 was a concession to “people who are a little racist and don’t want to see religious symbols anywhere in public.”

“It’s never enough,” said Bérard. “It’s a slippery slope.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: It’s scary out there. Live theatre is trying to make the most of it
stories.summary: In a time of great political and social unrest, the horror genre is picking up steam
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
It’s been a historic year for horror. Obsession and Backrooms are among the top 10 highest-grossing films of 2026, while Resident Evil , Scream 7 and Scary Movie are in the top 20. But this country’s renewed interest in the genre hasn’t stopped at the cinema: At live theatres across Canada, audiences are gobbling up all the scary stories they can get, and not just now, at the height of so-called spooky season.

Late last year, The Woman in Black , one of the West End’s longest-running shows, played Mirvish’s CAA Theatre; this summer, the stage version of Paranormal Activity ran down the street at the CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre to rave reviews and packed houses. Evil Dead , the bloody, cult favourite musical, is in full swing at cities across the country. And in January, a theatrical adaptation of Stephen King’s Misery will run at the Royal Manitoba Theatre Centre in Winnipeg before touring to rural communities in Manitoba and Ontario.

“We’re in a time of great political and social unrest, and as always happens in those moments, we’re seeing a renaissance in the genre,” said Eric Woolfe, artistic director of Eldritch Theatre (though he prefers to refer to himself as the company’s director of the uncanny).

Since 1999, Eldritch has specialized in ghoulish performances inspired by the likes of the Grand Guignol Theatre in Paris; most of its original works feature highly stylized puppets and costumes. Although attendance for Eldritch’s work at Toronto’s tiny Red Sandcastle Theatre creeps up around Halloween, the company produces eerie fare year-round.

“Every medium has its own set of conventions to make things work,” Woolfe explained, “and film works really well with the idea of control. We can control the frame, and where the viewer looks … In theatre, we can create those fears in people’s imagination. We don’t literally have to have a monster jump out of a box. We can force the audience to a place where they’re imagining it.” A puppet, he added, can encourage an audience to have a more emotional connection to the story at hand.

“Theatre is an outlet for our societal yearnings, for our values and our desires,” he continued. “When we’re scared, we like to be more scared. We like to share that fear with the people around us.”

Indeed, impactful horror stories have tended to cluster around societal instability. The films Dracula and Frankenstein came in 1931, in the depths of the Great Depression. Get Out , Jordan Peele’s psychological thriller about anti-Black racism in the U.S., landed in 2017, as the #BlackLivesMatter movement was crescendoing to the top of public discourse. Ari Aster’s 2019 Midsommar is largely regarded as an exploration of modern eco-fascism, an idea that’s only become more relevant in the age of climate change and water-guzzling data centres.

But by its very nature, live theatre offers a much more immediate sense of a given story’s stakes. (Troupes such as White Mills Theatre Company, best known for their site-specific Gothic work in Toronto, regularly take advantage of that haunted house-style intimacy.) Unlike in a film, a good horror play doesn’t just look and sound terrifying – it feels it, too.

That idea of experiencing horror live, and with a large group – not on a screen and not at home on the couch – is central to most of the blood-curdling plays that have cropped up across Canada in recent months. The Veil premiered in Crow’s Theatre’s studio space last September, and played a short run for Halloween at the Stratford Festival’s Meighen Forum this month. It’ll head to Calgary’s Vertigo Theatre in January.

The show hinges on proximity between its solo actor and the audience. In the play, written by Keith Barker and Thomas Morgan Jones, a buttoned-up lawyer inherits a curse which, try as he might, he just can’t shake.

In the show’s final moments, the audience, tasked with blowing out a real candle onstage, has to grapple with a choice: Should they break the cycle? Or save themselves from the terrors they’ve just seen unfold?

The first time The Veil played with a live audience was enlightening, said Jones. “People were laughing a lot,” he said. “People were audibly going, ‘Oh, no.’ A bunch of people put their hands on their faces. They were doing all of that just from the words being spoken onstage. These people were so invested in that character’s life and relationships that they had a physical reaction to it … people screamed. The fact that that could happen in a theatre felt really special.”

But what made The Veil stand out in its premiere – and what’s kept it popular enough to tour – isn’t just its intimacy. The play incorporates most of the senses, including smell, in its storytelling. Its sound design features naturalistic noises that lure the audience into a false sense of security that’s then abruptly shattered; visually, there’s far more to its spring-loaded set than meets the eye.

“There’s a huge appetite for that sort of adrenalin and excitement,” said Barker, also the Stratford Festival’s director of new plays, about The Veil ’s sensorial tricks. “I feel like theatre is uniquely positioned to give an experience that can scare the pants off people.”

Vertigo Theatre, where The Veil will play in 2027, just closed its production of The Lodger , a Canadian adaptation of Alfred Hitchcock’s 1927 silent thriller by Susie Moloney and Vern Thiessen. Not unlike Eldritch – though at a much larger scale – the company specializes in genre plays, including horror. (The company even has a specialty kitchen for mixing fake blood.)

Scary stories are a “blueprint for bad times,” mused Moloney. “People need to engage with something to purge their own fears. Fear is an extraordinary opportunity for people to come out and share that jump scare together,” she continued.

What are those fears? Take your pick, said Vertigo’s artistic director Jack Grinhaus. “People are scared of the economy. They’re scared of politics,” he explained. “I think people are feeling really destabilized, and horror is a great way to check the barometer of a society, and to feel connected.”

“Horror has always played that role, particularly for the vulnerable,” said Moloney. “The world is on fire right now. It’s a scary place to be. Watching somebody go through hell and come out the other end, I think, is soothing.”

stories.title: Kenora, Ont., fined for removing election signs during 2025 federal race
stories.summary: Kenora - Kenora, Ont., is facing a $1,000 fine from the Commissioner of Canada Elections after the office said city bylaw officers removed election signs while candidates were still campaigning during the 2025 federal race.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Kenora - Kenora, Ont., is facing a $1,000 fine from the Commissioner of Canada Elections after the office said city bylaw officers removed election signs while candidates were still campaigning during the 2025 federal race.

The office of the commissioner says it confirmed 102 election signs were removed by the City of Kenora without providing notice to the campaigns.

stories.title: Woman charged in connection with fake 911 reports
stories.summary: A woman has been charged in connection with fake 911 reports in Hanover.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A woman has been charged in connection with fake 911 reports in Hanover.

On Oct. 20 just after 2 p.m., police responded to an emergency call near 10th Avenue and 10th Street, which a woman allegedly reported gunshots were fired, and she was struck by a stray bullet.

The Hanover police arrived on scene and found the woman who said she needed an ambulance. Officers investigated and determined there was no evidence of a shooting, any injuries, or an emergency.

The woman has been charged with public mischief, failure to comply with a release order, and two counts of failure to comply with a probation order.

Police are now reminding the public that making false reports is a serious offence and takes away resources from those who need immediate help.

stories.title: Ottawa to invest up to $1.6B in Canadian AI firm Cohere
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.

He made the announcement in Montreal as he welcomed European Union leaders to a summit aimed at forging closer ties.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know or by whom we don’t trust. We’re building it right here in the right way,” Carney said.

In April, Cohere announced it would merge with Germany’s Aleph Alpha and said the company would be “anchored in” Germany and Canada.

On Thursday, Carney called the partnership a concrete example of what Canada and Europe can build together.

He also said that, under the agreement, Cohere will stay Canadian.

Carney said the government is making the announcement on “a commercial basis, alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell, and Germany’s Schwarz Group.”

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said at the announcement that the company, which was founded seven years ago, is now “one of the very few companies in the world building frontier AI technology at a global scale.”

He added that it’s the largest AI company outside the U.S. and China.

In a press release issued Thursday, the government said the funding would be provided in stages, with regular reporting on commitments made by the company.

Those commitments include creating at least 1,000 “new high-paying Canadian technical jobs” and committing at least $1.7 billion to building more computing infrastructure by 2030.

The government says Cohere will also maintain its Canadian headquarters and incorporation, invest in research partnerships, create opportunities for students and graduates and continue working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute.

“Cohere will now be able to develop far more advanced models and products, scale up its computing infrastructure, and expand its Canadian workforce to serve more businesses and governments in Canada and around the world,” the press release said.

“Building this capability at home ultimately means that Canadian businesses and governments will have more choice in how they adopt AI and greater control over their sensitive information.”

In 2024, the government announced it would provide up to $240 million to Cohere to boost its computing capacity. In 2025, Ottawa signed an agreement with the company to identify areas where AI can enhance public service operations.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon has often pointed to Cohere as an element of Canada’s strength in AI, saying Canada is one of only a few countries around the world with a large language model.

stories.title: European Commission head revives 'associate membership' for Canada on eve of meeting
stories.summary: Von der Leyen extolled the current partnership between allies while calling for even more integration with Canada.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Montreal — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday the EU and Canada can work together on “everything” as she renewed her call for the country to join the bloc as an “associate member.”

In a speech right before the start of a two-day Canada-European Union meeting in Montreal, von der Leyen extolled the current partnership between allies while calling for even more integration with Canada.

She notably began her speech reiterating her call for Canada to become the first ever “associate member” of the EU, pushing for “association without accession”.

Her doubling down on associate membership for Canada raised eyebrows because the term has become controversial in Europe, with some countries — notably Germany and half-dozen other countries — dismissing such a move.

A reference for “associate member” for Canada was removed from a draft joint statement between Canada and the EU circulated Wednesday ahead of the summit.

Instead, the Oct. 28 draft document (which could still be changed) referred to an “ever-closer association” between the EU and Canada that will be fully defined by next year’s bilateral summit.

Thursday, von der Leyen told attendees of a C.D. Howe Institute event that Canada and the EU “can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we’ve done before.”

She summarized associate membership as better alignment on policies like AI, climate, energy and security, shared governance work between both parliaments and courts, and more integration in certain EU ventures like student-mobility program Erasmus+ or its supercomputing infrastructure for AI.

“We are once again called upon to work on new frontiers together, because the current moment in history calls for it. We are witnessing a deeper decay in international order,” she said. “We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old world order.”

At a separate press conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed concerns about the nomenclature used to describe the new budding relationship between Canada and the EU.

“This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter. What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty,” he said.

In the past, he has emphasized a joint interest in developing AI and data-storage solutions outside of the U.S. and China as well as joint ventures in space technology and telecommunications.

Carney has repeatedly pointed to Elon Musk’s satellite telecommunications company Starlink as a technology he wants Canada to move away from.

Carney, von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday are expected to sign a final joint statement at the end of their trilateral summit on Friday.

According to the Oct. 28 draft statement viewed by National Post, Canada and the EU have concluded “substantive negotiations” on a new Digital Trade Agreement (DTA) that will supplement the existing free-trade deal between Canada and the EU. The DTA “will improve legal certainty and predictability, facilitate cross-border data flows, and enhance confidence in the digital economy for businesses and consumers.”

During a background briefing with reporters, senior European officials explained that the deal would harmonize rules on digital commerce and specifics like e-contracts and duties on electronic transmissions.

The Oct. 28 document also promises to look into faster money transfer solutions between Europe and Canada.

“We will also support work toward connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, lower cost and more seamless cross-border transactions, making it easier for Canadians and Europeans to conduct business, invest and transfer funds across the two economies.”

stories.title: A timeline of key events in the Regis Korchinski-Paquet case
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A coroner’s inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet has been adjourned until further notice after the presiding coroner said Thursday that an “unanticipated investigation” was required.

The 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020 : The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident. In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.

May 30, 2020 : Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.

June 3, 2020 : The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.

June 8, 2020 : Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.

June 10, 2020 : Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.

June 11, 2020 : The family holds a small funeral for her.

June 29, 2020 : Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.

July 25, 2020 : Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020 : The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

Feb. 3, 2021 : Toronto announces a pilot project to send crisis-support workers instead of police to certain 911 calls in the city. The pilot, set to begin the following year, comes after widespread calls for police reform, including improvements to how police deal with those experiencing mental-health crises.

May 26, 2021 : A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. The Oiprd confirms it is investigating but declines to comment further, citing confidentiality.

June 19, 2021 : Korchinski-Paquet’s relatives speak at Juneteenth event in Ottawa aimed at demanding accountability and changes to the justice system. Several Black and Indigenous families whose loved ones were harmed or killed by police also attend the event organized by Black Lives Matter Toronto.

The 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.
Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020 : The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident. In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.
May 30, 2020 : Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.
June 3, 2020 : The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.
June 8, 2020 : Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.
June 10, 2020 : Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.
June 11, 2020 : The family holds a small funeral for her.

June 29, 2020 : Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.
July 25, 2020 : Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020 : The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

May 26, 2021 : A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. stories.title: Churchill River energy agreement with Quebec not open for renegotiation, says N.L.
stories.summary: ST. John's - Newfoundland and Labrador's premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Newfoundland and Labrador’s premier says an agreement with Quebec to develop energy in Labrador is not open for renegotiation.

Tony Wakeham said Wednesday that the Newfoundland and Labrador government had already voted in favour of the non-binding agreement, which he unveiled in August alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney and former Quebec premier Christine Fréchette in St. John’s, N.L.

“Let me be clear: we will not be renegotiating the deal, and will not entertain an attempt by anyone else wishing to renegotiate the deal,” he said.

He made the remarks as reporters pressed him about whether final agreements would be signed before they were debated in the legislature. But there is also a new Parti Québécois government in Quebec that could ask for changes to the multibillion-dollar agreement.

Wakeham said he has not heard any rumblings about Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wanting changes.

“I think what I’m trying to do is just outline our position,” Wakeham told reporters in St. John’s.

The proposal — which the government has called a definitive co-operation and implementation agreement — lays out plans for Hydro-Québec and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro to expand the hydroelectric capacity of the Churchill River, which cuts through traditional Innu territory.

Carney has touted the proposal as “the largest clean energy investment in North American history” and his government has promised $10 billion in financing to help it along.

In a Facebook post Wednesday, the grand chief of the Innu Nation in Labrador said Innu were not included in the energy negotiations despite the agreement proposing projects on Innu land. Jodie Ashini pointed to a social media post by Carney saying he met with Wakeham recently in Ottawa, and a public statement from Wakeham pledging to “keep engaging respectfully with the Innu Nation.”

“How is meeting with the prime minister and discussing our lands and not having us at the table respectful?” she wrote. “There is no respect from the (Newfoundland and Labrador) government right now to the Innu.”

“Come to Sheshatshiu and speak with us,” she added, referring to an Innu community in central Labrador where the Innu Nation has its main office.

Ashini has accused Wakeham and his government of interfering with a cultural exhibit detailing Innu history in Labrador. She says the government believes Innu arrived about 300 years ago, after the Europeans. The position erases thousands of years of Innu history, she has said.

On Wednesday, Wakeham said he would table all final energy agreements in the legislature and propose a special debate about them. He would not answer directly when reporters asked if those agreements would already be signed, but he was clear they would not be open for changes.

The Parti Québécois did not immediately respond to a request for comment. St-Pierre Plamondon and his cabinet were sworn in last week, and Wakeham has not yet met with the new premier in person.

“It’s coming,” Wakeham said. “He wants to come to Newfoundland and Labrador for a meeting. He indicated that to me in our last conversation, and I’m looking forward to that.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Loss of Hockey Night in Canada a major blow to tradition, say majority of fans: poll
stories.summary: Nine-in-10 Angus Reid Institute survey respondents say hockey is an important or defining part of Canadian identity.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Just shy of three-quarters of Canadian hockey fans say the end of Hockey Night in Canada is a major loss for Canadian hockey and its traditions, according to a new Angus Reid Institute survey.

Polling found 74 per cent of Canadians who follow the NHL view the end of the traditional Saturday-night broadcast as a significant loss, following a 74-year run on CBC. The sentiment was strongest in Atlantic Canada, where 83 per cent say the loss is significant.

Just seven per cent see the change as a positive development, while another 12 per cent say they are disappointed but do not consider it a major loss.

Despite the changes, hockey remains deeply rooted in Canada’s national identity. Nine-in-10 (90 per cent) say hockey is an important or defining part of Canadian identity, up slightly from the 88 per cent found in 2015 polling.

The CBC’s Saturday-night broadcasts have long been a fixture for generations of Canadian viewers. Beginning Dec. 5, the national public broadcaster will instead use the Hockey Night brand to air eight Professional Women’s Hockey (Pwhl) games on Saturday nights.

The poll suggests there is uncertainty about how many Canadians will watch, however. Only one in five (20 per cent), say they are likely to watch a Pwhl game this season, while 69 per cent probably or definitely won’t.

That said, there is broad public support for women’s sports receiving increased visibility. Nearly two-thirds of respondents (64 per cent) say women’s pro sports deserve more Canadian television coverage. Still, among those who support more coverage, only 30 per cent say they’re likely to tune in.

The survey also points to widespread dissatisfaction with the growing reliance on streaming subscriptions to get their sports fix.

Among Canadians who follow the NHL, despite more overall games being available, 78 per cent say it’s bad that additional subscriptions are required. Only 10 per cent viewed more availability as a good thing.

Across the country, 70 per cent of Canadians say professional sports are spread across too many channels and platforms. Just six per cent disagreed and 23 per cent were unsure.

Subscription costs are another irritant for respondents.

Among subscribers to individual services, 63 per cent of those paying for Sportsnet+ say the monthly price is too much. That figure rises to 71 per cent for those on Dazn and 52 per cent for TSN+ users.

Amazon Prime Video, “which comes with the attached benefit of Prime delivery services,” is viewed more favourably on price, with 54 per cent of subscribers saying its cost is about right.

After the NHL and Rogers Sports & Media agreed to a 12-year, CA$11 billion broadcast extension last April to keep Sportsnet home for hockey in Canada until the end of the 2037-38 season, Amazon and Rogers signed a 12-year sub-license broadcasting this off-season, granting the streamer exclusive rights to Wednesday night broadcasts in both official languages on Prime Video. It replaces Amazon’s Prime Monday Night Hockey that ran for two years, but only in English.

The Monday night games now belong to Sportsnet, but are only available through its Sportsnet+ package. The upgrade is free for Rogers television subscribers, $12.99 monthly for other television service subscribers and $34.99 for those without.

For the most dedicated fan, the total cost can be especially challenging. Among Angus Reid survey respondents who follow the NHL very closely or just closely, 79 and 77 per cent, respectively, say it has become too expensive to follow their favourite teams. Even 63 per cent who don’t follow very closely say it’s getting too costly.

The online survey of 1,806 Canadian adults was conducted Oct. 19-22. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is plus/minus two percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
