Wednesday, October 28, 2026

As winter approaches, the City of London is getting streets ready for snow and ice. Some seasonal traffic-calming measures and bike lane bollards may be removed to create room for winter maintenance equipment to operate.
In the coming weeks, residents may see some signs, bollards and other temporary traffic-calming measures removed. These changes help crews clear snow and keep streets safe during the winter.
Seasonal traffic-calming measures will be put back in the spring, where needed.
Drivers are reminded to slow down, adjust their speed for road and weather conditions, and watch for people walking and cycling. Take extra care near schools, intersections and pedestrian crossings.
The City continues to work toward safer streets for everyone through street design, traffic calming and road safety education.

stories.title: Nearly $6-million raised towards $50-million goal to renovate 24 Sussex Drive
stories.summary: Funds raised as a result of donations from more than 4,000 Canadians, Rideau Hall Foundation CEO says
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
The effort to raise $50-million in donations to renovate the prime ministerial residence at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa has hit $5.7-million, according to new figures released by the Rideau Hall Foundation.

Although the newly released figure is only about 11 per cent of the goal, foundation president and chief executive officer Teresa Marques said she is pleased with the total, a result of donations from more than 4,000 Canadians.

“We’re very encouraged by the strong momentum behind this campaign and the support we’re seeing from Canadians across the country,” Ms. Marques said in a statement released on Tuesday.

“A $50 million goal is ambitious, but we believe it is achievable,” she said. “We’re confident in the opportunity before us and focused on building the support needed to reach our goal as quickly and efficiently as possible.”

The foundation is a nonpartisan, national charitable organization created to amplify the work of the Governor-General.

The target was set in June when Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a plan to renovate and reopen the residence, which was home to nine prime ministers from 1951 to 2015.

The physical decline of the property, initially built as a private home and first occupied in 1868, prevented prime minister Justin Trudeau from moving in with his family after he was elected in 2015.

Successive prime minsters took no steps to renovate the house, concerned about potential public opposition to providing a luxurious home for Canada’s leaders.

Mr. Trudeau moved into Rideau Cottage on the grounds of Rideau Hall, the residence and workplace of the Governor-General. He lived there through his time as prime minister. Mr. Carney moved into the cottage when he became prime minister in 2025.

The National Capital Commission, which manages official residences in the Ottawa region, cleared out 24 Sussex in 2023, removing its furnishings and finishes as it awaited a decision from the federal government on how to proceed.

Mr. Carney’s 24 Sussex plan has been the foundation for raising money from the public to cover the costs of the renovation. His government will cover security costs.

Firms interested in handling the renovation are being invited to submit their ideas to a competition that is being managed by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada.

The ideas will be judged by an institute committee led by acclaimed architect Moshe Safdie, the founding principal of Safdie Architects, who is a citizen of Canada, Israel and the United States. A winning plan is to be announced by Canada Day of 2027.

Also on Tuesday, the foundation announced the launch of the Council for 24 Sussex to help mobilize support for the fundraising appeal.

Inaugural council members listed Tuesday include acclaimed gardener Mark Cullen, former University of Toronto president Robert Prichard and Ed Clark, the former president of Canada Trust and former president of Toronto-Dominion Bank.

B.C. members include Roger Hardy, the co-founder and chief executive officer of Kits Eyecare, as well as John Montalbano, the former CEO of RBC Global Asset Management and a member of the foundation board.

Albertans on the council include Deanna Zumwalt, founder and chair of the Calgary Wild Women’s Football Club, and former University of Alberta chancellor Joanne Cuthbertson.

Aldéa Landry, a former New Brunswick deputy premier, is also on the council, as are Quebecers Anne-Marie Hubert, a foundation board member and chair of the Montreal Council on Foreign Relations, and Quebec businessman Evan Price.

stories.title: Expert explainer: Why sugar at Halloween shouldn’t be scary
stories.summary: Dietitian Danielle Battram explains the role sugar plays in our body and how to help children develop a healthy relationship with it.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
As Halloween nears, so does the amount of candy and chocolate on supermarket shelves. Sugary treats May be a big part of the spookiest night of the year, but figuring out how to navigate sweets, for ourselves and children, doesn’t need to be scary.

Danielle Battram – professor, dietitian and director of the Brescia School of Food and Nutritional Sciences in the Faculty of Health Sciences – dispels myths about sugar, breaks down the role it plays in the body and offers advice to help children foster a healthy relationship with food.

Danielle Battram (DB): Our whole body is designed to use sugar, or glucose, as fuel. And while we have the capacity to use other fuels, our cells often prefer glucose to other sources.

When glucose levels start to drop in our blood, our brain tells us to, ‘eat please, I need more fuel.’ So, when we eat, we satisfy this very basic and primitive need, and it feels rewarding.

DB: Like all food, sugar goes through a digestive process. As sugar is absorbed by your gut, blood glucose levels begin to rise, and the pancreas secrets insulin in response. Insulin is a hormone that acts like a key, allowing the glucose to enter your cells.

Once this happens, our brain receives a signal to decrease appetite; we have given our cells what they need, and now the body tells us we have satisfied that desire for fuel. When those blood sugar levels come back down, the signal to eat increases again, and the process repeats.

DB: The foods and beverages you consume, as well as how you eat and drink, will determine the rate at which your blood sugar rises and falls.

We’ve all had those days when we eat lunch, get busy throughout the day, and by the time we get home we’re feeling ravenous because our blood sugar has dropped. This can also happen when we consume a lot of sugar, particularly in beverage form. The body absorbs all that sugar quickly, leading to a swift drop in blood sugars resulting in what is often described as a ‘crash.’

To avoid this potential crash, eat regularly and consume foods that help keep your blood sugars stable; we don’t want these big hills and valleys of glucose in our blood, we want a steady supply throughout the day. For example, eating an apple is better than drinking apple juice because the sugar is absorbed more slowly, helping blood glucose levels rise gradually and stay stable for longer. These strategies help us fill satiated longer and helps control our appetite – often leading to better food choices.

DB:No. There have been a lot of studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses which all suggest that children do not get hyperactive from sugar itself.

Think about when kids usually have candy or sweets – often around an exciting event! Whether it’s a birthday party, Halloween or a sleepover, there’s a lot of excitement from the event itself. They’re in a stimulating environment, which leads us to wrongfully equate hyperactivity with sugar. If they’re hyper, it’s because they’re happy to be in the given environment.

Kids can certainly also experience a ‘crash’ if they don’t stay fueled properly like adults. So it’s important that we regulate their blood sugar by having them eat consistently and choosing nutritious foods as often as possible.

DB: No. A glucose molecule is a glucose molecule. When your body consumes glucose from a candy compared to an apple, it doesn’t know which one is which, it only recognizes the glucose. The difference is in how our blood glucose rises. It takes more time to digest and absorb the glucose in an apple than a piece of candy: that’s the difference. The fibre in the apple slows down the absorption of the sugar. It’s got nothing to do with where the molecule is coming from.

But there are other reasons to opt for the apple, too. We want people to choose the fruit because you’re getting a lot of nutrition, such as vitamins, minerals and fibre, at the same time as glucose or fuel. One concern we have as dietitians is that if you’re consuming a lot of excess sugar, you’re getting fuel, but not nutrients – that can lead to deficiencies.

We also want to make sure kids are consuming all the fruits, vegetables, protein and fibre they need in addition to glucose, because their brains and bodies are constantly developing, and they need all this nutrition to be healthy and grow.

DB: We’ve got to remember it’s the totality of what we do that determines our health. Our health is a marathon, not a sprint. Are we going to do significant damage to our children because they go out on Halloween and eat more candy for a week? Probably not. Candy is a part of Halloween, which is also associated with dressing up, running outside in the dark, being with your friends and family and an opportunity to engage with members of our community – all of which we want kids to experience.

As a parent, there are constraints you can place on Halloween and the candy they consume after the night is over, but Halloween is a short-term event. It’s what we do every day that matters. Making sure our kids have the foods they need for growth and development, helping them set healthy habits and ultimately having them enjoy a once-a-year activity with friends and family – that’s going to be more meaningful in the long run.

DB:Growing up, candy was never made a big deal in our house. When we had family nights, sometimes our movie snack would be candy, other times it would be carrot sticks and dip. Candy was just one of the many foods we ate.

We don’t want to set up a dynamic of sweets as a reward or something ‘special’, since too much restriction can actually enhance its appeal. Sweets are part of our food system, and yes, they taste good. If we can set an example of eating well, balancing foods and introducing sugar in a reasonable way, kids will be set up for success.

DB:Present a lot of different food options; you want to create variety. Keep introducing them to new foods, including a bit of everything in your family’s meals. Not setting up the war between what we would consider to be healthy, nutritious food and ‘treats’ will also go a long way.

We can also get children to participate in the food process. Data shows the more you get children involved in preparing meals, and teach them about the food system, the more likely they are to try new foods. It gives a sense of agency and ownership in the process. Some of my favorite moments in research have come from working with children in the kitchen – they are socializing and learning, without even realizing it.

Feeding kids can be challenging, but if we try to take the power struggle and stress out of it, while making it an engaging activity, it can make eating and mealtimes a more enjoyable experience.

DB: I’m still astounded at how much misinformation there is about sugar, and the fear messaging that suggests added sugar is as potent as a drug. There can be a lot of guilt over enjoying it, and that’s not what we want. Eating is supposed to provide us with the nutrients and fuel we need to live a good life, and allow us to do all the things we want to do.

As a dietitian, my role is to support people in cultivating an enjoyable and healthy relationship with food that supports all their needs. It means helping each person find what works for them, and making room for the foods they want to enjoy – including sugar.

We don’t need to fear sugar, we just need to be mindful of it. This Halloween, let’s lean into the excitement, and leave the fear for ghouls and zombies.

stories.title: Lumby to hold mayoral byelection after two back-to-back elections
stories.summary: Kevin Acton had previously said he would accept the provincial seat if he won both races and step down as mayor.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Kevin Acton is no stranger to election victories, but winning two elections just one week apart is a first for the longtime Lumby mayor.

Acton won re-election as mayor in the municipal election on October 17 before securing a provincial seat as the Conservative MLA for Vernon-Lumby on October 24.

He says he had planned to run provincially but expected the opportunity to come much later.

“All along, the plan was to run provincially if I got the nod from the party,” Acton said. “We just expected it to be two years from now, not a week after the election.”

Acton had previously said he would accept the provincial seat if he won both races and step down as mayor.

He said his decision was driven in part by a desire to improve the relationship between local and provincial governments.

“I absolutely love the job, love the community,” Acton said. “But there’s been some frustrations in dealing with provincial government that I think I can really help direct the province towards mending.”

He also pointed to what he described as ongoing tension between the province and local governments.

Acton’s departure means Lumby residents will soon be heading back to the polls for a third time to choose their mayor in a byelection.

“Sort of, but you’ve got to do what you’ve got to do,” resident Ann Verhage said when asked whether she was experiencing election fatigue.

Another resident, Paul Gilfillan, said he was not particularly concerned about another trip to the polls, while Irene Yaremcio joked that she was getting tired of voting and hoped it would be the last time.

The byelection is not expected to take place until the new year.

“We would be looking at the end of January, early February as a voting day,” said Bobbe Koenig, the village’s chief financial officer and acting administrative officer.

It means Lumby will go several months without an elected mayor.

“Once Kevin moved on to that MLA seat, we would have an acting mayor system similar to when he goes on vacation, ” Koenig said. “So the councillors that were in place would step on up on a rotating schedule that’s already established.”

Koenig estimates the byelection will cost between $5,000 and $10,000.

Acton has pledged to cover the cost personally, saying he does not want the expense to fall on Lumby taxpayers.

“It was the situation I was put in,” Acton said. “So I joke around sometimes and think that maybe David Eby should pay for half of it as well but I don’t think that’s going to happen. But no, I don’t want to put that responsibility on the taxpayer of Lumby.”

Acton is expected to be sworn in as the Conservative MLA for Vernon-Lumby in mid-November, formally beginning his transition from municipal politics to the provincial legislature.

I feel really excited about the final, the way it all worked out in the end,” Acton said. “I’m really excited to get to work.”

“We would be looking at the end of January, early February as a voting day,” said Bobbe Koenig, the village’s chief financial officer and acting administrative officer.
It means Lumby will go several months without an elected mayor.

“Once Kevin moved on to that MLA seat, we would have an acting mayor system similar to when he goes on vacation, ” Koenig said. “So the councillors that were in place would step on up on a rotating schedule that’s already established.”
Koenig estimates the byelection will cost between $5,000 and $10,000.
Acton has pledged to cover the cost personally, saying he does not want the expense to fall on Lumby taxpayers.

“It was the situation I was put in,” Acton said. “So I joke around sometimes and think that maybe David Eby should pay for half of it as well but I don’t think that’s going to happen. But no, I don’t want to put that responsibility on the taxpayer of Lumby.”
Acton is expected to be sworn in as the Conservative MLA for Vernon-Lumby in mid-November, formally beginning his transition from municipal politics to the provincial legislature.
I feel really excited about the final, the way it all worked out in the end,” Acton said. “I’m really excited to get to work.”

stories.title: Alberta Premier fends off leadership challenge and looks to squelch separatist discord
stories.summary: Candidates wanting to run for party board positions must declare that they’ll respect the provincial vote against holding an independence referendum
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith appears to have fended off a leadership challenge and is looking to smother discord within her United Conservative Party by requiring those seeking a seat on its provincial board to pledge they will respect the province’s majority vote against holding a separation referendum .

In an e-mail sent to UCP members on Tuesday evening, party president Rob Smith said at least 65 of the 87 constituency associations have passed motions in support of the Premier, whose authority has been questioned by pockets of the party’s membership following last week’s referendum and ahead of next year’s provincial election. At least 22 associations would need to vote in favour of a leadership review in order to force one.

“There will be NO UCP leadership review before our next general election,” wrote Mr. Smith, who holds no relation to the Premier. He added that Ms. Smith will be the leader for the foreseeable future.

With the possibility of a leadership review set aside, Ms. Smith confirmed the UCP is now requiring those wishing to serve on its 18-seat provincial board to pledge that they will respect the result of last week’s referendum on separation.

The requirement is contained in a mandatory declaration form that candidates applying to run for the party board must complete ahead of the Ucp’s annual general meeting in late November.

The declaration asks candidates to agree they “recognize, respect, and will abide by the majority decision made by Albertans on Question #10 of the 26/10/19 referendum,” referring to the ballot question that asked residents whether they wish to remain in Canada or have a second, binding secession vote.

The pledge is the first evidence that Ms. Smith and the UCP are taking steps to prevent separatist agitators from attempting to control the party apparatus.

Factions within the independence movement have threatened to take over the party’s governance structures in the wake of the Oct. 19 vote, in which roughly 75 per cent of Albertans rejected the prospect of a future independence referendum.

Ms. Smith has asked members to accept the result, warning that an internal civil war over separation would sink the party ahead of next year’s provincial election. Those wishing to turn the party into a vehicle for separation would not have a home in the UCP, she said.

She had been unclear, however, about what measures she was willing to take to snuff out the separatist fire.

Asked on Tuesday at an unrelated news conference about the new declaration requirement for board candidates, Ms. Smith said: “If you’re going to be a member of our party, you have to accept what Albertans told us.”

Some separatist leaders have angled to take control of the party board at the UCP AGM beginning Nov. 27 in Calgary, where certain positions will be up for grabs. Ms. Smith recently said the party had sold roughly 6,900 tickets to its AGM, which would break the party’s attendance record when nearly 6,100 party members showed up in Red Deer two years ago to reassert the Premier’s leadership.

The latest bid to defy her call for party unity and challenge her leadership happened on Monday night, when the Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul UCP constituency association in northern Alberta narrowly voted in favour of a leadership review. It was the fourth association to do so in the past two months.

Prominent separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre, who’s been vocal about his bid to stack the UCP board with pro-independence allies, is the association’s president.

The upcoming AGM and board elections are now the more pressing issues for Ms. Smith as advocates like Mr. Sylvestre push for like-minded members to vote for pro-independence candidates.

Ms. Smith reiterated her position that promoting separation is an incompatible position for those who speak on behalf of the UCP.

“If anyone wants to advocate for independence, we are not an independence party. That’s contrary to what Albertans told us,” she said.

“There’s lots of range for people to be able to advocate on policy, but just not that.”

Even so, people who emerged as prominent independence advocates are applying for board seats, indicating they support the Premier’s direction.

Chris Scott, a cafe owner in Mirror, Alta. , spent the summer roving the province in a camper van holding town halls on independence. He is applying to run for a board seat as the Ucp’s Central Alberta director and agrees with the pledge

“I have no problem doing that,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Scott said that while he still believes independence is “the only way to achieve the sovereignty Alberta needs,” the referendum result was decisive. For now, he said he’s content pursuing provincial autonomy within Canada, mirroring Ms. Smith’s pursuit of finding ways Alberta can wrest greater control over its affairs.

“This is an opportunity where both sides can set the nationhood thing aside for now and focus on the sovereignty things that we should be doing if we’re ever to prepare to be a nation anyhow,” Mr. Scott said.

Jason Lavigne, a podcaster who promoted the pro-independence camp during the referendum, also said he was pleased to sign the pledge. He’s putting his name forward to run for a board seat as vice-president of policy and governance.

“I was probably one of the first to respond in the affirmative,” he said.

Mr. Lavigne said pockets of the UCP membership have viewed the pledge as a “purity test or a gag order.”

He views it differently.

“What the party is asking for is, ON a policy and governance level, to head in the same direction, which is to respect the will of Albertans.”

With a report from Carrie Tait

stories.title: Tight mayoral race improved voter turnout: expert
stories.summary: Just over 30 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot in London's municipal election, up from 25 per cent tur...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
Just over 30 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot in London’s municipal election, up from 25 per cent turnout in 2022.

A political scientist said the slight jump in voter turnout could be attributed to a tighter mayoral race which ended Tuesday with incumbant Josh Morgan back in the mayor’s seat.

“Primarily, one of the reasons we had more turnout this year is due to more opposition from (Morgan’s closest rival candidate) Susan Stevenson,” said Martin Horak, an associate professor of political science at Western University. “Whenever we have competitive races like that it tends to drive more people to the polls.”

While municipal elections often fly under the radar as candidates talk about similar issues, Stevenson changed things up this year, basing her campaign on different ways to tackle some of the issues that have been a challenge for Morgan.

But even still, 31 per cent does not indicate a high level of engagement.

“Voting tends to be lower at the municipal level, partly because local politics get less media attention,” said Horak.

As London sees continued growth, voter turnout becomes a more prevalent issue. One of the aspects suggested as to bringing a low turnout is echo chambers online, lowering the public’s trust in government operations as a whole.

“The social media atmosphere we have now has a lot of negative and extreme views and tends to push voters away,” said Horak.

“Without the shorthand of political parties that stand one side or the other, it makes it difficult for voters to choose, as far as who stands for what causes.” stated Horak.

Susan Stevenson came second with 26 per cent of vote, holds a platform that frequently contends with Morgan’s.

This recent election has seen 11 incumbents and 4 new ward members.

New ward members include Ben Durham (Ward 3), Tom Cull (Ward 4), Johnathan Sher (Ward 7), and Jason King (Ward 14).

Voting sign outside of Stronach Arena (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

stories.title: Privacy commissioner opens investigation into Crime Stoppers data breach
stories.summary: Canada’s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into a reportedly massive Crime Stoppers data breach as police departments across the country have paused accepting tips through the platform.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into a reportedly massive Crime Stoppers data breach as police departments across the country have paused accepting tips through the platform.

The office of privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne says the probe will look into the cybersecurity incident involving Navigate360, the third-party company that manages the platform used by Crime Stoppers.

The investigation comes after CBC reported that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed when Navigate360 was hacked in March.

The U.S.-based company confirmed the breach last week, saying it immediately opened its own investigation, took “mitigation measures” and “implemented additional and enhanced safeguards” with the support of another cybersecurity firm after the discovery.

Police forces across Ontario, including several in the Greater Toronto Area, temporarily paused directing public calls to Crime Stoppers following the revelation.

Beyond Ontario, at least two police departments in Manitoba, including Winnipeg, have said that they would stop taking tips through the program as they review and assess the incident.

Saskatchewan Crime Stoppers told the public over the weekend to avoid sending tips through its platform.

“The pause is temporary. We will begin accepting new tips as soon as we are confident it is safe to do so,” it said in a statement.

The privacy commissioner’s office said it has reached out to Crime Stoppers programs to offer “expertise and guidance” in response to the breach.

“The investigation will examine the security safeguards that Navigate360 had in place at the time of the breach to determine the organization’s compliance with Canada’s federal private-sector privacy law,” it said in a statement Tuesday.

The watchdog also said it has contacted Navigate360, though it didn’t say whether the company has responded.

It said its engagement “with both organizations is focused on ensuring that the necessary steps are being taken to address the breach and protect Canadians’ personal information.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Regina dismantles Core Community Park encampment over fire safety concerns
stories.summary: Residents were not given notice that the site would be decommissioned, leaving some arriving at the park to discover their tents and belongings were gone.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Hannah Sangster
stories.content:
The City of Regina has dismantled an encampment at Core Community Park, also known as Pepsi Park, with fire officials citing an increased safety risk following a number of fires in recent days.

Police and fire crews cleared the encampment as streets surrounding the park were closed. City officials began erecting a fence around the property, while police placed tape reading “Do Not Cross” around tents.

About 150 people had been living at the encampment over the past three and a half months. Residents were not given notice that the site would be decommissioned, leaving some arriving at the park to discover their tents and belongings were gone.

Natalie, a former encampment resident whose last name was not provided, said she did not know the site was being cleared.

“My tent is gone. I didn’t even know this was happening at all,” she said.

The move also caught community organizers and at least one city councillor off guard.

“This problem just keeps getting worse and I know nobody wants to look at it, but it’s not going away,” community organizer Shawn Koch told Global News.

“This is not the way to deal with it.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This is not the way to deal with it."

Last November, city council approved changes to its encampment response strategy, including the creation of the Care Team and an approach focused on care rather than enforced removals.

Coun. Shanon Zachidniak said she did not know the encampment was being dismantled until the operation was already underway.

“I had no idea this was happening until I found out as it had already started,” she said. “And so I got here as quickly as I could to try and see what is going on, what is the plan, how can we ensure that folks are going to have a safe place tonight.”

Community organizers also raised concerns about what would happen to residents and their belongings.

“When you come back to the spot that you’ve called home for over three months, and nothing is going to be here, none of your friends are going to be there, and none of your belongings are going to be here,” community organizer Mandla Mthembu said.

He said those belongings could include keepsakes, as well as essential medication such as insulin.

Regina fire officials said the decision to clear the site followed an increase in fires and a high-risk assessment conducted over the weekend.

Mayor Chad Bachynski said the city had been working with the province to try to open some type of space where people could get out of the encampment and receive support.

“We were working with the province to try and open up some kind of space, whether it’s a triage space, a transitional space, something so they can get out of the encampment, out of the elements, and into somewhere where they can then navigate people on where they need to go,” Bachynski said.

Those displaced by the closure are now facing questions about what comes next as colder weather settles into Regina.

stories.title: Hello! London’s newest city councillors credit doorstep campaigning
stories.summary: Ward 3 councillor-elect Ben Durham has received more than 500 messages since defeating incumbent Peter Cuddy in northeast London.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Ward 3 councillor-elect Ben Durham has received more than 500 messages since defeating incumbent Peter Cuddy in northeast London.

Durham says he waited until every poll result was reported before celebrating a narrow 208 vote victory.

“We won!” the 32-year-old video producer recalled shouting alongside his supporters. “It was pretty incredible.”

The winning campaign included going door-to-door six, and sometimes seven days a week in northeast London since Durham registered as a candidate in May.

“It was consistency. I was out [door knocking],” he explained. “When you look at a map of how many addresses there are in this ward, oh my goodness, there are so many!”

Durham was the only challenger to defeat a member of council, joining three other rookie councillors who ran in races without an incumbent.

“I had on any given night, three to four people canvasing with me,” Cull told CTV News. “That enabled us to cover the ward once and then go back and talk to people again.”

Meanwhile, in northwest London, newly elected Ward 7 Councillor Jonathan Sher says doorstep discussions influenced his campaign.

“[Residents] are feeling squeezed by both rising property taxes, about 24 per cent this current term, and also what they see as a real slip in core services [like] snow removal, road capacity, and even safety,” Sher explained.

Trained as a lawyer and now teaching at Western Law, voters chose the former journalist from a field of eight candidates.

“You need to work cooperatively with other councillors, and you need to work respectfully with staff. That’s what I try to do as a journalist. That’s what I will try to do as an incoming councillor,” he added.

Jason King, the Ward 14 councillor-elect, will be the fourth newcomer taking a seat inside council chambers.

He takes over from Coun. Steve Hillier, who did not seek re-election.

The four will join the re-elected members of council taking their oath of office in a formal swearing-in ceremony on Nov. 17.

In the weeks that follow, they’ll face a number of critical decisions, including the endorsement of a deputy mayor and balancing the 2027 municipal budget.

Durham expects the learning curve to resemble trying to drink from a fire hose, “As a newbie on council I fully understand that I don’t understand everything, and I think acknowledging that can be a strength.”

“I’m analytical in my approach,” Sher said about his decision-making style. “I look for the best evidence. I look at practices in other jurisdictions across North America, even across the world.”

Tom Cull said he will look to collaborate with other councillors, “Finding common ground with my colleagues, figuring out what their ward residents need. Being able to articulate what my ward residents need.”

stories.title: Why talk of ending the 1876 Indian Act is raising big questions for Saskatchewan First Nations
stories.summary: In the wake of recent talks about reforming Canada’s Indian Act, Indigenous peoples are questioning what that change would look like.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Saskatoon, Sask. – In the wake of recent talks about reforming Canada’s Indian Act, Indigenous peoples are questioning what that change would look like.

Ernie Louttit is a member of the Missanabie Cree First Nation.

He is a status ‘Indian’ under the Indian Act, but his children are not due to certain rules under the current act.

He hopes reform would allow status to be easily passed down to his children.

“It just feels like you have to qualify your identity to the government,” Louttit told CTV News.

“It needs to be reformed, but it needs to be reformed with good intention.”

What is the Indian Act?

The Indian Act was enacted in 1876. The legislation gives the federal government authority over First Nations people, status registration, reserve lands and band governance.

The act attempted to assimilate First Nations.

“This exists to separate the Canadian populace from the First Nations populace,” said Jason Bird, a lecturer at the First Nations University of Canada.

“It seems like the goal of this whole thing is to rob Indigenous people of their status, identity and land.”

For years, Indigenous groups have questioned the purpose of the act.

“I don’t think anyone truly wants the Indian Act as a governing document over their societies,” Bird said.

The act prevented First Nations women from running for chief and would strip women of their status if they married a non-Indigenous man.

The Indian Act also paved the way for residential schools, banned cultural practices and developed the reserve system.

“The reserve system is a form of apartheid and really changed the dynamics of our communities in terms of hunting, fishing and housing,” said Katherine Strongwind, founder of Sixties Scoop Legacy of Canada.

Most of the reserve land given to First Nations was not optimal for farming, hunting, fishing or gathering, she said.

Previous repeal efforts

The Indian Act has been amended over the years.

Changes in the 1950s gave provinces jurisdiction over child welfare, which ultimately led to the Sixties Scoop, Strongwind explained.

“That is when we saw thousands of children taken from our homes and put into non-Indigenous homes,” said Strongwind, a Sixties Scoop survivor and advocate.

In 1969, the government of Pierre Trudeau attempted to completely abolish the act through a proposed policy known as the White Paper.

The move would have eliminated ‘Indian status’ altogether, among other controversial outcomes.

“The White Paper really aggravated and was an offence to First Nations leadership because it was not co-developed,” Strongwind said.

“It was another patriarchal decision to move towards abolishing the Indian Act and assimilating Indians, as we are called in Canada.”

Strongwind says recent talks about reforming the Indian Act are “somewhat reminiscent” of the White Paper.

She said she was surprised to hear the Indian Act come up in conversation at the First Ministers’ Meeting in Ottawa.

“I thought it came out of nowhere,” she said.

“For Premier Kinew to simply call out in a scrum to the prime minister without consulting with First Nations, and without the national chief there, is a little bit concerning.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said many Indigenous leaders have called for the elimination of the Indian Act.

Any reform or abolishment would only happen in partnership with First Nations, he added.

Strongwind believes this is an opportunity to redevelop legislation for the betterment of Indigenous communities.

The founder of Sixties Scoop Legacy of Canada went on to say that she hopes an opportunity to renegotiate the legislation, and define who is treaty and who belongs to the treaties presents itself.

She is hopeful replacement legislation can eventually be developed with more consultation with Assembly of First Nations chiefs, Indigenous leadership and survivors.

“It was another patriarchal decision to move towards abolishing the Indian Act and assimilating Indians, as we are called in Canada.”
Strongwind says recent talks about reforming the Indian Act are “somewhat reminiscent” of the White Paper.
She said she was surprised to hear the Indian Act come up in conversation at the First Ministers’ Meeting in Ottawa.
“I thought it came out of nowhere,” she said.
“For Premier Kinew to simply call out in a scrum to the prime minister without consulting with First Nations, and without the national chief there, is a little bit concerning.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney said many Indigenous leaders have called for the elimination of the Indian Act.
Any reform or abolishment would only happen in partnership with First Nations, he added.
Strongwind believes this is an opportunity to redevelop legislation for the betterment of Indigenous communities.
The founder of Sixties Scoop Legacy of Canada went on to say that she hopes an opportunity to renegotiate the legislation, and define who is treaty and who belongs to the treaties presents itself.
She is hopeful replacement legislation can eventually be developed with more consultation with Assembly of First Nations chiefs, Indigenous leadership and survivors.

stories.title: With no clear winner in Israel's election, here's what could happen next
stories.summary: The country's main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and Netanyahu's bloc to win 50.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
Israelis went to the polls in the highest turnout for decades on Tuesday, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning the next government will be formed by whoever can cobble together a coalition.

The country’s main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50.

Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.

Here are four possible scenarios:

The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.

President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government — not necessarily the party with the most seats, which the initial exit polls showed to be Netanyahu’s Likud.

The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot’s bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm’s length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.

For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.

Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.

Following the previous election in November 2022, it took Benjamin Netanyahu 58 days to form his government.

If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.

In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties — whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian — could play a critical role.

Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.

Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.

Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout “indicates a strong desire for partnership”.

Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.

“Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” Elovitz said.

Considering Israel’s extreme polarisation, a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.

Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.

Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.

A poll published on October 16 found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.

This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.

The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.

A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.

If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.

The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.

The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

Early Wednesday, Eisenkot spoke against this option, saying that Israel had chosen change and that he would seek to form a new government.

“In an election with such a high turnout, it would be a mistake to go to another round of elections.”

stories.title: Drawn lot decides mayor of Lytton, B.C., after tied election
stories.summary: Both candidates received 45 votes in the Oct. 17 election with only 198 voters registered in the village
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
The new mayor in Lytton, B.C., a tiny village razed by a raging wildfire in 2021, has been determined by the drawing of lots after a tied election.

The village says Jennifer Thoss is the winner in a process conducted in front of a judge, resulting in the defeat of incumbent Denise O’Connor.

Both candidates received 45 votes in the Oct. 17 election and the random draw was conducted after a judicial recount at the Kamloops Provincial Court produced the same tally on Tuesday.

A similar process determined the mayor of Peachland, B.C., in 2018.

Thoss and O’Connor have expressed differing views on the village’s recovery from the wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of Lytton’s structures, including its health centre, bank and municipal office.

Thoss, who was elected as a councillor in Lytton in 2022, has criticized the handling of the recovery and rebuilding process with O’Connor at the helm.

She told The Canadian Press last spring that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure funded largely by Ottawa would ultimately “bankrupt” the tiny village, where the shrunken tax base wouldn’t be able to sustain the operations costs.

O’Connor, who was elected mayor in 2022, defended the process, saying over the summer that Lytton wasn’t a typical municipality as it recovered from the fire and still required the recovery staff.

She said “dwelling on the negative” wouldn’t help Lytton rebuild and the village couldn’t attract new and returning residents if it lacked infrastructure and amenities.

The non-profit CivicInfo BC says Lytton has 198 registered voters, while the 2021 census, conducted just before the fire, put the total population at 210.

stories.title: Mayoral candidates pitch more policing as civic election nears in Winnipeg
stories.summary: Additional police and drones for surveillance won't reduce social issues despite mayoral candidates vowing to add more officers if elected, experts say.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Additional police and drones for surveillance won’t reduce social issues despite mayoral candidates vowing to add more officers if elected, experts say.

The Winnipeg Police Service receives 27 per cent or $370 million of the City of Winnipeg’s budget, according to the city’s 2026 budget. The city’s operating budget is at $1.49 billion.

“Per capita, we are pretty high. I think usually a lot of cities that are just slightly smaller than us are around $260-290 per citizen. Winnipeg is over $350 to $360 per citizen,” said Kevin Walby, University of Winnipeg criminologist. “When we put this percentage of our money into policing year after year after year, and we don’t see any reduction in any of those issues — in fact, visibly and statistically they are much worse. You have to start to wonder why are we doing that?”

Operating expenditures for policing in Canada totaled $22 billion in 2024-25, which is up 12 per cent from 2022-23, according to Statistics Canada.

“We are 100 police officers short of the very mere minimum of the per capita right now,” mayoral candidate Kevin Klein said on 680 Cjob.

“We need police officers, we do, we’re both committed to adding more police officers,” mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham said, also on 680 Cjob.

Mike Vogiatzakis said he would introduce drones as a tool to watch over the city and see where problems are at CBC Manitoba’s mayoral debate.

“As mayor, I’m going to instruct the police board and the police chief,” Vogiatzakis said. “I’ll sit with them within my first 30 days. I’ll sit with them and decide how we’re gonna change the city.”

The Winnipeg Police Service declined to comment.

stories.title: Doerkson tells of 'productive conversation' with Carney on supercharging B.C. economy
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says he and Prime Minister Mark Carney are aligned on the need to supercharge the economy, attract investment and create good-paying jobs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VICTORIA - British Columbia’s premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says he and Prime Minister Mark Carney are aligned on the need to supercharge the economy, attract investment and create good-paying jobs.

By The Canadian Press

Doerkson posted on social media that he had a productive conversation with the prime minister on Tuesday, just days after his B.C. Conservatives won two-thirds of the seats in the provincial election.

He says B.C. has an enormous role to play in driving Canada’s economic future and they are ready to lead.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Doerkson attached a readout from the Prime Minister’s Office about the same conversation, saying there was agreement to work together to increase growth and economic opportunities for B.C. and Canada.

It says Carney and Doerkson indicated their joint desire for a strong partnership, inclusive of all British Columbians, that can supercharge hope and opportunities for the province.

stories.title: Ford faces Ontario legislature after long summer break, pledges more landfills
stories.summary: Province introduced bill to streamline permits, increase dump capacity, while opposition grills government on scandals
stories.author: Laura Stone, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
The Ontario Legislature returned on Tuesday after an extended 21-week break, with Premier Doug Ford facing accusations from the opposition that he has been evading accountability, rewarding insiders and ignoring the plight of everyday people.

Responding in Question Period, Mr. Ford said he has taken 500 meetings since the legislature rose for summer break and defended his government’s record during trade strife with the United States.

Mr. Ford had vowed that his focus as MPPs return would be on measures to cut red tape to boost Ontario’s economy in the face of U.S. tariffs. On Tuesday afternoon, his government unveiled an omnibus bill it says would eliminate “nearly 220,000 days’ worth of permitting processing times” by streamlining or getting rid of the need for a range of permits and environmental processes.

Among the changes is a move to make it easier to receive approval for landfills and incineration or “energy-from-waste” facilities. Provincial Environment Minister Todd McCarthy said the change was needed in light of U.S. President Donald Trump’s announcement last week of new 50-per-cent tariffs on Canadian waste.

Mr. McCarthy said about 40 per cent of Ontario’s commercial waste is shipped to Michigan and New York and that the province has only 10 years of its own landfill capacity left. And while he said there would be “robust” public consultations and that he prefers “willing host communities,” the minister did not rule out imposing a facility over local objections.

The return of the legislature after a lengthy break was the first chance for opposition parties to question the Premier and his government since June 2. Mr. Ford’s government had said the hiatus was necessary so as to not interfere with Monday’s municipal elections in Ontario. But the opposition accuses Mr. Ford of trying to avoid scrutiny.

The Ontario NDP and Liberals both called for the resignation of Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, over concerns about how the government has handled questionable Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) payments at private career colleges.

Rising in the House, Liberal MPP Ted Hsu accused Mr. Ford of contempt in the legislature. He asked Speaker Donna Skelly to rule on whether the Premier breached his parliamentary privilege this summer when Mr. Ford said opposition requests to recall the legislature to address the tariff crisis were “gutter politics,” insisting Ontarians could just phone him instead.

“There’s a trend here that this government is making the legislature irrelevant. They just want to govern by Doug Ford’s cellphone,” Mr. Hsu told reporters after Question Period.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles accused Mr. Ford of forgetting about the people he promised to fight for, referencing his government’s purchase and hasty resale of a $28.9-million private jet last spring.

She also questioned the promotion of Toronto MPP Stan Cho, who resigned as tourism minister in July after it was revealed he spent $16,000 on hotels in the past three years, despite representing a riding not far from Queen’s Park. Mr. Cho last week was named parliamentary assistant to Education Minister Paul Calandra, a role that comes with a $22,500 raise.

“This minister made a decision at some point when he was in a hotel to give them either his own credit card or the taxpayer’s credit card, and he chose the latter,” Ms. Stiles told reporters after Question Period. “And I think it is outrageous that the Premier has decided to actually promote this this guy. And he’s taken no responsibility ultimately for his actions.”

Mr. Cho told reporters he made a mistake but took responsibility for his actions and repaid his expenses. He said he had a baby at home and had a hip replacement earlier this year.

“I made a decision that was convenient for my family. I wasn’t thinking about people in my riding working two jobs trying to make ends meet,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mr. Ford later told reporters he fired Mr. Cho. The MPP had characterized his departure from cabinet as a resignation.

“I don’t call it a promotion. He lost his job. I got rid of him,” the Premier said.

Also facing questions on Tuesday was Mr. Quinn, who has cut off access to student assistance for attendees of private career colleges after allegations of sweeping irregularities and skyrocketing payments at certain institutions.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser called the government’s handling of the file “colossal mismanagement” and said the province knew about suspicious activity for years, but failed to act.

Mr. Quinn has said he brought in Kpmg auditors and referred issues around the use of Osap to the Ontario Provincial Police for a potential investigation. He was asked why the government did not act sooner, despite warnings of potential problems dating back years.

“There were multiple investigations, individual investigations,” Mr. Quinn told reporters. “And then we realized across the sector there was a more of a broad issue, and that’s why we brought in a third-party investigator, Kpmg, to ensure that taxpayer dollars are respected and to ensure that there is compliance across the Osap system.”

stories.summary: The new mayor in Lytton, B.C., a tiny village razed by a raging wildfire in 2021, has been determined by the drawing of lots after a tied election.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The new mayor in Lytton, B.C., a tiny village razed by a raging wildfire in 2021, has been determined by the drawing of lots after a tied election.

DD[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/british-columbia/drawn-lot-decides-mayor-of-lytton-b-c-after-votes-are-tied-at-45-each/article_cbc6592c-2462-5cb0-85a2-760d166cf6cf.html)

By Brenna Owen The Canadian Press

The village says Jennifer Thoss is the winner in a process conducted in front of a judge, resulting in the defeat of incumbent Denise O’Connor.

Both candidates received 45 votes in the Oct. 17 election and the random draw was conducted after a judicial recount at the Kamloops Provincial Court produced the same tally on Tuesday.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

A similar process determined the mayor of Peachland, B.C., in 2018.

Thoss and O’Connor have expressed differing views on the village’s recovery from the wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of Lytton’s structures, including its health centre, bank and municipal office.

Thoss, who was elected as a councillor in Lytton in 2022, has criticized the handling of the recovery and rebuilding process with O’Connor at the helm.

She told The Canadian Press last spring that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure funded largely by Ottawa would ultimately “bankrupt” the tiny village, where the shrunken tax base wouldn’t be able to sustain the operations costs.

O’Connor, who was elected mayor in 2022, defended the process, saying over the summer that Lytton wasn’t a typical municipality as it recovered from the fire and still required the recovery staff.

She said “dwelling on the negative” wouldn’t help Lytton rebuild and the village couldn’t attract new and returning residents if it lacked infrastructure and amenities.

The non-profit CivicInfo BC says Lytton has 198 registered voters, while the 2021 census, conducted just before the fire, put the total population at 210.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

The Canadian Press

Vancouver - Hurricane, the sloth that has been hanging out at the Vancouver Aquarium for years, has died at the age of 29.

The aquarium says she was one of their “most beloved” residents.

stories.title: B.C. man who started dog rescue killed while saving animals in Ukraine
stories.summary: "The best thing I can say is Jesse was a force of nature," Penny Stone, executive director of the Victoria Humane Society, told Global News.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Kylie Stanton
stories.content:
A B.C. man who started a dog rescue has been killed while saving animals in Ukraine.

Jesse Adams founded RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, which is based in Victoria on Vancouver Island.

Last Friday, Adams posted on Facebook that he was heading out on a rescue mission in eastern Ukraine.

Two days later, an FPV (first-person view) drone struck the vehicle he was using to transport the animals, according to the rescue society.

Adams suffered severe injuries and underwent emergency surgery, but doctors were unable to save him.

“The best thing I can say is Jesse was a force of nature,” Penny Stone, executive director of the Victoria Humane Society, told Global News.

“He was unbelievably go, go, go. Wherever help was needed, Jesse was. It didn’t matter. And I mean, it shows in that he went to Kabul and he went to Ukraine a number of times. He was just like wherever they needed help the most.”

Stone said Adams was someone who always stepped up and was there for every animal.

“When he was in Ukraine, I know he was rescuing tigers and lions and different kinds of species, pigs and goats and stuff, and he would post about it and it was quite funny and we’d laugh about what he was doing,” she said.

“But I mean, he was just that guy, where it was needed.”

Stone said Adams also travelled to small communities to help the people living there.

“It’s a tragic loss. He was a real hero.”

Stone added that the space Adams left behind will be impossible to fill.

“He just believed every animal and every person deserved a chance and he never backed down for fighting for the little guy,” she said.

The RainCoast Dog Rescue Society posted to social media announcing Adams’ passing writing, “after a life lived in service to animal welfare, Jesse made the ultimate sacrifice to his beliefs on the front lines of Ukraine.”

Lori Kalef, the SPCA International Director of Programs, said she was stunned to hear the news.

“When I found out he passed away, I just couldn’t believe it,” she said.

“I still can’t believe it. I don’t think it has been properly processed.”

Adams is being remembered for his compassion, courage and the lives he worked to save.

It is estimated he and his team had evacuated as many as 1,000 animals from the war-torn country, including thousands more at home.

“Wherever there was a need, Jesse was there,” Kalef said.

“There is going to be a huge, huge hole. But I also feel that this is the kind of community that comes together, especially in the time of grief and the love for animals.

“I do believe that there is going to be a path forward.”

stories.title: Ontario government announces reforms for electricity distributors with rising demand in mind
stories.summary: There are long-standing concerns about ability of local distributors to maintain existing infrastructure, let alone pay for expansions
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Ontario’s government announced a slate of reforms on Tuesday intended to help the province’s several dozen electricity distributors prepare for a rapidly rising demand for power.

Stephen Lecce, Minister of Energy and Mines, said the government would introduce legislation on Tuesday afternoon in response to a series of recommendations received earlier this year from a four-member advisory group. The reforms include a new requirement that local distribution companies, or LDCs, produce 10-year plans “that include condition assessment, financing plans and work-force strategies.”

The government will also impose what it described as “a mandatory dividend stress test,” intended to ensure LDCs reinvest profits back into their grids.

“Because right now, across the board, that is not always the case,” Mr. Lecce said during a press conference in Toronto.

“Local utilities are facing aging infrastructure, rising capital requirements, work-force shortages and skyrocketing demands for connections. And so, notwithstanding very good efforts by our utilities, these challenges remain real, and they will imperil our economic growth if we don’t get it right today,” he said.

Ontario’s electricity is distributed by 58 LDCs that are mostly owned by municipalities. Many of them serve small numbers of customers, whereas other provinces are served by a single, monolithic Crown corporation such as Hydro-Québec.

Expectations of increasing demand for electricity have exacerbated long-standing concerns that many LDCs will be unable to maintain existing infrastructure, let alone pay for significant expansions. According to the Electricity Distributors Association, which represents Ontario’s LDCs, the tab for upgrading networks over the next couple of decades could amount to between $103-billion and $120-billion – an estimate the government has endorsed.

A year ago, the government convened a group called the Panel for Utility Leadership and Service Excellence, or Pulse, chaired by former Toronto Hydro Corp. president and chief executive Anthony Haines, to advise Mr. Lecce on potential reforms. Pulse’s recommendations, submitted in February and published Tuesday, warned that although LDCs have thus far managed to preserve reliability of their distribution systems, many have put off necessary capital investments for years.

Pulse warned LDCs are “increasingly misaligned with the scale, pace and complexity of growth in electricity demand now underway,” and that the pace at which Ontario can meet objectives such as building new housing, electrifying its industries and charging electric vehicles “increasingly turns on distribution system readiness.”

Pulse also found that while municipalities May, in some cases, be able to provide additional funding to LDCs, others must turn to alternative sources of capital such as pension funds and other institutional investors, or will need to merge with other utilities.

“Access to external investment, particularly from Canadian institutional investors, is likely to be a critical determinant of whether electricity distribution utilities can deliver required infrastructure on time and at reasonable cost,” its report concluded.

The government’s response to Pulse’s recommendations include imposing new governance requirements. Mr. Lecce said LDCs will be required to establish “independent, skills-based” boards of directors. Municipalities will be limited to having one member in a non-voting capacity – a departure from a status quo in which politicians occupy as much as half of LDC board seats.

Benjamin Dachis, vice-president of research at the energy think tank Clean Prosperity, said there’s strong evidence that independent directors who are not associated with municipal shareholders are more likely to promote investment by LDCs.

Teresa Sarkesian, president of the Electricity Distributors Association, expressed broad support for the reforms. She said her organization understands the government will later introduce further measures focused on removing barriers to greater private investment in LDCs.

“One of the most important things for us is to make sure that we have access to capital to properly fund the grid,” she said.

“There’s two times a year that they can implement those things: One is the fall economic statement, and one is the budget.”

Of particular interest is Pulse’s observation that when private ownership of an LDC exceeds a federally imposed threshold of 10 per cent, it’s deemed to have disposed of its assets at fair market value and faces a large departure tax. This has restricted LDCs’ access to outside investment.

Ms. Sarkesian said that while her organization supports long-term capital planning, inflation, supply chain challenges and the geopolitical environment make it difficult to forecast a decade out; five-year plans “would be more accurate and more meaningful.”

Thomas Timmins, who leads law firm Gowling Wlg’s energy practice, said the new governance and financial requirements are aimed at encouraging consolidation among the LDCs, without explicitly forcing them to do so.

The changes announced on Tuesday “put a compliance burden on the smaller utilities,” he said, “which will potentially push municipal shareholders to conclude that maintaining an independent utility is really a luxury that they can’t afford any more.”

He added: “Some of these LDCs are in financial trouble, and that is not okay. We are talking about keeping the lights and heating on – this is critical infrastructure.”

stories.title: Ontario Superior Court approves $213.5M settlement against Sun Life
stories.summary: The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has approved a $213.5 million class-action settlement against Sun Life.

A news release from law firm Kim Spencer McPhee Barristers P.C. says the action began in 2010 regarding alleged improper administration of three universal life insurance policies, including Universal Plus, Flexiplus, and OptiMet.

The policies were sold by Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. agents in Canada between 1987 and 1998.

The release says Sunlife has denied any wrongdoing, and the company did not immediately respond to a request for comment after hours.

The law firm says the settlement is the largest reported settlement in any life insurance policy dispute in Canadian history, concerning 70,000 eligible current and former Flexiplus and Universal Plus policyholders in Canada.

Eldon Fehr, representative plaintiff, says the settlement will provide significant benefits to current and former Sun Life policyholders.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Incumbent mayors, premiers losing jobs a result of Canadians not ‘getting ahead’
stories.summary: Many mayors in British Columbia and Ontario and premiers in B.C. and Quebec lost their jobs this month despite being incumbents in the race.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Cities and provinces across Canada have seen political change in recent months as frustrations over affordability and quality of life has meant incumbents being shown the door.

Multiple Ontario cities said goodbye to short and long-time mayors and councillors on Monday. A few days earlier, British Columbia ousted its NDP government and premier David Eby, following the trend of incumbent losses after several B.C. mayors were voted out of office. Those changes all came in a month that started with Quebec’s CAQ government losing every seat in the provincial election.

The back-to-back changes were a result of Canadians facing continued strain over tariffs from the U.S. administration, wavering inflation and uncertainty when affordability will get better, political experts said.

“If we think about the national mood right now in Canada … I think a lot of Canadians don’t feel like they’re getting ahead,” said Lewis Krashinsky, a political scientist and William Lyon Mackenzie King postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University. “Voters can be fickle.”

He said that when voters don’t feel like they’re getting ahead, they look for people they believe can bring new ideas.

Richard Johnston, professor emeritus of political science at the University of British Columbia, said the power of incumbency has decreased over decades. Previously, some provincial governments have served for decades such as the Progressive Conservatives in New Brunswick for 17 years, or the Alberta PCs for 43. The average length of a government now sits at about 10 years.

Incumbents have also faced multiple issues in recent months, with Johnston saying the handling of COVID-19, supply chain and inflation, and President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant Canadians are feeling worse off.

As a result, people are pointing the finger at politicians in city hall or the provincial legislatures and punishing them for it.

“In general, this has been a decade of sort of institutional failure, I think that’s actually unfair, but that’s how voters perceive it,” Johnston said. “There’s a sense in which governments of almost any stripe seem to have dropped the ball or they’re overwhelmed by forces beyond their control.”

But Krashinsky, originally from Toronto, added that voters can choose someone new for a number of reasons including anger.

“Perhaps that’s out of a sense of anger, resentment towards a political candidate who’s been in there for so many years; perhaps it’s a sense of optimism with what the new candidate could bring in,” said Krashinsky. “Perhaps it is a sense of just needing a better option; it’s a sense of almost desperation that we’ve tried this path over and over again, and we haven’t gotten ahead.”

Long-time incumbency ended for several mayors in Ontario Oct. 26.

Gord Krantz, Canada’s longest-serving, lost his first election since becoming mayor of Milton in 1980. Further south, Sarnia’s Mike Bradley ended his 38-year run in the mayor’s seat defeated by newcomer Carrie McEachran.

It wasn’t long-time incumbents who lost either. One-term mayors in B.C. including Port Moody’s Meghan Lahti and New Westminster’s Patrick Johnstone, and Mississauga’s Carolyn Parrish and Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath in Ontario also lost.

Hamish Telford, associate political science professor at the University of the Fraser Valley in B.C., said those short-term mayors were the victims of the public disappointed in their own choices within the previous four years.

“It’s frustration with lack of progress on core issues as a generality,” he said. “People look over the past four years and say, ‘my life or my city hasn’t improved like you promised it would,’ and obviously, they come to the conclusion that the direction that the mayor set was not the right one.”

Not all incumbents are losing though, with Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown and several B.C. mayors still keeping their jobs.

Krashinsky said the reasons can range from a mixture of relatability to there not being a strong enough opposition candidate to give voters another strong choice.

“Affinity for a candidate that you know and recognize and trust someone perhaps that you’ve met,” he said. “Being able to have that personal touch that you can be established really over time I think can really help these incumbents.”

Yet Telford added even likeability won’t help if voters are losing respect for the judgment of longer-serving incumbents creating that need for change.

“The winds of change of change blow every decade in Canada and that’s what we’re seeing lately,” Telford said.

— with files from Global News’ Aaron D’Andrea and Amy Judd

stories.title: Four and a half years on, the housing correction is an Ontario and B.C. story
stories.summary: The 2023 rebound was a false bottom. Where do home prices go from here?
stories.author: Hanif Bayat
stories.content:
After the recent rise in fixed mortgage rates and the expectation that variable rates will follow, the question many home buyers and sellers are asking is whether home prices in Canada will fall further.

The national benchmark home price fell to $651,400 in September, its lowest level since February, 2021, and 22.5 per cent below the March, 2022, high. The national average home price tells a similar story: At $666,538 in September, it was lower than in February, 2021.

Four and a half years after the peak, Canada’s housing correction isn’t over. But the national number hides the real story: This is now mainly a correction in two provinces.

Ontario’s benchmark home price is $736,300, down 26.7 per cent from its peak of just over $1-million. The typical Ontario home has lost about $269,000 in value. B.C. is down 16.7 per cent from its peak, down 4.7 per cent from a year ago. Worse, both have erased the 2023 rebound, which many buyers took as a sign the bottom had passed.

Quebec and Alberta, the other two big provinces, never had a 2022 bust. Alberta peaked later, in March, 2025, and is now only 3.6 per cent below that level. Quebec set a record this April and is still up 1.1 per cent from a year ago, the only annual gain among the four big provinces. Among the six smaller provinces, all but Nova Scotia are up from a year ago.

But momentum is fading almost everywhere. In September, the benchmark fell from the previous month in every province except PEI, though part of that is seasonal.

Given recent housing market activity and rising mortgage rates , I expect Ontario and B.C. housing prices will not rise next year and will most probably fall, possibly reaching their bottom. Home prices in Alberta and Quebec May not rise either.

Not everyone agrees. Ali Salarian, the broker at RE/MAX Success Realty in Mississauga, Ont., expects things to improve once the current renewal wave passes. Owners who locked in five-year rates below 2 per cent in 2021 are now renewing at much higher rates, pushing some to sell, while those who renew next year already have rates close to today’s. “Once this listing wave clears, expect gradual growth in 2027,” he said in an interview.

He is not the only one. Desjardins senior economist Kari Norman, for example, expects Ontario’s average home price to rise 2.4 per cent in 2027 , even though she anticipates two Bank of Canada rate hikes starting in late October.

Still, the economy is soft and borrowing costs are rising. Don’t be fooled by a good spring market. Benchmark home prices tend to rise in spring and stall in the fall. This year, a January-to-May bounce was followed by four straight monthly declines. The first sign of a bottom will be when annual price declines start to narrow month after month.

Hanif Bayat, PhD, is the CEO and founder of Wowa.CA , a Canadian personal finance platform.
