stories.title: Only firm approved to explore for N.S. offshore oil and gas misses deposit deadline
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia’s premier says the only company with rights to explore for offshore oil and gas in the province missed Monday's deposit deadline.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Nova Scotia’s premier says the only company with rights to explore for offshore oil and gas in the province missed Monday’s deposit deadline.

Tim Houston said in a social media post Monday that Nova Scotia’s Inceptio Oil and Gas would not be able to put down the more than $50 million that’s required to be granted an exploration licence.

In April, regulators approved a $210-million exploration bid from the company, led by Nova Scotian James Edens, who is also president of Scotland-based Inceptio UK.

Inceptio needed to put down 25 per cent of the bid price — about $52 million — in order to obtain a licence for activities such as seismic testing and drilling. Ottawa and the province had twice previously directed the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator to extend the deadline, in May and August.

Edens said in an email that the company was pleased with the support it received from the provincial and federal governments, including the extensions. He said there was significant interest in the project, but the company could not secure enough domestic investment in time to meet the deposit deadline.

“Foreign investment was sourced, but was limited by mandatory reviews for foreign ownership in natural resources, with incompatible timelines with our security-posting needs,” wrote Edens. “We will monitor the licensing framework proposed in future call for bids for supportive change.”

The regulator said in an email Tuesday that legislation requires an exploration licence to be issued within six months of the call for bids closing.

With the deadline passed, a new call for bids will have to be issued before Inceptio or any other company can seek to explore in Nova Scotia’s waters. Those calls are typically issued around mid-April.

Inceptio Ltd., which has common principal shareholders with Inceptio Oil and Gas but is a separate company, had previously been approved for an offshore exploration licence. However, the provincial and federal governments jointly vetoed the approval in 2023.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Natural Resources minister at the time, said the $1.5-million bid was small, raising questions around risk and complexity of the project.

Houston said in a social media post Monday that the lack of progress is a setback, but the province remains committed to developing its offshore resources.

“Hard things are hard but we will continue laying the groundwork for a stronger, more resilient Nova Scotia that can stand on its own and meet the challenges of tomorrow,” Houston said on social media.

The premier has pushed hard to kick-start Nova Scotia’s resource sector since his second term began in 2024. He has said the province needs to exploit its natural gas and other resources to better withstand economic challenges from the United States, including President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Along with a renewed focus on offshore oil and gas, his government has pursued wind and hydrogen development, and has lifted long-term bans on onshore natural gas fracking as well as uranium mining.

While the private sector has demonstrated interest in wind and hydrogen, there’s been little activity in Nova Scotia’s offshore fossil fuel sector since the Sable and Deep Panuke gas projects shut down in 2018. The projects combined to generate billions in royalties for the province over 25 years of offshore exploration and development.

There’s about 90-billion cubic metres of gas confirmed to exist on the Scotian shelf and a potential for more than 10 times that amount, says the province.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected article. A previous version incorrectly stated that Inceptio Oil and Gas was based in the U.K. In fact, the company is incorporated in Nova Scotia. While Inceptio Oil and Gas has principal shareholders in common with Inceptio Ltd. and Inceptio UK Ltd., the companies do not have ownership stakes in each another.

stories.title: Caat Pension Plan names OPTrust’s Peter Lindley as CEO
stories.summary: Plan’s leadership team has been in flux since oversight failures led to several departures
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Caat Pension Plan has appointed Peter Lindley as chief executive officer and plan manager, installing a new leader after a year of turmoil that led to the departure of most of the plan’s executive team.

Mr. Lindley is stepping down from another pension plan, OPTrust, where he has been CEO since 2019 . He starts at Caat on Jan. 6, 2027.

Caat’s leadership ranks have been in a state of flux after failures in the plan’s oversight spurred an abrupt overhaul early this year. Those issues included a $1.6-million vacation payout to previous CEO Derek Dobson, as well as a relationship he was having with a Caat employee.

Caat is a multiemployer pension plan with $25.4-billion in assets that serves Ontario’s colleges and about 850 public- and private-sector employers with more than 130,000 members. The Globe and Mail has been a participating employer since 2022.

In July, after a third-party review of the plan’s governance, Caat told members it was making “enhancements” to its governance procedures to improve oversight of executive compensation, workplace relationships and succession planning.

Caat board chair Janet Greenwood praised Mr. Lindley’s “depth of leadership, experience and perspective” in a statement.

“The board is confident Peter will keep members’ interests at the centre of the plan’s work, strengthen our partnerships with participating employers and continue to focus on the stability and strength of the plan,” she said.

Mr. Lindley was not available for an interview on Tuesday, but said in a statement that Caat “has done remarkable work expanding access to defined benefit pensions, and I’m drawn to the plan’s strong culture.”

OPTrust has appointed its chief risk officer, Dani Goraichy, as its interim president and CEO, effective immediately, and has launched a process to find a permanent CEO, the plan said in a news release.

Mr. Dobson left the plan in March as part of a settlement that required him to repay $1.6-million in vacation pay that became a central concern about the plan’s oversight.

Mr. Dobson was the plan’s CEO for nearly 17 years and oversaw a period of rapid expansion.

Since March, chief investment officer Kevin Fahey has led the plan as interim CEO, with a revamped executive team. He will stay on as CIO, and Ms. Greenwood said he created “a strong bridge to permanent leadership.”

Caat’s board initially stood by Mr. Dobson when multiple top executives sent a letter to trustees late last year that urged them to investigate Mr. Dobson’s conduct. Three of those executives subsequently left the plan in January, setting a governance crisis in motion.

Caat’s previous board chair, Don Smith, was then ousted in February and vice-chair Kareen Stangherlin resigned.

paragraphs: Caat Pension Plan has appointed Peter Lindley as chief executive officer and plan manager, installing a new leader after a year of turmoil that led to the departure of most of the plan’s executive team.
Mr. Lindley is stepping down from another pension plan, OPTrust, where he has been CEO since 2019 . He starts at Caat on Jan. 6, 2027.

Caat’s leadership ranks have been in a state of flux after failures in the plan’s oversight spurred an abrupt overhaul early this year. Those issues included a $1.6-million vacation payout to previous CEO Derek Dobson, as well as a relationship he was having with a Caat employee.

Caat is a multiemployer pension plan with $25.4-billion in assets that serves Ontario’s colleges and about 850 public- and private-sector employers with more than 130,000 members. The Globe and Mail has been a participating employer since 2022.

In July, after a third-party review of the plan’s governance, Caat told members it was making “enhancements” to its governance procedures to improve oversight of executive compensation, workplace relationships and succession planning.
Caat board chair Janet Greenwood praised Mr. Lindley’s “depth of leadership, experience and perspective” in a statement.

“The board is confident Peter will keep members’ interests at the centre of the plan’s work, strengthen our partnerships with participating employers and continue to focus on the stability and strength of the plan,” she said.

Mr. Lindley was not available for an interview on Tuesday, but said in a statement that Caat “has done remarkable work expanding access to defined benefit pensions, and I’m drawn to the plan’s strong culture.”

OPTrust has appointed its chief risk officer, Dani Goraichy, as its interim president and CEO, effective immediately, and has launched a process to find a permanent CEO, the plan said in a news release.
Mr. Dobson left the plan in March as part of a settlement that required him to repay $1.6-million in vacation pay that became a central concern about the plan’s oversight.
Mr. Dobson was the plan’s CEO for nearly 17 years and oversaw a period of rapid expansion.

Since March, chief investment officer Kevin Fahey has led the plan as interim CEO, with a revamped executive team. He will stay on as CIO, and Ms. Greenwood said he created “a strong bridge to permanent leadership.”

The search process to choose the plan’s permanent CEO formally started in June and was led by leadership advisory firm Egon Zehnder.

stories.title: No evidence stolen Crime Stoppers data used for fraud, provider says
stories.summary: The provider of software used by Crime Stoppers says it has found no evidence that personal information exposed in a cybersecurity breach has been used for fraud or identity theft.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The provider of software used by Crime Stoppers says it has found no evidence that personal information exposed in a cybersecurity breach has been used for fraud or identity theft.

Navigate360 acknowledged names, addresses, dates of birth, social security numbers and other sensitive information May have been affected, though it said the information involved varies by person.

The U.S.-based company said it first became aware of the incident on March 18 and has learned a third party accessed one of its systems, obtaining copies of some data between Nov. 21, 2025, and March 5, 2026.

Navigate360, which also provides software to some schools in the U.S., said phone numbers and email addresses were also exposed.

“We have no evidence of misuse of any personal information for fraud or identity theft,” the company said in its Oct. 23 statement.

“Please note the information impacted varies for each potentially impacted individual.”

Several Canadian police forces have suspended their use of Crime Stoppers as concerns grow over the breach.

Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said last week 176,859 tips submitted to the P3 software between January 2022 and November 2025 were affected, including 12,392 that May contain personal information. Navigate360 later supplied a separate list containing 14,973 names.

However, Sportun said the list “lacks detail necessary to measure the risk involved” because it did not identify who the names belonged to.

“We never ask for your name, and we don’t want it. But people sometimes include details to explain what they saw,” Sportun said.

“Before a tip goes to investigators, our practice is to remove those details. It has come to light that some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3.”

Toronto Crime Stoppers continues to press Navigate360 for details, he added.

The company said in its statement it remains dedicated to ensuring the privacy and security of the information in its control.

“Upon discovery of this incident, Navigate360 immediately instituted mitigation measures. Navigate360 promptly implemented additional and enhanced safeguards and enlisted the support of a leading cybersecurity firm to enhance the security of our network, systems, and data,” it said.

“Navigate360 also launched a comprehensive investigation, identified individuals who May have been affected, reported the incident to law enforcement, and notified regulatory bodies.”

Sean Sparling, a former deputy chief of the Sault Ste. Marie Police Service, previously told Global News officers across Canada use Crime Stoppers “on a daily basis.”

He said he relied on Crime Stoppers for many of his own investigations.

“Knowing Crime Stoppers and how well it’s organized, how well it works and its importance to the law enforcement community and the safety of our communities, I fully expect they’re going to recover from this,” Sparling said.

Police services that have suspended their use of Crime Stoppers said members of the public can submit information through regular police-reporting channels, although those methods are not anonymous.

Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 911.

“Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online or through the app,” Sportun said.

“Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.”

stories.title: Saab signs agreement with Halifax’s IMP for final assembly of Gripen E fighter jet
stories.summary: Agreement is conditional on Ottawa purchasing the Gripens instead of U.S.-made F-35 stealth jets
stories.author: Gavin John
stories.content:
Saab AB has chosen IMP Aerospace & Defence to run a Canadian final-assembly line in Halifax if the federal government chooses its Gripen E fighter jet.

Saab said in a news release on Tuesday that it has signed a teaming agreement with IMP covering the final assembly of the aircraft, as well as in-service support and training for any Canadian-made Gripens.

The Swedish aerospace and defence manufacturer also announced a memorandum of understanding with Magellan Aerospace Corp. of Mississauga to manufacture airframe and composite structures, and a training agreement with Montreal’s CAE Inc., after an earlier MOU.

“Canada’s fighter capability is a long-term national investment,” Micael Johansson, president and chief executive officer of Saab, said in the statement.

Saab describes the three companies as its “principal partners” and describes the agreement as the first step toward a national industrial program.

David Gossen, president of IMP, said in a statement that the Gripen contract positions “Canadian industry as an enduring part of the global Gripen program.”

The agreements are conditional on Ottawa purchasing the Gripens instead of its current order for U.S.-made F-35 stealth jets.

Prime Minister Mark Carney paused plans to proceed with a planned order for 88 F-35s, made by Lockheed Martin Corp., as the federal government considers whether to purchase all of those jets or instead have a mixed fleet that includes Gripen jets.

Mr. Carney launched a review of the purchase after U.S. President Donald Trump made trade and annexation threats. The review was supposed to have concluded a year ago.

The Royal Canadian Air Force announced last Friday that it has received its first pair of F-35 jets .

The IMP announcement coincides with the Canadian Aerospace Summit in Ottawa, where Mr. Johansson is scheduled to speak Tuesday afternoon. Defence Minister David McGuinty is also expected to speak at the summit.

The Globe and Mail reported in September that Saab had pitched a start-to-finish Canadian production line if Ottawa places an order. The production line would include roughly 10 prime partners, 250 suppliers and an invitation to join Sweden’s next combat aircraft program.

Tuesday’s news release contains no new details on estimated job numbers or the potential cost.

It also contains no details on the principal concern regarding the Gripen, its engine. The F414-GE-39E, made by General Electric, is the aircraft’s one purely American component and is subject to U.S. export control, allowing Washington to approve, restrict or refuse the sale of the American military technology. In August, Mr. Johansson told The Globe that “every contract that we secure is backed by a licence from the U.S.” and that it had “never been a problem.”

GE Aerospace and Magellan signed an MOU this July under which Magellan would be responsible for engine overhaul and maintenance in Mississauga.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said at The Globe’s defence summit on Oct. 14 that the decision on major defence procurements could come “within a couple weeks.”

Canada has 16 F-35s under contract and has paid long-lead costs on 14 more; the remaining 72 of the 88-jet order are under review.

Canada’s first two CF-35A Lightning II fighters were handed over to the Rcaf at Luke Air Force Base in Phoenix on Oct. 22. There are around 30 Canadian firms that are already suppliers to the global F-35 assembly operations.

stories.title: Ottawa demands plan to restore Stelco jobs before meeting Cleveland-Cliffs CEO
stories.summary: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is calling on the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. to provide a concrete plan and timeline to restore jobs at its Canadian steel mills.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is calling on the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. to provide a concrete plan and timeline to restore jobs at its Canadian steel mills before she will agree to meet with CEO Lourenco Goncalves.

Cleveland-Cliffs says it’s in full compliance with the promises it made as part of an Investment Canada Act review that allowed its purchase of Stelco in 2024.

The company also says Stelco has requested a meeting between Joly and Goncalves to talk about a path toward resuming full employment for workers who have been temporarily laid off.

Joly told reporters Tuesday that the government wants a plan to bring back laid off workers before she will sit down with the head of Cleveland-Cliffs.

She says the Ohio-based company has not respected its binding commitments, including a five-year commitment to maintain at least the same number of unionized workers and most non-unionized employees as when the deal was struck.

Joly says Ottawa could still take the company to court to enforce its commitments, seek financial penalties or require the sale of Stelco.

Cleveland-Cliffs has rejected Ottawa’s allegations, maintaining that it has met all its commitments.

“The facts are clear,” Goncalves said in a statement. “We made serious commitments to Canada when we acquired Stelco, and we have honoured them.”

He added that Stelco is in full compliance with all undertakings and in several important areas has even gone beyond what it committed to do.

“For galvanized products, the imports of non-automotive galvanized steel that continue to flood the Canadian market remain problematic,” he said

“We want to find a solution for Hamilton and its workers as soon as possible and believe common sense trade policy will make this a reality.”

Joly has accused Cleveland-Cliffs of failing to honour six binding commitments made when it purchased the Ontario steelmaker.

The minister has said the company must address its alleged violations, prove it has not broken its commitments or explain why it has failed to meet them.

However, in a letter to Joly, the company says it’s in full compliance with each of its 34 undertakings, including its promises regarding employment levels.

The company says Stelco will update its compliance report following the Oct. 31 close of the current reporting period.

stories.title: Hockey Canada brings back Order of Hockey in Canada after multi-year hiatus
stories.summary: Calgary — Hockey Canada is bringing back the Order of Hockey in Canada after a multi-year hiatus.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Calgary — Hockey Canada is bringing back the Order of Hockey in Canada after a multi-year hiatus.

A new nine-member selection committee, chaired by hockey broadcaster and producer John Shannon, will select three honourees each year based on their contributions to the growth and development of hockey in Canada.

Established in 2012, the Order of Hockey in Canada has recognized 36 individuals for their contributions to the sport. The most recent class was inducted in June 2022, one month after sexual assault allegations involving members of Canada’s 2018 world junior team became public.

The Class of 2026 is expected to be announced in the coming weeks.

The new selection committee includes four previous recipients: retired women’s hockey players Jayna Hefford (also executive vice-president of hockey operations for the Professional Women’s Hockey League), Angela James and France St-Louis, as well as former men’s hockey player Steve Yzerman.

The other members are Shannon, Pittsburgh Penguins general manager Kyle Dubas, Canadian para hockey captain Tyler McGregor, Own the Podium chief executive officer Anne Merklinger and Shawn Redmond, vice-president and general manager of Bell Media Sports.

“The Order of Hockey in Canada is an important initiative to celebrate some of the incredible and inspiring individuals who have positively impacted our National Winter Sport, and we are thrilled to announce its return,” said Katherine Henderson, president and chief executive officer of Hockey Canada, in a statement.

Shannon said the committee understands how significant the honour is to Canadians.

“As we look towards announcing the Class of 2026 and beyond, we know that telling the stories of the distinguished honourees will be extremely valuable to humanizing their accomplishments, and we couldn’t be more proud to begin our work,” he said in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Nova Scotia Power CEO Vivek Sood departing after less than a year on the job
stories.summary: Nova Scotia Power Inc. CEO Vivek Sood is leaving his post at the province’s privately owned utility less than a year after taking its top job.
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Nova Scotia Power Inc. CEO Vivek Sood is leaving his post at the province’s privately owned utility less than a year after taking its top job.

Sood became the Emera Inc. subsidiary’s chief executive in March 2026.

Nova Scotia Power said in a news release Tuesday that Sood has decided not to renew his contract.

The company says Chris Smith, its current executive vice-president of finance and commercial, will take over as CEO on Nov. 2.

Sood took the job when Nova Scotia Power was dealing with the fallout of a cyberattack that saw the personal information of hundreds of thousands of customers accessed by hackers.

He also stickhandled a contentious power rate hearing that will see a combined hike of seven per cent when the second of two price increases takes effect in January.

stories.title: Joly demands Cliffs come up with plan to restore Stelco jobs as condition for meeting
stories.summary: On Monday, U.S.-based Stelco owner said it believes it remains in compliance with Ottawa’s rules after announcing layoffs
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is demanding Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N come up with a plan to restore jobs at Stelco Inc. as a condition for meeting after she threatened to take the U.S. steelmaker to court for allegedly violating the terms of its 2024 acquisition of the company.

Ms. Joly was responding early Tuesday to the latest letter sent by Cliffs to her office on Monday. Ohio-based Cliffs said in a statement on Monday that it requested a meeting with her on Oct. 23 to “discuss a path toward resuming full employment” of 175 Hamilton workers who have been laid off.

Speaking to reporters in Ottawa before a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Ms. Joly said that she was willing to meet with Cliffs, but she made a stern demand.

“First and foremost, what I want is a plan to bring back the jobs, and I want a timeline,” she said. ”And of course, I’m always willing to sit down, but that’s the first condition."

On Sept. 28, Stelco announced that it was laying off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont. Not all of the layoffs have taken effect yet.

Late Monday, Cliffs reiterated in a statement that it believes it is complying with all of the promises it made to Ottawa as a condition for being allowed to acquire Stelco in 2024.

Cliffs said it expects Stelco’s “average annual employment” to be at least 1,879 for its unionized employees, which is 113 above the required level of 1,766. Salaried employment is expected to average at least 627 people, compared with the minimum requirement of 603, Cliffs said.

By reporting the average employment level for the 12-month period, and not the latest numbers, Cliffs appears to have leeway to lay off workers in Canada and still meet the minimum threshold allowed over the course of a year.

The Globe and Mail reached out to both Cliffs and Ms. Joly’s office for further clarification, but did not receive an answer.

Cliffs chief executive officer Lourenco Goncalves said in an interview on BNN Bloomberg this month that the company plans to report its annual job figures for Stelco to Ottawa in November, and said the company “will be in compliance” with its obligations.

Ms. Joly reaffirmed on Tuesday that the government believes Cliffs is in violation of its “undertakings” – the legally-binding promises it made in 2024.

Apart from allegedly not meeting its undertakings around job commitments, Cliffs did not live up to promises made around promoting free trade in steel between Canada and the United States, she said.

“They had a clear commitment to make sure that there would be advocating in favour of tariff-free access of Canadian steel to the U.S. and they’ve done completely the contrary.”

In her letter to Stelco last week, Ms. Joly pointed to multiple examples of Mr. Goncalves advocating against Canada after the U.S. imposed tariffs on steel imports last year, including several instances of him giving kudos to U.S. President Donald Trump for introducing them.

Ms. Joly has said multiple times over the past few weeks that Cliffs could face a lawsuit, and be forced to divest Stelco. On Thursday, she said she knew of potential buyers interested in acquiring Stelco.

But the Official Opposition doesn’t believe this is enough.

Conservative MP Michael Guglielmin, a former operations manager in the steel sector, said during question period on Tuesday that the Liberal government needs to be more aggressive in its approach against Cliffs.

“The government continues issuing warnings instead of taking legal action,” he said. “Enough letters, enough deadlines, it’s time to act.”

Cliffs boss Mr. Goncalves has repeatedly characterized the layoffs at Stelco as “temporary.” He has vowed to recall workers if Ottawa can reach a new deal with the U.S. that would see the steel tariffs either eliminated or fall significantly. He has blamed the closure of Stelco’s galvanized business on the 50-per-cent tariffs imposed by Washington, which he maintains have made it impossible for the company to compete in the U.S.

stories.title: Carney says Ottawa's Indian Act review might not end up abolishing the law
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney says a process to review the Indian Act won't necessarily lead to the controversial legislation's termination.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A new process to review the Indian Act won’t necessarily lead to the controversial law’s termination, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday as an activist with the Idle No More movement warned his government to tread carefully.

On Monday, during a historic gathering of federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in Ottawa, the prime minister said he was “very open to” the idea of abolishing the Indian Act.

The law, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do.

The Indian Act also dismantled traditional forms of governance and, at one point, outlawed ceremonial practices.

It even affects First Nations people after they die. The Indigenous Services minister is required to approve wills for people living on reserve and has the power to void them altogether.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, called for the repeal of the Indian Act during a break in the meeting in Ottawa on Monday.

Kinew, a member of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, held up his own First Nations status card and said abolishing the Indian Act should be high on the national political agenda. He said his proposal received an “open-minded reception” from other leaders in the closed-door meeting.

Previous prime ministers have tried and failed to reform or get rid of the Indian Act. In 1969, years before he became prime minister, Jean Chrétien introduced what was known as the “White Paper” when he was minister of Indian Affairs in the government of Pierre Trudeau.

The document called for the abolition of the Indian Act, an end to Indian status, the absorption of First Nations people as ordinary Canadian citizens, the termination of treaties and the privatization of reserve lands.

The proposal received widespread pushback from First Nations leaders led in part by Harold Cardinal and the Indian Association of Alberta. They called Chrétien’s plan assimilationist and warned it would lead to the erasure of their cultures.

“I’m sure that we were very naive in some of the statements we made in the paper. We had perhaps the prejudices of small ‘l’ liberals, and white men at that, who thought that equality meant the same law for everybody,” Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau said at the time.

“We have learned in the process that perhaps we were a bit too theoretical, we were a bit too abstract, we were not, as Mr. Cardinal suggests, perhaps pragmatic enough, or understanding enough, and that’s fine.”

Carney said the federal government will work with First Nations and the provinces and territories to review the Indian Act and suggest possible replacements for it.

“The suggestion of reforming, potentially abolishing and fully modernizing governance, is that a process, co-developed, needs to be put in place, and the federal government is open to that process,” Carney said Monday.

Carney agreed with Kinew that the idea of abolishing or modernizing the Indian Act was discussed openly in Monday’s meeting and said he was “very open to” the proposal.

“Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So it’s already starting from the right place in that it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done. It’s responding to a request,” Carney said.

Most First Nations chiefs agree the Indian Act is outdated and restrictive, but there is little consensus on what should replace it.

The main conversation about the Indian Act for the past year has been about how it determines status. The vast majority of First Nations agree that the federal government should move to a one-parent rule for passing on status rights.

But Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has signalled that approach will not be adopted by her government, despite calls from opposition parties in the House of Commons and the Senate for her to do so.

There are policies in place if a First Nation decides to opt out of the Indian Act and move toward self-government.

Gull-Masty’s community, the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi, is one of those self-governing communities under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement — the first modern land claim in Canada and one in which Chrétien played a leading role.

Talk of reforming or abolishing the Indian Act comes as Carney works to speed up development of major projects alongside the provinces and Indigenous Peoples.

His government’s Building Canada Act initially gave Ottawa the power to sidestep the Indian Act. That provision was removed in response to calls from the Conservatives and the Bloc Québécois.

Janice Makokis, a lawyer and Idle No More organizer, said the current talk of abolishing the Indian Act is an echo of federal efforts decades earlier that triggered unrest among First Nations people and leaders.

“We must scrutinize whether the language of modernization and economic partnership is being used to shift power away from our nations while opening our territories to development,” she said in the foyer of the House of Commons.

“Our rights existed before the Indian Act, they do not depend on the Indian Act. But abolishing it without a process directed by First Nations themselves risks another era of paternalism, of Canada deciding what our freedom should look like then writing the rules for us.”

Conservative MP Ellis Ross, the former chief councillor of the Haisla Nation in British Columbia, called the entire proposal a costly exercise that’s unlikely to lead to meaningful change.

“I can see this going on for years, and the academics making a career out of this, the lawyers making a career out of this, and it’ll go on and on,” Ross told The Canadian Press.

Ross said there are already ways for First Nations to exit the Indian Act or make it work in their favour. He said that when he led the Haisla Nation, he focused on economic development instead of relying on Indian Act funding agreements.

“How do you get 600-plus bands in Canada to agree to this?” he said.

“Don’t get us involved in a decades-long dispute process unless you have something of substance to offer us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Bazinet winds Goderich mayoral race in a landslide
stories.summary: Here’s what you need to know about the candidates running in Central Huron Mayor , Huron East Mayor , Morris-Turnberry Mayor , South Huron Mayor , Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh Mayor , Howick Reeve , North Huron Reeve , Arran-Elderslie Mayor , Brockton Mayor , Kincardine Mayor , Northern Bruce Peninsula Mayor , South Bruce Mayor , Saugeen Shores Mayor , South…
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff, Scott Miller
stories.content:
Here’s what you need to know about the candidates running in Central Huron Mayor , Huron East Mayor , Morris-Turnberry Mayor , South Huron Mayor , Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh Mayor , Howick Reeve , North Huron Reeve , Arran-Elderslie Mayor , Brockton Mayor , Kincardine Mayor , Northern Bruce Peninsula Mayor , South Bruce Mayor , Saugeen Shores Mayor , South Bruce Peninsula Mayor , and Huron-Kinloss Mayor

In a landslide victory, capturing nearly 85 per cent of the vote, Trevor Bazinet has been elected mayor of the Town of Goderich.

“Yeah, it is a dream come true. In my high school yearbook, the graduating question was future ambitions, and I wrote I wanted to become the Mayor of the Town of Goderich. So, yeah, you can’t write it any better, right?” said Bazinet.

In front of a crowd of supporters at Steve and Mary’s on the Square in Goderich, Bazinet celebrated the beginning of what is technically his second term as Goderich’s mayor. While this is the first time he has been voted in by Goderich’s electorate, Bazinet has served as the town’s mayor since August 2023, following the death of then-mayor Myles Murdock.

“I’m now elected as the Mayor. Before I was appointed. And, you know, you never want to become the Mayor the way that I became the Mayor, losing a dear mentor and friend of mine in Myles Murdock. But, you know, I can officially say that I have been elected as the Mayor of the Town of Goderich,” he said.

Bazinet received 3,098 votes to runner-up Steve Buchanan’s 587 votes.

“My mom’s no longer with me. And like I said to the people behind me here, it’s a very emotional moment for me, because my mom said several years ago that you would make a great Mayor one day, Trevor. And here I am now, the Mayor of the Town of Goderich, elected Mayor. So I’m very proud. And I think of her often. And I’m thinking of her right now as I talk to you about it,” said Bazinet.

Randy Carroll was acclaimed deputy mayor of Goderich. Liz Petrie, Vanessa McMillan, John Thompson, Jacob Bjerg and Chris Garnier make up the rest of Goderich council. Garnier beat Charles Oliver by just two votes for the final council seat, according to the unofficial results released by the Town of Goderich.

In a landslide victory, capturing nearly 85 per cent of the vote, Trevor Bazinet has been elected mayor of the Town of Goderich.

“Yeah, it is a dream come true. In my high school yearbook, the graduating question was future ambitions, and I wrote I wanted to become the Mayor of the Town of Goderich. So, yeah, you can’t write it any better, right?” said Bazinet.

In front of a crowd of supporters at Steve and Mary’s on the Square in Goderich, Bazinet celebrated the beginning of what is technically his second term as Goderich’s mayor. While this is the first time he has been voted in by Goderich’s electorate, Bazinet has served as the town’s mayor since August 2023, following the death of then-mayor Myles Murdock.

“I’m now elected as the Mayor. Before I was appointed. And, you know, you never want to become the Mayor the way that I became the Mayor, losing a dear mentor and friend of mine in Myles Murdock. But, you know, I can officially say that I have been elected as the Mayor of the Town of Goderich,” he said.
Bazinet received 3,098 votes to runner-up Steve Buchanan’s 587 votes.

“My mom’s no longer with me. And like I said to the people behind me here, it’s a very emotional moment for me, because my mom said several years ago that you would make a great Mayor one day, Trevor. And here I am now, the Mayor of the Town of Goderich, elected Mayor. So I’m very proud. And I think of her often. And I’m thinking of her right now as I talk to you about it,” said Bazinet.

Randy Carroll was acclaimed deputy mayor of Goderich. Liz Petrie, Vanessa McMillan, John Thompson, Jacob Bjerg and Chris Garnier make up the rest of Goderich council. Garnier beat Charles Oliver by just two votes for the final council seat, according to the unofficial results released by the Town of Goderich.

stories.title: ‘Local, capable, proven leadership’: Jeff Kohler elected as St. Thomas mayor
stories.summary: Jeff Kohler elected as St. Thomas mayor
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff, Brent Lale
stories.content:
Here’s what you need to know about the candidates running in Bayham , Central Elgin , Dutton Dunwich , West Elgin , Aylmer , Malahide , and Southwold

St. Thomas, Ont., voters decided to go with a council veteran over a newcomer in the 2026 municipal election.

Jeff Kohler, who has spent 22 years at city hall as a former mayor, alderman and councillor, received nearly 70 per cent of the vote to win.

“Our message of local, capable, proven leadership definitely resonated out there,” said Kohler at his victory party.

“We’re going to start off right away with fiscal responsibility. We need to make sure we put forward some responsible budgets where we’re not impacting the people of today to benefit the people of tomorrow and without cutting services. So that’s going to be a challenge for us. But that’s what we’re looking forward to.”

Kohler, who is succeeding two-term mayor Joe Preston, will also be leading a new council.

Three incumbents, Earl Taylor, Joan Rymal and Jim Herbert, were ousted by three newcomers, Mike Brisson, Joe Docherty Jr. and Kyle Yates, while former mayor Heather Jackson was elected councillor. Gary Clarke, Rose Gibson, Steve Wookey and Lori Baldwin-Sands were also re-elected.

Kohler said some of the new members will quickly realize their campaign promises won’t all happen due to financial restraints.

“At the end of the day, our commitment is going to be to maintain the momentum that they have without cutting services and without impacting the rate they are today with high-impact tax increases,” said Kohler.

As St. Thomas enters one of the most crucial eras in the city’s history, Kohler will be the one to lead the way.

“We are experiencing growth that we haven’t seen for generations,” he said.

“That experience of leading through where we can’t say yes to everything, but what makes it happen? Our transit plan is coming forward. How are we going to improve that? How do we grow that in a responsible way, but not add to the tax impact on taxpayers right now? It’s tough for people, especially seniors on fixed incomes, and we don’t want to add to that pressure.”

stories.title: ‘Encouraging step forward’: Canadian ovarian cancer treatment clears funding hurdle
stories.summary: Elahere is a targeted treatment option for Canadians living with FRα-positive, platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
This is an update to a story Speakers Corner has been following for several months : a specialized chemotherapy treatment for women living with ovarian cancer is one step closer to being covered by public drug plans in Canada after the drug maker and the Pan Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance (pCPA) announced a deal.

It follows a months-long stalemate between the two parties to get Elahere (mirvetuximab soravtansine) approved for funding—an issue CityNews has been covering since June.

Elahere is a targeted treatment option for Canadians living with FRα-positive, platinum-resistant ovarian cancer and had already been approved by both the FDA and Health Canada for use. Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA-AMC) also recommends it be reimbursed by public drug plans.

“The completion of pCPA negotiations is an encouraging step forward and brings eligible patients closer to accessing a new treatment through public drug plans,” said Tania Vrionis with Ovarian Cancer Canada.

Vrionis says the next step is to now work with provincial and territorial governments to support public reimbursement of the treatment for patients. While there’s no forecasted timeline, Vrionis says she and her members will be adding pressure to get through that process quickly.

“Women with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer don’t have time to wait. It’s critical to move this forward through the additional steps as quickly as possible,” Vrionis said.

stories.title: Incumbent mayors unseated in Kincardine, South Huron as election night brings surprises across midwestern Ontario
stories.summary: Incumbent mayors in Exeter and Kincardine were unseated in two of the most surprising results of Monday night.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Incumbent mayors in Exeter and Kincardine were unseated in two of the most surprising results of Monday night.

Ken Craig did not win a second term as Kincardine mayor, falling to former reeve and Bruce MPP Barb Fisher. Craig secured 2,001 votes to Fisher’s 2,283. Voter turnout was the highest in the region at 49 per cent..

In South Huron, George Finch was seeking a third term as mayor but was unseated by longtime South Huron councillor Ted Oke. Finch received 1,516 votes to Oke’s 2,033.

Martin Ritsma was also unseated in Stratford, finishing third in the mayoral race. Robert Ritz won with 4,246 votes, while Ritsma received 2,899.

In one of the closest mayoral races of the night, Mitch Wright defeated Trevor Seip in the Municipality of North Huron, 863 votes to 842. Forty-two per cent of North Huron voters cast a ballot.

Results: Here’s what voters decided in Huron and Bruce counties

In the Municipality of Bluewater, which includes Bayfield, Paul Klopp won back the mayor’s seat, securing 2,415 votes to Tyler Hessel’s 1,073.

Alvin McLellan is the new mayor of the Municipality of Huron East, securing 1,883 votes. Con Melady finished second with 526 votes. Only 33 per cent of Huron East voters cast a ballot.

Evan Hickey is the new mayor of Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, receiving 2,322 votes to Ben Van Egmond’s 558.

In Huron-Kinloss, Don Murray retained the mayor’s chair with 2,175 votes. Shawn Plante received 909 votes.

Luke Charbonneau won a third term as mayor of Saugeen Shores, defeating two first-time candidates. Charbonneau received 3,983 votes, ahead of Brian Putnam with 2,753 and Jeff James with 1,155.

In Owen Sound, Richard Thomas will be the new mayor after a convincing victory over a large field of candidates.

stories.title: With snowfall patchy, this three-generation ski hill looks beyond winter
stories.summary: The family behind Harper Mountain in Kamloops recognizes that the business’s next chapter likely includes expanding into year-round offerings to reduce its dependence on cold weather
stories.author: Jessica Huras
stories.content:
For more than five decades, the Daburger family has built its business around something it cannot control: the weather. Harper Mountain, their 400-acre ski hill near Kamloops, B.C., has withstood uneven winters by operating leanly, maintaining older equipment and making the most of the snow on its north-facing slopes.

But their model is under growing pressure. The effects of climate change make winters harder to plan around. Rising insurance, fuel, labour and equipment costs mean the hill is more expensive to operate.

As the second-generation owners Norm and Lisa Daburger consider passing the enterprise to their two sons, the family recognizes that Harper’s next chapter likely includes a reinvention that expands the business into the warmer months to reduce its dependence on snowfall.

“As our winters become shorter and less predictable, the transition to an all-season resort with a more diverse revenue strategy seems to be almost inevitable,” says Max Daburger, 23, the grandson and namesake of the founder.

Indeed, with little warm-weather business beyond hosting events such as weddings at Harper, Max flies floatplanes in northern British Columbia during the summer and returns to the resort each winter to assist his parents Norm, 61, and Lisa, 62, with operations and maintenance. His brother Ryan, 22, is Harper’s operations manager but takes a separate tree-planting job out of town each spring, returning in summer to prepare for ski season.

Busy winters make up for the quiet summers. The enterprise employs about 60 people during peak season but just four in the slow months, leaving much of its infrastructure underused for part of the year.

Lisa oversees the ski school, rentals, human resources and hiring. Norm manages the mountain, equipment and business strategy. Lisa estimates she works 90 hours a week during winter. “What Norm and I do is the jobs of about four people,” she says.

That lean operating model helps Harper compete on price against larger destination resorts. The family performs much of its maintenance in-house, buys used machinery and acquires compatible parts when bigger hills replace well-maintained lifts. Harper’s fees have risen more slowly than inflation, although there is no avoiding increases altogether, Norm says.

“An advantage that we have at Harper is we are small, we run efficiently and our prices are cheaper,” he explains. “There are certainly some people who don’t ski anymore because of the price, but there are also people who were skiing at a big resort and were paying a higher price, and they’re now opting to ski at a smaller resort like ours that has fewer facilities.”

Christopher Nicolson, president and CEO of the Canada West Ski Areas Association (Cwsaa), says small operations such as Harper can respond quickly to changing demand and keep infrastructure costs below those of destination resorts, allowing them to offer lower fees.

Unlike bigger enterprises, community ski hills depend primarily on locals and school groups rather than travellers, he says. Many customers buy season passes and return week after week, making smaller hills a recurring gathering place rather than an occasional getaway. “In many cases, they are kind of the de facto recreation centre,” Mr. Nicolson says.

Canadian ski areas recorded 19.5 million visits during the 2024-2025 season, up 8.6 per cent from the previous winter, according to Cwsaa. The Daburgers say increased visits have helped offset rising costs because many of Harper’s core expenses remain relatively constant once the hill is operating.

“You spend the same amount of money whether you have 20 people on the hill or if you have 2,000,” Lisa says. Harper records 18,000 to 22,000 skier visits yearly.

The facility opened in 1973 with a T-bar, handle tow and Bavarian-style lodge built from logs cleared from the property. The senior Max Daburger and his business partner financed its development largely through Max’s construction company. “We invested everything we had,” says Max’s widow, Elisabeth, 89.

The partner died in an accident in 1977, leaving Max to oversee the hill alone. Over the decades, the Daburgers depended on a small circle of relatives and long-term employees to operate Harper. Elisabeth managed the books and sold tickets, while the Daburgers’ five sons, including Norm, grew up helping wherever necessary.

stories.title: Ontario delayed inspections of 2 career colleges later given ‘fails’: court docs
stories.summary: Critics say it points to severe mismanagement of public money and the government has made the wrong people pay the price.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario delayed inspections of two career colleges that ultimately turned up serious concerns about student financial aid use, which meant the schools received a “fail” only after they had been approved for funding for another year, court records show.

Critics say it points to severe mismanagement of public money and the government has made the wrong people pay the price.

The Ministry of Colleges and Universities sent Academy of Learning locations in Toronto on Bay Street and in Brampton East notices of inspection on Oct. 1, 2024, according to court records, but did not start the in-person inspections until July and August of 2025, respectively.

“I apologize for the delay, which was due to transitions in roles and the implementation of new inspection procedures,” a ministry official wrote in an email to the Brampton East location, looking to schedule an on-site inspection.

That was four days after the schools were sent ministry notices approving their ability to accept Ontario Student Assistance Program-funded tuition for another year.

Correspondence between the schools and the ministry is among hundreds of pages of documents filed in court as Academy of Learning seeks judicial review of the ministry’s ultimate decision in 2026 to bar them from OSAP eligibility for a year, a ban that has now been extended to 2030.

Concerns about OSAP activity at the schools have been raised by various groups and governments, but no misuse has been proven in court. The schools deny allegations that anything improper occurred and have implemented a long list of corrective actions.

Their OSAP approval in 2025 came despite warnings months earlier from both the federal government and the industry’s own association, Career Colleges Ontario. That organization wrote a letter to the ministry in January 2025, flagging “irregularities” in OSAP usage at 10 schools, including the two Academy of Learning locations.

Growth in OSAP applications at most career colleges was flat between 2022 and 2024, Career College Ontario wrote, but the Bay location saw growth of 642 per cent, and Brampton East saw 527 per cent.

In May of 2025, the federal government told the province about serious concerns with those schools. As the federal government detailed to the schools a few months later, those concerns included unusually rapid growth and “evidence of systematic irregularities.”

The schools have said that instead of being viewed as an indicator of risk, growth represents “a reflection of program relevance, responsiveness to workforce needs, and public confidence in the institution’s delivery of quality education.”

Court records show the provincial inspections ultimately found, in September for the Bay location and in March 2026 for the Brampton East location, evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program.

Students may not have responded to the federal government’s verification attempts because they believed them to be scam calls, and other students having difficulty answering questions in interviews “can be reasonably attributed to situational and linguistic factors,” the school wrote in response to the government.

The Academy of Learning also suggests the government is interpreting IP address data incorrectly. Unusually rapid course completion warrants review, they have said.

Successful OSAP applications at those two schools, which share a parent company, totalled $173 million in grants alone in 2024-25, according to data previously obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request. The number rises to $219 million when a North York location that is a branch of Brampton East is added.

In comparison, students at all publicly funded colleges across the province that year received $385 million in provincial grants.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn drastically reduced the amount of OSAP grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of “sustainability” as the program was facing rising costs. Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges.

Quinn has also now paused OSAP payments to students at all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions as his government and an outside firm conduct a broader review of the issue.

Liberal colleges and universities critic Tyler Watt said those actions make Quinn’s delayed action on potential bad actors all the more baffling.

“Their recent actions, where they’ve completely pulled the rug out from every single student in the private sector, goes to show you that they are willing to take drastic action,” he said.

“It’s not OK at all what they’ve done to students and the people that are following the rules, but there’s no reasonable explanation why they let this go on and wasted this much of taxpayers’ money for as long as they did.”

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said the government has failed students and the public.

“This amounts to severe mismanagement of public money by the Ford government,” he wrote in a statement. “For years, this government has been aware of private career colleges breaking the rules and has allowed them to continue to benefit from OSAP.”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said the government should have acted earlier on the numerous warnings it received.

“The government still dragged its heels on conducting the investigation that it is obligated to do and then blames students for misusing OSAP grants and punishes the entire sector for its own incompetence,” she said.

A spokesperson for Quinn said the inspection process can be long and in-depth.

“As we have stated, these inspections are multifaceted, and include reviewing data within the ministry’s possession, data requested from the institution that is provided to the ministry Inspectors, and in-person inspections,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

“Due to the technical nature of this process, inspections and subsequent investigations can take over a year. The ministry cannot presume the outcome of these investigations until all steps have been completed.”

OSAP applications at those schools actually went down in 2025-26, the province said in court filings. In the case of the Brampton East location, the number of OSAP recipients dropped by 34 per cent from the previous year, compared to growth of 1,347 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

The decline is timed around the start of the ministry’s in-person inspections, the government says in a document filed in court.

The Academy of Learning says no single factor explains that decline.

“We reject any suggestion that the decline reflects wrongdoing,” the schools wrote in a statement.

“Enrolment fell during a period of significant uncertainty, as students received repeated communications questioning their OSAP funding and our eligibility. Many chose to withdraw, postpone or not start their studies. In the same period, we ended some community partner arrangements and added verification measures.”

stories.title: Nova Scotia committee to discuss $10B AI data centre planned for Cape Breton
stories.summary: A committee of Nova Scotia’s legislature is scheduled to discuss the controversial $10-billion AI data centre that’s been proposed in Cape Breton.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
A committee of Nova Scotia’s legislature is scheduled to discuss the controversial $10-billion AI data centre that’s been proposed in Cape Breton.

EverWind Fuels announced on Oct. 16 that U.S. AI company Anthropic had signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre facility in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

Nova Scotia’s standing committee on natural resources and economic development will meet this afternoon and hear from EverWind Fuels officials.

The County of Richmond’s warden and chief administrative officer will also be appearing as witnesses.

Deputy ministers and directors from the Department of Energy and the Department of Environment and Climate Change are also scheduled to speak at the meeting.

Opposition parties have slammed Premier Tim Houston’s government over a lack of regulations for the massive AI data centre project.

They have raised concerns over potential impacts to the environment, local water supply and electricity rates.

stories.title: Federal government to introduce bill restricting Maid for mental illness
stories.summary: A news release from the Department of Justice says "rigorous safeguards" will be put in place for advance requests that follow a diagnosis of an incurable illness.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The federal government is set to introduce changes to Canada’s medical assistance in dying law Tuesday to bar people suffering solely from a mental illness from accessing Maid , and to allow for advance directives.

The government put the legislation on notice last week and Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Heath Minister Marjorie Michel are set to answer questions Tuesday about the proposed changes.

The amendments are being tabled almost three weeks after Fraser said the government would not be extending access to assisted dying to people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

The government has repeatedly pushed back the date when mental illness could become a qualifying factor for an assisted death and asked a special parliamentary committee to study the issue.

The committee’s conclusion, reported in June, said the government should indefinitely exclude people suffering solely from a mental illness from accessing Maid.

Following that report’s release, Fraser’s office reviewed the evidence the committee considered and sought additional opinions on the deeply divisive issue.

“When I hear that there is a lack of consensus within the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern,” Fraser said on Oct. 7.

He said he’s also heard concerns about a lack of access to mental health care and worries that people who can’t get help might turn to Maid instead.

Fraser also said the government would be using the new bill to decriminalize advance requests, allowing those at risk of losing their capacity to consent to an assisted death to do so ahead of time.

A news release from the Department of Justice says “rigorous safeguards” will be put in place for advance requests that follow a diagnosis of an incurable illness.

Advance requests are documents that allow a person who suffers from a degenerative condition, such as dementia or ALS, to ask that an assisted death be carried out once they no longer have the capacity to consent.

The strict eligibility rules for Maid require that a qualifying patient be suffering from a grievous and irremediable medical condition and be able to consent at the time of the procedure.

Advocates have argued that requirement means people who know they are going to lose their capacity to consent must choose to end their lives earlier than they would want.

Some critics have asked Fraser not to put both mental illness and advance requests into the same bill in order to give the government more time to consult. He has indicated no plans to do so.

Fraser has said the legal change on advance requests will only affect the Criminal Code and it will be up to provinces to decide whether to provide advance requests through their own health systems.

The proposed bill will need to pass the House of Commons and the Senate before March 17 — the date on which the law states people with a mental illness as their sole underlying condition would become eligible for Maid.

stories.title: Seller of six-bedroom Toronto house takes firm offer with a quick close
stories.summary: Detached home sells for $3.08-million after 24 hours on the market
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
127 Strathallan Blvd., Toronto

Asking price: $3,295,000 (July, 2026)

Selling price: $3,080,000 (July, 2026)

Previous selling price: $607,000 (June, 1987)

Taxes: $17,714 (2025)

Days on the market: One

Listing agent: Andre Kutyan, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

Agent Andre Kutyan judged that the land alone this 100-year-old house stood on was worth somewhere between $2.7-million and $3-million. The 50- by 135-foot lot is down the street from Lytton Park in a prime residential area. The long-time owners set the asking price at just under $3.3-million this summer.

“Strathallan Boulevard is probably the best street in Lytton Park, west of Avenue Road, because of the consistency of lot sizes and calibre of homes there,” said Mr. Kutyan.

“This house had wide appeal because, although older, it was very big and in good shape. Someone could live in it the way it is, renovate, or tear it down.”

The six-bedroom home had 26 visitors. After 24 hours on the market, three buyers presented competing bids. The best was $3.08-million, with possession in three weeks.

“Given what we’d seen, in terms of online activity and in-person showings, it had enough critical mass to get three offers,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“There were a lot of factors in why [the sellers] took an offer that was less money; It was firm, and the closing was quick.”

This detached house has 4,260 square feet of living space across three floors, including formal living and dining rooms, a family room addition and a breakfast room off the kitchen with access to a south-facing deck.

The home has five bathrooms, a main-floor laundry room and a basement kitchenette.

Outside, there is a driveway to park four cars.

“It’s a nice location midblock,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“It’s almost 6,000 square feet, including the lower level; it’s massive.”

stories.title: Free labour movement not part of new Canada-EU transatlantic pact, ambassador says
stories.summary: They are expected to use the summit later this week to announce a new agreement on a number of issues including labour, critical minerals and energy
stories.author: David Baxter and Emilie Bergeron
stories.content:
Negotiations toward a new transatlantic pact between Canada and the European Union don’t include discussions for a full-scale free labour movement, but something more focused, Canada’s EU ambassador said ahead of the Canada-EU summit later this week in Montreal.

Canada and the EU are expected to use the summit to announce a new agreement that could touch on a number of issues including labour, critical minerals and energy.

Jonathan Wilkinson, who took the Canadian ambassadorship in Brussels earlier this year after spending more than five years in the Liberal cabinet, told The Canadian Press in an interview the labour discussions are focusing on “specialized areas” where employers from both places can benefit from access to a shared labour pool.

He said any measures that would make it easier for workers and students to move between the two jurisdictions need to be approached in a “thoughtful way.”

“We’re not talking about free movement of labour between Europe and Canada. But what we are talking about is in some specialized areas, it May be actually interesting and useful for both countries to have the ability to tap into labour pools,” Wilkinson said.

The ambassador did not cite specific sectors where labour mobility between Canada and the EU could be eased. The EU and Canada have been discussing increased collaboration on critical minerals, technology, defence and clean energy.

Wilkinson pointed to work already done by Canada and Europe on mutual accreditation for architects and said any future decisions about labour mobility would be focused on areas of “mutual benefit.”

Canada has also discussed joining Erasmus+, the European Union’s student exchange program, which offers study and training opportunities in member nations.

The exact nature of the new pact between Canada and the EU has been murky even from the leaders themselves.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in September a new alliance could make Canada an “associate” member of the 27-member bloc.

But “associate membership” does not actually exist in the EU and Canadian officials have downplayed the use of that term.

Prime Minister Mark Carney used the term “alliance of the future” to describe the deal, which was first made public when he spoke to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France, last month.

This week’s summit will be happening on the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Canada-Europe Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or Ceta.

Nine EU members – France, Italy, Belgium, Ireland, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece and Hungary – have not yet ratified that trade deal.

Wilkinson said he’s spoken with all 27 of his EU member nation counterparts since he moved to Brussels and there is momentum in Europe to get more countries behind Ceta. He did not name specific nations.

“I think there are a number of countries that will be moving in that direction over the coming months. So that’s a process that will go along with the rest of this deepening of the relationship,” he said.

One of the EU’s leading nations May have a new government soon. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is the current polling favourite to succeed Emmanuel Macron as president this spring.

Le Pen delivered a nearly hour-long speech to supporters Sunday that focused on her party’s nationalist, anti-immigrant positions.

Wilkinson said politics is always dynamic and Europeans and Canadians will go on sharing values regardless of which party is in power in a particular nation.

“I think in France, it’s a very important debate that they are having. And I think that if in fact the government were to change, people will have to take stock of that,” he said.

“But I do think that the European Union is a much bigger project than any one government in any one country. And I have a lot of confidence that Europeans will find their way through this and be just fine.”

Wilkinson said energy and critical minerals – including natural gas, hydrogen and nuclear power – will play a crucial role in the enhanced partnership between Canada and the EU.

“We’re looking at … how can we, for example, encourage significant additional European investment in Canadian minerals projects. We’re talking about how can we think about things like stockpiling together so that we actually can help to stabilize the market,” Wilkinson said.

The European Investment Bank applied for an exemption from Canadian foreign banking rules earlier this month that would allow the state investor to operate in Canada as part of a critical minerals agreement.

Wilkinson said Canada and the European Union are both looking for ways to build up more infrastructure to refine and ship critical minerals and reduce China’s market dominance.

“That’s not a dependency that’s good for Canada. That’s not a dependency good for the European Union. So we are looking at that,” he said.

stories.title: Your governments are to blame for high gas prices: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: Canadians pay an average of $1.85 a litre, but that's less than Norway, the U.K., Australia and Mexico, where taxes are even higher.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada, a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

The next time you pull up to the gas pump and grumble about the soaring cost of filling up the tank, take solace you don’t live in Norway or Mexico.

Those two countries are among a number of energy-producing democratic nations whose gas prices are far higher than what Canadians pay, according to an analysis by Benchmark Canada, a Macdonald-Laurier Institute project that compares Canada with its peers.

Which doesn’t make it cheap. Canadians paid an average of about $1.85 a litre for gas by mid-October, the Benchmark Canada data shows, but that’s less than Norway, the United Kingdom, Australia and Mexico. Only Americans, who pay the cheapest at roughly $1.57 a litre in equivalent Canadian dollars, and Brazilians pay less for gas.

In almost all the countries surveyed, government taxes and policy are driving higher prices.

“The underlying cost of the commodity is roughly the same,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “It May vary slightly, but it’s all in taxes and potential rules and regulations.”

Taxes make up about 21 per cent of the Canadian pump price at normal rates (17 per cent if you take account of the federal excise tax, which is suspended until next January). In Norway, which has more oil per person than any other of the seven democracies highlighted by Benchmark Canada, they make up 51 per cent, the data showed. Again, American drivers enjoy the lowest gas tax at about 12 per cent.

Prices vary across the country due to various provincial taxes and regulations. Drivers in Alberta, which has suspended its provincial fuel tax, enjoy some of the cheapest gas in the country at $1.55 a litre, compared with $2.165 in Newfoundland and Labrador and $2.12 in Metro Vancouver, the Benchmark Canada data shows.

Canadians quickly falling behind on their mortgages: Benchmark Canada

There are other variables too. Dan McTeague, a former Liberal MP and president of Canadians for Affordable Energy who has carved out a niche analyzing gas price movements since 2015, said Benchmark Canada’s finding that roughly 20 per cent of prices come from taxes doesn’t include federal clean fuel regulations. Those regulations encourage energy suppliers to reduce their carbon footprint, either by buying carbon credits or blending in more ethanol to gasoline.

“There’s no way you can consider that this isn’t a tax,” said McTeague, whose has long campaigned against carbon pricing. His back-of-the-envelope math puts taxes and carbon-policy costs at roughly a quarter of the pump price in Ontario and Vancouver.

Global pricing also explains why being a major oil producer doesn’t help Canadians get cheaper gas.

“It’s a global commodity, not just a Canadian commodity,” De Haan said. “Just because it’s produced in Canada doesn’t mean it stays there.”

Nowadays, the Canadian dollar threatens to trade below the 70-cent mark against the greenback, which makes it more expensive to buy from gas refiners, which typically sell in U.S. dollars. The currency impact comes even as global oil prices soar past the $100-per-barrel mark, which typically helps oil producers in Western Canada and generally helps Canada’s so-called “petro-dollar.”

“I’ve been doing this for a long time, and never have I seen the Canadian dollar not respond to an energy crunch,” said McTeague. “It did this time. It refused to move.”

Figures from fuel-pricing firm Kalibrate show the average Canadian price at the pump was $1.843 a litre at the end of September, about 40 cents higher than it was a year earlier. Diesel prices are up more than a dollar per litre from a year earlier.

“Regardless of whether you drive or not, you’re paying more for everything,” McTeague said.

Barring any major global currency developments or a seismic change in geopolitical events that would send oil prices to new lows, the best way Canadians should expect to see some gas price relief would be through lower taxation.

In Eastern Canada, getting rid of the HST would be “the biggest target” for potential relief, because it’s a percentage tax that grows with the price, McTeague said. “You’re actually turbocharging the higher cost of energy,” he said. “There’s no rhyme or reason why that should still be there.”

De Haan doesn’t necessarily buy that tax relief would be a salve on the wallets of Canadian drivers. An easing of tensions between the U.S. and Iran, and between Russia and Ukraine, would be “the biggest overnight improvement,” he said.

De Haan also warns that cutting fuel taxes while supply is tight could spur demand, and wouldn’t necessarily solve the pricing problem.

“That would be probably the wrong time to lower fuel taxes,” he said.

Blaming the gas station company itself May be misguided as well. Gas stations typically post profit margins of roughly a dime a litre that are often whittled down to a few cents by the end of the day, McTeague said. The real money, he noted, is through selling coffee, car washes and snacks like candy or beef jerky.
