stories.title: How a new medical school in Surrey, B.C. could transform its downtown
stories.summary: The new school will serve Canada’s growing need for family medicine doctors
stories.author: David McPherson
stories.content:
Simon Fraser University in Surrey, B.C., will soon welcome its first class of future primary-care doctors at its new medical school in the city’s Central Business District.

Amid a countrywide doctor shortage, the SFU Stephens Family School of Medicine will do double duty: It will educate future physicians, while its new building will better integrate amenities in a growing city.

“[The development] brings higher education, health care, research, office and retail space together on one site next to Surrey Central Station,” says Bill Aujla, president and chief executive of the Surrey City Development Corp., a real estate development company. “That mix is what turns a city centre into a true downtown.”

Centre Block, a massive two-phased master plan for municipal land adjacent to the city’s Central SkyTrain Station and the former site of a now-demolished recreation centre, supports Surrey’s long-term vision for economic growth, innovation and education.

The development is expected to add roughly two million square feet of office and retail space. It’s also one of several infrastructure projects under way to meet the demands of the rising population of Surrey, one of Canada’s fastest-growing major cities.

Other continuing developments include the Newton Community Centre and a new 10,000-seat City Centre Arena as Surrey posts population growth averaging 10,877 people a year for the past five years, largely owing to immigration. Dubbed British Columbia’s “second downtown,” it’s on its way to surpassing Vancouver to become the province’s most populous city, with a projected population of 783,690 by 2041 .

Sfu’s Stephens Family School of Medicine is hoping to close the gaps in Canada’s health care system, with a long-term goal of educating and training more family-medicine practitioners.

According to the Canadian Medical Association , more than one in five Canadians don’t have a family doctor or nurse practitioner they see regularly.

“We saw the need for a medical school focused on family practice and primary care,” says Peter Hall, vice-provost and associate vice-president of academics at SFU.

Set to open in 2030, the new SFU medical school building will anchor downtown Surrey’s new Centre Block development, serving as a multiuse hub that’s easily accessible by transit.

It will occupy the former site of the North Surrey Recreation Centre, demolished in 2025 , and sit directly adjacent to the SFU Surrey campus and Surrey Central Station. It will also be located to the south of City Hall, a public plaza and the City of Surrey’s municipal hub.

“This site is an integral part to connecting that urban landscape together, as well as the bus and the SkyTrain transit systems to create a real active node and a sense of community,” says Darren Burns, vice-president of design and innovation for buildings at Stantec, the project’s architect-of-record and main consultant who jointly partnered with Revery Architecture on Centre Block.

Sfu’s Stephens Family School of Medicine is Western Canada’s first new med school since the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine was founded in 1967. It will take over seven floors of the 12-storey mixed-use development and feature retail at grade, in addition to four floors of office space for the City of Surrey.

“This Centre Block project aligns well with Surrey’s official community plan and the desire to have a civic hub and to expand an academic hub,” Mr. Burns says.

SFU already has a strong presence in Surrey’s city centre, with an academic campus that includes the School of Interactive Arts and Technology, the School of Mechatronic Systems Engineering and the School for Sustainable Energy Engineering.

The university’s new medical school will include high-tech classrooms, research spaces, administrative offices, an outpatient clinic and a 49-space child-care centre. The publicly accessible family outpatient clinic will occupy the second floor of the building and incorporate educational training and other community health services. Five floors of academic space will also sit directly above the clinic and right below Sfu’s dedicated floor for child care.

“The building is activated at the street level, at the pedestrian level and 360 degrees around to make it feel really connected and bring in the community,” Mr. Burns says.

The structure’s design looks like sculpted stacked buildings, similar to a Jenga game, that seamlessly blend with what’s happening inside the building, while connecting to downtown Surrey and the area’s exterior cityscape.

Inside the building, an open atrium will welcome visitors and is surrounded by multilevel gathering places, including dedicated Indigenous student spaces.

“We have an Indigenous consultant on our team to help with that engagement and to help with reaching out to the community,” Mr. Burns adds, saying the team has engaged with Indigenous knowledge keepers and a steering committee to incorporate Indigenous themes into the building.

As the university’s new urban campus grows in Surrey, Mr. Hall is hopeful that the school can secure funding to build additional student services such as health and wellness programs and housing.

“Our Surrey campus until now has been a bit fragmented,” says Mr. Hall, adding that the SFU is hoping the new med school building will provide a sense of identity, cohesion and integration.

He points to Britain’s University of London as a hub worth emulating as SFU intends for its new med school building to serve Surrey’s civic and business communities.

“The University of London prides itself on being halfway between the old commercial city of London and Westminster and acting as an integration point between commerce and government,” Mr. Hall says. “There May be something here, eventually, like that.”

Centre Block, a massive two-phased master plan for municipal land adjacent to the city’s Central SkyTrain Station and the former site of a now-demolished recreation centre, supports Surrey’s long-term vision for economic growth, innovation and education.

The development is expected to add roughly two million square feet of office and retail space. It’s also one of several infrastructure projects under way to meet the demands of the rising population of Surrey, one of Canada’s fastest-growing major cities.

Other continuing developments include the Newton Community Centre and a new 10,000-seat City Centre Arena as Surrey posts population growth averaging 10,877 people a year for the past five years, largely owing to immigration. Dubbed British Columbia’s “second downtown,” it’s on its way to surpassing Vancouver to become the province’s most populous city, with a projected population of 783,690 by 2041 .
Sfu’s Stephens Family School of Medicine is hoping to close the gaps in Canada’s health care system, with a long-term goal of educating and training more family-medicine practitioners.
According to the Canadian Medical Association , more than one in five Canadians don’t have a family doctor or nurse practitioner they see regularly.
“We saw the need for a medical school focused on family practice and primary care,” says Peter Hall, vice-provost and associate vice-president of academics at SFU.
Set to open in 2030, the new SFU medical school building will anchor downtown Surrey’s new Centre Block development, serving as a multiuse hub that’s easily accessible by transit.

It will occupy the former site of the North Surrey Recreation Centre, demolished in 2025 , and sit directly adjacent to the SFU Surrey campus and Surrey Central Station. It will also be located to the south of City Hall, a public plaza and the City of Surrey’s municipal hub.

“This site is an integral part to connecting that urban landscape together, as well as the bus and the SkyTrain transit systems to create a real active node and a sense of community,” says Darren Burns, vice-president of design and innovation for buildings at Stantec, the project’s architect-of-record and main consultant who jointly partnered with Revery Architecture on Centre Block.

Sfu’s Stephens Family School of Medicine is Western Canada’s first new med school since the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine was founded in 1967. It will take over seven floors of the 12-storey mixed-use development and feature retail at grade, in addition to four floors of office space for the City of Surrey.
“This Centre Block project aligns well with Surrey’s official community plan and the desire to have a civic hub and to expand an academic hub,” Mr. Burns says.

SFU already has a strong presence in Surrey’s city centre, with an academic campus that includes the School of Interactive Arts and Technology, the School of Mechatronic Systems Engineering and the School for Sustainable Energy Engineering.

The university’s new medical school will include high-tech classrooms, research spaces, administrative offices, an outpatient clinic and a 49-space child-care centre. The publicly accessible family outpatient clinic will occupy the second floor of the building and incorporate educational training and other community health services. Five floors of academic space will also sit directly above the clinic and right below Sfu’s dedicated floor for child care.
“The building is activated at the street level, at the pedestrian level and 360 degrees around to make it feel really connected and bring in the community,” Mr. Burns says.

The structure’s design looks like sculpted stacked buildings, similar to a Jenga game, that seamlessly blend with what’s happening inside the building, while connecting to downtown Surrey and the area’s exterior cityscape.
Inside the building, an open atrium will welcome visitors and is surrounded by multilevel gathering places, including dedicated Indigenous student spaces.

“We have an Indigenous consultant on our team to help with that engagement and to help with reaching out to the community,” Mr. Burns adds, saying the team has engaged with Indigenous knowledge keepers and a steering committee to incorporate Indigenous themes into the building.
As the university’s new urban campus grows in Surrey, Mr. Hall is hopeful that the school can secure funding to build additional student services such as health and wellness programs and housing.
“Our Surrey campus until now has been a bit fragmented,” says Mr. Hall, adding that the SFU is hoping the new med school building will provide a sense of identity, cohesion and integration.
He points to Britain’s University of London as a hub worth emulating as SFU intends for its new med school building to serve Surrey’s civic and business communities.

“The University of London prides itself on being halfway between the old commercial city of London and Westminster and acting as an integration point between commerce and government,” Mr. Hall says. “There May be something here, eventually, like that.”

stories.title: Ontario’s delayed inspections of two career colleges was after funding approval, records show
stories.summary: The schools received a ‘fail’ only after they had been approved for funding for another year
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario delayed inspections of two career colleges that ultimately turned up serious concerns about student financial aid use, which meant the schools received a “fail” only after they had been approved for funding for another year, court records show.

Critics say it points to severe mismanagement of public money and the government has made the wrong people pay the price.

The Ministry of Colleges and Universities sent Academy of Learning locations in Toronto on Bay Street and in Brampton East notices of inspection on Oct. 1, 2024, according to court records, but did not start the in-person inspections until July and August of 2025, respectively.

“I apologize for the delay, which was due to transitions in roles and the implementation of new inspection procedures,” a ministry official wrote in an e-mail to the Brampton East location, looking to schedule an on-site inspection.

That was four days after the schools were sent ministry notices approving their ability to accept Ontario Student Assistance Program-funded tuition for another year.

Correspondence between the schools and the ministry is among hundreds of pages of documents filed in court as Academy of Learning seeks judicial review of the ministry’s ultimate decision in 2026 to bar them from Osap eligibility for a year, a ban that has now been extended to 2030.

Concerns about Osap activity at the schools have been raised by various groups and governments, but no misuse has been proven in court. The schools deny allegations that anything improper occurred and have implemented a long list of corrective actions.

Their Osap approval in 2025 came despite warnings months earlier from both the federal government and the industry’s own association, Career Colleges Ontario. That organization wrote a letter to the ministry in January 2025, flagging “irregularities” in Osap usage at 10 schools, including the two Academy of Learning locations.

Growth in Osap applications at most career colleges was flat between 2022 and 2024, Career College Ontario wrote, but the Bay location saw growth of 642 per cent, and Brampton East saw 527 per cent.

In May of 2025, the federal government told the province about serious concerns with those schools. As the federal government detailed to the schools a few months later, those concerns included unusually rapid growth and “evidence of systematic irregularities.”

The schools have said that instead of being viewed as an indicator of risk, growth represents “a reflection of program relevance, responsiveness to work force needs, and public confidence in the institution’s delivery of quality education.”

Court records show the provincial inspections ultimately found, in September for the Bay location and in March, 2026 for the Brampton East location, evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework – sometimes entire courses in one day – and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program.

Students May not have responded to the federal government’s verification attempts because they believed them to be scam calls, and other students having difficulty answering questions in interviews “can be reasonably attributed to situational and linguistic factors,” the school wrote in response to the government.

The Academy of Learning also suggests the government is interpreting IP address data incorrectly. Unusually rapid course completion warrants review, they have said.

Successful Osap applications at those two schools, which share a parent company, totalled $173-million in grants alone in 2024-25, according to data previously obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request. The number rises to $219-million when a North York location that is a branch of Brampton East is added.

In comparison, students at all publicly funded colleges across the province that year received $385-million in provincial grants.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn drastically reduced the amount of Osap grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of “sustainability” as the program was facing rising costs. Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges.

Quinn has also now paused Osap payments to students at all career colleges and other private postsecondary institutions as his government and an outside firm conduct a broader review of the issue.

Liberal colleges and universities critic Tyler Watt said those actions make Quinn’s delayed action on potential bad actors all the more baffling.

“Their recent actions, where they’ve completely pulled the rug out from every single student in the private sector, goes to show you that they are willing to take drastic action,” he said.

“It’s not OK at all what they’ve done to students and the people that are following the rules, but there’s no reasonable explanation why they let this go on and wasted this much of taxpayers’ money for as long as they did.”

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said the government has failed students and the public.

“This amounts to severe mismanagement of public money by the Ford government,” he wrote in a statement. “For years, this government has been aware of private career colleges breaking the rules and has allowed them to continue to benefit from Osap.”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said the government should have acted earlier on the numerous warnings it received.

“The government still dragged its heels on conducting the investigation that it is obligated to do and then blames students for misusing Osap grants and punishes the entire sector for its own incompetence,” she said.

A spokesperson for Quinn said the inspection process can be long and in-depth.

“As we have stated, these inspections are multifaceted, and include reviewing data within the ministry’s possession, data requested from the institution that is provided to the ministry Inspectors, and in-person inspections,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

“Due to the technical nature of this process, inspections and subsequent investigations can take over a year. The ministry cannot presume the outcome of these investigations until all steps have been completed.”

Osap applications at those schools actually went down in 2025-26, the province said in court filings. In the case of the Brampton East location, the number of Osap recipients dropped by 34 per cent from the previous year, compared to growth of 1,347 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

The decline is timed around the start of the ministry’s in-person inspections, the government says in a document filed in court.

The Academy of Learning says no single factor explains that decline.

“We reject any suggestion that the decline reflects wrongdoing,” the schools wrote in a statement.

“Enrolment fell during a period of significant uncertainty, as students received repeated communications questioning their Osap funding and our eligibility. Many chose to withdraw, postpone or not start their studies. In the same period, we ended some community partner arrangements and added verification measures.”

stories.title: A chance for B.C. to step back from the fiscal brink
stories.summary: The newly elected Conservatives need to show a plan for getting control of the province’s debt spiral
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
David Eby, inadvertently, did British Columbia an enormous favour in his fateful and politically fatal gamble on an early election call. The decisive rejection of the BC NDP in Saturday’s vote spares the province two more years of fiscal malpractice by Mr. Eby and his party.

Under the NDP, the deficit has soared to record heights , the debt burden is accelerating and the province has amassed a string of credit downgrades. There were many reasons for the defeat of the NDP in the Oct. 24 vote, but the utter lack of fiscal discipline by the Eby government – a marked and disappointing contrast to the NDP under the late John Horgan – was part of the mix.

Now, it will fall to the BC Conservatives, and premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, to fix what Mr. Eby, who resigned as BC NDP Leader on Saturday, has broken. As we wrote ahead of the vote, Mr. Doerkson has not yet presented a cohesive plan for restoring sanity to B.C.’s finances. (The party’s release of its full platform late in the campaign did little to fill in any blanks.)

He will need to do so, soon. On Sunday, Mr. Doerkson said one of his first acts in office will be to commission an independent review of B.C.’s finances. Incoming governments are typically shocked, so very shocked, to discover that their predecessors somehow cooked the books. A truly arms-length review of the province’s budget could be helpful in avoiding that partisan buck-passing.

Whatever the verdict, the Conservatives face some difficult choices, made all the harder by some ill considered campaign commitments, most notably a pledge to cut most taxpayers’ bills by $1,000 by boosting the basic personal exemption. It’s a tax cut that B.C. simply cannot afford.

But it’s unlikely that the Conservatives will abandon one of their marquee promises. In addition, the party has pledged to not increase taxes. (However, the Conservatives have not said they will undo the Ndp’s de-indexing of personal income tax brackets for the next four years, a stealth tax hike that will deliver hundreds of millions in revenue during that time.) And Mr. Doerkson has said he will not cut back services. If anything, his rhetoric around health care points to increased expenditures.

The Conservative plan to reduce the deficit leans heavily on economic growth, a triumph of wishful thinking over fiscal experience. Mr. Doerkson will need to do more than hope that a rising economy floats a surplus his way.

Luckily for him, so to speak, the NDP has bequeathed him the means. There are substantial savings waiting to be wrung out of core government operations. Under the NDP, the core bureaucracy (a measure that excludes front-line workers such as nurses and teachers) soared by 41 per cent between 2018 and the current fiscal year, or by more than 14,000 jobs.

The Conservatives are stuck with the bill for the the Ndp’s capitulation to public sector unions’ wage demands. But they can, and should, take action to roll back the size of the bureaucracy. The NDP, for its part, had sketched out its intention to start to undo its hiring spree in coming years.

An effort to downsize the bureaucracy, and a focus on simply not spraying cash in all directions, should start to turn British Columbia away from its current perilous fiscal path.

Those public sector unions will not surrender meekly. B.C.’s storied history of tumultuous labour relations is about to get a new chapter. Expect many a press conference about the horrendous effects of heartless Conservative cuts.

B.C. residents should keep a couple of realities in mind. One is not to mistake the fire department for the person who set the house ablaze. It is the NDP – specifically the Eby government – that has run up the deficit, handed outsized raises to the bureaucracy and undermined decades of fiscal restraint. That includes undermining Mr. Horgan’s prudent fiscal stewardship. The Conservatives inherit the privilege of cleaning up the mess.

The other reality is that the Conservatives can deliver modest austerity now, or British Columbia can experience a hard-edged version a few years down the line, dictated by bond markets. The warning signs, in the form of multiple credit downgrades, could scarcely be any clearer.

The Conservatives have won power, earlier than anyone, themselves included, could have expected. Mr. Doerkson’s government has an opportunity to restore British Columbia’s finances to their customary prudent state. We look forward to hearing how he proposes to do so.

stories.title: Results from mayoral races in major Ontario cities
stories.summary: Alvin Tedjo pulled off a victory in Mississauga, Keanin Loomis declared victory in Hamilton and Mark Sutcliffe cruised to re-election in Ottawa
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
Municipal elections in Ontario toppled some incumbents, elevated new names and returned some familiar faces to city halls across the province.

Monday’s vote was headlined by the mayoral race in the country’s biggest city, where Toronto’s Olivia Chow fended off challenger councillor Brad Bradford to win re-election.

Here are the results from five other mayoral races from around Ontario.

In one of the night’s biggest upsets, Alvin Tedjo pulled off a victory in Mississauga.

Tedjo, a city councillor and former Ontario Liberal leadership hopeful, defeated incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.

Tedjo, who finished second in the 2024 mayoral by-election, started out as a longshot but began to rise in the polls as the front-runners clashed, culminating in a heated back-and-forth between Parrish and Crombie at a debate earlier this month.

Tedjo will now be expected to make good on a platform headlined by a promise to freeze property taxes for two years, and allow certain seniors to defer that tax bill until they sell or transfer their home.

It’s another disappointing setback for Crombie, who left Mississauga’s top job in 2024 after she took over as Ontario Liberal leader. The party added seats in the 2025 snap provincial election but fell short of expectations, and Crombie resigned as leader in January of this year.

Keanin Loomis, CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, declared victory after garnering more than 40 per cent of the vote with the majority of polls reporting Monday night.

He unseated incumbent Andrea Horwath, who trailed in third place.

The race was a rematch of the 2022 contest, when Loomis lost to Horwarth by just 1,663 votes.

The race in Hamilton was held under the shadow of layoffs at Stelco, a U.S.-owned steelmaker.

Mark Sutcliffe cruised to re-election in Ottawa.

Sutcliffe’s main challenge came from Jeff Leiper, a longtime councillor who ran as the progressive alternative to the incumbent mayor.

But voters stuck with Sutcliffe, who pledged to keep property taxes low, maintain a hiring freeze on non-front-line workers and create free trade with neighbouring Gatineau.

Patrick Brown, the former Progressive Conservative leader, easily won his re-election bid.

Brown had secured a majority of the votes with most polls reporting Monday night.

He ran on a platform of more front-line policing and stronger action on extortion and auto theft, along with expanded transit and health-care facilities.

Brown took over the city’s top job in 2018 in the aftermath of sexual misconduct allegations that led to his resignation as PC leader. He has vehemently denied those allegations and no criminal charges were ever laid.

The winds of change were blowing in southwestern Ontario.

Windsor, the tariff-vulnerable capital of Canada’s auto sector, elected Fred Francis.

The city councillor put an end to incumbent Drew Dilkens’ 12-year tenure as mayor, in an election that took place amid the U.S.-Canada trade war.

Francis, the younger brother of former mayor Eddie Francis, pledged to hold the line on taxes, make city hall more transparent, eliminate strong mayor powers and cap transit fees.

stories.title: Toronto election 2026: Who’s in and who’s out at city hall
stories.summary: Toronto voters elected seven new councillors Monday, defeating several incumbents and returning one former councillor to City Hall.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto voters elected seven new councillors Monday, defeating several incumbents and returning one former councillor to city hall.

Longtime councillor Frances Nunziata and mayoral candidate Brad Bradford are among those leaving council, while former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith and former councillor Mike Layton are among the incoming members. Eighteen incumbents were returned to council.

Bradford lost his mayoral bid to Olivia Chow, who will serve her first full term as mayor after winning the 2023 mayoral byelection.

Here’s the full list of who’s in and who’s out at Toronto City Hall, along with the councillors returning to office.

Diana Chan McNally will represent Ward 4 Parkdale-High Park. The ward was previously represented by longtime councillor Gord Perks, who retired earlier this year.

After multiple attempts at securing the job, Chiara Padovani will replace Nunziata – the longest-serving member of city council – as the councillor for Ward 5 York South-Weston.

Former councillor Mike Layton is returning to city hall as the representative for Ward 11 University-Rosedale. The seat was vacated by Dianne Saxe, who ran in Ward 14 Toronto-Danforth.

Curran Stikuts will represent Ward 13 Toronto Centre, taking over the job from incumbent Chris Moise.

Sara Ehrhardt will become councillor for Ward 14 Toronto-Danforth. It was previously represented by Paula Fletcher, who announced her retirement this summer. Saxe finished third in the race.

Nate Erskine-Smith, a former MP who sought the leadership of the Ontario Liberal Party earlier this year, will represent Ward 19 Beaches-East York – the seat vacated by Bradford.

Former Liberal MP Shaun Chen, who resigned from federal politics in August citing lingering health effects from a car crash, will represent Ward 23 Scarborough North – defeating incumbent Jamaal Myers.

stories.title: Edmonton judge rejects 'unhinged' sentence proposed for Indigenous stabber
stories.summary: The defence and Crown both recommended a sentence of 180 days in jail for the assault. Instead, the judge tripled that to 18 months.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Edmonton judge has rejected a joint sentence recommendation as “unhinged” for an Indigenous man who stabbed a stranger in the buttocks during a group mugging less than two months after he was released on bail on conditions prohibiting him from possessing any weapons.

Shaye Riley Bird, who still had the bloody knife on him, as well as blood on his pants when police picked him up, pleaded guilty in Alberta’s Court of Justice to the May 3, 2026, assault causing bodily harm and breaching the conditions of his release in March. Both his defence lawyer and the Crown recommended Bird get 180 days in jail for the assault, and another 30 days to be served concurrently, for the bail breach.

“This case features several errors in principle. They result in a proposition that constitutes one of those rare instances — a joint submission that is unhinged from what would be reasonable,” Justice Steven Bilodeau wrote in an Oct. 21 decision.

The judge concluded he could not accept the recommended sentence for three reasons.

“First, it does not adequately reflect the gravity of this random group attack with a knife,” Bilodeau said.

“Second, it gives no meaningful effect to the serious and lasting impact upon the victim. Third, the proposed concurrent sentence leaves the separate breach of the weapons condition without any meaningful sanction.”

Instead, the judge sentenced Bird to 18 months in jail — 14 months for the assault and another four months for the bail breach to be served consecutively — tripling the recommendation from defence and Crown lawyers, while noting “it is no small thing” to reject their joint submission.

Bird’s “conduct bears many of the hallmarks of a street mugging,” Bilodeau said. “It has been long-settled law in Alberta that these merit significant incarceration if they are to be deterred effectively, if at all.”

The attack was “perpetrated by a group or mob,” said the judge. “Being outnumbered changes the entire dynamic of the assault.”

The bail breach would have been serious if Bird had “merely been found carrying a pocketknife,” Bilodeau said. “Instead, he was found with what was effectively a hunting knife, covered in the victim’s blood, which he admits he used to stab the victim. It is hard to imagine a more significant breach of the order.”

The court heard that Bird was with a group of other people at Churchill Square on the evening of May 3. They approached a man wearing headphones at 9:12 p.m. and attacked him.

“During this assault the victim was stabbed with a knife in his buttocks causing a one-inch wound that bled heavily. The assailants took the victim’s headphones, which were worth about $100, and fled the scene,” the judge said.

The victim immediately reported the stabbing to police, who identified Bird through surveillance video.

“A search of the downtown area quickly located him still wearing the clothing described by the victim and seen in the video,” said the decision. “He was in possession of the bloody knife and had blood clearly on his pant leg.”

The victim told court that the attack affected him “emotionally” and changed how he interacts with Edmontonians.

He had just moved to Edmonton five days before the attack and now suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder.

“I walk around the city with fear and distress all the time since it was an unprovoked action,” the victim said.

Bird, 23, has done time for a May 2025 assault and for being in possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose this past January. His lawyer “highlighted” Bird’s Indigenous background, the judge noted.

His family belong to the Paul Brand First Nation, part of the Cree Nakoda Nation near Duffield, Alta.

An Indigenous Background Report described how Bird “feels very connected to his Indigenous roots,” said the decision.

For Bird, “returning there is an important part of his stated plan, and he intends to reconnect with his family, culture, and establish greater stability within his community.”

Bird, who grew up mostly living with his family and six siblings, “described alcohol and substance use as a regular part of their growth years. There was also some domestic turmoil which could get physical.”

Bird’s mother described him as being the “man of the house,” after she separated from her husband.

“He was exposed to despicable racist attitudes surrounding his community, sufficient to drive him out of playing hockey, which he used to love playing. This also crept into his school life.”

That had an impact on Bird’s self-confidence, according to his mother and grandmother.

“It drove him to using marijuana and alcohol, and he eventually withdrew from school altogether in Grade 11.”

Bird’s mother and her parents attended residential schools, said the decision.

“The consequences of the treatment and derision that they underwent transposed into alcohol struggles and, as (his mom) puts it, part of an ongoing ‘family cycle.’ They were stripped of their cultural identities and traditional ways. These were not passed down the generations, and that negatively impacted all of them.”

The judge noted that he’s directed by Gladue principles set out in a Supreme Court of Canada decision that say sentencing judges must consider the unique circumstances of Indigenous offenders, as well as systemic issues like the impact of residential schools.

“In considering Mr. Bird, there can be no doubt that the effects of colonialization have impacted his family and made their way through the generations onto him,” Bilodeau said. “He described his response to the racism and discrimination. He said that he turned into a bully himself as a sort of defence mechanism.”

While the judge said he could see that Bird is not a fundamentally dangerous person, he needs “further persuasion that the prior convictions and sentences did not achieve.”

The judge saw it as “concerning” that Bird’s “short-term plan” was to embrace his “support from his family, community, and nation,” then return to Edmonton.

“It seems that as soon as he can, he wants to divert back to the environment which gave him the opportunity to consort with other bullies,” Bilodeau said.

Shaye Riley Bird, who still had the bloody knife on him, as well as blood on his pants when police picked him up, pleaded guilty in Alberta’s Court of Justice to the May 3, 2026, assault causing bodily harm and breaching the conditions of his release in March. Both his defence lawyer and the Crown recommended Bird get 180 days in jail for the assault, and another 30 days to be served concurrently, for the bail breach.

“This case features several errors in principle. They result in a proposition that constitutes one of those rare instances — a joint submission that is unhinged from what would be reasonable,” Justice Steven Bilodeau wrote in an Oct. 21 decision.
The judge concluded he could not accept the recommended sentence for three reasons.
“First, it does not adequately reflect the gravity of this random group attack with a knife,” Bilodeau said.

“Second, it gives no meaningful effect to the serious and lasting impact upon the victim. Third, the proposed concurrent sentence leaves the separate breach of the weapons condition without any meaningful sanction.”

Instead, the judge sentenced Bird to 18 months in jail — 14 months for the assault and another four months for the bail breach to be served consecutively — tripling the recommendation from defence and Crown lawyers, while noting “it is no small thing” to reject their joint submission.

Bird’s “conduct bears many of the hallmarks of a street mugging,” Bilodeau said. “It has been long-settled law in Alberta that these merit significant incarceration if they are to be deterred effectively, if at all.”
The attack was “perpetrated by a group or mob,” said the judge. “Being outnumbered changes the entire dynamic of the assault.”

The bail breach would have been serious if Bird had “merely been found carrying a pocketknife,” Bilodeau said. “Instead, he was found with what was effectively a hunting knife, covered in the victim’s blood, which he admits he used to stab the victim. It is hard to imagine a more significant breach of the order.”
The court heard that Bird was with a group of other people at Churchill Square on the evening of May 3. They approached a man wearing headphones at 9:12 p.m. and attacked him.

“During this assault the victim was stabbed with a knife in his buttocks causing a one-inch wound that bled heavily. The assailants took the victim’s headphones, which were worth about $100, and fled the scene,” the judge said.
The victim immediately reported the stabbing to police, who identified Bird through surveillance video.

“A search of the downtown area quickly located him still wearing the clothing described by the victim and seen in the video,” said the decision. “He was in possession of the bloody knife and had blood clearly on his pant leg.”
The victim told court that the attack affected him “emotionally” and changed how he interacts with Edmontonians.
He had just moved to Edmonton five days before the attack and now suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder.
“I walk around the city with fear and distress all the time since it was an unprovoked action,” the victim said.

Bird, 23, has done time for a May 2025 assault and for being in possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose this past January. His lawyer “highlighted” Bird’s Indigenous background, the judge noted.
His family belong to the Paul Brand First Nation, part of the Cree Nakoda Nation near Duffield, Alta.
An Indigenous Background Report described how Bird “feels very connected to his Indigenous roots,” said the decision.
For Bird, “returning there is an important part of his stated plan, and he intends to reconnect with his family, culture, and establish greater stability within his community.”

Bird, who grew up mostly living with his family and six siblings, “described alcohol and substance use as a regular part of their growth years. There was also some domestic turmoil which could get physical.”
Bird’s mother described him as being the “man of the house,” after she separated from her husband.
“He was exposed to despicable racist attitudes surrounding his community, sufficient to drive him out of playing hockey, which he used to love playing. This also crept into his school life.”
That had an impact on Bird’s self-confidence, according to his mother and grandmother.
“It drove him to using marijuana and alcohol, and he eventually withdrew from school altogether in Grade 11.”
Bird’s mother and her parents attended residential schools, said the decision.

“The consequences of the treatment and derision that they underwent transposed into alcohol struggles and, as (his mom) puts it, part of an ongoing ‘family cycle.’ They were stripped of their cultural identities and traditional ways. These were not passed down the generations, and that negatively impacted all of them.”

The judge noted that he’s directed by Gladue principles set out in a Supreme Court of Canada decision that say sentencing judges must consider the unique circumstances of Indigenous offenders, as well as systemic issues like the impact of residential schools.

“In considering Mr. Bird, there can be no doubt that the effects of colonialization have impacted his family and made their way through the generations onto him,” Bilodeau said. “He described his response to the racism and discrimination. He said that he turned into a bully himself as a sort of defence mechanism.”
While the judge said he could see that Bird is not a fundamentally dangerous person, he needs “further persuasion that the prior convictions and sentences did not achieve.”
The judge saw it as “concerning” that Bird’s “short-term plan” was to embrace his “support from his family, community, and nation,” then return to Edmonton.
“It seems that as soon as he can, he wants to divert back to the environment which gave him the opportunity to consort with other bullies,” Bilodeau said.

stories.title: Alto’s high-speed rail project: A Plan B is needed
stories.summary: It would be wiser and more pragmatic to carefully evaluate the efficient, reliable and less expensive option represented by high-frequency rail
stories.author: Jacques Roy, Jean Mercier, Pierre Filion
stories.content:
Jacques Roy is professor emeritus of logistics and operations management at HEC Montréal.

Jean Mercier is an adjunct professor in the department of political science at Université Laval.

Pierre Filion is professor emeritus at the school of planning at University of Waterloo.

The Crown corporation Alto is managing the high-speed rail project between Quebec City and Toronto. Normally, such a major project would be subject to a cost-benefit analysis. However, according to Alto, an analysis is impossible because current estimates of the rail’s construction costs are too preliminary. Based on high-speed rail projects elsewhere in the world, Alto claims the cost will range from $60-billion to $90-billion for the 1,000-kilometre route. The Parliamentary Budget Officer has recently released a report estimating the construction to cost between $75-billion and $113-billion.

The Alto and PBO forecasts are optimistic given the recent extreme cost overruns of the Californian and British high-speed rail projects, and to a lesser extent of a recent French line project between Bordeaux and Toulouse. Also, the recent election of the Parti Québécois (which is opposed to Alto’s project) has only increased the need to examine this project carefully and rationally.

Via Rail’s current record for on-time performance is unacceptable. However, there is another solution - conventional trains on existing rail rights-of-way: the high-frequency rail. In its most recent promotional document, Alto opposes the high-frequency rail, claiming that it would cost nearly as much as the high-speed rail - between $45-billion and $75-billion - without citing any supporting studies.

However, the high-frequency rail project proposed by Via Rail was projected to cost $12-billion in 2021, with dedicated tracks (without interference from freight trains), using existing rail rights-of-way (without agricultural expropriation) and electrifying the entire route.

Alto assumes the high-frequency rail must travel at 200 kilometres an hour, which requires rebuilding the entire infrastructure to avoid railroad crossings. This was not part of the original high-frequency rail plan, which called for trains to slow down at railroad crossings to comply with Canada’s speed limit of 177 km/h. Even at an average speed of 150 km/h, the high-frequency rail would be very competitive with cars. Alto did not compare the high-speed rail’s costs to those of Via Rail’s high-frequency rail, but rather to another, slower high-speed rail. No wonder people prefer the 300 km/h high-speed rail.

In any public transportation project, we must also assess the direct benefits to users (time savings and cost savings from not using a car) and the benefits to society (reductions in GHG emissions, traffic congestion and traffic accidents). Alto’s most recent estimate for the direct benefits is $49.5-billion over 60 years. These benefits are insufficient to justify investments of $60-billion to $90-billion, let alone costs that are likely to exceed $125-billion.

So, Alto adds indirect benefits to the equation, such as the creation of 50,000 jobs over the decade it will take to build the high-speed rail line. However, it might be possible to create just as many jobs by investing in other infrastructure maintenance projects (hospitals, schools, urban public transit, roads, etc.) which are priorities today.

Alto also cites indirect benefits such as hypothetical productivity gains and agglomeration effects that could amount to $24.5-billion annually in the long term. However, Alto is extremely vague about how the high-speed rail could generate such benefits. A study by the C.D. Howe Institute published in 2025 estimates the present value of the benefits over 60 years (not annually as in the case of Alto’s projections) from a potential high-speed rail line - including the oft-cited agglomeration effects - to be in the range of $15-billion to $27-billion. Furthermore, the same study puts the economic benefits of the high-frequency rail at $11-billion to $17-billion, which is close to those of Alto’s high-speed rail.

These benefits are based on ridership projections that vary widely depending on the source. Alto forecasts up to 24 million passengers in 2055 and 43 million by 2084, according to its most optimistic scenario. A recent study by McGill University, however, forecasts ridership of 10.5 million passengers in 2050, which could rise to 17.5 million when strong induced demand is factored in. But long-term forecasts are always uncertain – let’s not forget the 50 million passengers originally projected for Mirabel Airport.

Our main concern is that the exorbitant costs and questionable estimations of Alto’s high-speed rail will lead to its abandonment, as has happened in the past. It would be wiser and more pragmatic to carefully evaluate the efficient, reliable and less expensive option represented by the high-frequency rail. That way, when in-depth studies show that Alto’s high-speed rail is too costly for the expected benefits, the government will have an alternative solution to propose.

stories.title: New bill coming today to amend Canada’s medical assistance in dying regime
stories.summary: Justice Minister Sean Fraser will be introducing legislation Tuesday to amend Canada’s medical assistance in dying regime, both to indefinitely exclude those whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness from qualifying, and to allow advance directives to be issued in certain cases.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello
stories.content:
Justice Minister Sean Fraser will be introducing legislation Tuesday to amend Canada’s medical assistance in dying regime, both to indefinitely exclude those whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness from qualifying, and to allow advance directives to be issued in certain cases.

Fraser first signaled the policy changes were coming earlier this month .

Accompanied by Health Minister Marjorie Michel, Fraser will speak to reporters about the updates to Canada’s medical assistance in dying (Maid) law at 1 p.m. ET in Ottawa.

Ahead of that, senior government officials will brief reporters on the details of the bill and the specific changes being proposed.

Halting expansion for mental illness

According to the justice minister, the federal government has decided – after an extensive study by MPs and ahead of a March deadline – not to move ahead with the expansion scheduled in the Criminal Code of Canada to permit assisted death in circumstances where mental illness is the sole factor.

Instead, the legislation is expected to be updated to “indefinitely exclude” persons whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

This approach was precisely what was recommended to the government by the special joint parliamentary committee tasked with assessing a potential expansion.

That panel heard from dozens of experts, the majority of which opposed expanding eligibility. To qualify for Maid in Canada, a person must be suffering from a grievous and irremediable medical condition, a determination that can be very challenging to make in the case of a mental illness.

Allowing advance directives

Tuesday’s bill is also expected to include provisions for people who make advanced requests for medical assistance in dying if they have been diagnosed with an illness that will cause them to lose capacity in the future.

Known as advance directives, the minister signalled that what the federal government would propose, would still have to comply with provincial legislation.

Several jurisdictions currently have differing positions on the issue of allowing adults to consent in advance to receive Maid at a later point, following a diagnosis of an uncurable illness expected to eventually take away their ability to make that decision.

Certain Canadians have had access to Maid since 2016 and amendments were made to the eligibility criteria in 2021. Further expansion of Maid has been highly controversial, amid reports of existing safeguards failing in complex cases.

This is a developing story, check back for updates…

content_blocks.text: Allowing advance directives

Tuesday’s bill is also expected to include provisions for people who make advanced requests for medical assistance in dying if they have been diagnosed with an illness that will cause them to lose capacity in the future.
Known as advance directives, the minister signalled that what the federal government would propose, would still have to comply with provincial legislation.

Several jurisdictions currently have differing positions on the issue of allowing adults to consent in advance to receive Maid at a later point, following a diagnosis of an uncurable illness expected to eventually take away their ability to make that decision.

Certain Canadians have had access to Maid since 2016 and amendments were made to the eligibility criteria in 2021. Further expansion of Maid has been highly controversial, amid reports of existing safeguards failing in complex cases.

stories.title: RCMP probe potential fraud, money laundering in Alberta health care procurement controversy
stories.summary: Letter filed to court shows charges are being pursued as police investigate the province’s health contracts
stories.author: Carrie Tait, Tom Cardoso
stories.content:
The RCMP is investigating fraud, breach of trust and money laundering in connection with Alberta ’s health care procurement controversy, according to a letter filed in court that reveals for the first time the potential criminal activity police are examining.

The Mounties confirmed in early 2025 that they launched an investigation into the province’s health care purchasing practices, and earlier this year executed searches as part of their inquiry, but the RCMP have otherwise remained silent on the offences they’re considering.

The letter, dated Oct. 15 and addressed to several parties involved in a civil dispute in Alberta connected with the procurement affair, provides a rare glimpse into the probe. It is signed by Tom Andreopoulos, a Crown prosecutor with the Complex Prosecutions Bureau at Ontario’s Ministry of the Attorney-General.

“Our office is responsible for the provision of advisory support and the prosecution of any charges that May arise from the ongoing Royal Canadian Mounted Police criminal investigation into fraud, breach of trust, and money laundering arising out of procurement processes and practices at Alberta Health and Alberta Health Services,” Mr. Andreopoulos says in his letter.

The letter copies two other Ontario Crown prosecutors assisting with the probe, Niall Gilks and Alana Rodrigo.

Both the RCMP and Ontario’s Ministry of the Attorney-General declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.

The prosecutor’s letter is addressed to lawyers for the government of Alberta, provincial health agency Alberta Health Services and Athana Mentzelopoulos, the agency’s former chief executive.

Ms. Mentzelopoulos sued the government and the health authority in February, 2025 for wrongful dismissal, setting off a political firestorm when she alleged that she faced pressure from government officials to drop an internal investigation into her agency’s contracting processes and ties between private businesses and senior Alberta government officials.

The government says it fired Ms. Mentzelopoulos because she failed to execute its vision for the health care system.

None of the allegations have been tested in court.

The parties in Ms. Mentzelopoulos’s lawsuit have been jousting over whether records she has held – at least some of which were seized by the RCMP, according to Mr. Andreopoulos’s letter – were confidential to the government or protected under solicitor-client privilege.

Last month, Justice Michael J. Lema ruled that most of the materials at issue were privileged or confidential and ordered Ms. Mentzelopoulos to return or destroy those records.

A lawyer for Ms. Mentzelopoulos filed the Ontario prosecutor’s letter in court after Justice Lema’s decision, arguing that it shows the intent behind her retention of records was not “ill-placed.”

Mr. Andreopoulos’s letter says the Crown is aware of the judge’s decision and will be asking the Alberta Court of King’s Bench for help in determining how to handle the privilege review of the seized materials. He also explains that Edmonton criminal lawyer Alexandra K. Seaman has been tapped as a third-party “referee” to work through those issues. Ms. Seaman did not respond to a request for comment.

The letter does not elaborate on the alleged potential offences or who is the subject of the investigation, and does not specify why Ontario Crown prosecutors are involved in the RCMP’s probe in Alberta. (Provincial justice departments sometimes appoint prosecutors from other provinces when dealing with politically sensitive cases in which a potential conflict of interest May arise.)

The Alberta Premier’s office did not acknowledge requests for comment.

The government has been embroiled in the health care procurement controversy for more than a year and a half. The investigation ordered by Ms. Mentzelopoulos focused, in part, ON contracts awarded to Edmonton-based medical supplier MHCare Medical Corp., which received roughly $614-million in business from Alberta Health Services since 2020. That included $70-million for children’s pain and fever medication, only a third of which was delivered.

The fired executive’s lawsuit alleged that Jitendra Prasad, a senior purchasing official at Alberta Health Services, had a potential conflict of interest with MHCare.

Mr. Prasad had an MHCare e-mail address just before the agency entered into a contract with the company for the children’s pain and fever medication, according to a court filing by Ms. Mentzelopoulos.

A lawyer for Mr. Prasad did not respond to a request for comment.

MHCare is owned by businessman Sam Mraiche, who The Globe and Mail has reported joined Premier Danielle Smith’s inner circle in a hotel suite in 2023 to watch the province’s election results. He has also played host to the Premier, cabinet ministers and senior political staff in private boxes for National Hockey League games.

Mr. Mraiche has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing in connection with the controversy, and he is not a party to Ms. Mentzelopoulos’s lawsuit.

In an unsigned letter addressed to the government in April, 2025, MHCare said the suggestion that the company has benefited because of Mr. Mraiche’s relationships rather than on merit is “untrue and a plainly unfair characterization.”

The Globe reported in June that Mr. Andreopoulos, a veteran prosecutor, was attached to the case, but he declined to specify his role at the time.

His involvement in the Alberta procurement probe came to light after he responded to inquiries from a consortium of media outlets – including The Globe – that applied to unseal search-warrant materials filed in court as part of the RCMP’s investigation.

In March, the Mounties executed searches at the offices of MHCare and Jaberson & Associates Inc. , an accounting and tax-preparation business owned by Sam Jaber, who has acted as MHCare’s chief financial officer.

Mr. Jaber was appointed by the Premier to the board of Invest Alberta, a Crown corporation designed to attract foreign investment to the province. Shortly after the RCMP searched Mr. Jaber’s accounting firm, Invest Alberta said the businessman was taking a leave of absence from its board.

A lawyer for Mr. Jaber has previously said his client “steadfastly maintains his innocence.”

The Globe also reported in June that Alberta Health Services had been ordered to hand documents over to the RCMP as part of the police’s investigation.

stories.title: An inside look at the animals behind Parliament's walls (no, not those ones)
stories.summary: You May know about of the animals inside the walls of Parliament, in this video we introduce you to the critters that live just outside.
stories.author: Mick Gzowski
stories.content:
Ottawa — While most of us are aware of the antics of the animals inside the walls of Parliament, in this video we introduce you to the critters that live just outside.

Parliament Hill sits atop a limestone cliff surrounded by 25 acres of forested land adjacent to the Ottawa River.

Its natural setting makes our seat of government unique in G7 capital cities. Directly behind Parliament is a steep, wild and tree-covered hill that drops directly into a major and very clean river, the Ottawa.

The mighty Ottawa River is both one of Canada’s greatest and cleanest major rivers. It has never hosted significant industrial activity, except for its historic forestry industry and the Chalk River nuclear research facility in Deep River. The river’s ecological health is demonstrated by the many, many reptiles and amphibians that live there. Both of those species are bellwethers for pollution, and they are abundant around Parliament Hill.

Much of the Nature Museum’s collection lives at the Natural Heritage Campus in Gatineau. The scientists describe this modern, non-public building as being the dimensions of six olympic-sized pools. The campus houses natural world specimens carefully stored in climate controlled rooms. Scientists from across the world use this collection to study our fauna, some of it more than a century old. Big and small, fish and fowl, the campus also boasts the world’s largest collection of polar bear parts.

Watch this video and get as excited about these creepy crawlies as the scientists are.

stories.title: Dementia doctors, provinces differ on question of advance consent in Maid
stories.summary: Toronto - As the federal government prepares to table new legislation that would allow advance requests for medical assistance in dying, the stark difference in opinion between two provinces highlights an ongoing debate about what constitutes true consent among people who have dementia.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - While proposed new federal legislation would allow advance requests for medical assistance in dying, the stark difference in opinion between two provinces highlights an ongoing debate about what constitutes true consent among people who have dementia.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser introduced a bill on Tuesday to decriminalize providing Maid to people with dementia and other conditions that take away the capacity to consent if they ask for it in advance while they’re still mentally capable.

Bill C-41 states that “a person would have to be experiencing intolerable suffering at the time Maid is provided, even if all the conditions in their advance request have been met.”

It’s up to provincial governments to decide whether — and how — to allow people to make advance requests and have those wishes fulfilled in the future.

The positions of two provinces are already clear. Quebec legalized advance requests in 2024.

Alberta, ON the other hand, passed legislation last March that bars advance requests — and the federal government’s legislation won’t change that position, said Maddison McKee, press secretary to Adriana LaGrange, the province’s minister of hospital and surgical health services.

“Ending a person’s life when they can no longer confirm their wishes raises profound concerns about consent and the protection of vulnerable people, which is why the safeguards we enacted last spring will remain in place,” McKee said in an email on Oct. 7.

Quebec had 3,463 registered advance requests as of Oct. 4 this year, Marie-Christine Patry, spokesperson for the province’s ministry of health and social services, said in an email.

The number of advance requests that have led to Maid being carried out in Quebec is not available, but is expected to be included in a report by the province’s commission on end-of-life care later this fall, she said.

Dying with Dignity has said that without advance requests in the rest of country, people with dementia have lost precious time with loved ones because they have chosen to receive Maid while they still have the ability to consent, instead of risking not being able to die when their condition has deteriorated to an intolerable state of suffering.

Earlier in October, Fraser said the Liberal government believes allowing advance requests is the right thing to do and reflects the will of many Canadians.

“I have conversations with people who’ve received a diagnosis of early onset Alzheimer’s, who want desperately to be able to know that they’re not going to subject their families to pain and suffering,” he said.

The minister acknowledged that advance requests will spark debate and discussion in the provinces over “the next number of months and years.”

The issue is “complicated,” said Dr. Samir Sinha, a geriatrician and clinical scientist at Sinai Health and University Health Network in Toronto.

Sinha, who was part of an expert panel that looked at the issue, said the trickiest cases will be when someone makes an advance request for medically assisted death to be administered when their dementia takes certain effects — such as not being able to recognize their children — but when that condition happens and it’s time for Maid, the patient seems happy in their current life.

”(The question is) does your present self and your present views truly reflect what your future self and future views will actually be? Nobody knows,” Sinha said.

For him, there’s no issue if the patient made an advance request for Maid and is clearly not experiencing a good quality of life.

“There’s no happiness, and this is kind of what you said would be intolerable suffering, and we all see it. Well, there’s clarity there,” Sinha said.

When it’s not so “black or white” and the person’s quality of life is more of a grey area, “that’s where I get nervous,” he said.

Dr. Catherine Ferrier, a geriatric physician at McGill University Health Centre in Montreal who treats patients with dementia, said she simply doesn’t see how advance consent to death can be valid from a medical ethics perspective.

“This is like signing a paper trying to imagine yourself several years down the road when you’re in a different condition and what might be troubling you at that time and saying, ‘I predict that it will be so bad that I would prefer to be dead.’ And there’s a lot of assumptions there,” said Ferrier, who is president of the Physicians’ Alliance Against Euthanasia.

Instead, the focus should be on providing more services to patients with dementia and their families so they can live comfortable and fulfilling lives, as well as ensuring the staff caring for them — both in long-term care and home care — are properly trained, she said.

According to its website, the alliance sees “any law allowing doctors to intentionally end the life of their patients as contrary to the goals of medicine and the good of our patients, especially the most vulnerable and those who cannot speak for themselves.”

But Dr. Laurent Boisvert, a family and emergency physician who provides Maid in Quebec, said the opposite is true — that someone can only truly give consent when they have the mental capacity to do so.

A patient’s advance request for Maid reflects that person’s true wishes — even if they “seem” to be happy later when dementia has taken away what they valued, he said.

”(That’s) the real suffering,” said Boisvert, who is the president of Association québécoise pour le droit de mourir dans la dignité — Quebec’s equivalent to Dying with Dignity.

He said that when he prepares advance requests with patients who have dementia, it brings them great relief.

“When everything is complete, I said to them, ‘now you forget that and have fun. When you will have (a) big problem, your advance request is there as you ask(ed), and that is what you want,’” he said.

“At this moment they say, ‘oh doc, phew, I’m really fine with that and I’m very happy that I can put that behind me.”

In Quebec, advance requests must specify effects of their illness that would signal they would want Maid at that time.

The most common conditions Boisvert sees listed by patients with dementia include no longer being able to recognize their family, not being able to go to the toilet themselves, not being able to eat without assistance, not knowing where they are and becoming aggressive.

In a technical briefing on Tuesday, government officials said that two physicians or nurse practitioners would assess the patient at the time their advance request conditions for Maid have been met to determine if they are experiencing intolerable suffering.

If a person seems happy at that time, that’s “one piece of information that a practitioner will have to take into consideration,” they said.

Quebec also allows people making advance requests to designate one or two “trusted third person(s)” who know the patient’s wishes and will advocate to make sure they are known and respected by health and social service providers. They can inform the patient’s care team if they see the conditions outlined in the advance request happening.

A physician or specialized nurse practitioner then assesses the patient to decide if they have reached the stage of “unbearable physical or psychological suffering that cannot be relieved under conditions considered tolerable,” according to the Quebec government website. A second doctor or nurse practitioner must confirm the assessment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa raking in billions more than expected thanks to inflation and natural resource revenue
stories.summary: The government May be on track to take in almost $20-billion more this year than had been expected less than six months ago.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
The federal government May be on track to take in almost $20-billion more in taxes and other revenue this year than had been expected less than six months ago, National Post has learned, potentially handing Prime Minister Mark Carney much more room in his second budget to cut taxes, trim Canada’s massive deficit or spend.

In its Spring Economic Update in late April, the government said it expected to rake in $529.6-billion this fiscal year, which would have been an increase of 3.5 per cent over the previous year.

But instead, according to government figures up to the most recent month, Ottawa has so far this year taken in 7.4 per cent more than the previous year, more than double the pace of growth that had been expected. If the growth continues throughout the year, that translates to $549.4-billion, or $19.8-billion more than what had been expected in April.

Economists say the federal government, like the provinces and territories, is sitting on extra cash this year due to higher-than expected income tax payments, a small jump in inflation, and strong markets for many natural resources, particularly oil. That means increases in both corporate income tax and sales tax.

Trevor Tombe, professor of economics at the University of Calgary and director of fiscal and economic policy at the School of Public Policy, said he’s surprised at the federal government’s revenue spike, although he emphasized that Ottawa shouldn’t assume that those increases will continue.

Canada’s trade relationship with the U.S. remains uncertain while growth has been sluggish and the government’s fiscal situation is dire, leading to questions about how long the revenue spike will continue, economists say.

“It’s hard to count on anything,” said Tombe.

Some had expected an increase in federal revenue, just not this big.

In an update issued earlier this month, the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) also forecast a healthy increase in federal revenue, a jump of 5.4 per cent or $538.7-billion this fiscal year over the previous year, or $9.1-billion higher than what had been forecast in the spring update.

With the Carney government scheduled to unveil its budget on Nov. 5, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and Finance Canada officials are poring over options what to do with the extra money.

John Fragos, a spokesman for Champagne, declined to comment on what Ottawa’s revenue numbers will look like in the budget.

But economists warned that it would be a mistake for the government to view the extra revenue as a windfall or a long-term trend. Tombe said the government should be thinking long term, particularly about future growth and how to pay for such things as support programs for seniors and the defence spending plans that have already been announced.

“That’s where the government should be focused,” said Tombe.

Don Drummond, former senior executive at the Department of Finance and now a fellow-in-residence with C.D. Howe Institute, warned that it would be a big mistake for the Carney government to assume that any revenue increase will continue.

Oil prices May not remain this high, population growth has waned and productivity remains low, said Drummond, and the government has already allocated big bucks for new spending promises and tax cuts.

Ottawa should take a prudent approach and assume modest economic growth in the coming years, Drummond said.

“The bottom line is there is no windfall available for new initiatives in the (upcoming) budget,” Drummond wrote in a memo for the C.D. Howe Institute that is expected to be released later this week. “And even if there was, it should be applied to lowering the deficit and debt.”

Although reducing the deficit hasn’t so far been a government priority, the Carney government seems to have taken a more long-term approach to the economy than the previous regime under Justin Trudeau. Carney has focused much of his effort since taking office on trying to solidify the pillars of the Canadian economy: infrastructure for exports and transportation of goods, improving the investment climate and supporting trade relationships.

The government announced a so-called mega-deduction last month, for example, at an international investment summit in Toronto that it hopes will spur investment, particularly in capital-intensive industries such as energy, mining, transportation, and technology.

The changes, which have not yet become law but May well be included in the budget, are expected to cut Canada’s projected tax rate on new investment, a key metric for large investors, by slightly more than half, to about 6.4 per cent from 13 per cent. The price tag for the changes is an estimated $36.5-billion over the next five years.

For those concerned about Canada’s fiscal problems, Champagne has not provided much relief in recent months. He has described Canada’s fiscal position as the best in the G7 and has said the government will continue to make what he calls economic “investments,” instead of reducing the deficit.

“I think Canadians can understand that we have a strong fiscal position and we’re investing in the things that will generate growth to the country,” he said in July.

But Ottawa is staring at an increasingly large pile of red ink. In the government’s spring update, Champagne said the 2025–26 deficit was projected to be about $66.9 billion, down from the $78.3 billion that had been projected in last fall’s budget. That drop was due largely to a fiscal windfall from higher oil prices.

The federal government has now accumulated more than $1.3 trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last five years.

stories.title: United Arab Emirates, Canada to share details of strategic partnership today
stories.summary: Ottawa — Abu Dhabi's crown prince is in Ottawa for meetings today as Canada and the United Arab Emirates work to cement their trade ties.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a free trade deal on Tuesday they say was reached in a “record” time of 47 days, and have also agreed to start talks on an extradition treaty.

The trade deal was one of a handful of trade and infrastructure agreements signed during the crown prince of Abu Dhabi’s visit to Ottawa on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to Parliament Hill. The crown prince’s motorcade was escorted onto the Hill by four RCMP horses.

It’s just the latest example of the Carney government’s outreach to nations with questionable human rights records as it works to redirect Canada’s trade around an increasingly erratic United States.

Carney was in Turkey last week to discuss deeper economic and social ties with the Nato ally. In recent months, Turkish authorities have targeted multiple Lgbtq+ groups and individuals — detaining dozens of activists, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts.

The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. But the country has been accused of fuelling a militia in Sudan that conducted what Washington has called a genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

Asked Tuesday about human rights concerns linked to the UAE, International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said “human rights never takes a back seat with Canada.”

“It’s important that we continue to engage, being at those tables to make sure that we raise whatever we need to raise in terms of human rights,” he said.

At home, Human Rights Watch says the UAE is responsible for “rampant systemic human rights violations,” particularly with regard to freedom of speech.

Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan.

The letter, signed by the Trade Justice Network, Amnistie internationale Canada francophone and Equality Fund, said as Canada looks to diversify its trade, it needs to assert support for human rights as a core Canadian value.

“Our prosperity cannot be built at the expense of the lives and futures of the Sudanese people,” said the letter.

Ministers from Canada and the UAE have also signed agreements pledging investments in clean power and energy infrastructure and collaboration on diplomatic training.

They’ve signed an agreement on defence co-operation covering military education and training, joint exercises, cybersecurity and information sharing, as well as the creation of a joint military committee.

Stephanie Kusie, Conservative MP and critic for international trade, said in a social media post Tuesday that it’s “tiresome” to see the prime minister holding “yet another flashy meeting with no tangible outcomes for Canadians, as he did today with the UAE.”

“Instead of another fancy ceremony, Canadians deserve clear information about the number of jobs and the names of projects involved, not another vague ‘strategic partnership’ that lacks any real details on how it would improve their lives,” she said.

The Prime Minister’s Office said the trade deal will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 per cent of current Canadian exports to the UAE once it’s fully implemented.

The office says the agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including those in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental and engineering sectors.

The Prime Minister’s Office said the trade agreement is expected to take effect next year.

During the visit, Canada and the UAE also announced they will launch negotiations on an extradition treaty and a mutual legal assistance treaty.

During a meeting with the crown prince in his West Block office, Carney said the visit would reinforce the countries’ partnership, which has grown substantially over the past year.

At a state dinner for the crown prince hosted by Carney in downtown Ottawa on Monday, the prime minister said the two countries are united in their determination to “build for the future.”

Carney travelled to the United Arab Emirates last year. At the end of that November visit, the prime minister said Ottawa was working on a $1-billion project to expand critical minerals processing capacity in Canada.

At the same time, the UAE pledged to invest about $70 billion in Canada.

Sidhu said Tuesday that sum could include new investments in mining, logistics, energy and digital technology.

“They are actively looking at deploying that as soon as possible,” he said. “They’ll have more to say publicly soon.”

The Prime Minister’s Office said the visit led to “significant progress” on the Uae’s commitment to invest in Canada.

It said Emirati multinational logistics company DP World has signed an agreement with the Arctic Gateway Group and CentrePort Canada to advance trade opportunities and develop a transportation corridor linking the Port of Churchill, the Hudson Bay Railway, CentrePort Canada and DP World’s global logistics network.

It said agreements were signed between renewable energy company Masdar and Natural Resources Canada on green energy projects, and between Invest in Canada and the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce and Industry on sharing information and coordinating visits.

The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade. The government’s spring economic update said non-U.S. goods and services exports increased by $33 billion in 2025 compared to 2024.

In 2025, Canada’s two-way merchandise trade with the UAE was valued at $3.5 billion, with $2.8 billion in exports and $679.1 million in imports.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

-With files from Dylan Robertson

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press
