stories.title: Timeline of events in Osap career colleges warnings, probes
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government is coming under increasing fire for how it has handled Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at private career colleges.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government is coming under increasing fire for how it has handled Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at private career colleges.

Critics say the government set the stage for the system to possibly be exploited, did not properly oversee the billions of dollars going out the door, then made students pay the price.

The following timeline is based largely on documents filed in court as Academy of Learning career college locations that share a common owner try to fight a government decision to deny them Osap eligibility.

Academy of Learning denies any wrongdoing and the government’s allegations have not been proven in court. The Academy says the schools have instituted a large number of corrective actions in response to ministry concerns.

The loss of access to Osap grants, and now loans, amid fraud allegations at 8 schools is sparking fears for the future.

2020: Ontario allows online-only programs, including those without live instruction, to qualify for Osap.

January 2023: Career Colleges Ontario raises concerns about “indicators consistent with suspicious activity” in a meeting with the government, as well as at meetings in May and November of that year.

Oct. 1, 2024: The Ministry of Colleges and Universities sends routine notices of inspection to Academy of Learning locations on Bay Street in Toronto and in Brampton East.

Jan. 15, 2025: Career Colleges Ontario writes to the ministry noting 10 schools in particular with Osap usage showing significant anomalies, including the two Academy of Learning locations. Names of the other eight schools are redacted.

May 2025: The federal government tells Ontario about concerns with several schools, including the two Academy of Learning locations.

July 8, 2025: Ministry starts in-person inspection at Academy of Learning — Bay.

Aug. 8, 2025: Both Academy of Learning locations are approved for Osap for the 2025-26 year.

Aug. 12, 2025: Ministry starts in-person inspection process for Academy of Learning — Brampton East, sending them an email apologizing for “the delay, which was due to transitions in roles and the implementation of new inspections procedures.”

Sept. 17, 2025: Ministry shares its Academy of Learning — Bay inspection report with the school. Among other concerns, it alleges inspectors found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program.

December 2025: Ministry tasks its forensic investigation team to provide advice to further strengthen oversight of career colleges and Osap.

Feb. 12, 2026: Minister Nolan Quinn announces that due to rising pressures on Osap, career college students will no longer be eligible for grants, and students at publicly funded colleges and universities will receive a maximum of 25 per cent of their financial aid as grants, down from 85 per cent.

Feb. 26, 2026: Career Colleges Ontario sends Quinn a second letter, asking the ministry to inspect 14 campuses it has identified as having “possible suspicious” Osap activity.

March 9, 2026: Ministry shares its Academy of Learning — Brampton East inspection report with the school. It details concerns about “compromised participation” in programs delivered asynchronously online.

May 1, 2026: Ministry decides the two schools and a few others will not be eligible for Osap for the 2026-27 year, a decision the schools are now challenging in court.

August 2026: Ministry asks Kpmg to audit Osap use at private post-secondary institutions.

Oct. 2, 2026: Ministry refers concerns from audit’s preliminary findings to the Ontario Provincial Police and says many of the concerns stem from online-only programs.

Oct. 6, 2026: Quinn announces pause on Osap payments to all private post-secondary institutions across the province, leaving thousands of students in limbo.

October 2026: Ministry begins in-person inspections at eight career colleges but does not name them.

Fall 2026: Government intends to table legislation to exclude “predominantly online-only programs” at career colleges from Osap.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario delayed inspections of two career colleges later given 'fails': court docs
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario delayed inspections of two career colleges that ultimately turned up serious concerns about student financial aid use, which meant the schools received a "fail" only after they had been approved for funding for another year, court records show.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario delayed inspections of two career colleges that ultimately turned up serious concerns about student financial aid use, which meant the schools received a “fail” only after they had been approved for funding for another year, court records show.

Critics say it points to severe mismanagement of public money and the government has made the wrong people pay the price.

The Ministry of Colleges and Universities sent Academy of Learning locations in Toronto on Bay Street and in Brampton East notices of inspection on Oct. 1, 2024, according to court records, but did not start the in-person inspections until July and August of 2025, respectively.

“I apologize for the delay, which was due to transitions in roles and the implementation of new inspection procedures,” a ministry official wrote in an email to the Brampton East location, looking to schedule an on-site inspection.

That was four days after the schools were sent ministry notices approving their ability to accept Ontario Student Assistance Program-funded tuition for another year.

Correspondence between the schools and the ministry is among hundreds of pages of documents filed in court as Academy of Learning seeks judicial review of the ministry’s ultimate decision in 2026 to bar them from Osap eligibility for a year, a ban that has now been extended to 2030.

Concerns about Osap activity at the schools have been raised by various groups and governments, but no misuse has been proven in court. The schools deny allegations that anything improper occurred and have implemented a long list of corrective actions.

Their Osap approval in 2025 came despite warnings months earlier from both the federal government and the industry’s own association, Career Colleges Ontario. That organization wrote a letter to the ministry in January 2025, flagging “irregularities” in Osap usage at 10 schools, including the two Academy of Learning locations.

Growth in Osap applications at most career colleges was flat between 2022 and 2024, Career College Ontario wrote, but the Bay location saw growth of 642 per cent, and Brampton East saw 527 per cent.

In May of 2025, the federal government told the province about serious concerns with those schools. As the federal government detailed to the schools a few months later, those concerns included unusually rapid growth and “evidence of systematic irregularities.”

The schools have said that instead of being viewed as an indicator of risk, growth represents “a reflection of program relevance, responsiveness to workforce needs, and public confidence in the institution’s delivery of quality education.”

Court records show the provincial inspections ultimately found, in September for the Bay location and in March 2026 for the Brampton East location, evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program.

Students May not have responded to the federal government’s verification attempts because they believed them to be scam calls, and other students having difficulty answering questions in interviews “can be reasonably attributed to situational and linguistic factors,” the school wrote in response to the government.

The Academy of Learning also suggests the government is interpreting IP address data incorrectly. Unusually rapid course completion warrants review, they have said.

Successful Osap applications at those two schools, which share a parent company, totalled $173 million in grants alone in 2024-25, according to data previously obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request. The number rises to $219 million when a North York location that is a branch of Brampton East is added.

In comparison, students at all publicly funded colleges across the province that year received $385 million in provincial grants.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn drastically reduced the amount of Osap grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of “sustainability” as the program was facing rising costs. Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges.

Quinn has also now paused Osap payments to students at all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions as his government and an outside firm conduct a broader review of the issue.

Liberal colleges and universities critic Tyler Watt said those actions make Quinn’s delayed action on potential bad actors all the more baffling.

“Their recent actions, where they’ve completely pulled the rug out from every single student in the private sector, goes to show you that they are willing to take drastic action,” he said.

“It’s not OK at all what they’ve done to students and the people that are following the rules, but there’s no reasonable explanation why they let this go on and wasted this much of taxpayers’ money for as long as they did.”

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said the government has failed students and the public.

“This amounts to severe mismanagement of public money by the Ford government,” he wrote in a statement. “For years, this government has been aware of private career colleges breaking the rules and has allowed them to continue to benefit from Osap.”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said the government should have acted earlier on the numerous warnings it received.

“The government still dragged its heels on conducting the investigation that it is obligated to do and then blames students for misusing Osap grants and punishes the entire sector for its own incompetence,” she said.

A spokesperson for Quinn said the inspection process can be long and in-depth.

“As we have stated, these inspections are multifaceted, and include reviewing data within the ministry’s possession, data requested from the institution that is provided to the ministry Inspectors, and in-person inspections,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

“Due to the technical nature of this process, inspections and subsequent investigations can take over a year. The ministry cannot presume the outcome of these investigations until all steps have been completed.”

Osap applications at those schools actually went down in 2025-26, the province said in court filings. In the case of the Brampton East location, the number of Osap recipients dropped by 34 per cent from the previous year, compared to growth of 1,347 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

The decline is timed around the start of the ministry’s in-person inspections, the government says in a document filed in court.

The Academy of Learning says no single factor explains that decline.

“We reject any suggestion that the decline reflects wrongdoing,” the schools wrote in a statement.

“Enrolment fell during a period of significant uncertainty, as students received repeated communications questioning their Osap funding and our eligibility. Many chose to withdraw, postpone or not start their studies. In the same period, we ended some community partner arrangements and added verification measures.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

Growth in Osap applications at most career colleges was flat between 2022 and 2024, Career College Ontario wrote, but the Bay location saw growth of 642 per cent, and Brampton East saw 527 per cent.

In May of 2025, the federal government told the province about serious concerns with those schools. As the federal government detailed to the schools a few months later, those concerns included unusually rapid growth and “evidence of systematic irregularities.”

The schools have said that instead of being viewed as an indicator of risk, growth represents “a reflection of program relevance, responsiveness to workforce needs, and public confidence in the institution’s delivery of quality education.”

Court records show the provincial inspections ultimately found, in September for the Bay location and in March 2026 for the Brampton East location, evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program.

Students May not have responded to the federal government’s verification attempts because they believed them to be scam calls, and other students having difficulty answering questions in interviews “can be reasonably attributed to situational and linguistic factors,” the school wrote in response to the government.
The Academy of Learning also suggests the government is interpreting IP address data incorrectly. Unusually rapid course completion warrants review, they have said.

Successful Osap applications at those two schools, which share a parent company, totalled $173 million in grants alone in 2024-25, according to data previously obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request. The number rises to $219 million when a North York location that is a branch of Brampton East is added.
In comparison, students at all publicly funded colleges across the province that year received $385 million in provincial grants.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn drastically reduced the amount of Osap grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges could receive in the name of “sustainability” as the program was facing rising costs. Those costs were later revealed by The Canadian Press to largely be due to activity at a small number of career colleges.
Quinn has also now paused Osap payments to students at all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions as his government and an outside firm conduct a broader review of the issue.
Liberal colleges and universities critic Tyler Watt said those actions make Quinn’s delayed action on potential bad actors all the more baffling.
“Their recent actions, where they’ve completely pulled the rug out from every single student in the private sector, goes to show you that they are willing to take drastic action,” he said.

“It’s not OK at all what they’ve done to students and the people that are following the rules, but there’s no reasonable explanation why they let this go on and wasted this much of taxpayers’ money for as long as they did.”
Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said the government has failed students and the public.

“This amounts to severe mismanagement of public money by the Ford government,” he wrote in a statement. “For years, this government has been aware of private career colleges breaking the rules and has allowed them to continue to benefit from Osap.”
NDP critic Peggy Sattler said the government should have acted earlier on the numerous warnings it received.

“The government still dragged its heels on conducting the investigation that it is obligated to do and then blames students for misusing Osap grants and punishes the entire sector for its own incompetence,” she said.
A spokesperson for Quinn said the inspection process can be long and in-depth.

“As we have stated, these inspections are multifaceted, and include reviewing data within the ministry’s possession, data requested from the institution that is provided to the ministry Inspectors, and in-person inspections,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

“Due to the technical nature of this process, inspections and subsequent investigations can take over a year. The ministry cannot presume the outcome of these investigations until all steps have been completed.”

Osap applications at those schools actually went down in 2025-26, the province said in court filings. In the case of the Brampton East location, the number of Osap recipients dropped by 34 per cent from the previous year, compared to growth of 1,347 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25.
The decline is timed around the start of the ministry’s in-person inspections, the government says in a document filed in court.
The Academy of Learning says no single factor explains that decline.
“We reject any suggestion that the decline reflects wrongdoing,” the schools wrote in a statement.

“Enrolment fell during a period of significant uncertainty, as students received repeated communications questioning their Osap funding and our eligibility. Many chose to withdraw, postpone or not start their studies. In the same period, we ended some community partner arrangements and added verification measures.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: American steel — not overseas dumping — dominates Canadian imports, trade data shows
stories.summary: Federal trade figures show American steel makes up more than half of Canada's imports of galvanized and coated steel, complicating Cleveland-Cliffs' argument that an influx of cheap overseas steel is one of the top causes of Stelco layoffs.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
American steel makes up more than half of Canada’s imports of galvanized and coated steel, federal trade figures show, raising questions about Cleveland-Cliffs’ argument that an influx of overseas steel is one of the top causes of Stelco layoffs.

Global Affairs Canada import data show that 54.1 per cent of the country’s 625,726 tonnes of galvanized and coated steel sheet imports during the first nine months of 2026 came from the United States.

Stelco’s owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, has blamed the idling of cold-rolled and coated steel operations at its Hamilton, Ont., plant partly on what it describes as dumped offshore steel imports in Canada.

It argues that Ottawa’s trade protections have failed to create a viable market for Canadian producers.

Colin Mang, assistant professor of economics at McMaster University, said the latest trade figures challenge claims that Canada is being flooded with dumped steel from overseas.

“Canada does import a lot of this stuff but much of it comes from the United States, not from other countries, and accusing them of dumping the steel into Canada at artificially low prices is not a fully accurate depiction,” he said.

Canada’s largest sources of galvanized and coated steel sheets outside the United States were South Korea, Taiwan and Germany, accounting for 13.4 per cent, 7.6 per cent and seven per cent of imports, respectively.

The United States supplied more than four times as much as the second-largest source, South Korea, the data shows.

Still, Mang said Canada continues to import large quantities of steel even as domestic demand weakens, putting additional pressure on Canadian producers like Stelco.

“There has been a drop in demand for their product,” he said. “The main issue really is that there’s just less market demand from not just the auto sector, but also from construction and then from exports.”

Dan Ciuriak, director and principal of Ciuriak Consulting, said the bigger problem for Canadian steelmakers is collapsing exports, not foreign imports.

“There’s no flood of imports coming in,” he said. “The problem in terms of Canada’s trade balance is the collapse of exports to the U.S. because of the tariffs.”

Ciuriak said Cleveland-Cliffs actively supported the U.S. tariffs that have hurt Stelco because the levies benefit the company’s American operations by restricting foreign competition and keeping U.S. steel prices high.

He said those higher prices are particularly important to Cleveland-Cliffs, which carries a heavy debt load and relies on strong steel prices to bolster its financial performance and share price.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has argued that Canada’s galvanized steel market is too small to accommodate two domestic producers alongside what he called “an avalanche of imports.”

In a statement Monday, Goncalves pointed specifically to imports of galvanized steel used outside the automotive sector as a problem for Stelco.

“For galvanized products, the imports of non-automotive galvanized steel that continue to flood the Canadian market remain problematic,” he said.

In an Oct. 9 letter to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Stelco president and general counsel Paul Simon blamed the company’s difficulties in part on the “market-depressing impact of dumped, offshore imports” and U.S. tariffs.

In response, Joly pointed to federal measures restricting overseas steel imports, including tighter quotas introduced in Dec. 2025. Imports from the United States and Mexico remain exempt from those quotas.

However, Canada has since raised tariffs on certain U.S. steel imports, including galvanized steel, to 50 per cent on Sept. 8, potentially making American steel more expensive for Canadian buyers.

Ciuriak said the new tariffs could reduce galvanized steel imports into Canada, given that the United States is the country’s largest supplier.

Cleveland-Cliffs announced plans on Sept. 28 to lay off up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., citing U.S. tariffs and challenging market conditions.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada's Eurovision finalists to be announced today by CBC
stories.summary: Toronto - Who will be Canada’s first Eurovision star?
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Montreal dance-pop artist Rêve has spent years watching Eurovision’s over-the-top performances from her couch. Now, with a chance to become Canada’s first contestant, she’s ready to put on a spectacle of her own.

“How big am I willing to go? As big as they let me and their insurance allows,” said the artist born Briannah Donolo.

The Juno winner and self-described Eurovision superfan was named Tuesday as one of five finalists vying to represent Canada at the 2027 song contest.

The five finalists vying to represent Canada at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest are making their pitches. They are Montreal dance-pop artist Rêve, Quebec vocalist William Cloutier, Ottawa pop-rocker Talk, New Brunswick singer-songwriter Josiane and B.C. pop crooner Tyler Shaw. (Oct. 27, 2026)

Joining her are Quebec vocalist William Cloutier, Ottawa pop-rocker Talk, New Brunswick singer-songwriter Josiane and B.C. pop-crooner Tyler Shaw.

CBC/Radio-Canada revealed the contenders at a splashy media event in Toronto, where the artists made their pitches for a spot on one of the world’s biggest music stages.

For Rêve, whose music draws on Eurodance, disco and contemporary pop, the competition’s elaborate performances have long felt like a natural fit.

“I’m a theatre kid at heart. I’m a maximalist at heart,” she said Tuesday.

The public broadcaster says 325 artists applied earlier this year for a chance to become Canada’s inaugural representative. The public will be invited to vote, with the winner set to be announced in December.

Canada will make its official debut at the 71st Eurovision Song Contest, taking place next May in Burgas, Bulgaria. It will be the first new country to join since Australia in 2015.

The winning artist will work with music-industry talent to develop Canada’s song and performance.

Rêve said she became hooked on Eurovision after watching Austrian drag queen Conchita Wurst’s winning performance of “Rise Like a Phoenix” in 2014. Its mix of vocal power, staging and message showed her a different kind of singing competition.

Despite her success – including winning the Juno for dance recording of the year in 2023 for her hit “Ctrl + Alt + Del” – she never imagined entering the competition herself.

“It is my Super Bowl.”

For Josiane, the opportunity is also a chance to introduce international audiences to her Acadian roots.

The 25-year-old from Dieppe, N.B. said her ability to shift seamlessly between French and English could distinguish her in the competition, while giving her community a global platform.

She was in a car with her mother when she received the news she had made the shortlist. As Josiane became emotional on the phone, her mother pulled over and began crying, too.

“It’s a beautiful moment I got to live with my family,” said the artist, whose full name is Josiane Comeau.

Josiane hopes Canada’s participation will give other artists in the country permission to dream bigger.

“We have a place, we truly do, and I believe in Canada.”

Shaw, meanwhile, said he feels as though he has spent 14 years preparing for the opportunity, working his way from performing in coffee shops to arenas.

A tour of Germany last May strengthened his belief that his music could connect with European audiences.

“It’s, like, normal for me to hear Canadians sing back my music, but to hear other countries sing my music is mind-blowing to me,” said Shaw, who first broke out in 2012 with his hit “Kiss Goodnight.”

Shaw, who described his background as Chinese and Polish-Ukrainian, said he also wants to offer the kind of representation he felt was missing while growing up.

“I’ve had a long struggle with self-identity for the longest time because I had no one to look up to,” he said.

Cloutier pointed to two years performing across Europe and Quebec in the musical “Starmania” as preparation for Eurovision’s demanding stage. His wish list for a performance includes sparkles, fireworks and possibly water.

“I want to push my limit doing something crazy on stage,” he said.

Talk, known for his flashy and eccentric stage theatrics, was fairly direct about his ambitions.

“I think any of the finalists would be a great choice. But I really think this opportunity was built for me and I’m ready to win,” he said virtually, unable to attend the event in person.

Born Nicholas Durocher, Talk won the Juno for breakthrough artist of the year in 2024.

CBC/Radio-Canada says its music teams made initial selections before a seven-member jury chose the finalists at an Oct. 8 meeting in Toronto.

Jennifer Dettman, Canada’s head of delegation and CBC’s executive director of unscripted content, said vocal ability and the capacity to deliver a mesmerizing performance were central considerations.

With limited preparation time in Canada’s first year, organizers also sought artists with experience performing on large stages, she said.

Asked about the absence of Black and Indigenous finalists, Dettman said representing the country’s diversity is important to the broadcaster and promised more outreach in future years.

Those conversations take time, she said, particularly when many Canadian artists are still unfamiliar with Eurovision and the opportunities it offers.

“We’re really making sure with Indigenous music organizations, with Indigenous artists, with Black artists, that we are talking with them, that we’re listening to them,” she said.

Canada’s arrival comes as the competition faces continued controversy over Israel’s participation amid the crisis in Gaza.

Five public service broadcasters — from Ireland, the Netherlands, Spain, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted this year’s event.

Ireland’s RTÉ has confirmed it will neither participate in nor broadcast next year’s contest. The Netherlands is also withdrawing again, reversing a decision in September to return to the show.

Dettman said CBC/Radio-Canada respects other broadcasters’ decisions, while viewing Canada’s participation as an opportunity for its artists.

“It’s not a comment or a thought about what countries are participating or not,” she said.

“It’s about our participation with that Canadian artist to give them this incredible opportunity to showcase their music and their artistry to the world.”

Dettman declined to disclose how much it will cost to send Canada’s entrant.

Organizers say more than 130 million viewers across 35 markets watched this year’s Eurovision, a competition that has helped propel acts including Abba, Céline Dion and Måneskin to international fame.

For Rêve, it’s a chance to show audiences a different side of a country already known for its musical exports.

“Sometimes we only get to know Canadians on a global scale when they’ve already left,” she said.

“But we’re all still here.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Liberals set to table bill restricting access to Maid in cases of mental illness
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal government is set to introduce changes to Canada's medical assistance in dying law Tuesday to bar people suffering solely from a mental illness from accessing Maid, and to allow for advance directives.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A new law introduced in the House of Commons on Tuesday would allow Canadians to make advance requests for medically-assisted death — but their access is likely to vary depending on where they live.

Bill C-41 would amend the Criminal Code to allow people to make advance requests to access Maid. It would be up to provincial governments to decide whether to fulfil those requests through their own health systems, and to enact legislation.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser told reporters Tuesday he wasn’t certain how many provinces would do so. Quebec is the only province that already has an advance request regime in place. Alberta has passed legislation to bar the use of advance requests.

“I expect there will be more, but I hesitate to make announcements on behalf of provincial governments who are not here to represent themselves,” he said.

Under Canada’s current laws, a medically assisted death is available to individuals who are at least 18 years old, have a serious and incurable physical illness, disease or disability, and are in an advanced or irreversible state of decline. They also must be able to make a voluntary request and give informed consent for the procedure, including at the time it is administered.

An advance request would allow a person who suffers from a degenerative condition, such as dementia or ALS, to ask that an assisted death be carried out once they no longer have the capacity to consent.

The government said in a press release the decision to request Maid must be “voluntary, free from external pressure, and remain protected by rigorous safeguards.”

Fraser told reporters that while he’s somewhat concerned about the prospect of a patchwork of different rules across the country, he would be “more concerned about extending access without the safeguards in place, including the safeguards that must be legislated by provincial governments.”

The safeguards for advance requests included in the federal bill include a requirement that two independent medical or nurse practitioners agree the person meets the criteria.

The legislation also says the procedure will not be administered “if the person demonstrates, by words, sounds or gestures, refusal or resistance to have the substance administered to them.”

It says if the person demonstrates such refusal or resistance, “medical assistance in dying can no longer be provided to them on the basis of that request.”

Bill C-41 also would stop a scheduled expansion of Maid access to those suffering solely from a mental illness. The government said in the press release that “serious concerns remain about whether these cases can be assessed safely and consistently.”

The government has repeatedly pushed back the date when mental illness could become a qualifying factor for an assisted death and asked a special parliamentary committee to study the issue. The committee concluded in June that people suffering solely from a mental illness should be indefinitely excluded from accessing Maid.

Bill C-41 will need to pass the House of Commons and the Senate before March 17 — the date on which the law states people with a mental illness as their sole underlying condition would become eligible for Maid.

Fraser said Tuesday the consequences of not passing the bill before that deadline would be “extraordinarily serious.”

He said he wants to see the bill pass through the House of Commons before the parliamentary sitting ends in December.

Fraser said this would give “ample time for the Senate, where I know there are individuals who have unique perspectives on this issue, to raise their concern, to participate in debate, but ultimately pass this law before we face the potential consequence of the lapsing of the existing timeline.”

The group Dying with Dignity Canada called the government’s approach to the bill fundamentally flawed.

“By requiring provinces and territories to adopt further legislation before advance requests are allowed in their jurisdiction, the federal government has effectively given each province and territory a veto on advance requests,” the group said in a press release.

It said it’s also concerned that the legislation requires a subjective assessment of intolerable suffering.

“Individuals should be allowed to define what they consider to be physical and psychological intolerable suffering, as part of the advance request, and medical practitioners should base their decision on that objective standard. Any other approach risks ignoring an individual’s documented wishes,” the group said.

Conservative MP Tamara Jansen said on social media Tuesday that Maid in Canada is “already facing serious concerns about failing safeguards, weak oversight and vulnerable Canadians falling through the cracks.”

“Just 20 days ago, the Liberals voted down my bill to permanently stop this expansion. Mental illness and advance requests are separate issues, one has been extensively studied and has broad consensus, the other does not,” she said. “With the March 17 deadline approaching, the Liberals are holding Parliament ransom.”

Fraser said Tuesday the medical practitioners will use their expertise to confirm a person is living with an intolerable level of suffering.

Cardus, a Christian think-tank that opposes Maid, said in a release it was “deeply concerned” about expanding Maid to allow advance directives. It said data is limited because not many international jurisdictions allow the practice.

“Advance euthanasia requests introduce heightened risks for patients and providers, including significant risks of wrongful deaths,” it said.

Disability rights group Inclusion Canada said advance requests “allow assisted death after a person has lost the capacity to consent, leaving consequential judgments about their suffering and expressions of refusal to others.”

The group said it is worried “that discriminatory assumptions about disability, dependence and quality of life could influence those judgments.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

— With files from Hannah Alberga in Toronto and Catherine Morrison in Ottawa

stories.title: Five Things: The key topics at play as Canada and the EU discuss deeper ties
stories.summary: Ottawa - The next step in the relationship between Canada and the European Union is set to be unveiled by Prime Minister Mark Carney and EU President Ursula von der Leyen at a summit in Montreal on Thursday and Friday.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The next step in the relationship between Canada and the European Union is set to be unveiled by Prime Minister Mark Carney and EU President Ursula von der Leyen at a summit in Montreal on Thursday and Friday.

This summit comes just over a month after Carney delivered a speech to the European Parliament calling for closer ties with the 27-nation bloc.

Here are five things to look out for at the Montreal summit:

Ursula von der Leyen made waves last month when, in her own address to the European Parliament, she opened the door to Canada becoming “the first associate member of the EU.” Canadian officials were quick to downplay the likelihood of that name.

Canada’s EU Ambassador Jonathan Wilkinson pointed out that Carney described the arrangement as an “alliance of the future” when speaking with reporters after von der Leyen’s speech.

Since there’s no such thing as “associate membership” in the EU, the exact nature of the planned agreement with the EU has been a topic of much speculation.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has insisted Canada will never be an EU state and has said he doesn’t support EU taxes, laws or “reckless European-style immigration.”

Carney has said that any agreement will be brought to Parliament to be debated and voted on.

It was more than half a century ago, but there are many modern echoes in the twists and turns of this earlier attempt at securing our economy.

Freedom of movement is a central element of EU membership — European citizens are able to live in any member nation visa-free for up to three months. Those looking to work or study in a different country still face administrative obstacles that vary from country to country.

Wilkinson told The Canadian Press the two sides are not talking about free labour mobility between Canada and Europe. Rather, he said, Canada and the EU are looking at specific sectors which could benefit from shared labour pools.

There also has been talk of Canada joining Erasmus+, the EU’s study and training program that facilitates exchanges between member nations.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu was in Ireland last week to push forward negotiations on a digital trade agreement with the EU that would make it easier for Canadian and European businesses to buy and sell across borders.

Sidhu said in a statement the goal is to create “less friction” on e-signatures, e-contracts, paperless trade and cross-border data flows.

The Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or Ceta, is celebrating its 10th anniversary on Friday.

Nine EU members — France, Italy, Belgium, Ireland, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece and Hungary — have not yet ratified that trade deal.

Wilkinson said he’s met with all 27 of his EU counterparts and senses “momentum” in efforts to get more nations on board with Ceta.

The EU sees Canada as a valuable partner for developing clean, low-carbon energy. Canada has vast mineral resources that can be put toward hydrogen, nuclear and wind power projects.

Wilkinson said the two sides are talking about ways they can invest in boosting critical mineral refining and supply on both sides of the ocean to cut into China’s market dominance.

Natural Resource Minister Tim Hodgson signed a critical mineral partnership with Europe earlier this year focused on opening up more avenues to get European money invested in Canadian projects.

The European Investment Bank applied earlier this month for an exemption from foreign banking rules that would allow it to back Canadian projects.

Critical minerals are also vital to modern weapons manufacturing. Canada recently chose a German-Norwegian partnership over a South Korean competitor as its new submarine supplier, and this summit could see even closer ties emerge with Europe on defence.

Finance Minister Francois Philippe-Champagne recently announced a Nov. 30 summit in Luxembourg where Canada will gather its partners to sign an agreement to establish the new Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.

That bank will have headquarters in both Canada and Luxembourg.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Free labour movement not something Canada and EU considering in new pact: ambassador
stories.summary: Ottawa — Negotiations toward a new transatlantic pact between Canada and the European Union don't include discussions for a full-scale free labour movement, but something more focused, Canada's EU ambassador said ahead of the Canada-EU summit later this week in Montreal.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Canada-EU Summit being held this week in Montreal will serve to launch more formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the next year, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday.

Carney will meet with European Union President Ursula von der Leyen and other EU officials on Thursday and Friday in Montreal, where they are expected to announce the next stage of an enhanced alliance.

“This is the launch of further formal discussions, negotiations, over the course of the next year,” Carney said on his way into the weekly cabinet meeting.

The exact nature of the pact between Canada and the EU has been unclear — even to the leaders themselves.

In September, von der Leyen said the new arrangement could make Canada an “associate” member of the 27-member bloc. But “associate membership” does not actually exist in the EU and Canadian officials have downplayed the use of that term.

“It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians, in terms of opportunities to study work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities,” Carney said Tuesday, adding it could open up new research opportunities as well.

Carney used the term “alliance of the future” to describe the deal, which was first made public when he spoke to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France, last month.

Jonathan Wilkinson, who took on the Canadian ambassadorship in Brussels earlier this year after spending more than five years in the Liberal cabinet, told The Canadian Press the labour policy discussions with Europe are focused on “specialized areas” where employers on both sides of the Atlantic could benefit from access to a shared labour pool.

He said any measures that would make it easier for workers and students to move between the two jurisdictions must be approached in a “thoughtful way.”

“We’re not talking about free movement of labour between Europe and Canada. But what we are talking about is, in some specialized areas, it May be actually interesting and useful for both countries to have the ability to tap into labour pools,” Wilkinson said.

The ambassador did not cite specific sectors where labour mobility between Canada and the EU could be eased. The EU and Canada have been discussing increased collaboration on critical minerals, technology, defence and clean energy.

Wilkinson pointed to work already done by Canada and Europe on mutual accreditation for architects and said any future decisions about labour mobility would be focused on areas of “mutual benefit.”

Canada has also discussed joining Erasmus+, the European Union’s student exchange program, which offers study and training opportunities in member nations.

Michelle Rempel Garner, the Conservative immigration critic, has called on the government to explain what these negotiations mean for people coming to Canada.

“Canadians are already struggling with the cost of living due to immigration levels which are too high and have contributed to jobs becoming more scarce and workers getting paid less. Canadians deserve transparency on any EU immigration deal and how it would impact our jobs, homes, and health care,” she said in a statement.

The summit appears to be a source of friction between Carney and the new Parti Québécois government in Quebec.

A spokesperson for Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon St-Pierre Plamondon said in a written statement that Ottawa denied the premier the chance to speak at the summit and refused to allow Quebec to host a reception on the sidelines, following a request submitted by the former government in mid-September.

Following the cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney said in French that St-Pierre Plamondon declined an invitation to join him and the other premiers for a dinner with European officials during the summit. Carney said the federal government has had three consultation sessions with Quebec about the talks with the EU.

Joel Lightbound, Carney’s Quebec lieutenant, said Tuesday that St-Pierre Plamondon is welcome to attend the summit and the dinner but this is still a meeting between Canada and the EU.

This week’s summit will take place on the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Canada-Europe Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or Ceta.

Nine EU members — France, Italy, Belgium, Ireland, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece and Hungary — have not yet ratified that trade deal.

Wilkinson said he’s spoken with all 27 of his EU member nation counterparts and there is momentum in Europe to get more countries behind Ceta. He did not name specific nations.

One of the EU’s leading nations May have a new government soon. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is the current polling favourite to succeed Emmanuel Macron as president this spring.

Le Pen delivered a nearly hour-long speech to supporters Sunday that focused on her party’s nationalist, anti-immigrant positions.

Wilkinson said politics is always dynamic and Europeans and Canadians will go on sharing values regardless of which party is in power in a particular nation.

“I think in France, it’s a very important debate that they are having. And I think that if in fact the government were to change, people will have to take stock of that,” he said.

“But I do think that the European Union is a much bigger project than any one government in any one country. And I have a lot of confidence that Europeans will find their way through this and be just fine.”

Wilkinson said energy and critical minerals — including natural gas, hydrogen and nuclear power — will play a crucial role in the enhanced partnership between Canada and the EU.

“We’re looking at … how can we, for example, encourage significant additional European investment in Canadian minerals projects. We’re talking about how can we think about things like stockpiling together so that we actually can help to stabilize the market,” Wilkinson said.

The European Investment Bank applied for an exemption from Canadian foreign banking rules earlier this month that would allow the state investor to operate in Canada as part of a critical minerals agreement.

Wilkinson said Canada and the European Union are both looking for ways to build up the infrastructure to refine and ship critical minerals and reduce China’s market dominance.

“That’s not a dependency that’s good for Canada. That’s not a dependency good for the European Union. So we are looking at that,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press.

David Baxter and Emilie Bergeron, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Politicians return to Ontario legislature after 147-day break
stories.summary: The house is expected to sit for 23 days in a short but intense session, a hallmark under Premier Doug Ford's government since he won his third election in 2025.
stories.author: Liam Casey and Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Tuesday he feels “terrible” for honest students caught up in a career college system where financial aid is now unavailable, but opposition leaders say the students are only in that situation because of him.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at all private post-secondary institutions earlier this month after he said preliminary findings of a Kpmg audit turned up significant concerns.

Critics say the ministry should have acted sooner on a spike in Osap usage at a relatively small number of career colleges, and they question why the solution is to make all students pay the price.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he feels "terrible" for honest students caught up in a career college system where financial aid is now unavailable. Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at all private post-secondary institutions earlier this month after he says preliminary findings of a Kpmg audit turned up significant concerns. (Oct. 27, 2026)

“They’re all being penalized because these guys screwed up royally, and I don’t know whether it’s just total incompetence or complicity or some mixture of both, but it’s bad,” said interim Liberal leader John Fraser.

The opposition parties spent much of question period on the first day of the legislature returning from a 147-day break calling for Quinn to be fired for his handling of the issue.

In February, Quinn announced that the amount of Osap grants that students at publicly funded colleges and universities could receive would be cut because the program was becoming “unsustainable.”

But data obtained by The Canadian Press through a series of freedom-of-information requests showed that usage at colleges and universities was relatively flat, but career college usage was skyrocketing. Much of that was due to large year-over-year increases from a small number of schools.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said Quinn blamed students when his government should have been keeping a closer eye on the money.

“For more than three years, this government has been shovelling hundreds of millions of Osap grant funding to a handful of private career colleges without any oversight, monitoring, or accountability,” she said in the legislature.

“That’s why Osap costs were rising. If this isn’t gross incompetence, it’s something worse, and all the details will soon be coming out. Will the premier take responsibility for the Osap fiasco and fire his minister of colleges and universities?”

Ford defended Quinn, saying he is doing “an incredible job,” and directed his ire at the career colleges he accuses of being bad actors.

“Do you know who I feel terrible for?” Ford said. “These honest students that got trapped in the private college system ... There’s some good operators there, but got caught with the bad apples.”

Quinn said the pause was a necessary step.

“I do really sympathize for the students that are caught up in this, the good students that are really caught up in this, but we have to make sure that taxpayer dollars are respected,” he said.

Quinn said his ministry acted when it received tips and complaints, but critics say it should not have taken outside tips for the ministry to act on its own data showing rapidly increasing Osap usage at some schools.

“Well, recognizing that it is a tips-based system, we’ve investigated over 3,200 different Osap complaints since 2020, and we’ll continue to do that, ensuring that there is compliance across the Osap,” he said.

Quinn has referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, who are reviewing the information to determine whether to launch an investigation.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at all private post-secondary institutions earlier this month after he said preliminary findings of a Kpmg audit turned up significant concerns.
Critics say the ministry should have acted sooner on a spike in Osap usage at a relatively small number of career colleges, and they question why the solution is to make all students pay the price.

“They’re all being penalized because these guys screwed up royally, and I don’t know whether it’s just total incompetence or complicity or some mixture of both, but it’s bad,” said interim Liberal leader John Fraser.

stories.title: Five takeaways from Ontario’s municipal elections
stories.summary: Along with her win in the mayor’s race, key ward races appeared to go Olivia Chow’s way
stories.author: Laura Stone, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
The incumbent mayor staved off her main challenger, former councillor Brad Bradford, to win re-election. With almost all votes counted, Ms. Chow had 54 per cent of the vote, compared to Mr. Bradford’s 41 per cent. In her victory speech, she said she spoke with both Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who called to congratulate her, and that she looks forward to working with both governments to deliver for the people of Toronto. She also pledged to keep investing in police, paramedics, emergency response and community programs, and said she would keep Toronto’s water “in public hands,” a reference to Mr. Bradford’s promise to hive off the Toronto Water department into a separate, publicly owned company. His critics alleged this was a step toward privatization. He denied it.

The results in several key ward races appeared to go Ms. Chow’s way: In University-Rosedale former councillor Mike Layton – her stepson and son of the late Jack Layton, former leader of the federal NDP – won a return to city hall easily. In Parkdale-High Park, where left-leaning Gord Perks had stepped down, he will be replaced by Diana Chan McNally, an advocate for the homeless.

In Toronto-Danforth, long-time councillor Paula Fletcher’s chosen successor, former school trustee Sara Ehrhardt, defeated former councillor Mary Fragedakis. The second runner-up in the ward was Dianne Saxe, the sitting councillor in University-Rosedale, where she would have faced Mr. Layton. Ms. Saxe withdrew her candidacy there to run in Toronto-Danforth instead.

In Toronto Centre, a dense downtown ward, self-described progressive candidate Curran Stikuts unseated Chris Moise, a former police officer and health care worker. Mr. Stikuts, a young and articulate former activist with The 519, a community group based in the Gay Village, had the endorsement of Kristyn Wong-Tam, the NDP MPP and former city councillor. A third candidate, Daniel Tate, who posted graphic videos showing urban disorder in the city, came third.

The election also saw the defeat of long-time city hall fixture Frances Nunziata, who has spent 16 years as speaker of council and had been a councillor since Toronto was amalgamated in 1998. Before that, she was mayor of the city of York, already deep into a career in municipal politics that began in the 1980s. In her third attempt, social worker and local activist Chiara Padovani beat Ms. Nunziata in the ward of York South-Weston.

In Scarborough North, former Liberal MP Shaun Chen defeated Chow ally Jamaal Myers, who has served as Toronto Transit Commission chair.

In Beaches-East York, former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith, who has pledged to work with Ms. Chow, won easily in the ward Mr. Bradford had vacated to run for mayor. Mr. Erskine-Smith attempted to make the leap to provincial politics, but was unsuccessful in his bid to become the Ontario Liberal nominee in neighbouring Scarborough Southwest, and abandoned his plan to run for Ontario Liberal leader. He beat Natalie Johnson, a former CTV reporter.

In one of the evening’s early surprises, Alvin Tedjo was elected mayor of Mississauga. The first-term city councillor beat incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor and one-time Ontario Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie, who returned to municipal politics after losing the 2025 provincial election. The dynamic between Ms. Parrish and Ms. Crombie grew heated at times. Mr. Tedjo, a 43-year-old father of three, ran on a platform that focused on affordability and community safety.

Incumbent mayor and former Ontario NDP Leader Andrea Horwath was soundly defeated in her re-election bid. She came third, capturing just 14 per cent of the vote according to early returns, while winner Keanin Loomis won more than 40 per cent of the vote. Mr. Loomis, the former President and chief executive officer of the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce, now works in the steel construction industry, which has been hammered by U.S. tariffs. Mr. Loomis ran a campaign focused on respecting taxpayers, a responsive city hall, and getting the basics right.

With reports from Patrick White and Marcus Gee

stories.title: Business leaders and Emirati officials on guest list for Carney’s dinner with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince
stories.summary: A guest list of nearly 120 names shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of the ruling circle
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is courting wealthy Gulf investors, hosted a dinner in Ottawa on Monday for Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.

A guest list of nearly 120 names obtained by The Globe and Mail shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of Abu Dhabi’s ruling circle.

The dinner capped the first day of a two-day visit to Canada by the Crown Prince, whose father is the president of the UAE.

The blossoming relationship between Canada and the UAE has included the inking of a free trade agreement in July and an investment protection treaty that went into force in May. Mr. Carney came back from a visit to the country last fall touting a UAE commitment to invest $70-billion in Canada.

Ottawa is deepening ties with the UAE and other foreign trade partners as part of a push by the Prime Minister to lessen Canada’s economic reliance on the United States.

One of the most prominent invitees to the dinner was former prime minister Stephen Harper. The list leaned toward companies and investors with stakes in defence and security, energy, critical minerals, infrastructure, international development, space, advanced communications, quantum computing and artificial intelligence – all areas in which the Prime Minister’s Office has said the two countries will expand relations.

The invitees also included lawyers, consultants and lobbyists representing business interests in Ottawa, as well as provincial representatives, hospital and university leaders, museum administrators and representatives of Indigenous communities.

Members of the Desmarais family, long synonymous with Power Corporation of Canada, were on the list. André Desmarais, deputy chairman of Power Corporation of Canada, and Paul Desmarais III, a senior vice-president, were both listed, along with executives from Power Sustainable, a Power Corp. investment arm.

Also among the invitees were representatives of several large industrial companies, including Gregory Ebel, chief executive of Enbridge Inc.; Ian Edwards of engineering firm AtkinsRéalis; Alexandre L’Heureux of WSP Global; Kieran Hawe of construction company EllisDon; Bruce Power’s chief operating officer, James Scongack; and Eric Desaulniers, head of graphite developer Nouveau Monde Graphite.

Victor Dodig, recently appointed chief executive of Telus Corp., was also listed, as was Éric Martel, chief executive of Bombardier Inc.

Members of the tech industry were invited, including Joelle Pineau, chief AI officer at Cohere, and Valérie Pisano, chief executive of Mila.

Big investors and lenders were also on the list, including Deborah Orida, chief executive of PSP Investments; Alison Nankivell of Export Development Canada; and Geneviève Bouthillier, an executive vice-president at BDC Capital. So were government-relations heads from Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Hoopp and Sun Life, and venture investor Chris Arsenault of Inovia. Gurinder Grewal, named chief executive of Invest in Canada on Aug. 31, was also on the list.

Many members of Mr. Carney’s inner circle were listed, including Marc-André Blanchard, his chief of staff; Michael Sabia, Clerk of the Privy Council; David Morrison, a senior diplomatic adviser; Scott Gilmore, principal secretary; and Jennifer MacIntyre, a deputy chief of staff. The ambassadors to the United States and the UAE, Mark Wiseman and Angad Dhillon, were also on the list. So was Sébastien Carrière, Global Affairs Canada’s chief of protocol.

Many of the Emiratis who were invited work for the Abu Dhabi Crown Prince’s Court. Sheikh Khalifa bin Tahnoon Al Nahyan, the court’s chairman, and Saif Ghobash, chairman of the Crown Prince’s Office and secretary-general of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, were listed, as was Sultan Al Jaber, who is both the Uae’s minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.

Among the rest of the Emirati contingent on the list were representatives of DP World, a Dubai-based port operator that on Monday announced a memorandum of understanding with the owner of Manitoba’s Port of Churchill to explore further development of an expanded northern shipping corridor. Douglas Smith, chief executive officer of the company’s operations in Canada, was invited, as was Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, chairman of Dubai Chambers, who also sits on DP World’s board.

paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is courting wealthy Gulf investors, hosted a dinner in Ottawa on Monday for Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.
A guest list of nearly 120 names obtained by The Globe and Mail shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of Abu Dhabi’s ruling circle.
The dinner capped the first day of a two-day visit to Canada by the Crown Prince, whose father is the president of the UAE.

The blossoming relationship between Canada and the UAE has included the inking of a free trade agreement in July and an investment protection treaty that went into force in May. Mr. Carney came back from a visit to the country last fall touting a UAE commitment to invest $70-billion in Canada.
Ottawa is deepening ties with the UAE and other foreign trade partners as part of a push by the Prime Minister to lessen Canada’s economic reliance on the United States.

One of the most prominent invitees to the dinner was former prime minister Stephen Harper. The list leaned toward companies and investors with stakes in defence and security, energy, critical minerals, infrastructure, international development, space, advanced communications, quantum computing and artificial intelligence – all areas in which the Prime Minister’s Office has said the two countries will expand relations.

The invitees also included lawyers, consultants and lobbyists representing business interests in Ottawa, as well as provincial representatives, hospital and university leaders, museum administrators and representatives of Indigenous communities.

Members of the Desmarais family, long synonymous with Power Corporation of Canada, were on the list. stories.title: CPP and OAS payments land in bank accounts tomorrow. Here’s what you need to know
stories.summary: Canadians over the age of 60 can apply to receive hundreds of dollars in monthly benefits.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
Benefits from the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and the Old Age Security (OAS) program will be arriving in eligible Canadians’ bank accounts on Wednesday.

These plans offer monthly payments to millions of Canadians above the age of 60. Whether you are already receiving these benefits, or curious about your eligibility, this is the guide for you.

Here’s what you need to know.

The amount you receive monthly from the CPP retirement pension is based on your age, your contributions to the CPP and your average earnings when you were working. Your OAS payment is dependent on your age, net income and the number of years you’ve lived in Canada as an adult.

This year, the maximum monthly payment for the retirement pension is $1,507.65, and the average for new beneficiaries is $858.34.

Maximum monthly payments for seniors receiving OAS range from $762.50 to $838.75, depending on your age.

Starting your CPP pension later in life will result in higher payments per month. Starting before the age of 65 will result in payments decreasing by a small percentage each month. Starting after 65 will result in payments increasing by a small percentage each month. The maximum monthly payment is reached at age 70 and will not increase past then.

OAS payments work similarly.

You can calculate your approximate OAS payment using the Benefits Estimator tool on the Canadian government’s website. You can use your My Service Canada Account (Msca) in order to see your CPP contributions and calculate your approximate monthly CPP benefits.

Payment amounts for OAS benefits are reassessed quarterly in order to reflect the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Notably, payments will only increase if the CPI goes up, payments will never decrease if the CPI goes down.

The Canada Revenue Agency has said that based on changes in the CPI, OAS benefits increased by 1.4 per cent for the October to December 2026 quarter, for an increase of three per cent over the past year, from October 2025 to October 2026.

If you have lived in Canada for 10-40 years after the age of 18, you are only eligible for a partial OAS pension. Using the Benefits Estimator tool can help you figure out the payments to expect.

In order to qualify for CPP payments, you must be 60 or above and have made at least one valid contribution to the plan. Contributions to the CPP are automatically deducted from your paycheque. If you are self employed, you contribute when you file your taxes.

You do not need to be retired to qualify for the CPP retirement pension, working will not reduce the amount you are paid or impact your eligibility.

If you are a Canadian citizen or legal resident aged 65 or above you May qualify for the OAS benefit. If you have lived in Canada for less than 20 years as an adult, your eligibility May be impacted.

The OAS benefit is not contingent on your current or previous working status, however, there is a maximum income threshold.

People aged 65 to 74 must have an annual net income less than $152,062 to qualify. If you are 75 or above, your income must be less than $157,923.

You must submit your tax return each year in order to receive CPP and OAS benefits.

The CPP primarily provides benefits to Canadians outside of Quebec. However, if you have lived or worked in Quebec, you May still be eligible for CPP benefits. If you are unsure of your eligibility, check with Retraite Québec .

If you have lived or worked outside of Canada, you May be eligible to receive CPP pension and a pension from the other country.

Even if you are eligible, you will not be automatically registered for CPP payments, you must apply. You have the option to apply online through your Msca or apply by mail using a paper form.

Those who apply online can expect to receive a decision within 28 days, whereas applications by mail May take up to 120 days to receive a decision. If you would like the decision you received to be reconsidered, you will have 90 days to submit a request for reconsideration .

Most people will be eligible to apply online, but there are some exceptions. Before applying online, be sure to check if you qualify . If you apply online, you will be able to track the status of your application using your Msca.

Beyond retirement benefits, the CPP also provides disability benefits, benefits for children of CPP contributors and benefits for surviving dependants of deceased CPP contributors.

Most eligible Canadians over the age of 65 will be automatically enrolled in OAS and receive a confirmation letter from Service Canada. If you are eligible, but Service Canada is lacking necessary information to register you for the program, you May need to apply.

The final two dates for 2026 pension benefits will be Nov. 26 and Dec. 22.

stories.title: Stolen vehicle spotted in drive-thru
stories.summary: London, ON (October 27, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service arrested two after a stolen vehicle was spotted in a drive-thru near the downtown core yesterday morning.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 27, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service arrested two after a stolen vehicle was spotted in a drive-thru near the downtown core yesterday morning.

On Monday, October 26, 2026, at approximately 3:45 a.m., a vehicle entered a drive-thru in the area of Oxford Street West and Wharncliffe Road North followed by an officer in an unmarked cruiser.

While in the drive-thru, the officer learned that the vehicle was stolen. The officer followed the vehicle, requested additional resources, and the vehicle was stopped in a nearby laneway. Both suspects were taken into custody without incident.

As a result of the investigation, Ryan Robert Mercer, 46, and Amber Leigh Cottrelle, 37, both of London, have been charged jointly with possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000.

Amber Leigh Cottrelle has additionally been charged with fail to comply with release order and possession of a Schedule 1 substance.

Both of the accused have upcoming court dates.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Premier Doug Ford said there will be "zero tolerance" for any fraud in the Osap system
stories.summary: Questions about the government’s handling of the student aid controversy dominated the first day back at Queen’s Park.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford said there will be “zero tolerance” for any fraud in the OSAP system — but that he feels sorry for students at private career colleges caught up in the temporary ban on student aid .

Questions about the government’s handling of the student aid controversy dominated the first day back at the legislature after a 21-week break , with opposition critics asking the government why it didn’t act sooner, and why students at all private colleges are being penalized for what, so far, is a handful of rogue institutions.

“For more than three years, this government has been shovelling hundreds of millions of OSAP grant funding to a handful of private career colleges without any oversight, monitoring or accountability,” said New Democrat MPP Peggy Sattler, her party’s post-secondary critic. “That’s why OSAP costs were rising.

“This government’s failure to act earlier has protected bad-actor institutions and you are attacking students instead,” she said in the legislature Tuesday.

Earlier this month, Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced that his ministry notified the Ontario Provincial Police after a third-party audit uncovered irregularities in the OSAP system around a number of private career colleges, and that he was banning all career colleges from the aid system until the new year when a new, more stringent process will be rolled out.

Quinn has also permanently removed online-only programs at private colleges from OSAP eligibility.

The loss of access to OSAP grants, and now loans, amid fraud allegations at 8 schools is sparking fears for the future.

He had previously changed the OSAP system that was heavy on non-repayable grants to loans, citing ballooning costs. However, The Canadian Press later revealed that much of that increase was because of seven private career colleges, which received $385 million in 2024-25, the same amount that all public colleges received that same year.

The third-party audit continues, and police say they are still reviewing the referral from ministry.

In the meantime, Ford said it is “heartbreaking” for students but that the government had to act on the alleged fraud.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he feels "terrible" for honest students caught up in a career college system where financial aid is now unavailable. Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at all private post-secondary institutions earlier this month after he says preliminary findings of a KPMG audit turned up significant concerns. (Oct. 27, 2026)

“That’s who I feel sorry for,” the premier said when asked about those who have not received previously approved funds to pay their tuition.

While not wanting to “paint a broad brush against all colleges — because there are really good private career colleges — but there’s some really bad, bad people and we’re auditing the system right across the board,” Ford said, adding “there will be zero tolerance for any fraud. They’re going to jail. We’re going to hold them accountable, simple as that.”

Opposition critics accused the government of ignoring the problem for years, even after an auditor report in 2021, and Career Colleges Ontario reaching out with its concerns in 2023.

Minister Nolan Quinn asks Ontario Provincial Police to investigate “criminal allegations.”

Speaking to reporters at the legislature, Quinn said the government brought in the third-party auditor after his ministry’s own investigations, “recognizing that we saw some similarities across the inspections that we have done.”

He said he has sympathy for students, “but we have to remember these are serious criminal allegations. These are bad actors, and they’ve had to act to protect taxpayer dollars.”

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said “here’s the story for thousands and thousands of students receiving OSAP: They’re approved, they’re enrolled and then they’re abandoned in a period of seven weeks.”

The province has promised it will work with financial institutions to help facilitate loans in the meantime, but no further details have been released.

Some of the 242 colleges that had been eligible for OSAP have allowed students to continue classes in the interim .

With files from Robert Benzie

This article was updated from a previous version that misstated the number of private career colleges that had been eligible for OSAP as almost 300. In fact, it is 242.

stories.title: Althia Raj: What B.C.‘s Conservative win and Alberta’s referenda should teach Pierre Poilievre
stories.summary: Hanging on to the Conservative party’s most extreme members comes at a long-term cost, Althia Raj suggests.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
As Conservative MPs gather for their weekly caucus meetings, some are attempting to read the tea leaves from last week’s Alberta referenda and British Columbia’s big Conservative win.

Saturday, David Eby’s early election gamble — two years into his NDP government’s mandate — failed spectacularly . B.C. interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson won a majority after running a disciplined campaign and uniting his party — and the conservative movement — around his leadership.

On X, federal B.C. Conservative MP Aaron Gunn posted that Doerkson and his team had articulated a compelling vision for the province “and did so Without abandoning key conservative priorities or principles, including Dripa (the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act ), Sogi (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) and ending safe supply. “Those trying to use this victory to argue the federal Conservative Party needs to abandon its conservative principles in order to win an election are doing so either disingenuously or ignorantly,” he wrote.

Despite his rodeo announcer background, Doerkson did not create a stampede to the polls . Only 48 per cent of the B.C. electorate showed up to vote. The Conservatives obtained fewer votes than they did in 2024 — 862,688 to 911,153.

What led to the party’s large majority is that 273,768 NDP voters from 2024 failed to show up for their party.

Some likely voted Green, others Conservative, but many simply stayed home.

That is a success of the Conservative campaign.

And it isn’t because Doerkson and his team flexed on controversial issues, like Sogi — it’s precisely because they didn’t.

Since Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from “a bad deal” with the U.S. in August, his popularity has reached new heights. This makes the

What the B.C. Conservatives presented, through careful messaging, was a Conservative leader that British Columbians did not need to fear. Doerkson seemed like a nice positive guy, talking about running a competent government and lowering taxes. He was a blank slate. With not much of a record to defend, his campaign successfully stripped centrists and progressive voters of a reason to mobilize. And the NDP failed to make a compelling case otherwise.

Depressing an opponent’s turnout can be as important as turning out your own voters.

While the NDP made a series of own goals, from calling an election they were ill-equipped to fight, to having no clear message, to Eby’s subsidized child-care revelation , the Conservatives amplified the setbacks. NDP voters were left unmotivated.

Gunn May believe that Dripa and Sogi policies led British Columbia to turn blue and that the same strategy will pay off for Poilievre. But not only does the data suggest that is not true — Research Co.’s exit poll found fewer than 30 per cent of respondents said those were vote drivers — Poilievre is no Doerkson. Voters have already made up their minds about Poilievre, and poll after poll suggests they don’t like him. Recent figures from Abacus Data suggest 45 per cent of the country does not like him; Liaison suggests the number is 55 per cent; an Ekos survey this month pegs it at 70 per cent .

This isn’t because voters can’t see beyond admiration for Prime Minister Mark Carney . According to Liaison, NDP Leader Avi Lewis’s negatives are dropping. But Lewis is just becoming known; Poilievre is a known quantity.

During the 2025 federal election, a major vote driver was U.S. President Donald Trump and his 51 st state threats, but dislike for Poilievre also sent voters to the Liberal camp.

Those voices are defining the party’s agenda to one that a majority of swing voters cannot support — voters that the Conservatives need without a stronger NDP splitting the Liberals’ base of support.
