stories.title: Outgoing Winnipeg councillor reflects on increasing polarization, hostility towards elected officials
stories.summary: Outgoing city councillor Janice Lukes says a lot has changed during her 12 years at city hall.
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
Outgoing Waverley West councillor Janice Lukes is reflecting on her 12 years at Winnipeg city hall: the good, the bad, and the ugly.

“I’m ready to go, I made up my mind, so I’m excited. It’s like a new beginning for me,” Lukes told Global News.

She says a lot has changed since she first started as city councillor.

“The world has become very polarized, everything is black and white now it seems. Very different even from 12 years ago when I started. I attribute it to a lot of it to the orange man down south and the disrespect(ful) language that he uses,” she said, adding that economic instability, global conflict and mental health issues all play a role.

“There’s a lot of upset people, a lot of unrest, a lot of polarization, and people take that out on elected officials, (while) driving, people at Tim Horton’s, wherever. People are frustrated in the world right now.”

Lukes says while she hasn’t had many issues with the residents in her ward, the increased cases of threats and hostility often come with chairing a committee and being involved with broader decision making at city hall.

“People coming into this role have to understand very clearly that you’re not going to make everybody happy at all,” she said.

“And you’re making decisions that impact people’s lives, income, (and) livelihoods. You’re making very big decisions here at city hall and not everybody is going to agree with that, so it makes you a target for comments and feedback and probably some other things.”

Lukes has taken her own safety precautions. Last year, she hired private security to attend a community event following concerning comments online. She’s also consulted with police to know what to do in the event of an emergency at city hall.

“I met with a police officer. We sat down in my office and he told me what to do if there is a shooting or a break in or whatever,” Lukes said. “So I am mentally all prepared for all that, I have my baseball bat, I know what window to jump out of.”

While it May be amplified in recent years, hostility towards elected officials isn’t new, if you ask former Winnipeg mayor Susan Thompson.

She says during the 1990s, security measures at city hall were nearly non-existent.

“Even in my day, I had some really bad situations. And I mainly had to handle them personally, and that’s not right,” Thompson said.

“It was not until I got a bomb threat, and my car keyed, and tires slashed, and death threats that (security) began to evolve.”

Last year, Manitoba NDP cabinet ministers Nahanni Fontaine and Bernadette Smith had their constituency offices set on fire. A man was arrested and charged in that case.

Kelly Saunders, a political science professor at Brandon University, says social media has played a role in heightening hostility, particularly towards marginalized communities.

“Women politicians, people of colour – those politicians are unfortunately experiencing even high threats of violence compared to everyone else,” Saunders said.

She also says it’s having an impact on how many people want to run for office.

“It really has a chilling impact,” she said. “I mean how many people are willing to subject themselves and their families to this kind of vitriol of hatred, of violence.”

As for Lukes, her message to the next council is to be prepared.

“Always be aware of your surroundings, know that you’re not going to make everyone happy, know that the world is unstable, that people are unstable,” she said.

“You have to think about these things, because you are making decisions that are impacting lives, and that’s very big stuff.”

stories.title: What is ‘advance directive,’ the principle at heart of Ottawa’s new Maid law?
stories.summary: The principle of advance directives is “profoundly ethically complex,” one expert said, adding that it can be hard to predict how a person’s disease will progress.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The federal government is set to update the law on medical assistance in dying (Maid) in Canada, permitting Canadians to decide whether they want to end their lives ahead of time.

On Wednesday, Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Health Minister Marjorie Mitchel are scheduled to reveal more details about Canada’s new Maid law, which will include changes to include changes to the Criminal Code to ensure that a doctor who provides medical assistance in dying to someone who is eligible on an advance directive “will not be treated as a criminal in Canada going forward.”

Speaking in Ottawa earlier this month, Sean Fraser said the government will “grant access to medical assistance in dying to people who have provided consent at a time when they still have capacity but know that they have been diagnosed with an illness that will take that capacity from them subsequently.”

This is sometimes referred to as an “advance directive” or “advance request” in medical parlance.

It often involves a mentally competent person making a written request for Maid, with the intention that it would be honoured later, if and when they lose the capacity to make the decision for themselves: for example, in people suffering from worsening Alzheimer’s or dementia.

“That means, specifically, I give my consent in advance in this capable state to receive medical assistance in dying (at a later time),” said University of Toronto bioethicist Kerry Bowman.

In 2024, Quebec became the first, and so far only, province in Canada to allow residents to authorize an early request for Maid.

In Quebec, only a person who has been diagnosed with “a serious and incurable illness leading to incapacity to give consent to care” May give advance request for Maid. They must also identify a physician or specialized nurse practitioner who agrees to assist in the process.

Bowman said the principle of advance directives is “profoundly ethically complex,” adding that it can be hard to predict how a person’s disease will progress.

“The concern is you’ve almost got a stranger making a decision for a stranger. Do we really know ourselves in that state?” he said.

The Quebec law allows a patient to withdraw or modify their Maid request. However, the question of withdrawing consent becomes complicated when some patients have “no capacity to withdraw” in the advanced stages of illness, Bowman said.

“I’m not necessarily against it. But I do think most of us are enormously underestimating how ethically complex this is,” he said.

Advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada, which has long advocated for advance directives, says the federal government’s approach is “fundamentally flawed” because it downloads implementation to the provinces and territories.

“At best, this legislation will create a patchwork of systems across the country, thus further increasing inequity in Maid access, instead of a federal framework that would ensure that all people across Canada could have access to advance requests for Maid if they are eligible,” Helen Long, the group’s CEO, said in a statement.

“At worst, some people in Canada May never have access to advance requests in their province or territory,” she added.

Equitable access to advance requests is fundamental to death with dignity, Long said.

“Without the option of an advance request, Canadians are forced to make an impossible choice: die earlier than they want to in order to ensure they have capacity to consent… or risk losing capacity and be forced to live in a situation they would find intolerable,” she said.

stories.title: These punk musicians became city councillors in B.C. – and brought their progressive politics to the table
stories.summary: D.O.A.’s Joe Keithley and Needs’s Sean Orr have both pressed for housing to be recognized as a human right
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Joe Keithley has lived most of his life by a simple slogan: Talk Minus Action Equals Zero . He’s never much cared for rhetoric; making the world a better place requires work. The philosophy has coloured his nearly 50-year career as the front man of D.O.A., the trailblazing, innovative and deeply progressive B.C. punk band that has played and organized hundreds of benefit concerts for anti-racist, anti-war, environmental and many other causes.

So when Keithley was first elected to Burnaby, B.C.’s city council as a member of the local Green Party in 2018 by a margin of just a couple hundred votes, he was happy to see that voters understood his ethos. “At first, they were like, ‘Oh, it’s a punk rock guy,’” he says, “but then were like, ‘No, no, he actually takes these issues seriously.’”

The 70-year-old has since helped push the city to affirm housing as a human right and to boost its supply of affordable units, including when old buildings are knocked down for new development. During B.C.’s municipal elections earlier this month, Keithley’s reputation as a councillor took him even further than his reputation as a musician. Running this time as a member of the social-democratic Burnaby Citizens Association, he won the most votes of any aspiring councillor.

He wasn’t, remarkably, even the only punk-rock front man in the Lower Mainland to pull off that feat. Sean Orr, vocalist of the hardcore-punk band Needs – and a longtime civic-affairs writer, housing activist and artist – took home the most votes of any Vancouver council candidate on Oct. 17 as a member of the Coalition of Progressive Electors, or Cope, party.

Punk rock and progressive politics have been intertwined since the Ramones and Sex Pistols first brought the genre to the masses in the seventies. The connection only deepened at the turn of the eighties, when the genre’s rougher, tougher second wave more openly and deeply wrapped inclusivity into its scenes. It May have taken a few decades since D.O.A. helped christen that more aggressive wave and its descendants as hardcore punk, but the progressive politics of the genre are now firmly entrenched in two of the biggest municipal governments in B.C. (The provincial government is another matter, however, with the B.C. Conservatives winning a majority in last weekend’s vote.)

“I really like the metaphor of the mosh pit – if somebody falls down, you pick them up,” Orr says. “Extrapolating that out to politics, into the world in general, it’s like the spirit of looking out for each other and protecting each other.”

His band Needs, which is now dormant, made both its politics and its sense of humour quite clear with several releases last decade. Its song titles include The Only Good Condo Is a Dead Condo and Eat the Rich... People’s Leftovers , but also We Don’t Know Why We Are Protesting Is Why We Are Protesting .

“I’ve written songs about limitations around punk rock and change, in terms of how it kind of gets co-opted by the big machine,” Orr says, acknowledging that there are “limitations to being a city councillor as well.”

Orr, 48, felt limited in his ability to push an agenda after first being elected to Vancouver council in a 2025 by-election. Not only was he Cope’s only councillor for that truncated term, he had a terse-at-best relationship with now-outgoing mayor Ken Sim after Sim falsely accused Orr, a supporter of harm-reduction approaches for drug users, of distributing illegal drugs. While Sim later apologized, Orr has since launched a defamation suit against him.

Despite being on the outside, Orr made serious efforts to get his voice heard in his brief first year-and-change on council. He co-introduced a successful motion for landlords to be fined for preventing tenants from running air conditioners; fought for more library funding and seven-day-a-week service; and, like Keithley in Burnaby, pressed to recognize housing as a human right.

He said that being part of Cope, now part of a largely progressive Vancouver council, keeps him grounded. “We’re a party that is connected to a lot of movements on the ground, and we are super aware of the limitations of we can do at City Hall – and that we have to kind of have that door open to those movements.”

Keithley ran for politics a half-dozen times before winning a Burnaby council seat. Before that, he was mostly known by a stage name that does not adhere to The Globe and Mail’s editorial style guide. And while he still performs with the band between council sessions, often in sleeveless shirts, these days you might catch him walking around Burnaby City Hall in a suit jacket – or at least a T-shirt with sleeves.

It’s only a slight lifestyle change for a man whose band once issued a record with a famed photo of Ojibwa warrior Brad Larocque staring down a soldier during the Oka Crisis on its cover, and which has also put out albums titled Something Better Change and, yes, Talk - Action = 0 . (D.O.A. also released a song about American assimilation called 51st State – in 1987.)

Keithley’s political career has caught the attention of everyone from documentarian Scott Crawford – whose film, also titled Something Better Change , chronicles the musician’s 2022 council campaign – to Beto O’Rourke, the Texas Democrat who came up in the same music scene as members of At the Drive-In and The Mars Volta. Punk didn’t exist when Keithley first got into music; he made it his own. “These people stood up and said something,” he said of his contemporaries. So did he.

Though both their past and present careers overlapped thematically, Orr and Keithley have only met briefly in passing. But the geographic coincidence of both winning the most votes among council candidates in their respective cities nonetheless highlights the way progressive politics emerges organically in the Vancouver area.

“If you look at Vancouver, we’re kind of isolated from the rest of the country, and we’ve prided ourselves on this long history of activism,” Orr says. “Look at Greenpeace, look at Adbusters, look at all these organizations that are now international – that started in Vancouver, because of that spirit of fighting back against institutions and power.”

Punk rock and progressive politics have been intertwined since the Ramones and Sex Pistols first brought the genre to the masses in the seventies. The connection only deepened at the turn of the eighties, when the genre’s rougher, tougher second wave more openly and deeply wrapped inclusivity into its scenes. It May have taken a few decades since D.O.A. helped christen that more aggressive wave and its descendants as hardcore punk, but the progressive politics of the genre are now firmly entrenched in two of the biggest municipal governments in B.C. (The provincial government is another matter, however, with the B.C. Conservatives winning a majority in last weekend’s vote.)

“I really like the metaphor of the mosh pit – if somebody falls down, you pick them up,” Orr says. “Extrapolating that out to politics, into the world in general, it’s like the spirit of looking out for each other and protecting each other.”

His band Needs, which is now dormant, made both its politics and its sense of humour quite clear with several releases last decade. Its song titles include The Only Good Condo Is a Dead Condo and Eat the Rich... People’s Leftovers , but also We Don’t Know Why We Are Protesting Is Why We Are Protesting .

“I’ve written songs about limitations around punk rock and change, in terms of how it kind of gets co-opted by the big machine,” Orr says, acknowledging that there are “limitations to being a city councillor as well.”

Orr, 48, felt limited in his ability to push an agenda after first being elected to Vancouver council in a 2025 by-election. Not only was he Cope’s only councillor for that truncated term, he had a terse-at-best relationship with now-outgoing mayor Ken Sim after Sim falsely accused Orr, a supporter of harm-reduction approaches for drug users, of distributing illegal drugs. While Sim later apologized, Orr has since launched a defamation suit against him.

Despite being on the outside, Orr made serious efforts to get his voice heard in his brief first year-and-change on council. He co-introduced a successful motion for landlords to be fined for preventing tenants from running air conditioners; fought for more library funding and seven-day-a-week service; and, like Keithley in Burnaby, pressed to recognize housing as a human right.

He said that being part of Cope, now part of a largely progressive Vancouver council, keeps him grounded. “We’re a party that is connected to a lot of movements on the ground, and we are super aware of the limitations of we can do at City Hall – and that we have to kind of have that door open to those movements.”

Keithley ran for politics a half-dozen times before winning a Burnaby council seat. Before that, he was mostly known by a stage name that does not adhere to The Globe and Mail’s editorial style guide. And while he still performs with the band between council sessions, often in sleeveless shirts, these days you might catch him walking around Burnaby City Hall in a suit jacket – or at least a T-shirt with sleeves.

It’s only a slight lifestyle change for a man whose band once issued a record with a famed photo of Ojibwa warrior Brad Larocque staring down a soldier during the Oka Crisis on its cover, and which has also put out albums titled Something Better Change and, yes, Talk - Action = 0 . (D.O.A. also released a song about American assimilation called 51st State – in 1987.)

Keithley’s political career has caught the attention of everyone from documentarian Scott Crawford – whose film, also titled Something Better Change , chronicles the musician’s 2022 council campaign – to Beto O’Rourke, the Texas Democrat who came up in the same music scene as members of At the Drive-In and The Mars Volta. Punk didn’t exist when Keithley first got into music; he made it his own. “These people stood up and said something,” he said of his contemporaries. So did he.

Though both their past and present careers overlapped thematically, Orr and Keithley have only met briefly in passing. But the geographic coincidence of both winning the most votes among council candidates in their respective cities nonetheless highlights the way progressive politics emerges organically in the Vancouver area.

“If you look at Vancouver, we’re kind of isolated from the rest of the country, and we’ve prided ourselves on this long history of activism,” Orr says. “Look at Greenpeace, look at Adbusters, look at all these organizations that are now international – that started in Vancouver, because of that spirit of fighting back against institutions and power.”

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Peel regional police say they were called shortly before 5 a.m. Sunday on reports of a stabbing in the parking lot of an industrial area near Tomken and Kamato roads.

They say officers found an injured man who died at the scene.

Police say they have identified a 35-year-old man from Brampton, Ont., as the suspect.

stories.title: Victims sought after London man charged in child luring investigation: LPS
stories.summary: A London man has been charged in a child luring investigation and police are looking for more potential victims.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A London man has been charged in a child luring investigation and police are looking for more potential victims.

On Oct. 20, police said a man started speaking with a person online that he believed was a 14-year-old girl. Officers said during their exchange, the suspect offered to pick her up and take her for a drive.

The suspect allegedly gave his phone number, continuing the conversation via text, which became sexual in nature, police said. Sexually explicit photos were reportedly sent and the suspect allegedly asked for photos back.

The LPS said the suspect also agreed to meet the girl in person.

Police identified the suspect as a London man who was using Snapchat with the username “biskylover”.

On Oct. 22, officers arrested 25-year-old Dylan Jonathan Carter. He has been charged with:

Making sexually explicit material available to a person under or believed to be under 18 years of age

Luring a person under 18 years of age by telecommunication

The LPS is looking for any other potential victims, releasing the accused’s picture in an effort to do so. Anyone with information or who had any similar interactions with him is asked to contact the LPS at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Crown withdraws criminal charges against Montreal protesters arrested at bank sit-in
stories.summary: Montreal - The Crown has withdrawn all criminal charges against pro-Palestinian protesters arrested during a sit-in at a downtown Montreal bank more than two years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Crown on Monday dropped criminal charges against pro-Palestinian protesters arrested during a sit-in at a downtown Montreal bank in 2024, ending a legal battle that protesters say raises broader questions about the right to demonstrate.

The Crown withdrew the remaining criminal mischief charges against 14 protesters after they agreed to plead guilty to violating a municipal noise bylaw and pay $300 fines.

The defendants were among 44 people arrested in April 2024 after staging a sit-in at a Scotiabank branch, demanding that the bank divest from Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems amid the war in Gaza.

“We want to make sure people can continue to fight things like this,” protester Eli Tareq said at a news conference Monday at Montreal municipal court. “If a citizen gets treated this way, what will happen when people do anything that’s deemed more violent?”

Defence lawyer Barbara Bedont said most of the other protesters had already resolved their cases through community service.

She said the remaining defendants had a strong constitutional case and warned that criminalizing peaceful sit-ins threatens freedom of expression and the right to protest.

The case comes to an end months after Scotiabank’s investment management subsidiary disclosed it had sold its remaining shares in Elbit Systems, which protesters celebrated as a victory for their campaign.

“We set out to pressure a Canadian bank to stop profiting from genocide, and in that case we won,” protester Harar Hall said at the press conference.

But protesters said the resolution of their criminal cases fell short of the accountability they had sought from police and the justice system.

Protester Mara Farrokh said the defendants had challenged their arrests under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, arguing that police had violated their constitutional rights.

But she said they eventually agreed to the fines in order to put an end to the proceedings. She alleged that the judge overseeing their case was treating them unfairly.

“We knew that getting justice out of this court system wouldn’t be possible,” she said in an interview Monday.

Footage of the sit-in was shown at the Montreal municipal court in April.

Farrokh alleged the security camera footage included a sequence showing officers in riot gear stepping on a protester, as demonstrators were surrounded.

Farrokh said the judge watched the footage but refused to acknowledge what the protester described as evidence of excessive police force.

The allegations have not been independently verified, and the Canadian Press has not viewed the footage described by Farrokh.

In an email, Montreal police said they acknowledged the municipal court’s decision, adding that anyone who believes they were mistreated during a police intervention can file a complaint with the force or an independent body.

The protesters say they have filed a complaint with Quebec’s judicial council against the judge, ’‘to have a committee review her behaviour throughout the case,’’ said Farrokh, adding the judge treated them in a way she described as ’‘unacceptable’’ and showing ’‘bias’’ against the protesters.

During hearings in April, a manager at the Scotiabank branch testified that the protesters had not threatened anyone or damaged property. He also said he had locked the doors and called police without first asking the demonstrators to leave.

At the time, protester Felix Bradley questioned why the demonstrators were still facing criminal charges when the bank had already divested from Elbit Systems.

“We really want to draw attention to this so that more Canadians can be informed and then that more Canadians can exercise their right to protest,” Bradley said in April.

The sit-in was part of a broader wave of pro-Palestinian demonstrations following the outbreak of the war in Gaza in October 2023.

Pro-Palestinian activists accused Scotiabank of profiting from Israel’s military operations through its investment in Elbit Systems, which supplies weapons and military technology to the Israeli military.

Regulatory filings disclosed in February showed that Scotiabank’s subsidiary, 1832 Asset Management, had sold its remaining shares in Elbit Systems.

Hall previously said the protesters believed they had been treated more harshly because of their political views.

“We would not have faced this treatment from the police, from the bank, from institutions, if we were not pro-Palestinian protesters,” Hall said in April.

The Crown declined to comment at the end of the hearings.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

— with files from Erika Morris in Montreal

stories.title: A tale of a B.C. election in three speeches
stories.summary: As Lorne Doerkson reached beyond his base, David Eby apologized to his and Emily Lowan sparked divisiveness
stories.author: Marsha Lederman
stories.content:
David Eby wore it in his words and his face on Saturday night, his terrible decision to call an election two years into a four-year mandate. The hubris was a turnoff for an electorate already dissatisfied, the desire for change evident in B.C.’s municipal elections a week earlier that, in Vancouver, brought in a new mayor and many new councillors.

But it was worse than hubris. It was the calculated nastiness of it all: to take advantage of an opposition party in disarray; the fresh departure of a wildly unpopular leader who had sent MLAs fleeing from the party to sit as independents or start their own parties; a new guy whom many people in the province had never heard of suddenly in charge. Two days after Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s unexpected resignation, two days into Lorne Doerkson’s surprise leadership, Mr. Eby called the election anyway. He said he was doing it for stability in the face of the Trump threat. Voters weren’t buying it.

Mr. Eby’s public career trajectory has seen him go from advocate in the Downtown Eastside with the Pivot Legal Society, to the B.C. Civil Liberties Association, to politics, where eventually as Premier, he disappointed some of his base with his climate and addiction and mental-health policies.

He’ll now forever be known as the premier who blew it with the early election call.

“A number of my colleagues, some of the hardest-working MLAs I know for their communities, were not elected tonight,” Mr. Eby said on Saturday, looking older than he did when he called the election just over a month earlier. “It breaks my heart and I accept full responsibility for that outcome.” He announced his resignation as party leader.

And now the guy who nobody had heard of is going to be Premier. Lorne Doerkson, who is said to be a decent guy, reflected that decency in the way he recognized Mr. Eby in his victory speech, and how he seemed to recognize the B.C. voters who did not choose the Conservatives.

“I want to say a word to the people who aren’t in this room,” Mr. Doerkson said. “There is a place for you here. Bring your ideas. Bring your family. Bring your ambitions.”

He mentioned First Nations and young British Columbians; there are people in both constituencies feeling wary right now.

There was a point when Mr. Doerkson went off and sounded a bit, dare I say, Trumpish – “we will cut red tape like it’s never been cut before” – but you can forgive the guy for a moment of hyperbole amid his jubilation.

On Sunday, B.C.’s next Premier was more collected as he thanked Mr. Eby again, outlined his priorities – cutting government spending, fixing health care, building the pipeline – and again reached out beyond his base.

“To the British Columbians who voted for another party yesterday, I heard you. Starting today, I am your Premier as much as anyone else’s. You will have a government that listens to you, works for you and respects you, however you marked your ballot.”

The Green Party retained two seats, including that of its new leader. Emily Lowan is very young, only 26, so we can keep that in mind when we scrutinize her election night speech, in which she failed to congratulate Mr. Doerkson for his win or to recognize Mr. Eby for his service.

Her words lacked grace and at times felt unnecessarily mean-spirited. About the party that had just won the confidence of the province with a majority government, Ms. Lowan said the Greens “are the only party who is equipped to stand against the Conservatives and their existence.” There were laughs and cheers.

The word “existence” came after a pause as she appeared to be talking off the cuff. Still, that is not what we need right now. No thank you to the divisiveness that has dominated the discourse to the south of us. No thank you to politicians who care more about ideology than governance through collaboration, who use the platform of an election night speech to jab an opponent, rather than assure the electorate.

Mr. Eby was far more gracious in his moment of humiliation over his ill-conceived election call, as he detailed another call he made – a phone call, to congratulate Mr. Doerkson.

“I wished him the best, and quite sincerely,” Mr. Eby said in his concession speech. “This is an important time. This is a critical time for our province and for our country, and I hope for all British Columbians that he protects British Columbians, looks after us, and looks after the province.”

Yes. You’re going to be in charge, Mr. Doerkson. We’re counting on you.

stories.title: A look at Ontario’s current negotiations with its education unions
stories.summary: Here is where each union currently stands in the process
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
The Ontario government is hoping to reach deals with five major education unions, all of which have been without a contract since the end of August.

Bargaining has been stalled over a dispute regarding which issues should be addressed centrally with the government and which should be handled at the local table with school boards.

Usually, large issues such as salaries, class sizes and sick days are negotiated centrally, while school board-specific issues such as operational and administrative policies are negotiated locally.

The matter will be decided by Ontario’s Labour Relations Board. Its ruling is expected in early November.

In the meantime, all five unions have set dates for members to vote on giving their leadership a mandate to strike in November.

Here is where each union stands in its negotiations with the province and school boards.

Represents: 84,000 members, which include elementary teachers, occasional teachers, education-support personnel, professional-support personnel and early-childhood educators.

Latest: The union will vote on a strike mandate from Nov. 9 to 18.

Represents: About 60,000 members, which include high-school teachers, occasional teachers, educational assistants, psychologists and speech-language pathologists.

Latest: The union has scheduled its strike vote for Nov. 6 to 16.

“Our members want fair, negotiated contracts that address the realities they are seeing in schools every day,” Osstf president Martha Hradowy said in a press release .

“A strike vote gives us an opportunity to strengthen our bargaining position and sends a clear message to the Ford government that Osstf/Feeso members are united behind the bargaining priorities we will bring to the table.”

Represents: About 45,000 members, including elementary, secondary and occasional teachers.

Latest: The union has scheduled its province-wide strike vote for Nov. 12 and 13.

Represents: More than 13,000 teachers in French-language elementary and secondary schools in Ontario, both Catholic and public, as well as professional and support staff working in various Francophone workplaces.

Latest: The union’s strike vote is scheduled for Nov. 16 and 17.

Represents: About 57,000 Cupe education workers in the public, Catholic, English, and French school systems across Ontario.

Latest: The union’s strike vote has been scheduled for Nov. 4 to 18.

stories.title: Man and woman who yelled, stripped on Newfoundland flight fined $4,000 each
stories.summary: Corner Brook - A man and woman in Newfoundland have each been fined $4,000 for endangering the safety of an airline flight by refusing to remain in their seats, yelling at passengers and crew and removing some of their clothing.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Corner Brook - A man and woman in Newfoundland have each been fined $4,000 for endangering the safety of an airline flight by refusing to remain in their seats, yelling at passengers and crew and removing some of their clothing.

A court in Corner Brook, N.L., heard that on Aug. 28, 2024, Corey Pancer and Deborah Bojman were aboard a Flair Airlines flight headed to Deer Lake, N.L., when Pancer got out of his seat and refused to follow instructions from the crew.

stories.title: Vehicle ends up on its roof following multi-car crash in London
stories.summary: Emergency crews were called to the intersection of Wonderland Road and Glanworth Drive at about 10:20 a.m. Monday.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
One vehicle ended up on its roof following a multi-vehicle crash in London’s south end.

Emergency crews were called to the intersection of Wonderland Road and Glanworth Drive at about 10:20 a.m. Monday.

At the scene, responders found a pickup truck and a sedan that had collided.

It remains unclear whether other vehicles were involved.

The sedan came to rest on its roof with one person trapped inside. Firefighters removed a door from the vehicle and extricated the occupant.

London police said one person was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Wonderland Road and portions of Glanworth Drive were closed until around noon.

stories.title: Police ethics commissioner and watchdog investigating Montreal police
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - Quebec's internal security minister says a provincial police ethics commissioner and an independent watchdog will both investigate the suspension of a Montreal police officer over allegations of criminal conduct in interactions with homeless people.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - Quebec’s internal security minister says a provincial police ethics commissioner and an independent watchdog will both investigate the suspension of a Montreal police officer over allegations of criminal conduct in interactions with homeless people.

Oct. 26, 2026

By The Canadian Press

Guy Jr. Lapointe says in a news release that an independent investigation was needed to maintain public trust.

Lapointe says the Montreal police chief had informed him of a criminal allegation involving an officer.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Image 9Image 10

The daily newspaper La Presse was the first to report allegations of misconduct by two police officers from a station in the city’s downtown area.

One officer allegedly urinated on unhoused people while on duty, while another officer allegedly posed for photos mocking a suspect placed in a humiliating position during an arrest.

Lapointe says he asked both the watchdog and the commissioner to conduct their own investigation into the criminal allegation and of the conduct of the officer or officers involved.

Police confirmed on Oct. 16 that two of its officers were suspended and were subject to internal investigations by the professional standards unit.

“This isn’t a vote of non-confidence toward the Montreal police, nor is it calling into question the quality of their investigation,” Lapointe said. “Rather, it is a question of transparency. It is clear to me that, in this specific case, the investigation needs to be done by an external body in order to maintain public trust.”

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada praised the minister’s decision in a social media post on Sunday evening.

She said the alleged behaviour by police was unacceptable and had no place in society.

“The trust of citizens in our institutions is based on respect, integrity and transparency,” she said. “Citizens have the right to have answers. It is essential to shed light on the facts and (ensure) accountability is at the heart of the process.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Poilievre asks Carney to repeal B.C.’s oil tanker ban
stories.summary: Poilievre was one of several Opposition MPs who signed a letter to Carney as a federal Tory bill to scrap the tanker ban goes for second reading this week.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has asked Prime Minister Mark Carney to repeal the oil tanker ban on British Columbia’s northern coast months after Canada inked a deal not to change it.

Poilievre was one of several Opposition MPs who signed a letter to Carney as a federal Tory bill to scrap the tanker ban goes for second reading this week.

The group says the tanker ban “effectively donates” billions of dollars to the United States by forcing Canada to sell discounted oil profiting American refineries.

The MPs point to a proposal by Calgary-based Strathcona Resources to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day on existing railroad tracks through Prince Rupert, B.C., and across the Pacific Ocean.

For the proposal to be considered, the tanker ban would have to be lifted, and the letter says the federal government is the only thing standing in the way.

Carney and then-B.C. Premier David Eby signed an agreement in July that included a promise by Ottawa to maintain the north coast tanker ban “without alteration, suspension, or narrowing of scope.”

The letter says the Opposition would also be willing to discuss amendments to the ban that would allow the Prince Rupert project to move forward.

Eby’s New Democrats lost the B.C. election on Saturday, as Lorne Doerkson’s provincial Conservatives swept to power with about two-thirds of the 93 seats in the provincial legislature.

After Carney signed the deal with B.C., Alberta formally submitted a pipeline proposal to the major projects office — but with a southern route.

The plan would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline from Bruderheim, Alta., to an export terminal in Delta, B.C.

The letter says lifting the ban would give Alberta and British Columbia “an opportunity to build prosperity together.”

stories.title: U.K. says no to Canadian-led defence bank, backs partnership
stories.summary: The British government has turned down Ottawa’s attempts to have it join the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, though London says it will work in lockstep with Canada to meet Nato spending targets.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The British government has turned down Ottawa’s attempts to have it join the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, though London says it will work in lockstep with Canada to meet Nato spending targets.

The Dsrb is meant to reduce borrowing costs for military spending by pooling credit strength among allies.

Canada has tried for months to convince the U.K. to join the project, but London has instead been pursuing its own program called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.

Both countries agreed Sunday to craft a framework for cooperation between both banks, “having mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions.”

The two will “work in close partnership” on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.

The Dsrb will be based in Canada and has the support of countries such as Belgium, Turkey and Ukraine.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadians are borrowing money more than ever for food – what does this mean for the Canadian economy?
stories.summary: In a recent study conducted by the University of Dalhousie Economics found that on average nearly 20% of Canad...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
In a recent study conducted by the University of Dalhousie Economics found that on average nearly 20% of Canadians were either using their savings or borrowing money just to afford food.

They have also noted that Canadians reported a nearly 76% increase in food costs over the past year. Many Canadians now have to focus on the affordability of the foods rather than the quality and quantity of them.

This is also putting a large strain on the local food banks “it has in London, We have seen a 30 percent increase in individuals accessing our food” said Stacey Martin, a worker at the London food bank.

This trend could spell danger for the Canadian economy as business and economics teacher at Fanshawe College Mike Tucker points out “Our population growth has slowed which also slows the economy down…when you dwindle down your savings it leaves little room for unexpected circumstances”

Although the main concern is the increase in food costs and ability to afford them, many Canadians are also facing similar issues in areas such as transportation, with ever rising gas prices.

But Canadians can work towards keeping their savings through good budgeting as Mike discusses “many people don’t budget, it is amazing the amount of money you can find if you look at what’s coming in and what you’re spending your money on”.

stories.title: Charges laid after serious two-vehicle collision in Lucan Biddulph
stories.summary: A 25-year-old from Zurich has been charged following a two-vehicle collision in Lucan Biddulph last week
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 25-year-old from Zurich has been charged following a two-vehicle collision in Lucan Biddulph last week that left three people injured, including one person with life-threatening injuries.

Middlesex County OPP, paramedics and firefighters were called to the intersection of Elginfield Road and Prospect Hill Road at approximately 6:32 a.m. on Oct. 21 for a collision involving an SUV and a pickup truck.

Police said three people travelling in the SUV were taken to hospital. Two suffered non-life-threatening injuries, while a third sustained life-threatening injuries.

The driver of the pickup truck was not injured.

The accused has been charged under the Highway Traffic Act with two counts of careless driving causing bodily harm.

stories.summary: British Columbians have chosen Lorne Doerkson as their next premier. His victory follows a snap-election call by former Premier David Eby late last month, after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned from her role as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party after some three months on the job. Doerkson was since tapped to become interim leader of the […]
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
British Columbians have chosen Lorne Doerkson as their next premier.

His victory follows a snap-election call by former Premier David Eby late last month, after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned from her role as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party after some three months on the job. Doerkson was since tapped to become interim leader of the party.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Andrew MacLeod, the B.C. legislative bureau chief with The Tyee , to discuss how Doerkson and his majority government will meet British Columbians where they’re at, what this means for the province’s relationship with Indigenous communities, and whether or not Eby is regretting his snap-election call.

stories.title: One dead, one in critical condition after Barrie, Ont., house fire
stories.summary: Barrie - Police say one person is dead and another is in critical condition after a weekend fire in Barrie, Ont.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Investigators say they were called to Livingstone Street East and St. Vincent Street in the city’s north end on reports of a fire around 6:30 p.m. on Sunday.

They say five people were in the home when the smoke alarms sounded, and three were able to escape without getting injured.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Police say a 51-year-old man went back into the house to help someone believed to be in the basement, and was seriously injured in the process.

They say he was taken to hospital and remains in critical condition.

Police say firefighters found someone dead inside the home, which was heavily damaged in the fire. They say that person has not yet been identified.

The fire marshal’s office has been called to look into the cause of the fire.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Eric Bauza, Canadian voice actor behind Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies at 46
stories.summary: Among Bauza’s credits are TV shows such as The Looney Tunes Show, SpongeBob SquarePants and Bob’s Burgers
stories.author: Nicole Thompson
stories.content:
Eric Bauza, the Toronto-born voice actor who breathed fresh life into some of Hollywood’s most iconic cartoon characters, has died at 46.

His family announced his death in a brief post on his official social media channels.

The Los Angeles Medical Examiner says he died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease on Sunday.

Bauza, who was born and raised in Scarborough, was known as a modern successor to Mel Blanc, who originated the voices of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck.

Bauza carried the torch in recent years. In 2018, he became the first non-white actor to voice Bugs Bunny. He went on to voice Bugs, Daffy and more in Looney Tunes Cartoons , which ran on HBO Max for six seasons starting in 2020.

He reprised the roles numerous times, including in the film Coyote vs. Acme , which came out this summer , years after it was filmed.

It almost didn’t see the light of day after Warner Bros. canned the finished film as a tax write-off; but a campaign to release it, led in part by Bauza, convinced the production company to put the project up for sale.

He pushed the hashtag #ReleaseCoyoteVsACME on social media, and at the 2024 Annie Awards made the case from the podium in the voice of Daffy Duck.

“He’s the go-to cartoon character above anyone else when it comes to begging and pleading,” Bauza said while promoting the film. “It seemed appropriate.”

Eventually, an independent distributor bought the film and released it to glowing reviews.

A lifelong lover of cartoons, Bauza described the surreality of becoming a pillar of the scene.

“We grew up watching this stuff as it was happening. I was buying those Transformers as they were being made,” he told The Canadian Press in 2022.

“Fast forward, and I’m auditioning for the reboots — I buy a toy that I’m voicing, which is a Transformer that my son’s now into, so it’s kind of like a cat eating its tail.”

Bauza’s lengthy list of credits also includes SpongeBob SquarePants and Bob’s Burgers .

Comedian Kristen Schaal, who voices Louise Belcher on Bob’s Burgers , paid tribute to Bauza on Instagram on Monday.

“When I found out he was coming to a Bob’s Burgers table read it honestly felt like we had been blessed by the Elvis of voice actors,” she wrote.

“I obviously didn’t know him that well. I only knew his immense talent.”

Bauza was a regular on the convention circuit, and spoke on a panel at Lightbox Expo in Pasadena, Calif., the day before he died.

Jerry Beck, an animation historian, moderated that panel and wrote about it on the website Animation Scoop after Bauza’s death.

“He was vibrant and alive,” Beck wrote. “To demonstrate a classic piece of Looney Tunes comedy he performed as Bugs Bunny doing the square dance call from ‘Hillbilly Hare’, while the classic cartoon ran on a large screen beside us, to an packed room full of hopeful artists, cartoonists and budding voice over performers.”

In an online tribute, fellow voice actor Josh Keaton said Bauza was a gifted and humble performer.

“He let his talent speak for itself and made everyone feel like he was their biggest fan,” Keaton said on social media.

“He will always be a legend but I’m devastated that I’ll never be able to give him a hug, or hear him joke or see him smile again.”

stories.title: Trade war with Canada could end ‘pretty soon,’ Trump says during rally
stories.summary: Trump told a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, ON Sunday that Canada had been "ripping off" the U.S. on trade and that the U.S. had no choice but to impose levies on Canadian goods.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump says he expects his ever-evolving trade war with Canada to end “pretty soon.”

Trump told a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, ON Sunday that Canada had been “ripping off” the U.S. on trade and that the U.S. had no choice but to impose levies on Canadian goods.

He said the ongoing trade dispute between the two nations would be settled “pretty soon” and that Canada was “willing to give us anything at this moment.”

The Prime Minister’s Office did not immediately return a request for comment.

Diplomacy between Canada and the U.S. has been dicey since the Carney government walked away from formal trade talks in August after the Americans made unreasonable last-minute demands.

In response, Washington imposed tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, and Ottawa followed suit with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

“Canada has been ripping off the United States for years, OK? For years. And I had to do it. We’ll have that settled pretty soon. They’re willing to give us anything at this moment,” Trump said Sunday.

Trump’s trade war with Canada has been a key issue in the November midterm elections, especially in tight races.

With the midterms less than two weeks away, Trump announced Friday he will lift some of those 50 per cent tariffs at the end of the month, while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

It came at the request of Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, an eastern state on the Canada-U.S. border hit hard by the trade dispute.

stories.title: Above-seasonal warmth expected across London through Halloween week
stories.summary: The London area is in for a mild stretch of late-October weather, with temperatures expected to climb well above seasonal normals by midweek.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The London area is in for a mild stretch of late-October weather, with temperatures expected to climb well above seasonal norms by midweek.

Environment Canada is forecasting a mix of sun and cloud Monday, becoming cloudy through the day with a high of 16 C. Skies will clear overnight with a low of 2 C.

Tuesday is expected to be mainly sunny with a high of 13 C, followed by cloudy periods and an overnight low of 6 C.

The warmest day of the week is expected Wednesday, when cloudy skies accompany a forecast high of 20 C. Clear conditions are expected Wednesday night with a low of 10 C.

Temperatures remain mild through the latter half of the week. Thursday will bring a mix of sun and cloud with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 19 C. Similar conditions are expected overnight.

Cloudy skies are forecast Friday with a high of 17 C and a low of 10 C. Halloween on Saturday is expected to be cloudy, with a daytime high of 16 C.

No significant precipitation is currently forecast for the London area through the week, with temperatures remaining well above freezing overnight after Tuesday.

stories.title: How higher grocery prices affect farmers
stories.summary: Local farmers are seeing a rise in sales as food cost increases in stores, says one local farmer...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Local farmers are seeing a rise in sales as food cost increases in stores, says one local farmer.

“It’s great to see students come out and to support a local farm and also care about their nutrients,” said Kristina Courey a Co-Founder of New Moon Homestead in Ailsa Craig at a Fanshawe College Farmers market on the October 22. With the food cost increasing over the years, Courey stated her prices have almost match the prices of processed food.

“It’s great to be at a farmers market as you not only get to support farmers, but its a way to put a face to the farm and know who you’re buying from is someone in your community”

Courey did mention her food prices have gone up from a few years ago, stating they are the same if not less than what stores sell for. From the Canada food price report it found food prices are 27% higher now than five years ago, with the average family expected to spend almost $1,000 more this year compared to last year.

“We don’t use any chemicals in our food which makes it last longer, it’s all grown from the ground and harvested when ready using all natural materials from our farm,” Courey stated.

stories.title: Provincial police investigate death at prison in Gravenhurst, Ont.
stories.summary: Gravenhurst, ONT. - Ontario Provincial Police say they are investigating a death at a prison in Gravenhurst, Ont.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OPP say they were notified Saturday evening of an altercation that had occurred at Beaver Creek Institution earlier in the day and involved inmates.

They say a man was taken to hospital, where he later died.

Police say the man has been identified as 45-year-old Devon Paskimin, of Gravenhurst, Ont.

Article continues below

They say an autopsy will be conducted to determine the cause of death.

Beaver Creek is a clustered security facility that includes minimum- and medium-security units.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Poilievre pitches bill that would end B.C.’s tanker ban
stories.summary: Conservative Leader was one of several Opposition MPs who signed a letter to Carney as a federal Tory bill to scrap the tanker ban goes for second reading this week
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Conservative members of Parliament are calling on Ottawa to repeal the West Coast oil tanker ban, arguing it’s hurting Canada’s prosperity.

They pushed for the repeal during debate Monday in the House of Commons on a private member’s bill to scrap the tanker ban, a day after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Prime Minister Mark Carney about it.

Poilievre was one of several Opposition MPs who signed the letter to Carney ahead of debate on the bill. The vote on it was set for Wednesday as the Liberals asked for a recorded vote.

The existing law, the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, prohibits tankers from carrying more than 12,500 metric tonnes of crude oil in areas along the northern coast of British Columbia.

Bill C-264, sponsored by Calgary MP David McKenzie, would repeal the law entirely.

“Passing this legislation would not approve a single new pipeline or tanker terminal. It would not give an oil company permission to do whatever it wants, and it would not remove Canada’s other marine safety or environmental laws,” Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie said in the House of Commons.

“It would simply repeal the existing tanker moratorium, allowing future proposals to be considered under the other laws and approval processes that apply to it.”

Leslie said decisions about whether a project should have access to shipping on the north coast should be made on the merits and risks.

“How can we seriously talk about opening new markets while maintaining a law that rules out an entire region of potential export opportunities?” he said.

“I don’t believe that protecting the environment and developing our natural resources must be competing objectives. We should in fact be able to walk and chew gum. I think it is perfectly reasonable to take another look at whether this tanker ban still makes any sense.”

The letter to Carney from Poilievre and other Conservative MPs argued the tanker ban “effectively donates” billions of dollars to the United States by forcing Canada to sell discounted oil profiting American refineries.

The MPs point to a proposal by Calgary-based Strathcona Resources to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day on existing railroad tracks through Prince Rupert, B.C., and across the Pacific Ocean.

For the proposal to be considered, the tanker ban would have to be lifted. The letter says the federal government is the only thing standing in the way.

The Liberals don’t appear likely to repeal the tanker ban.

“I think it is important that we continue to look at ways in which we can encourage and support that collaborative approach at dealing with building a stronger and healthier Canada,” said Kevin Lamoureux, parliamentary secretary to the government leader in the House of Commons.

Carney signed an agreement with British Columbia in July that included a promise by Ottawa to maintain the north coast tanker ban “without alteration, suspension, or narrowing of scope.”

A day later, Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the route for their proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast would go south to respect the tanker ban.

The plan would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline from Bruderheim, Alta., to an export terminal in Delta, B.C.

On Monday, Smith joined the calls for the tanker ban’s repeal.

“Canada cannot become a global energy superpower while federal policies continue to stand in the way of getting our energy to the world. Repealing the tanker ban is an important step toward securing better prices for our resources and building a stronger, more prosperous Canada,” Smith said in a statement.

The Conservative letter to Carney says the Official Opposition also would be willing to discuss amendments to the ban that would allow the Prince Rupert project to move forward.

The provincial Conservatives swept to power in B.C. on Saturday after winning about two-thirds of the seats and defeating the NDP, which had governed the province since 2017.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has said he supports the new Pacific Link pipeline.

stories.title: Meet Lorne Doerkson, B.C.'s accidental premier
stories.summary: Doerkson’s public profile got a big boost when former NDP Premier David Eby called a provincial election early.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Last month, Lorne Doerkson was a well-liked but little-known B.C. MLA, a former rodeo rider and small-town newspaper publisher. Then, while he was on a layover at Amsterdam’s airport returning from a parliamentary association meeting in South Africa, he heard from Conservative Party of B.C. officials.

They asked him to take the party’s helm. Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay had been forced out by a caucus revolt. It was only supposed to be an interim role, but NDP premier, David Eby called an early election, hoping to capitalize on the Conservatives’ disarray. Suddenly, he was the main man.

Early polls showed a tight race, but Doerkson’s calm, solid demeanour proved popular and the gap grew. By Saturday, election day, the Conservatives won by 11 points, with 48% of the popular vote. That was good for 64 seats, more than double the combined opposition.

Doerkson, 58, literally bounced onto the victory party stage, walked up to the mic and shouted: “B.C. is definitely blue!”

“Man, I am out of breath. I am so excited,” he exclaimed.

He later admitted he’d possibly been over-caffeinated. But party members loved it, as well as his quick, unlikely rise to become premier of Canada’s third largest province. He did it by unifying an opposition party that had been fractured by waves of defections under the former leader.

“(W)hen his colleagues asked him to lead British Columbians through the 45th General Election, he accepted, and within 48 hours, brought the party back together as one team,” states his bio on the B.C. Conservative party website .

Doerkson’s highest educational attainment is a high school degree. He is described on the party website, not as “a guy working the room with talking points,” but instead, “one you’d find at the rodeo … doing the work quietly, locally, and without forgetting who he serves.”

Most of his six years in the B.C. Legislative Assembly was as assistant deputy speaker, not a role that gets much notice.

Doerkson is a long-time Cariboo-region resident who has spent close to 30 years in the communities that he represents. Born in New Westminster and raised in Surrey, he went on to build his life in Williams Lake, spending 20 years as a newspaper publisher before moving into financial planning. He has also been Rotary president, a rodeo announcer and a volunteer, voted Stampede volunteer of the year in 2019.

As MLA, Doerkson focused his time on his riding in a region struggling to cope with wildfires and hospital emergency room closures, reports the Victoria Times-Colonist .

Then Eby took his gamble. “I didn’t expect this, I certainly didn’t seek this and I certainly did not plan two years ago to somehow put all of these stars into alignment,” Doerkson said in a campaign interview.

Doerkson and the Conservatives went on to consistently lead in opinion polls , as Eby struggled with intense criticism over his early election call.

Doerkson was first elected as MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020, winning 51.25 per cent of the vote. At the time, Doerkson ran as a Liberal, taking the riding with a significant margin over the NDP (32.46 per cent).

The B.C. NDP went on to form government following the 2020 election, leaving the B.C. Liberals — later renamed B.C. United — as Opposition. Doerkson served as Opposition critic for rural development and as the party’s deputy whip.

But in the spring of 2024, Doerkson crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. “This is the toughest decision I have made in my life,” he said, according to the Vancouver Sun .

“I have spent countless hours listening to my constituents in recent months … They want to see David Eby defeated and they want to see a common sense Conservative government in Victoria,” he said then.

In 2024, Doerkson was re-elected as a Conservative, winning 69.59 per cent of the vote over the Ndp’s 30.41 per cent. After the election, he was named assistant deputy speaker.

During the election campaign, the Conservative platform promised to create $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years, while shrinking the deficit to $10.8 billion by 2030. It said a Conservative government would chop spending by freezing outside hiring, cutting consultants, and review spending on numerous government ministries.

The Conservatives promised to reduce income taxes by $1,000 per year, cut contribution taxes and charges, drop the PST on some business expenses, and build a new Massey bridge, scrapping the tunnel plans, among other pledges.

The New Democrats said they costed Doerkson’s promises and argued income tax cuts and taking the PST off Canadian alcohol and other items would reduce revenues by more than $4.3 billion a year and boost the deficit by 33 per cent. The NDP said Doerkson had a budget gap of $6 billion after announcing items such as a new women and children’s hospital.

But Doerkson said unlocking business confidence will pay for all this by filling the province’s coffers with new tax revenue.

“Together, we voted for a better British Columbia,” he said Saturday night. “And from here, I will do everything in my power to get British Columbia back on track.”

Early polls showed a tight race, but Doerkson’s calm, solid demeanour proved popular and the gap grew. By Saturday, election day, the Conservatives won by 11 points, with 48% of the popular vote. That was good for 64 seats, more than double the combined opposition.
Doerkson, 58, literally bounced onto the victory party stage, walked up to the mic and shouted: “B.C. is definitely blue!”
“Man, I am out of breath. I am so excited,” he exclaimed.

He later admitted he’d possibly been over-caffeinated. But party members loved it, as well as his quick, unlikely rise to become premier of Canada’s third largest province. He did it by unifying an opposition party that had been fractured by waves of defections under the former leader.

“(W)hen his colleagues asked him to lead British Columbians through the 45th General Election, he accepted, and within 48 hours, brought the party back together as one team,” states his bio on the B.C. Conservative party website .

Doerkson’s highest educational attainment is a high school degree. He is described on the party website, not as “a guy working the room with talking points,” but instead, “one you’d find at the rodeo … doing the work quietly, locally, and without forgetting who he serves.”
Most of his six years in the B.C. Legislative Assembly was as assistant deputy speaker, not a role that gets much notice.

Doerkson is a long-time Cariboo-region resident who has spent close to 30 years in the communities that he represents. Born in New Westminster and raised in Surrey, he went on to build his life in Williams Lake, spending 20 years as a newspaper publisher before moving into financial planning. He has also been Rotary president, a rodeo announcer and a volunteer, voted Stampede volunteer of the year in 2019.
As MLA, Doerkson focused his time on his riding in a region struggling to cope with wildfires and hospital emergency room closures, reports the Victoria Times-Colonist .

Then Eby took his gamble. “I didn’t expect this, I certainly didn’t seek this and I certainly did not plan two years ago to somehow put all of these stars into alignment,” Doerkson said in a campaign interview.
Doerkson and the Conservatives went on to consistently lead in opinion polls , as Eby struggled with intense criticism over his early election call.

Doerkson was first elected as MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020, winning 51.25 per cent of the vote. At the time, Doerkson ran as a Liberal, taking the riding with a significant margin over the NDP (32.46 per cent).

The B.C. NDP went on to form government following the 2020 election, leaving the B.C. Liberals — later renamed B.C. United — as Opposition. Doerkson served as Opposition critic for rural development and as the party’s deputy whip.
But in the spring of 2024, Doerkson crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. “This is the toughest decision I have made in my life,” he said, according to the Vancouver Sun .

“I have spent countless hours listening to my constituents in recent months … They want to see David Eby defeated and they want to see a common sense Conservative government in Victoria,” he said then.
In 2024, Doerkson was re-elected as a Conservative, winning 69.59 per cent of the vote over the Ndp’s 30.41 per cent. After the election, he was named assistant deputy speaker.

During the election campaign, the Conservative platform promised to create $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years, while shrinking the deficit to $10.8 billion by 2030. It said a Conservative government would chop spending by freezing outside hiring, cutting consultants, and review spending on numerous government ministries.

The Conservatives promised to reduce income taxes by $1,000 per year, cut contribution taxes and charges, drop the PST on some business expenses, and build a new Massey bridge, scrapping the tunnel plans, among other pledges.

The New Democrats said they costed Doerkson’s promises and argued income tax cuts and taking the PST off Canadian alcohol and other items would reduce revenues by more than $4.3 billion a year and boost the deficit by 33 per cent. The NDP said Doerkson had a budget gap of $6 billion after announcing items such as a new women and children’s hospital.
But Doerkson said unlocking business confidence will pay for all this by filling the province’s coffers with new tax revenue.
“Together, we voted for a better British Columbia,” he said Saturday night. “And from here, I will do everything in my power to get British Columbia back on track.”

stories.title: Canada receives first F-35 fighter jets from U.S.
stories.summary: Ottawa is still deliberating how many of the American planes it will buy
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada has received its first pair of new F-35 fighter jets, with Ottawa still deliberating how many of the American planes it will buy.

The Royal Canadian Air Force announced Friday on social media that it received the two Lockheed Martin jets, sharing a photo from Phoenix showing one plane with a maple-leaf roundel.

The air force did not immediately say when it will start training pilots with the new planes, which U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra recently hailed as “the best fighter in the world.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has paused plans to proceed with a planned order for 88 of these stealth fighter jets, and Ottawa May instead have a mixed fleet that includes Gripen jets made by Saab.

Carney launched a review of the purchase amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated trade and annexation threats, and the review was supposed to have concluded a year ago.

Last year, Trump mused about providing allies with jets that have limited capabilities in order to maintain American supremacy, and former foreign minister Lloyd Axworthy warned in a Saturday blog post that Washington controls software used by F-35 jets.

stories.title: ‘They buy because it’s easy’: Legal shops want more than enforcement to fight illegal pot
stories.summary: Though the Ford government says it’s planning to introduce new measures to crack down on illicit cannabis sales, legal retailers are questioning why it took eight years following legalization for enforcement tools to be bolstered. Several legal sellers told Global News they want Ontario to take the new rules a step further, by allowing the...
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Though the Ford government says it’s planning to introduce new measures to crack down on illicit cannabis sales, legal retailers are questioning why it took eight years following legalization for enforcement tools to be bolstered.

Several legal sellers told Global News they want Ontario to take the new rules a step further, by allowing the legal market to innovate and modernize cannabis sales by lifting some restrictions on how and where pot can be sold.

Increasing the appeal and ease of the legal product is what the industry truly needs to combat illegal enterprises, said Mike Dunn, the owner and founder of 1922 Cannabis in Toronto, a licensed cannabis dispensary.

“People don’t buy illegally because they want to break the law. They buy because it’s easy,” said Dunn.

On Monday, the Ministry of the Attorney General announced the Ford government will introduce new legislation to “strengthen enforcement” against illegal cannabis sales by providing “new tools” to the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario to tackle unauthorized sellers.

The legislative changes would include “the authority to conduct inspections, seize illegal cannabis products and equipment and issue administrative monetary penalties,” said the attorney general in a news release this week.

The illegal market for cannabis sales in Ontario has been prolific. When cannabis was legalized in October, 2018, the legal market was only responsible for 5.4 per cent of purchases, according to the Canadian Press. Legal sales only overtook illegal sales for the first time at the end of 2021.

Now, illegal cannabis retailers make up about 30 per cent of cannabis sales in Ontario, according to the ministry.

Omar Khan, with High Tide, the parent company of retail chain Canna Cabana, said the new legislation will allow the Alcohol and Gaming Commission to seize products and issue fines without the burden of proof needed for criminal prosecutions.

Anytime a new illegal seller emerges near any store, legal enterprises are threatened, he said. There are about 1,800 legal retailers across the province, according to the Ministry of the Attorney General.

“We’re encouraged by this move,” he said. “Every indication that I’ve heard says that the government is taking this seriously.”

But the province has faced criticism for its approach to shutting down illegal pot shops over the last few years.

In early 2025, Carleton Grant, Toronto’s executive director of municipal licensing and standards, said the city hadn’t been given adequate municipal funding to enforce rules against illegal stores.

Ford should have shored up enforcement on illegal retailers soon after cannabis was legalized, according to some legal sellers. Now, they say, the government has an opportunity to make legal sales more appealings and further discourage illegal sales.

Some illegal vendors offer late night delivery options, with cannabis products just a text away on a customer’s phone. Cannabis can be delivered legally in Ontario but hours are restricted from 9 a.m. to 11 p.m. Dunn’s retailer, 1922 Cannabis, does offer delivery using bike couriers to try to tap into the ease customers are looking for.

“Enforcement can close doors. It can’t make the legal option easier,” said Dunn.

Khan said the new tools will only work if the Alcohol and Gaming Commission is provided with enough resources. He also agrees with Dunn that Ontario’s retail framework for cannabis needs modernization.

“Whetheter that’s looking at the potential for consumption spaces, consumption lounges for cannabis drinks or cannabis edibles,” he said. Ontario could follow Alberta, which allows temporary cannabis store licences for adults-only music festivals, he said.

“A lot of provinces are letting cannabis stores sell munchies and snacks and a few other things to increase revenue lines. We hope and encourage the Ontario government to take a look,” he said.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles said she wants to see what the Ford government firmly proposes before determining if the legislation will be effective.

“They talk a lot before they come back to the legislature, but we need to see the details of what they’re proposing,” she said.

The planned new legislation has not been released yet. The legislature is not sitting, as it was put on a 21-week long summer break that began in June. MPPs are scheduled to return on Oct. 27.

stories.title: Voters head to the polls across Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area
stories.summary: Voters across Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area will head to the polls Monday to elect mayors, councillors and school board trustees.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Voters across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton area head to the polls Monday to elect mayors, councillors and school board trustees.

After weeks of campaigning, several high-profile races are set to be decided. Toronto’s mayoral contest between incumbent Olivia Chow and main challenger Brad Bradford is one of them.

Both frontrunners hit the pavement daily in the final week to reach undecided voters. Chow and Bradford have been quick to trade barbs throughout the campaign, with Chow last week accusing her opponent of neglecting residents in his own ward during his time as a city councillor. Bradford has claimed Chow has failed to address the city’s traffic and transit woes.

Chow’s key promises include measures to help lower grocery prices in the city, offer free lunches in schools and build more affordable housing units. Meanwhile, Bradford has pledged to freeze property tax rates in his first year as mayor and scrap the land transfer tax for homes under $1.1 million.

In neighbouring Mississauga, former mayor Bonnie Crombie is attempting to reclaim her old job.

Crombie left the post at the beginning of 2024 to become leader of the Ontario Liberal Party. She had won a landslide victory in the 2022 municipal election. Crombie held Mississauga’s top job for nearly a decade, serving as the successor to Hazel McCallion who held the post for 36 years.

Crombie led the Liberals to a third-place finish in the 2025 provincial election, although the party secured roughly 30 per cent of the popular vote.
