stories.title: How the war in Iran could impact your home heating oil bill this winter
stories.summary: Since the start of the war in Iran, the average retail home heating oil prices have jumped 42 per cent in most of Canada, sitting at $2.50 per litre this week.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The Iran war isn’t just making it costlier to fill up the tank of your car at the pump, it May also be making the cost of heating your home go up this fall.

Heating oil is similar in composition to diesel fuel, the price of which has hit records above US$6.50 per gallon following disruptions in the Middle East caused by the Iran war. The Trump administration also blames high prices on Ukrainian attacks on refineries in Russia.

Canada, too, has been hit with higher heating oil prices.

Since the start of the war, heating oil prices have jumped 42 per cent in most of the country. Average retail price for furnace oil in Canada was just under $2.50 per litre on Tuesday, according to Natural Resources Canada, a sharp jump from the $1.76 just before the Iran war began and almost a full dollar higher than the $1.56 per litre seen in January.

There is “no question” that the higher prices are “linked to the war,” said Behrouz Bakhtiari, a supply chain expert and professor at McMaster University’s DeGroot School of Business.

“There are other aspects also. There May be some panic in the market. There May lower inventories, but really the link is directly tied to the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.

Adding to the pressure is the fact that many refineries close down temporarily for the fall, Bakhtiari said.

While in most years it is a routine shutdown, this year it could add pressure to prices.

“This year, because there was already shortage in the market, those maintenance schedules would add to the pain,” he said.

The Trump administration is offering to loan up to nearly a third of the one-million-barrel U.S. emergency heating oil reserve, the Department of Energy said on Wednesday, in a bid to tame surging prices.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration was “committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs.” The department said there would be a competitive bidding process for the loans for both fuel retailers and terminal holders to allow the fuel to flow into areas facing shortages.

The U.S. has only tapped the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve once since Hurricane Sandy struck the region in 2012. The emergency stockpile is held at sites in New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Maine.

About one-third ​of New England homes use heating oil, including about half of homes in Maine.

In Canada, the pain is likely to be concentrated in Atlantic Canada, Bakhtiari said. As of 2022, 305,900 homes in Atlantic Canada used oil to heat their homes, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that the federal government will launch a new heat pump rebate program early next year as part of ongoing work over recent years to get consumers onto alternative heating options, but program details haven’t been finalized.

Ottawa is in the process of winding down an existing program to subsidize purchases of heat pumps for homes heated with oil.

Last month, Finance Minister Francois-Phillipe Champagne said the current pause on the federal excise tax on fuel would be extended until February.

For Atlantic Canada with its long winters, this would mean that heating oil costs could rise further in March.

A single cold snap could mean an additional $600-$700 per household for that period, Bakhtiari estimates.

Higher heating oil prices, along with the end of the fuel tax holiday, would mean “$3,000 to $4,000 dollars added to the cost of the energy bill,” he said.

In his announcement, Carney announced $2 billion in spending to retrofit one million homes across Canada with heat pumps, which he said would mean $1,400 in annual savings on energy bills for households heating with oil, propane and electric resistance.

–with files from Reuters and Canadian Press

stories.title: Federal agency reports nearly 600% increase in licenses stripped from money services firms
stories.summary: Fintrac will report that it stripped the licences last year of more than seven times as many money services operations as the previous year.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s financial intelligence agency will report Monday that it stripped the licences last year of more than seven times as many money services operations as the previous year, part of an increased emphasis on a sector that can play a key role in money laundering and some other financial crimes.

The Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (Fintrac) will say in its annual report that it revoked licences for 82 money services businesses in Canada in 2025-26, compared to 12 a year earlier and 17 in 2023-24.

The report says last year’s dramatic increase in that element of the financial services industry was part of a year characterized by record levels of enforcement actions as Fintrac and its police allies battled fraud, extortion, human trafficking, fentanyl and a wide range of illegal activities.

At the same time, the challenge for financial intelligence officials continues to grow as the growth of the digital world has led to an increasingly large and sophisticated number of online criminals.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre has said that Canadians were scammed out of $704-million in online fraud in 2025, about three times the figure from just five years earlier. The federal government has said that less than 10 per cent of these types of scams are reported to authorities.

The money service business is divided into those with store fronts, including big players such as Western Union and Money Mart, and those who operate online only, including many that are based overseas. The industry, which includes those who transfer money or exchange currencies, has 3,396 registered operations, a sharp increase from 2,778 in the previous year.

According to its annual report, Fintrac also fined nine money services businesses for a total of more than $198 million for a variety of violations, including failing to register and other forms of non-compliance, and not reporting large virtual currency transactions.

In one of the larger cases, Fintrac imposed an administrative monetary penalty in July, 2025 of $19.6-million on Peken Global Limited (which also operates as KuCoin) for failing to register with Fintrac, failing to report large virtual currency transactions on 2,952 separate occasions, and “failing to report suspicious transactions” on 33 occasions. Some of those transactions were linked to darknet marketplaces, questionable gambling sites and illegal activities.

In another case, where a company hadn’t registered, the investigation led in September 2025 to the RCMP seizing more than $56-million in cryptocurrency, the largest crypto seizure in Canadian history.

The information gathering within the sector can be “crucial to our ability to ensure and enforce compliance and track the proceeds of crime across jurisdictions,” Fintrac chief executive officer Stéphane Sirard wrote in the report.

Like online crime, authorities’ efforts have also been on the climb.

Fintrac reported last year that it easily set a new record in the number of cases that it sent to police for possible criminal investigation. And the organization said this spring that extortion cases have increased more than sixfold over the first four months of the year, with a growing number of those crimes committed against Canadians by criminal organizations with direct ties to India and elsewhere in south Asia.

The annual report says Fintrac generated 122 financial intelligence disclosures in support of police investigations of extortion over the last year, for example, leading to the identification of 336 people of interest.

Local police forces in larger communities and the federal government have taken steps to try to respond to the growth of online crimes. The Liberal government announced late last year that it would launch a new Financial Crimes Agency, aimed at trying to improve Canada’s ability to tackle online scams, money laundering and other types of fraud

The fight against such crimes also got some help earlier this year from legislative changes to the Bank Act. The new rules require banks and other financial institutions to play a bigger and more proactive role in detecting and fighting fraud.

Many local police forces, particularly in larger cities, have also made the fight against financial crimes a priority in recent years, allocating resources to new technology and hiring specialists.

Fintrac reported last year that it easily set a new record in the number of cases that it sent to police for possible criminal investigation. And the organization said this spring that extortion cases have increased more than sixfold over the first four months of the year, with a growing number of those crimes committed against Canadians by criminal organizations with direct ties to India and elsewhere in south Asia.

The annual report says Fintrac generated 122 financial intelligence disclosures in support of police investigations of extortion over the last year, for example, leading to the identification of 336 people of interest.

Local police forces in larger communities and the federal government have taken steps to try to respond to the growth of online crimes. The Liberal government announced late last year that it would launch a new Financial Crimes Agency, aimed at trying to improve Canada’s ability to tackle online scams, money laundering and other types of fraud

The fight against such crimes also got some help earlier this year from legislative changes to the Bank Act. The new rules require banks and other financial institutions to play a bigger and more proactive role in detecting and fighting fraud.
Many local police forces, particularly in larger cities, have also made the fight against financial crimes a priority in recent years, allocating resources to new technology and hiring specialists.

stories.title: Sydney man showcases incredible collection of over 175 vintage cameras
stories.summary: For as long as John Duffy can remember, he said he has always been passionate about cameras and photography.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Sydney, N.S. - For as long as John Duffy can remember, he said he has always been passionate about cameras and photography.

“When I was young, I bought a couple of cameras and took a few courses,” said Duffy who landed a job at a camera shop after finishing high school. “Customers would bring old cameras in and see if they were worth getting repaired and if they weren’t, they would say, ‘toss them out’. And they were just too gorgeous to throw them away.”

So, Duffy kept them and eventually started his own camera collection.

“I went to yard sales and auctions,” said Duffy. “The more I got, the more I got into it and then the more I got really into it.”

Duffy now has more than 175 cameras. Most are from the early to mid-20 th century with slower shutter speeds and they all still work.

Each one is a conversation piece.

“This one is from the 1950s and the original film is still in the camera” said Duffy as he described his collection.

He also has several century-old accordion-style expandable bellows cameras which are his favourites.

His oldest cameras date back to the early 1900s.

“I have one from 1901 and the one next to it is from 1902,” said Duffy, who also has a tiny James Bond-style spy camera, which were popular in movies in the 1960s and 1970s.

Duffy is especially nostalgic about his four film projectors which hold home movies of his parents from more than 70 years ago.

“In those days you would take your film and send it away and two weeks later you would get the film with movies back,” he said.

Duffy also said, as he examines his collection, he is reminded of how photography has changed over the years, especially compared to digital photography.

“These older cameras were much easier and user-friendly. A lot of smartphone cameras today don’t come with a proper manual and it is very hard for someone in my age to buy a phone and figure out all the hidden features,” said Duffy. “But old cameras back in the day, had a four-page manual and if you read it, you were good to go.”

He cannot pin down the exact date when he began collecting these cameras, but Duffy estimates it was roughly 45 years ago. Now as he approaches his retirement years he would like to donate this collection to a museum, but he has two conditions: the collection would stay intact and always be properly displayed.

“I don’t want to put it in boxes or put it in storage,” he said.

Tech analyst Carmi Levy said a collection like this is a treasure and would be a valued addition to any museum or photography school.

“This collection excites me and we need to preserve this history for ourselves to understand how we got to where we are, and why we appreciate all the things we use today,” said Levy. “If we don’t, we could lose that sense of history.”

Duffy said it is more than a hobby or a just fun collection.

It’s a throwback to a long-lost era of photography, a living history of the evolution of cameras.

stories.title: Toronto-born voice actor Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dead at 46
stories.summary: Born in Scarborough, Canadian voice-actor Eric Bauza built a celebrated career in animation and voice acting.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Toronto-born voice actor Eric Bauza, best known as the modern voice behind iconic Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, has died at the age of 46.

His family announced his death in a statement shared on social media Sunday .

“Eric Bauza, Emmy award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away. More details to come,” the statement read.

No additional details were immediately released by the family.

A report by the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner says Bauza died at his home of hypertensive cardiovascular disease.

Born in Scarborough, Bauza built a celebrated career in animation and voice acting. Over the years, he voiced a wide range of beloved characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Tweety Bird, Elmer Fudd, Marvin the Martian and Road Runner.

Beyond his work in the Looney Tunes universe, Bauza lent his voice to characters in productions such as Teen Titans Go!, Muppet Babies, The Super Mario Bros., Woody Woodpecker, Puss in Boots, Avatar: The Last Airbender and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

Bauza earned multiple Emmy Awards during his career, including recognition for his work on Looney Tunes Cartoons.

Bauza most recently reprised several classic Looney Tunes roles in the feature films The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie and Coyote vs. Acme, with the latter film earning critical acclaim.

His other 2026 voice-acting credits include The Super Mario Galaxy Movie (Toad General), the horror film Buddy (Mr. Mailbox, Worry Well, Couchy, Trashy, Pee Flower) and Forgotten Island (Gen. Button Wutton and Sarangay).

In an online tribute, fellow voice actor Josh Keaton said Bauza was a gifted and humble performer, and remembered him for having a warm smile and always being sincere.

“He let his talent speak for itself and made everyone feel like he was their biggest fan,” Keaton said on social media.

“He will always be a legend but I’m devastated that I’ll never be able to give him a hug, or hear him joke or see him smile again.”

He is survived by his wife and son.

With files from Aaron Sousa of The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian Blood Services says longtime plasma donor’s death not connected to donation
stories.summary: Charity’s CEO said person’s death earlier this fall was from natural causes
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
Canadian Blood Services says a plasma donor recently died a day after making a donation, but the charity believes the death was not connected to the donation itself.

Blood collectors such as CBS are required under federal regulations to report to Health Canada if a donor has died within 72 hours of making a donation. The initial report must be made within 24 hours of the collector learning about the death.

It is the first time CBS has reported such an incident since at least 2018, the earliest that records are available.

The safety and oversight of plasma donation has come under scrutiny in the past year after the deaths of two donors who gave plasma at Grifols, a Spanish pharmaceutical company that operates collection facilities in Canada through a partnership with CBS. Health Canada found operational deficiencies at multiple Grifols locations and suspended the licence of one site in September. The company temporarily paused operations in Canada, but announced last week it was going to gradually reopen.

Plasma is a golden-coloured fluid found in blood that is used as a key ingredient of some medicines, such as immunoglobulin.

The latest incident involved someone who died the day after giving plasma at a CBS facility.

CBS said it is withholding nearly all the details of the incident to protect the donor’s privacy. The charity, which runs the blood system everywhere in Canada but Quebec, would not provide any details about the donor, where the incident happened or precisely when it occurred, preferring to say it happened “earlier in the fall.”

CBS chief executive officer Graham Sher told The Globe and Mail on Friday that a long-time donor and volunteer died a day after making a plasma donation. Dr. Sher said CBS only found out three weeks later, when the donor’s family told the staff of a CBS clinic.

Dr. Sher said CBS quickly reported the death to Health Canada. He said CBS then reviewed the records of the donor and the donation. He said that nothing unusual happened during the donation and the donor appeared fine when they left. He said the donor’s family told CBS that doctors had described the death the following day as being due to natural causes.

“I just want to put it this way: Donors are normal people with normal lives, and donors will have things that happen to them in their lives: motor vehicle accidents, illnesses, falls, trips,” Dr. Sher said in an interview. “Anything can happen to a donor. The same is going to happen to anyone else. And this, an event of a natural cause death, just happened to be temporally related to a previous donation.”

Health Canada said it received notice of the death from CBS on Sept. 25, which would suggest the death occurred in early September.

Health Canada said it could not provide any more information about the incident, such as the date and location it occurred, out of concern for the donor’s privacy.

Earlier this year, the regulator provided The Globe and other media outlets the date and location of two other such deaths, which happened in Winnipeg on Oct. 25, 2025, and on Jan. 30, 2026. Health Canada did not immediately answer a question Friday about why it provided the information in previous cases but not in this one. Health Canada also disclosed earlier this year that it had received a report of a death on June 4, 2018, that also came from Winnipeg.

Health Canada said that, under federal regulation, CBS holds the responsibility to conduct a thorough investigation of this incident.

The regulator said it reviewed documentation provided by CBS, which said the charity followed appropriate procedures and there was no suggestion of equipment failure or malfunction. Health Canada did not say it was taking any further actions.

Health Canada has previously told The Globe that as a regulator of blood and plasma products, it “does not determine the cause of death, including whether the donation process may have contributed to a death.”

CBS reports annual statistics on the number of “adverse reactions,” which is defined in federal regulations as an “undesirable response” associated with the collection of blood or plasma. CBS reported 28 adverse reactions in the 2025-26 year, which was lower than previous years.

Dr. Sher said the recent death is not classified as an adverse reaction because CBS believes it is unrelated to the donation.

Grifols announced in August that it had revised its own reports of serious adverse reactions, which involve incidents of injury or death, and believed there were only six such incidents that had occurred at its facilities since 2018, much lower than the 25 incidents the company had previously reported to Health Canada.

Hema-Québéc, the blood authority in Quebec, has reported three serious adverse reactions in that time.

None of CBS’s adverse reactions since 2018 have been classified as “serious.”

Globally, deaths connected to plasma donation are very rare. In the U.S., where millions of plasma donations are made annually, there are only a handful of deaths each year that may be connected to a donation, according to reports from the Food and Drug Administration.

stories.title: Trump says he expects trade war with Canada to end 'pretty soon'
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump says he expects his ever-evolving trade war with Canada to end "pretty soon."
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - U.S. President Donald Trump says he expects his constantly evolving trade war with Canada to end “pretty soon” as Prime Minister Mark Carney suggests Washington could be moving closer to Ottawa’s demands.

Trump told a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, ON Sunday that Canada had been “ripping off” the U.S. on trade and he had no choice but to impose levies on Canadian goods.

He said the trade dispute would be settled “pretty soon” and that Canada was “willing to give us anything at this moment.”

At a news conference Monday, Carney was asked if there had been any movement on the trade file in the past week.

“To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” Carney responded.

“Canada’s ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians, all Canadians. We have very clear bottom lines — red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August.”

Diplomatic relations between Canada and the U.S. have been dicey since Carney’s government walked away from formal trade talks in August. The prime minister accused the Americans of making unreasonable last-minute demands.

In response, Washington imposed tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, and Ottawa followed up with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

“Canada has been ripping off the United States for years, OK? For years. And I had to do it. We’ll have that settled pretty soon. They’re willing to give us anything at this moment,” Trump said Sunday.

Trump has repeatedly insisted Canada has treated the United States unfairly despite the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade that was negotiated during his first term.

A spokesperson for Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office said the two sides “remain in constructive dialogue” on a “range of priorities.” The spokesperson said Canada is ready to work constructively on a mutually beneficial deal that “respects Canada’s interests.”

Trump’s trade war with Canada has been a key issue in the November midterm elections, especially in tight races. The Republicans currently control both the House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate but polls suggest they are in danger of losing one or both of those chambers after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Trump announced Friday he will lift some of the 50 per cent tariffs on Canada at the end of the month, while adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

The tariff changes reportedly came at the request of Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, an eastern state on the Canada-U.S. border hit hard by the trade dispute.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

-with files from David Baxter in Ottawa and Aaron Sousa in Edmonton

stories.title: Doerkson won't rule out shortened fall session after provincial election win
stories.summary: Victoria - B.C.'s newly minted Conservative government could take its seats in the legislature soon, but the premier-designate is not ruling out a shortened fall session.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - The lawyer for the Cowichan Tribes said they will make a proposal in January that protects private property rights in the landmark Aboriginal title case that the B.C. Conservatives have said calls into question who controls British Columbia.

Lawyer David Rosenberg said that if it has “the right attitude,” the incoming Conservative government will find it easier to resolve the Cowichan case than to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, known as Dripa.

The 2025 Cowichan ruling on a portion of Crown, city and private land in Richmond, B.C., found that Aboriginal title is a “senior interest” compared with fee-simple title, and sections of B.C.‘s Land Title Act that establish fee-simple title as “indefeasible” do not apply to Aboriginal title.

It has triggered concerns about the impact on private property rights and values, but Rosenberg said the tribes will go to court in the new year with a solution to respect and protect private property and its value, as well as Cowichan Aboriginal title.

“That is what negotiations are supposed to be leading to,” he said.

He said the case has nothing to do with the repeal of Dripa, which premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has said is his top priority after Saturday’s election victory.

Rosenberg said Doerkson’s election could be seen as a fresh start in resolving the Cowichan case.

“That a new government could come to the issue with a positive attitude, and show some leadership, and take the high road, and say, ‘We’re going to recognize Aboriginal title and we’re going to protect property interests,’” he said.

While Rosenberg said it could be easier to resolve the Cowichan case, former B.C. Conservative leader John Rustad said Dripa can be repealed quickly, while the Cowichan Tribes case could drag on for years.

Rustad, who didn’t seek re-election, said last year that “Indigenous rights and private property cannot coexist,” and called on the Supreme Court of Canada to resolve the conflict as soon as possible.

He said in an interview on Monday that the case cannot be allowed to drag on because of the uncertainty it has created around private property rights.

Rustad said the incoming government must argue in its appeal for the extinguishment of Aboriginal title, something the previous government did not do in the original case.

“Private property is the foundation of society,” he said. “If you are going to take private property rights, which the court is now in the process of doing, you completely undermine society,” he said.

Extinguishment, however, does not rule out some agreement that would compensate First Nations, said Rustad, who was the Aboriginal relations minister under the former B.C. Liberal government.

But Rosenberg said neither British Columbia nor the federal government could extinguish existing Aboriginal title, unless the Constitution were amended, and he warned against conflating Dripa with the Cowichan Tribes case. He added that the City of Richmond had argued for extinguishment, and was unsuccessful.

“I don’t believe the repeal of Dripa would in substance affect what the court ordered,” he said, referring to the ruling that British Columbia must negotiate in good faith how to reconcile fee-simple interests with Cowichan Aboriginal title.

Rosenberg said the tribes’ proposal on private property will be filed when the court hears requests for the Cowichan judgment to be stayed pending appeal.

The Conservatives’ resounding election win, in which they secured a two-thirds majority, has raised concern among First Nations leaders.

The First Nations Leadership Council said Monday that B.C. is at a crossroads with the incoming government that could result in either a “battleground” or reconciliation.

Doerkson said at a postelection news conference on Sunday that he is “completely committed to working with First Nations” but would stick with his election promise to repeal Dripa.

He said the declaration act brought in by the New Democrat government had caused more problems.

“So, I am committed with working on a great path forward of respect, partnership, friendship and conversation.”

Rustad said the situation facing the new government is how to reconcile private property rights with outstanding Indigenous rights.

“The Indigenous question is the elephant in the room,” Rustad said. “You cannot get your economy going without finding a path forward, working with First Nations, which means you can’t do all these other things that you want to do.”

The leadership council, made up of executives from three main First Nations groups in B.C., said in a statement that it was ready to work with the government to advance reconciliation and uphold rights and title.

Grand Chief Stewart Phillip of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said outgoing Premier David Eby’s loss on Saturday was “hugely disappointing.”

“We are at a historical crossroads: Battleground B.C. or reconciliation through the principles and road map of the Declaration Act,” he said.

B.C. Assembly of First Nations Regional Chief Terry Teegee said in the statement that some provincial politicians in the recent past have campaigned on anti-Indigenous racism.

“We call on premier-designate Doerksen to uphold a zero-tolerance policy for racism, discrimination or hatred in his caucus, including holding his members accountable for some of the reprehensible statements made during the election,” he said.

First Nations Summit Chief Shana Thomas said no economic projects in the province could happen without involvement of First Nations.

A statement from the office of the clerk of the legislative assembly said swearing-in ceremonies can’t take place until the election results are certified and provided by the chief electoral officer, which is expected Nov. 18.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Federal Conservatives pitch bill that would end B.C.'s tanker ban
stories.summary: Ottawa - Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has asked Prime Minister Mark Carney to repeal the oil tanker ban on British Columbia's northern coast months after Canada inked a deal not to change it.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Conservative members of Parliament are calling on Ottawa to repeal the West Coast oil tanker ban, arguing it’s hurting Canada’s prosperity.

They pushed for the repeal during debate Monday in the House of Commons on a private member’s bill to scrap the tanker ban, a day after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Prime Minister Mark Carney about it.

Poilievre was one of several Opposition MPs who signed the letter to Carney ahead of debate on the bill. The vote on it was set for Wednesday as the Liberals asked for a recorded vote.

The existing law, the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, prohibits tankers from carrying more than 12,500 metric tonnes of crude oil in areas along the northern coast of British Columbia.

Bill C-264, sponsored by Calgary MP David McKenzie, would repeal the law entirely.

“Passing this legislation would not approve a single new pipeline or tanker terminal. It would not give an oil company permission to do whatever it wants, and it would not remove Canada’s other marine safety or environmental laws,” Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie said in the House of Commons.

“It would simply repeal the existing tanker moratorium, allowing future proposals to be considered under the other laws and approval processes that apply to it.”

Leslie said decisions about whether a project should have access to shipping on the north coast should be made on the merits and risks.

“How can we seriously talk about opening new markets while maintaining a law that rules out an entire region of potential export opportunities?” he said.

“I don’t believe that protecting the environment and developing our natural resources must be competing objectives. We should in fact be able to walk and chew gum. I think it is perfectly reasonable to take another look at whether this tanker ban still makes any sense.”

The letter to Carney from Poilievre and other Conservative MPs argued the tanker ban “effectively donates” billions of dollars to the United States by forcing Canada to sell discounted oil profiting American refineries.

The MPs point to a proposal by Calgary-based Strathcona Resources to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day on existing railroad tracks through Prince Rupert, B.C., and across the Pacific Ocean.

For the proposal to be considered, the tanker ban would have to be lifted. The letter says the federal government is the only thing standing in the way.

The Liberals don’t appear likely to repeal the tanker ban.

“I think it is important that we continue to look at ways in which we can encourage and support that collaborative approach at dealing with building a stronger and healthier Canada,” said Kevin Lamoureux, parliamentary secretary to the government leader in the House of Commons.

Carney signed an agreement with British Columbia in July that included a promise by Ottawa to maintain the north coast tanker ban “without alteration, suspension, or narrowing of scope.”

A day later, Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the route for their proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast would go south to respect the tanker ban.

The plan would largely follow the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline from Bruderheim, Alta., to an export terminal in Delta, B.C.

On Monday, Smith joined the calls for the tanker ban’s repeal.

“Canada cannot become a global energy superpower while federal policies continue to stand in the way of getting our energy to the world. Repealing the tanker ban is an important step toward securing better prices for our resources and building a stronger, more prosperous Canada,” Smith said in a statement.

The Conservative letter to Carney says the Official Opposition also would be willing to discuss amendments to the ban that would allow the Prince Rupert project to move forward.

The provincial Conservatives swept to power in B.C. on Saturday after winning about two-thirds of the seats and defeating the NDP, which had governed the province since 2017.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has said he supports the new Pacific Link pipeline.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

— with files from Nick Murray in Ottawa and Aaron Sousa in Edmonton

stories.title: Osap, affordability questions likely to dominate as Queen's Park resumes sitting
stories.summary: Toronto - Provincial politicians are returning to the Ontario legislature Tuesday for the first time in 21 weeks with some new faces thanks to three byelections, a rejigged cabinet and a new cloud of scandal hanging over the government's head.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Provincial politicians are returning to the Ontario legislature Tuesday for the first time in 21 weeks with some new faces thanks to three byelections, a rejigged cabinet and a new cloud of scandal hanging over the government’s head.

The spotlight in question period is expected to largely focus on Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn, who is under fire for his government’s handling of Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to career colleges.

Provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled from 2023-24 to the next year, when the amount hit almost $1 billion. Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request points to larger-than-usual increases at some schools.

That includes seven whose approximately $385 million in Osap grants in 2024-25 matched the amount that went to students at all publicly funded colleges in the province.

The industry’s association, Career Colleges Ontario, began warning the government of what they allege were suspicious usage patterns at a small number of schools in 2023, but it wasn’t until May of this year that the government banned six schools from Osap eligibility.

Quinn’s office says it regularly reviews complaints and monitors Osap activity, and expanded its reviews in May 2025 when it received warnings about usage at a few schools from the federal government.

Quinn has since engaged Kpmg to conduct an audit of the sector and referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, but critics say the ministry should have taken action long ago.

Now part of Quinn’s solution is making matters worse, critics say. Not only did Quinn drastically reduce the amount of grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges can receive in the face of rising Osap usage driven primarily by a few career colleges, he has now also paused Osap payments to all students at career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions until 2027.

It is leading many of those students to scramble to figure out how to pay their living expenses while they study, in addition to the tuition that Osap was supposed to cover.

The Liberals plan to go hard at Quinn on Osap with the legislature back in session.

“It still shocks me what’s happening to people out there because of the mess up with Osap and this government’s failure to act over three years,” interim Liberal leader John Fraser said.

“It is causing so much hardship and so much hurt that we can’t ignore it.”

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said Quinn has a lot to answer for.

“Nolan Quinn and the Ford government cut Osap, and we also know that they mismanaged the way in which private colleges use the Osap program, and it should be those private colleges that pay the price for that, not the students,” he said.

“So we are calling on this government reverse the cuts to Osap and have the backs of students.”

Affordability is another key priority for the Greens during this six-week sitting, Schreiner said. They plan to introduce a motion calling for a wealth tax on the ultra rich.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said she also plans to focus on the cost of living.

“The reality right now for most people out there in Ontario is life is just deeply unaffordable,” she said. “People are concerned about the state of our health-care system and the state of our economy, and I think we’re going to be speaking about all of those issues.”

The government will likely also face questions on nursing jobs that are being cut at hospitals across the province, funding to help tariff-affected industries, and potential looming showdowns with teachers, who will take strike votes next month.

Three new faces will enter the legislature after a set of September byelections: Progressive Conservative Jeff Beattie for Hamilton East–Stoney Creek, Progressive Conservative Susan Lahey for York–Simcoe, and New Democrat Fatima Shaban for Scarborough Southwest.

The most prominent cabinet positions are unchanged from when the legislature last sat in June, but Premier Doug Ford did make several moves in a shuffle last month.

Those include a move from Labour to Infrastructure for David Piccini, who is under investigation by the integrity commissioner after the auditor general raised questions about his handling of the $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund.

It is not known when the long-awaited report from the integrity commissioner will be published, but if it comes before the legislature rises in December for its winter break, it could knock the government off its preferred messages on the economy and infrastructure.

The government is focused this session on cutting red tape, protecting workers, and keeping costs low for businesses and families, a spokesperson for Ford said.

“As the world faces economic uncertainty caused by tariffs, our government is relentlessly focused on delivering on our plan to protect Ontario by building a more competitive, resilient, and self-reliant economy for future generations,” Hannah Jensen wrote in a statement.

The first week of the sitting is set to be a busy one, with the fall economic statement – a mini-budget of sorts – to be tabled on Thursday. As well, Quinn has indicated that he will table legislation to exclude predominantly online programs at career colleges from Osap eligibility.

The Ford government first extended Osap eligibility to those programs during the COVID-19 pandemic, then later made it permanent.

The spotlight in question period is expected to largely focus on Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn, who is under fire for his government’s handling of Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to career colleges.

Provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled from 2023-24 to the next year, when the amount hit almost $1 billion. Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request points to larger-than-usual increases at some schools.
That includes seven whose approximately $385 million in Osap grants in 2024-25 matched the amount that went to students at all publicly funded colleges in the province.

The industry’s association, Career Colleges Ontario, began warning the government of what they allege were suspicious usage patterns at a small number of schools in 2023, but it wasn’t until May of this year that the government banned six schools from Osap eligibility.

Quinn’s office says it regularly reviews complaints and monitors Osap activity, and expanded its reviews in May 2025 when it received warnings about usage at a few schools from the federal government.
Quinn has since engaged Kpmg to conduct an audit of the sector and referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police, but critics say the ministry should have taken action long ago.

stories.title: Toronto votes in tight mayoral race as Chow looks to hold off Bradford
stories.summary: Toronto - The next leader of Toronto is set to be decided on Monday, as Olivia Chow looks to hold off a challenge from city councillor Brad Bradford in what's shaped up to be one of the most tightly contested re-election bids by a sitting mayor.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Olivia Chow won a decisive re-election victory in Toronto’s mayoral race Monday, fending off a challenge from councillor Brad Bradford and convincing voters to stay the course on her progressive agenda highlighted by expanded renter protections and transit affordability.

Chow held a double-digit lead over councillor Brad Bradford with most polls reporting Monday night.

Her campaign watch party, held at the same west-end venue where she celebrated her 2023 byelection victory, erupted into chants of “Olivia” as television broadcasters called the election for Chow.

“My friends, tonight we celebrate. Tomorrow, we get back to work. Because an election victory isn’t the finish line. It is a responsibility,” Chow told the raucous crowd shortly after 10:30 p.m.

Her re-election pitch rested largely on her track record, highlighted by the deal to upload city expressway costs to the province, tighter rules for bad-faith evictions, and reduced 911 wait times. She will be expected to make good on new promises, including capping transit fares at 10 rides a week, building more affordable rental housing and expanding a school nutrition program.

She vowed to create a task force to pursue landlords with the worst track records and empower the city to complete more repairs in buildings where owners had chronically refused court-ordered work.

Bradford’s campaign attempted to cast Chow as out of touch with the city’s anxieties and grievances, leaning hard on issues of crime, transit safety and traffic congestion. Opinion polls in the waning days suggested the race could be a dead heat.

Some observers speculated that tightening race could mirror a broader Canadian political climate driven by voter dissatisfaction and a growing desire for change, citing recent incumbent defeats in British Columbia and Quebec elections. Mayoral incumbents in Mississauga and Hamilton were both unseated by wide margins on Monday night.

But in Toronto, it was Chow’s message that triumphed. Unofficial results on election night suggested she secured more than 50 per cent of the vote in what was a two-way race with Bradford.

Chow was raised in a highrise apartment in St. James Town, a familiar landing in the downtown core for working-class newcomers, after her family immigrated from Hong Kong when she was 13. She was first elected as a school board trustee in 1985, sat for 13 years on Toronto city council until 2005, and then went to Ottawa as an NDP MP alongside her late husband, former federal New Democrat leader Jack Layton.

She made a failed bid for mayor in 2014 only to successfully return in the 2023 byelection after John Tory’s resignation. Chow, 69, heads into a full four-year term with several key allies also winning their own re-election bids and other new progressive faces ascending to city hall.

“I have never forgotten what Toronto gave my family, and I have spent my life trying to give back because Toronto is a city that believes in people, a progressive city, a city of compassion, a city to welcome newcomers. A city that stands up for working people, celebrates our differences and believes everyone deserves a fair chance,” she said.

Results were delayed by over an hour in Toronto as the city said it extended voting at some locations to accommodate those still in line. Results began to trickle in after 9 p.m. with the first batch of votes showing Bradford with a slim lead. That lead, and the initial buzz at his campaign headquarters, vanished as more polls reported.

Bradford conceded defeat and congratulated Chow on her re-election.

“I implore all of us, everybody in a leadership position here in Toronto, to make sure that we spend the days, weeks, and months ahead bringing this city back together, healing this city, making sure that this is a city for everybody — a city that’s safe for everybody and a city where nobody is left behind,” Bradford said.

At the council level, Mike Layton, Chow’s stepson, was poised to reclaim his former seat in University-Rosedale after stepping away from municipal politics. The ward incumbent Dianne Saxe, who instead opted to run in Toronto-Danforth to avoid a faceoff with Layton, lost that race to Sara Ehrhardt.

Diana Chan McNally, one of the city’s most vocal defenders of people experiencing homelessness, won in Parkdale-High Park, the seat left open by the retirement of longtime progressive councillor Gord Perks.

While Chow held off her challenger, other councillors were not so successful. Monday’s election put an end to more than four decades of city politics for Frances Nunziata, who lost to progressive opponent Chiara Padovani in York South-Weston. Shaun Chen, the former federal Liberal MP who resigned earlier this year, unseated transit chair Jamaal Myers in Scarborough North.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

—With files from Kathryn Mannie and Maan Alhmidi

stories.title: Voters across Ontario head to the polls for municipal elections
stories.summary: It's election day in Ontario, with voters in more than 400 municipalities set to pick their local representatives.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Municipal elections in Ontario toppled some incumbents, elevated new names and returned some familiar faces to city halls across the province.

Monday’s vote was headlined by the mayoral race in the country’s biggest city, where Toronto’s Olivia Chow fended off challenger councillor Brad Bradford to win re-election.

Here are the results from five other mayoral races from around Ontario.

In one of the night’s biggest upsets, Alvin Tedjo pulled off a victory in Mississauga.

Tedjo, a city councillor and former Ontario Liberal leadership hopeful, defeated incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.

Tedjo, who finished second in the 2024 mayoral byelection, started out as a longshot but began to rise in the polls as the front-runners clashed, culminating in a heated back-and-forth between Parrish and Crombie at a debate earlier this month.

Tedjo will now be expected to make good on a platform headlined by a promise to freeze property taxes for two years, and allow certain seniors to defer that tax bill until they sell or transfer their home.

It’s another disappointing setback for Crombie, who left Mississauga’s top job in 2024 after she took over as Ontario Liberal leader. The party added seats in the 2025 snap provincial election but fell short of expectations, and Crombie resigned as leader in January of this year.

Keanin Loomis, CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, declared victory after garnering more than 40 per cent of the vote with the majority of polls reporting Monday night.

He unseated incumbent Andrea Horwath, who trailed in third place.

The race was a rematch of the 2022 contest, when Loomis lost to Horwarth by just 1,663 votes.

The race in Hamilton was held under the shadow of layoffs at Stelco, a U.S.-owned steelmaker.

Mark Sutcliffe cruised to re-election in Ottawa.

Sutcliffe’s main challenge came from Jeff Leiper, a longtime councillor who ran as the progressive alternative to the incumbent mayor.

But voters stuck with Sutcliffe, who pledged to keep property taxes low, maintain a hiring freeze on non-front-line workers and create free trade with neighbouring Gatineau.

Patrick Brown, the former Progressive Conservative leader, easily won his re-election bid.

Brown had secured a majority of the votes with most polls reporting Monday night.

He ran on a platform of more front-line policing and stronger action on extortion and auto theft, along with expanded transit and health-care facilities.

Brown took over the city’s top job in 2018 in the aftermath of sexual misconduct allegations that led to his resignation as PC leader. He has vehemently denied those allegations and no criminal charges were ever laid.

The winds of change were blowing in southwestern Ontario.

Windsor, the tariff-vulnerable capital of Canada’s auto sector, elected Fred Francis.

The city councillor put an end to incumbent Drew Dilkens’ 12-year tenure as mayor, in an election that took place amid the U.S.-Canada trade war.

Francis, the younger brother of former mayor Eddie Francis, pledged to hold the line on taxes, make city hall more transparent, eliminate strong mayor powers and cap transit fees.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Bank of Canada now expected to hike key rate as it faces ‘pivotal decision’
stories.summary: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise interest rates this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to Lseg Data & Analytics. The central bank’s planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings.

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven’t significantly spread throughout the economy yet.

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions.

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

“While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike,” the note reads.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations.

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

“All the economic data that we’ve had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates,” Janzen said.

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, “and that’s what’s starting to change the calculus.”

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.

“There’s interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space,” Ercolao said.

“Overall, Canada’s economy is growing, but it’s not necessarily overheating by any means.”

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said.

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent.

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy.

“On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces,” he said.

“But at the same time, it’s households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases.”

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute “fairly well” by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

“That said, there’s still that acute pressure that’s being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney, premiers to meet with First Nations leaders in Ottawa for first time in years
stories.summary: Ottawa — First Nations leaders meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney and some of the country's premiers today in what the Assembly of First Nations is calling a historic occasion.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A historic meeting between Prime Minister Mark Carney, premiers and First Nations was meant to build bridges between communities and work out issues related to major projects development, the respecting of rights, health and public safety amid rising tensions.

But it ended with calls from Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew to abolish the controversial Indian Act, and agreement from Carney something must be done about the legislation from 1876 that governs First Nations — something protestors outside the Ottawa venue were warning about before the announcement was even made, and something likely to generate heated debate.

Carney said he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act, which he said could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether. He said changes would only be made in partnership with First Nations leadership.

The Indian Act gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including by defining who qualifies for recognition, what reserves can and can’t do, dismantles traditional forms of governance and, at one point, outlawed ceremonial practices.

It even governs First Nations people after death, with the Indigenous Services minister required to approve of wills for people living on reserve, or to void them altogether if they see fit.

While there is a general consensus among First Nations chiefs the legislation is outdated and restrictive, there is little consensus on if it should repealed, and, if it is, what takes its place. There is broad support, however, for changing rules on how the Indian Act determines who qualifies for status, but the federal government and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty have not committed to changing registration rules.

Earlier in the day, Kinew told reporters during a break in the meeting that Canada needs a relationship between First Nations and the government “that reflects who Indigenous people are as Canadians.”

Kinew, a member of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, held up his own status card and said abolishing the Indian Act should be high on the national political agenda, and that he received an “open-minded reception” from leadership in the closed-door meeting when he made the pitch.

“The suggestion of reforming, potentially abolishing and fully modernizing governance, is that a process, co-developed, needs to be put in place, and the federal government is open to that process,” Carney said.

Carney echoed Kinew’s remarks that the idea of abolishing or modernizing the Indian Act was discussed openly in the room — and an idea he was similarly “very open to.”

“Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So it’s already starting from the right place in that it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done. It’s responding to a request,” Carney said.

“I think this was the spirit of this meeting — certainly the spirit I took — the ability to sit down together and develop that co-development, gives me hope that we can we can finally move forward from this.”

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there are some protections in the Indian Act for First Nations, and First Nations should be able to decide how to move forward.

“Look, that’s a question that was just posed today in the room among First Nations. Some First Nations; others would be very reserved,” Woodhouse Nepinak.

“But there is, you know, a diversity of First Nations from coast to coast to coast, where in every province and territory in this beautiful country that we all share. And that question is going to be up to them to decide.”

Protestors outside the venue were warning that their representatives in the meeting, who were largely made up of regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations, would inappropriately discuss First Nations rights without a mandate from community members.

Mohawk policy analyst and protest organizer Russ Diabo has frequently accused the Assembly of First Nations of working toward Indian Act abolition with the federal government. Asked about Woodhouse Nepinak telling the room in her opening remarks she has a mandate from chiefs to discuss rights, Diabo said the AFN charter does not represent the grassroots.

“Our traditional governments are direct democracies where the people are involved in decision-making,” Diabo told The Canadian Press on the sidewalk in front of the Diefenbaker Building..

“What we should be returning to is traditional forms of government which involve people in decision making, otherwise we see manipulation happening all the time.”

After Kinew’s remarks, Diabo said governments were already working on abolishing it without consent.

The chief of Onion Lake Cree Nation, which reportedly sent a cease-and-desist letter to the Assembly of First Nations ahead of the meeting to make clear the body does not represent his community or negotiate on its behalf, expressed concern about the future of the Indian Act.

“First Nations must determine their own path toward self-determination. That cannot be a process designed in Ottawa and presented to our nations for approval. It must be developed with us, respect our treaty relationships and proceed only with our free, prior and informed consent,” Chief Pete Chief said in a media statement.

“But that future must be determined by First Nations themselves, not dictated by the federal government or negotiated on our behalf by organizations we have not authorized to represent us.”

First Nations chiefs are frequently critiqued by members of their community when they meet with premiers or Carney behind closed doors.

Asked about those critiques already forming online regarding talk of Indian Act abolition, Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations should be able to determine for themselves how they’re governed.

“I know those conversations are hard to have, but if we don’t have them, you’ll see the disputes,” she said.

Lawyer Pam Palmater likened the talks of abolishment to the Stephen Harper era, saying the federal government would love nothing more than to drop its fiduciary and treaty obligations to First Nations.

“Saw this coming with Carney’s conservative extractive agenda,” Palmater wrote on social media.

Monday’s closed-door meeting is the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities.

The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office just a few months later.

This meeting came as Carney’s government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.

Jeronimo Kataquapit, who was protesting the major projects push outside the meeting venue in Ottawa, chided the federal government and the Assembly of First Nations over the lack of youth representation at the meeting.

“These major projects cannot move forward without our free, prior and informed consent, and it’s the youth that stand to be the most impacted by the decisions made today by all leadership, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous alike,” Kataquapit said from the sidewalk in front of the Diefenbaker Building.

Protester Katisha Paul, an advocate for youth and women, questioned the Assembly of First Nations’ mandate to negotiate on First Nations’ behalf.

“I’m not in that room today but I can imagine and speculate that the voices of our ancestors are not being heard, they’re not being voiced and they’re not being amplified because many of those elected band council chiefs have lost their ways,” Paul said.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation.

But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario. In many cases, it’s youth who are pushing back on First Nations leaders, the premiers and prime minister.

Carney said Monday in his opening remarks it’s “sobering” to consider that this is the first meeting to bring together federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in two decades.

“Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” he said.

“And secondly, our task is to live our values fully of a fair and inclusive Canada.”

While some First Nations are opposed to Carney’s development agenda and those of the provinces, others are open to the idea of increasing economic activity in their territories.

Nisga’a Nation President Eva Clayton told reporters ahead of the meeting she supports Carney’s plans and that she and other modern treaty holders are at the meeting to support Canada.

Chiefs in the meeting room told reporters the talks behind closed doors were constructive and that they felt their voices were heard, but that they wanted more action on actively involving their communities in the Natural Resources Transfer Acts. That call was pushed for by former Assembly of First Nations national chief Matthew Coon Come.

The British Columbia Assembly of First Nations said in a media release after the meeting it failed to live up to its potential.

“The structure, format and agenda of this meeting were solely reflective of federal and provincial interest,” Regional Chief Terry Teegee said.

“The prime minister and premiers have an obligation to meet directly with First Nations to engage in reciprocal dialogue on issues of shared importance, not simply those items which align with this government’s priorities.”

After the meeting, Carney committed to looking into a First Nations sovereign wealth fund that would allow for communities to invest in major projects in an easier way, funding for First Nations policing and improving First Nations health.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray

stories.title: Did Ontario's minimum wage just go up?
stories.summary: There are four categories of workers affected by the province's minimum wage hikes.
stories.author: Soma Ray-Ellis
stories.content:
Q: I’m a minimum wage earner in Ontario, and my pay has recently gone up. Can I expect it to keep increasing annually?

A: Ontario’s minimum wage rates are subject to annual increases based on the rate of inflation measured through the province’s Consumer Price Index (CPI). Minimum wage is the lowest amount an employer is allowed to pay a worker by law.

This index measures changes in the cost of goods and services purchased by Ontario consumers, including food, transportation and shelter.

Ontario’s minimum wage is adjusted annually based on the CPI. The government announces the new rate by April 1, and the new rate takes effect on Oct. 1.

This year, as you’ve mentioned, minimum wage has increased.

The Ontario government states that about 35 per cent of minimum wage workers are employed in the retail trade sector, while about 24 per cent work in accommodation and food services.

Overall, there are four categories of workers affected by minimum wage hikes in Ontario.

The first is general minimum wage workers, which includes employees in the retail trade, accommodation, and food services sectors.

As of Oct. 1, 2026, their wage has increased to $17.95 per hour from $17.60 per hour.

The second category is student minimum wage, which applies to students younger than 18 who work 28 hours a week or less while school is in session, or work during school breaks or summer holidays.

Their wage has increased to $16.90 per hour from $16.60 per hour.

The third category covers employees who work as hunting, fishing and wilderness guides.

A wilderness guide is an employee who guides, assists or teaches groups/individuals participating in activities in the wilderness.

This includes backcountry skiing, snowshoeing, canoeing, hiking and survival training.

Wages for this group are based on blocks of time rather than by the hour.

Their rate for working less than five consecutive hours in a day is now $89.75, up from $88.05.

Their rate for working five or more hours in a day is now $179.50, up from $176.15.

The last group of minimum wage earners to receive a rate hike are homeworkers.

A homeworker is defined as an employee who is paid to perform work in their own home.

This includes those who write software for a high-tech company, call centre employees, and employees who sew for a manufacturer.

Their rate is now $19.70 per hour, up from $19.35 per hour.

Keep in mind that students of all ages employed in this category must receive the homeworker’s minimum wage.

Ontario maintains the second-highest minimum wage rate among provinces in Canada, second to British Columbia, where it is $18.25 per hour.

If a minimum wage increase comes into effect partway through an employee’s pay period, it will be treated as two separate pay periods, and the employee will be entitled to at least the minimum wage that applies in each of them.

Additionally, if an employee’s pay is based wholly or partly on commission, it must amount to at least the minimum wage for each hour the employee has worked.

stories.title: Ontario promised four hours of daily care in long-term care homes, but records show nearly 300 are failing
stories.summary: Internal records show nearly 300 Ontario long-term care homes fail to meet the promised four hours of daily resident care.
stories.author: Frédérik Plante
stories.content:
At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in November 2020, Ontario Premier Doug Ford promised more hands-on care for long-term care homes’ residents.

“By increasing the hours of daily direct care for residents, we will improve their quality of life and ensure they are more comfortable and safe,” Ford said at the time.

His government pledged to reach four hours of daily care by nurses and personal support workers for each long-term care resident by 2024-25. But records obtained by the Star through a freedom-of-information request reveal large disparities between homes and widespread failure to reach the standard.

A year past the government’s deadline, nearly 300 long-term care homes still don’t meet the promised standard of four hours of daily care, the records show.

Research has shown that more daily hours of care is associated with better outcomes for long-term care residents , including better mood, fewer falls and lower use of antipsychotic drugs .

The Canadian Institute for Health Information found that short-staffed long-term care homes had a higher risk of infection and a higher mortality rate. Ontario’s Long-Term Care COVID-19 Commission recommended in 2021 that the minimum of four hours of hands-on care by personal support workers and nurses should be implemented “ on an urgent basis .”

A Ministry of Long-Term Care spokesperson said that Ontario is “making record investments to ensure people at every stage of life can access the care they need.” This includes $44.1 million in the province’s 2026 budget “to ensure every resident continues to receive an average of four hours of direct care each day,” the Ministry said in an unsigned statement.

The Ford government said it met its goal, with the provincial average increasing slightly above four hours of daily care last year. But far from every resident benefits from that minimum.

The COVID-19 Commission found that the government’s promised timeline was “too slow” and that, by the time the standard would be reached, four hours of daily care would likely be insufficient as the “acuity of long-term care residents continues to increase.”

The facility that provided the least amount of direct care to residents in the first three quarters of 2025-26 — the most recent data obtained by the Star — was St. Lawrence Lodge in Brockville. St. Lawrence, a not-for-profit home with 224 licensed beds, recorded an average of two hours and 21 minutes of care per resident over that period, with a low of one hour and 16 minutes during the second quarter.

An unrelated Ministry of Long-Term Care inspection conducted in the fall of 2025 shows numerous other issues at St. Lawrence, including unspecified allegations of staff to resident physical and emotional abuse, neglect and retaliation. The inspection found several deficiencies, including a resident with a documented bed sore who was not assessed and another whose wounds were not treated properly.

Lisa Harper, the administrator of St. Lawrence, did not return the Star’s calls.

Ninety-one long-term care homes did not have data on care provided in 2025-26 because of various “data quality issues,” according to Ministry records. Among those without recent data, 73 had previously failed to provide four hours of care per resident, ON average, between 2023 and 2025.

This means that less than half of Ontario’s 705 long-term care homes have met the provincial government’s promised standard.

Among the 20 facilities giving the least amount of daily care per resident, four homes belong to the same for-profit licensee: Caressant Care Nursing and Retirement Homes Limited.

An August routine compliance inspection at one of these, the Caressant Care home on McLaughlin Road in Lindsay, found that staff “were verbally abusive when providing care” to a resident, did not provide sufficient personal care, failed to properly address a resident’s pain and put others “at increased risk of heat-related illness” when their rooms were left at temperatures above 26°C. The inspection resulted in several written notifications and orders to remedy deficiencies, but no penalty.

Betty Hazen, the facility’s executive director, declined to answer the Star’s questions. Natalie Dechert, Caressant Care’s Vice President of Operations, said that “while many of our homes are consistently meeting or exceeding these provincial targets, we recognize there is ongoing work to do in certain locations to ensure consistency.”

She said that the company is making progress and “remains deeply focused on delivering the safe, compassionate care our residents deserve.”

An August routine compliance inspection at one of these, the Caressant Care home on McLaughlin Road in Lindsay, found that staff “were verbally abusive when providing care” to a resident, did not provide sufficient personal care, failed to properly address a resident’s pain and put others “at increased risk of heat-related illness” when their rooms were left at temperatures above 26°C. The inspection resulted in several written notifications and orders to remedy deficiencies, but no penalty.

Betty Hazen, the facility’s executive director, declined to answer the Star’s questions. Natalie Dechert, Caressant Care’s Vice President of Operations, said that “while many of our homes are consistently meeting or exceeding these provincial targets, we recognize there is ongoing work to do in certain locations to ensure consistency.”
She said that the company is making progress and “remains deeply focused on delivering the safe, compassionate care our residents deserve.”

ByThames Valley District School Board - Oct 26, 2026

General News

All Notices and Updates

Thames Valley District School Board congratulates Kim Davy, a valued art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary School, for receiving the prestigious Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award from the Canadian Society for Education through Art (CSEA/SCEA) and the journal Canadian Art Teacher (CAT).

Kim Davy is one of just five educators from across Canada named as award recipients this fall, and the only recipient representing Ontario. The Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award is a national recognition program that celebrates outstanding K-12 art educators who contribute to sharing knowledge and fostering meaningful learning through the visual arts.

Kim was nominated for the award by a BealArt alumna who wanted to honour the exceptional impact she has had on students through her work in the classroom.

"I am deeply passionate about the power of Art Education to drive personal growth and development," said Kim Davy. "As an educator, my primary mission is to support and empower students as they find their voice, build technical skills, and expand their creative awareness. I encourage them to focus on their unique artistic journeys—where "mileage on the hands" reflects a dedication to practice, and deep research fosters an authentic voice. By inviting students to take risks, I help them learn to trust the creative process."

"Within the Bealart community, staff and students uplift one another through coordinated teamwork, critical dialogue, technical growth, and conceptual exploration. Ultimately, my hope is that our students cultivate lifelong skills that extend far beyond the classroom, shaping them into future creators and engaged community members."

As part of the recognition, Kim participated in a CAT Conversation on October 15, joining fellow award recipients in an 80-minute discussion focused on creative programming and art education.

Congratulations to Kim Davy on this outstanding achievement and recognition of her work in art education!
