stories.title: Political hubris claims another victim – the Ndp’s David Eby
stories.summary: Former Ontario premier David Peterson has gained some new company in the realm of snap election cautionary tales
stories.author: Gary Mason
stories.content:
British Columbians took a huge political gamble this weekend, handing power to someone they barely know who leads a party that looked like it was imploding only a few weeks ago.

But such was the level of anger and disgust over NDP Leader David Eby’s move to call a snap election – amid provincewide municipal elections no less, and with two years left in his mandate – that the public decided B.C. Conservative Party Leader Lorne Doerkson sounded normal enough to trust.

It’s impossible to overstate the enormity of the challenge now confronting him and his party.

First, we must say a few words about the man they vanquished – Mr. Eby. Since first being elected as an MLA in 2013, knocking off then-Liberal premier Christy Clark, Mr. Eby was viewed as a rising political star. As attorney-general, he became the heir apparent to much-loved NDP premier John Horgan. When Mr. Horgan resigned in the fall of 2022 because of illness, Mr. Eby was virtually handed the job.

But governing never came easy to him. He was unquestionably bright, but lacked the natural charm and easygoing nature of his predecessor. Where Mr. Horgan was a delegator, Mr. Eby centralized decision-making. He also treated the treasury as an ATM, using it to pay for things his government couldn’t afford, including grossly irresponsible public sector contracts.

Provincial debt soared to historic levels under his watch. Meantime, emergency rooms across the province were halting services for short periods because of staffing shortages, while doctors and specialists were resigning because of workload issues.

And that only begins to scratch the surface of the many problems Mr. Eby left behind for Mr. Doerkson and his party to clean up.

Had Mr. Eby been paying more attention, he would have detected the public wasn’t in the mood for an early election and that calling one was likely to make people even more ornery.

Still, he couldn’t resist pouncing on the opportunity that an opposition party in disarray offered. The disastrous new leadership of the Conservatives’ Kerry-Lynne Findlay was too juicy a situation to pass up. But when she resigned unexpectedly and the party announced that the relatively unknown Lorne Doerkson was being named interim leader, Mr. Eby didn’t pause his plan to go to the polls.

A more savvy politician would have slammed the brakes on his election plan right then and there. But Mr. Eby, no doubt pushed by advisers who showed him public opinion polling in his favour, decided to push forward.

It was a fatal mistake.

He isn’t the first politician to be punished for his political hubris. The scrap bin of history is full of them. And there are some, like former Ontario premier David Peterson, who will doubtlessly be overjoyed by Saturday’s outcome in B.C. Now, Mr. Peterson is unlikely to be cited as frequently or as instantaneously as a cautionary tale of the hazards of snap elections. He called one in 1990 when his Liberal government had a healthy majority. So disgusted was the public over the cynical move, it gave the NDP a majority. Mr. Peterson lost his own seat.

There needs to be something said here about Mr. Doerkson’s leadership. In a short period of time, he united the Conservative Party caucus, bringing back to the fold many of those MLAs who had left it over Ms. Findlay’s extreme lurch to the right. The new leader was not interested in making culture wars his priority.

Mr. Doerkson showed people he is a “normal” Conservative, whose priority is the big issues facing the province – health care, the economy, education – and not trans athletes in women’s sports.

As long as he continues to act and lead as a regular, middle-of-the-road conservative, he should be just fine. The moment he caves to loud voices promoting fringe issues, he will get himself in trouble. The premier-designate needs to remember he is leading a centre -right coalition, one previously represented by the BC Liberal Party, and Social Credit Party before that.

Managed properly, this type of coalition has shown it can rule B.C. for long periods of time, in fact decades longer than any other political alliance in the province’s history.

As for the NDP, well, they know the position in which they find themselves all too well. While its caucus has been drastically reduced in size, the party will still have several experienced MLAs who will constitute what should be a formidable Opposition.

With Mr. Eby announcing his resignation as leader Saturday, the party will soon need to begin the process of replacing him.

The pollsters said the B.C. public was demanding change in this election. Well, they got it. We’ll soon find out what that means.

stories.title: BC premier-designate Doerkson says province ‘chose change’ in election
stories.summary: The man who was previously a relatively unknown backbench MLA took the reins of the party as an interim leader heading into the election.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
B.C. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said he was “deeply humbled” by his party’s victory and vowed to earn the trust British Columbians have placed in him.

Doerkson’s BC Conservatives won a resounding victory on Saturday night, with Global News projecting a majority government less than an hour after polls closed.

“I’m very excited that yesterday British Columbians chose change and they chose that,” Doerkson said Sunday in his first official news conference after election day. “People in every corner of this province, from the Peace to the island, from the Kootenays to the Coast placed their trust in us … It was lent to us for purpose and it must be earned back every single day.”

The man who was previously a relatively unknown backbench MLA took the reins of the party as an interim leader heading into the election after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned amid numerous departures.

On Sunday, his party was projected to win 64 seats, a total no party has surpassed since the BC Liberals won 77 seats in 2001.

Outgoing premier David Eby triggered the election less than two years into his mandate, initially saying it was necessary in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, though he later shifted his focus to affordability issues, a key part of Doerkson’s campaign.

Doerkson stressed he was an ally of British Columbia when asked about Trump reposting about the Conservatives’ win on his Truth Social platform.

“I’m an ally to British Columbia and we should have taken the opportunity years ago to protect ourselves against these attacks,” Doerkson said. “My focus is going to be to supercharge our economy … It’s just about endless, where I believe we can support different industries that will protect us against these attacks.”

Work was already underway in forming government, with the premier-designate saying he’s spoken with Lt. Gov. Wendy Cocchia and named Kim Henderson as chair of the government’s transition team.

“When this party is sworn in, it will be ready on day one and it will hit the ground running,” he said.

He said his government will launch an independent review of the province’s finances on day one to “know where things stand,” promising residents would have a “full picture” before a budget is tabled.

He also reiterated campaign promises, stating within the first 100 days an expert commission would look into keeping emergency rooms open and cutting wait times.

But the first priority, Doerkson said, was raising the basic personal exemption to $32,000, amounting to about $1,000 a year “back in the pocket” of working British Columbians.

“These are serious times, people are stretched, the economy has stalled and too many British Columbians have stopped believing government can get anything done,” he said.

Though the BC Conservatives won a resounding victory, they also achieved a majority with the lowest voter turnout in decades. Preliminary figures from Elections BC show 48 per cent of those eligible voted. Prior to this year, no provincial election in recent history has seen turnout fall below 50 per cent.

Doerkson’s party was projected to win 64 seats with 48.05 per cent of the votes, with the NDP receiving 27 seats and 37.38 per cent. The Green Party won two seats and received 10.97 per cent.

During the campaign, Eby questioned if Doerkson would remain as premier going forward. As interim leader of the party, he is not currently permitted to run in an eventual leadership race.

Asked whether he would stay, Doerkson said that’s an “administrative detail” that will see information provided “imminently.”

“But I will remain leader of the party and I am thrilled to be the premier-elect of British Columbia right now,” he added.

The next premier also faced questions on his stance on repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Dripa).

He stressed he was committed to working with First Nations as premier, but remained firm on his plan.

“It has not worked in this province, and frankly, it has caused more problems to date than I think potentially anything else,” Doerkson said, questioning what it has done to solve problems in the province.

Congratulations for the premier-designate have come in from across the province and country, with Doerkson adding he’s heard from “a number of First Nations,” including in his riding of Cariboo Chilcotin.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew congratulated Doerkson on his win and thanked Eby for his friendship over the past few years.

Kinew did have caution though when questioned about Doerkson’s policies on Dripa and Indigenous rights.

“I think the election results in BC should concern every elected politician and every consultant out there for this reason,” Kinew said. “It’s a reminder that what we’re doing is not a game. When you’re elected to serve the people of your province or of your country, it is a serious responsibility that isn’t to be played with.”

A date for when Doerkson’s government will be sworn in has yet to be announced and he did not say if there would be a fall session, though he didn’t rule it out.

— with files from Global News’ Amy Judd

stories.title: Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank, sources say
stories.summary: Two countries say they will develop framework for co-operation between defence-funding initiatives
stories.author: Reuters
stories.content:
Britain will not join the planned Canada-led multinational defence financing bank, opting instead to work toward a separate defence procurement entity after weeks of negotiations.

In a joint statement released Sunday, the two countries said they have “mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions that work in partnership.”

A senior Canadian government official confirmed that Britain will not be joining the institution, known as the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (Dsrb). The official said the two sides determined that it would be better to have the Canadian-headquartered bank focused on providing low-cost capital and the British initiative focused on procurement issues.

Meanwhile, the Dsrb is working toward being operational by next year, with a charter-signing ceremony set to take place in the last week of this November, according to two other Canadian sources with knowledge of the situation.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources as they were not authorized to comment publicly on the matter.

The development adds to growing pains for the Dsrb, envisioned as a way for Nato members and other allies to work together on raising the capital needed for vast military buildouts as geopolitical dangers multiply.

The nascent institution so far consists of a small group of founding countries: Canada, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine.

The bank’s creation was first proposed in 2024, and Canada was announced as the host country in April of this year.

Negotiations between Britain and Canada broke down after government officials spent much of the summer working on a potential merger of the two countries’ defence-finance and procurement mechanisms: the Dsrb and the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.

Britain’s MDM is not dissimilar to existing programs within the European Union and Nato. For example, there is the Security Action for Europe instrument, which Canada can also participate in.

The mechanism currently has four countries committed: Britain, the Netherlands, Finland and Poland. It is working toward being set up by 2027. However, little has been said publicly about it since early July, and few details have been made available about its structure.

Britain has been touch-and-go on joining the Dsrb since last year. In September, 2025, Britain’s Treasury told Reuters that it had ruled out joining the initiative. A year later, after a change in government, the door to Britain joining seemed to reopen . Prime Minister Mark Carney even headed to Britain to catch a soccer game with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to help seal the deal of the country’s decision.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne also met with his British counterpart, Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, in London the same week to discuss the subject.

However, despite the concerted effort by Ottawa, the sources with knowledge of the negotiations said ultimately that Britain made Canada an offer it could not accept. This included moving the headquarters from Canada to Europe and changing the mandate of the Dsrb to focus more heavily on procurement, rather than financing.

At least nine countries will be present at the Dsrb signing ceremony planned for November, with the possibility for others to still join before then. After the signing of the charter, further details, such as the Canadian city where the bank will be headquartered as well as the name of its chief executive officer, will follow.

For now, Canada and Britain have agreed to continue working on their respective initiatives to improve defence financing and procurement, with the caveat that one does not compete with the other.

The rest of the countries participating in the Dsrb were informed of the breakdown of negotiations between Canada and Britain on Saturday, the sources say.

In the joint statement released Sunday by Canada and Britain, the two sides said they have been working closely to consider how the Canadian bank “can best advance our shared objectives.”

The statement said that as they are operationalized, the two institutions will be designed “to work in close partnership, so that they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges. Together, they will provide complementary tools to strengthen the defence-industrial base and enhance collective defence readiness.”

stories.title: $6-million gift to establish first national myeloma research biobank in London
stories.summary: An anonymous $6-million donation will help establish Canada’s first national biobank dedicated exclusively to multiple myeloma research at London Health Sciences Centre.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
An anonymous $6-million donation will help establish Canada’s first national biobank dedicated exclusively to multiple myeloma research at London Health Sciences Centre.

The Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank will be housed at the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute and developed through a collaboration between the London Health Sciences Foundation and the Canadian Myeloma Research Group.

The gift is among the largest donations to multiple myeloma research in Canada and the largest known gift from a Canadian philanthropist dedicated to the disease, according to the organizations.

The biobank will collect, store and make biological samples available to approved researchers across the country, helping advance discoveries, improve diagnostics and develop new treatment options.

Multiple myeloma is a complex blood cancer that begins in plasma cells, a type of white blood cell that produces antibodies. The disease can damage bones, cause anemia and kidney problems, and weaken the immune system. An estimated 4,400 Canadians will be diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2026. While treatments such as chemotherapy, stem cell transplants and immunotherapy can help control the disease, there is currently no cure.

The new biobank will bring together blood, bone marrow and other biological samples collected with patients’ consent. Researchers will be able to study samples taken at different stages of the disease, including diagnosis, after treatment and relapse. The goal is to better understand how the cancer develops, why some treatments work better for certain patients and how the disease becomes resistant to treatment.

The biobank will also complement the Canadian Myeloma Research Group’s national database, which contains disease-specific information on more than 12,000 Canadian patients.

The anonymous donor, who is living with multiple myeloma and received immunotherapy through a clinical trial in Boston, said the experience highlighted both advances in treatment and the barriers some Canadians face in accessing care.

“I also know the cost and frequent travel required to access these treatments can put them out of reach for many Canadians,” the donor said.

The donor said the gift is intended to strengthen research in Canada and support efforts to find a cure.

Engin Gul, chief executive officer of the Canadian Myeloma Research Group, said the biobank will expand access to high-quality samples and help researchers collaborate on more precise and effective treatments.

Dr. Chris McIntyre, interim vice-president of research and scientific director of the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute, said studying patient samples could help explain why treatments produce different results and lead to improvements in care.

Planning and implementation are underway, with the biobank expected to become operational in 2027. Once established, it will support research collaborations across Canada and internationally, including studies into early detection, personalized treatments and ways to improve outcomes for people living with multiple myeloma.

stories.title: Old South church helps ‘Fill the Van’ for London Food Bank
stories.summary: For more than 20 years London Food Bank (LFB) co-executive directors Glen Pearson and Jane Roy have been members of Wesley-Knox United Church (Wkuc) in Old South.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
For more than 20 years London Food Bank (LFB) co-executive directors Glen Pearson and Jane Roy have been members of Wesley-Knox United Church (Wkuc) in Old South.

That means the congregation knows the dire straits Londoners are facing in 2026.

Wkuc held a rapid response food drive Sunday as they filled a van to help the LFB.

“They really pulled in this week for the food drive and so we really appreciate it.”

Organized by EJ Lamb, the chair of leadership at Wkuc, the drive pulled sponsors, businesses, church members and others to help.

“About a week and a half before the Thanksgiving program that the London Food Bank was doing, they were down 25 per cent compared to last year’s donations,” said Lamb.

“We decided to do the ‘Fill the Van’ event and it has been a really cool event for the community. The church is obviously involved, but we have renters as the Shout Sisters Choir. The Spiritualist Church also runs their business here as well, so they’ve helped contribute. We had a Halloween Bingo last night and they brought food and neighbours are bringing stuff in, and some of the local businesses were also involved.”

Throughout the afternoon people were consistently bringing bags of food and non-perishable items. Pearson believes most of the donated items will go to local agencies.

“One thing you know is all this food will be gone within 48 hours,” said Pearson.

“The food comes in the Food Bank, and it’s just gone. Sixty per cent of the food that came in during the (Thanksgiving) food drive goes out to other agencies, so it doesn’t even get to the Food Bank. It goes straight to them.”

Pearson says every week agencies are coming to the LFB asking for help as cutbacks are happening.

While they try to manage that, Wkuc is just trying to do anything they can to help.

“It’s very much a community event and the community is very passionate about it,” said Lamb.

“We all know we can help others, and this is a wonderful way to do it.”

stories.title: 'He's earned it': Conservatives want Doerkson as premier amid constitutional question
stories.summary: Vancouver - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson's B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do the same to change their constitution to allow an interim leader to become permanent.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson’s B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do the same to change their constitution to allow an interim leader to become permanent.

The party’s constitution prohibits an interim leader from seeking leadership in subsequent ballot, and change would require the support of two-thirds of the party’s members.

The party’s board said after the election was called that if Doerkson became the premier, he would remain leader and that it would pursue appropriate means “to give effect to this intention.”

Doerkson moved quickly on Sunday to disabuse people of the idea that he not be the party’s leader and become premier because of the constitutional clause.

“I am leader and that’s an administrative detail that there’ll be more information on that imminently,” he told reporters.

“But I will remain as leader of the party and I’m thrilled to be the premier-elect of British Columbia right now.”

He said his party is “united” and the election results “decisive.”

Conservatives celebrated the win Saturday, praising the premier-designate for uniting the party after a tumultuous few months under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who quit days before the election was called.

Caroline Elliott lost to Findlay for the leadership race by a few percentage points but she won the riding of West Vancouver-Capilano on Saturday.

She said that Doerkson was the “right person” to lead the party to victory as “things were splintering.”

“He’s earned it. He’s earned the trust of British Columbians. He has earned more votes in this general election than we could ever dream of in a leadership race, and so, for me, that’s mandate enough and I’ll support him for as long as he wants to stay on,” she said Saturday.

Findlay congratulated Doerkson in a post to social media on Saturday, calling the election a “historic victory.”

“I am hopeful that under his leadership British Columbians will see the changes to how our province is governed that I, and so many others, have long advocated for,” she said.

Doerkson became the party’s interim leader just days before the snap election was called Sept. 22 by outgoing New Democrat premier David Eby, and the victory ends nearly a decade of NDP government in the province.

But how the party’s board would ensure Doerkson will lead Conservatives remains unclear.

“A premier chosen by British Columbians deserves the certainty of leading his party. This amendment will provide it,” the board’s statement said in a social media post on Sept. 23.

Doerkson also has the support of former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell, who called him a “decent, honest, straightforward guy.”

“He gets people to understand how good they are and where we can be. We can be a province of possibility and promise again, and I think that’s what we’re going to get to,” Campbell said while attending the Conservative election-night celebration.

Hamish Telford, an associate professor in political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said it’s an interesting situation because a large portion of the party’s base wanted to make sure there was no taint of the B.C. Liberals, as was made clear in the leadership results and Findlay’s win.

“And now they want to represent themselves as a reincarnation of the B.C. Liberals. How is the base going to react to this new direction of the party? This is now a mainstream business-oriented party, that’s not the party they wanted,” he said.

Doerkson was elected in 2020 as a B.C. Liberal, which became B.C. United, but he jumped to the Conservatives before the 2024 provincial election to win again in Cariboo-Chilcotin.

As recently as the 2020 election, the party received less than two per cent of the vote, but the collapse of BC United paved the way for its rise to official Opposition status and now government.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

- With files from Brenna Owen and Wolfgang Depner

stories.title: Funeral for soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire is held in Edmonton
stories.summary: Sgt. Morgan Wong remembered as dedicated brother, friend
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Family, friends and Armed Forces members filled the pews of an Edmonton funeral home on Sunday as one of the soldiers killed in the devastating Canadian Forces Base Wainwright fire was laid to rest.

All rose as Sgt. Morgan Wong’s casket was carried in by pallbearers, draped in a Canadian flag that was then carefully folded and presented to one of Wong’s loved ones.

In a eulogy, Wong’s sister Megan remembered her brother as a loyal friend and problem-solver who dedicated himself to serving his community and country.

“Long before he was the fearless soldier many of you came to know, he was one of the bravest and funniest people I have ever met,” she said.

The 26-year-old reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, was one of four killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright. Thirty-nine more were injured.

Buddhist practitioners sang and prayed for Wong, whose photo sat on an altar alongside bowls of white rice and plates of oranges and apples.

Those gathered at the funeral heard how the soldier joined the Armed Forces at 17, advanced through the military ranks and volunteered in 2024 to be deployed to Latvia.

There, he would ultimately meet his wife.

“They were married last December,” Wong’s sister said. “He was so excited to (build) an incredible life and family with her.”

After Wong returned from Latvia, he trained and mentored new recruits and was preparing for a second deployment abroad when he was killed in the fire at Wainwright.

Lt.-Col. Bryn Wright, the commanding officer of Wong’s regiment, said Wong quit a civilian job earlier this year to be an instructor for the Armed Forces.

“Dedicated to service, reliable, willing to put the regiment ahead of himself. That was Morgan Wong,” he said.

Wright said the soldier’s cap badge and regimental coin, sometimes called a challenge coin, will be returned to his family.

“Soldiers often challenge one another by producing their coin, and if the other soldier doesn’t have theirs, they lose. If they do, they win. Morgan carried his coin with him right to the end. In classic fashion, it was still in his pocket,” Wright said.

Megan said she was proud to be Wong’s big sister and that she hopes his life serves as a reminder “to use the time we have to achieve a life we would be proud of.”

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said after the service that Wong had an impact on the city.

“(We) heard from so many of the people who had stories to share today that it’s not just his military service, it was his service to family, to loved ones, to friends, to community, that this is somebody who, no matter who you are, he was there to support you,” Knack said in an interview outside the funeral home, located in the city’s north end.

“It’s impossible to replace someone like that, who’s given so much. And yet I hope that we all take this opportunity as Edmontonians and as Canadians to live up to that legacy.”

While the exact cause of the fire at CFB Wainwright is unclear, Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, head of the military police, said it was sparked during a routine training event at an anti-grenade launcher range on the grounds.

The fire was considered sufficiently under control that training exercises were allowed to continue, before high winds caused it to spread, said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division.

Military officials wouldn’t say why training continued during the fire. Hanrahan said it’s part of the military police investigation.

The City of Prince Albert said a vigil would be held Sunday afternoon in Memorial Square for Pte. Shaun Farrell, another soldier who died in the tragedy at Wainwright.

Police in the northern Saskatchewan city posted a video Saturday showing a procession of police and other emergency vehicles accompanying a hearse into the city, passing underneath a Maple Leaf flag that was hanging from the extended ladder of a fire truck.

“Today, Prince Albert showed up with love, compassion, and respect as we welcomed Private Shaun Farrell home,” a message with the post said.

“Behind every uniform is a person, a family, and a story. And today, we were reminded that when one of our own comes home, they do not come home alone.”

stories.title: New Canadian procedure could revolutionize AFib treatment
stories.summary: Atrial fibrillation is the most common type of irregular heart rhythm in the world, but a new approach could change the game for patients.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A new Canadian approach to treating a common heart rhythm condition could change the game for patients who deal with atrial fibrillation or AFib.

AFib is considered the most common arrhythmia and occurs in the upper chambers of the heart.

Affecting one to two per cent of the general population, the irregular heartbeat can cause symptoms such as shortness of breath and fatigue, but can lead to severe consequences such as stroke or heart failure.

Fatigue caused Jon Davies of Edmonton to suspect something was wrong.

“I used to go mountain hiking and played a lot of squash and then that sort of quickly went away as I got into my early 50s,” he told Global News in an interview. “I just figured it was old age and having a desk job and not enough exercise maybe.”

His wife, Nora, said he was often tired and would sleep a lot.

He was eventually diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, but when speaking about treatment options he was left in shock.

“They told me that my heart had enlarged so much that it wouldn’t make sense for them to treat it surgically, so that’s when they said you’re going to stay on blood thinners,” Davies said.

Until this year, he said he’s had to accept the “status quo,” adding he got a second opinion with the same result.

People with AFib often receive treatment either through medication or with what’s known as “catheter ablation.”

“Patients are usually sedated or put to sleep entirely and we put little tubes in the groins and we pass wires into the heart, cross over to the left side of the heart and what we try and do is kill the tissue around the pulmonary veins,” said Dr. Paul Angaran, cardiac arrhythmia director at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto.

The process involves creating tiny scars in an area of the heart, according to the Mayo Clinic. During AFib, faulty signals can tell the heart to beat irregularly. The scars prevent those faulty signals from reaching their target.

“Typically we burn, so we use energy sources that overheat the tissue and sometimes we can use energy sources that freeze the tissue,” said Dr. Gianluigi Bisleri, the director of minimally invasive and robotic cardiac surgery at St. Michael’s Hospital. “But either way, we create these scars that become permanent and stop the irregular heart rate.”

But Angaran said not everyone with AFib will see such a treatment be effective.

Angaran joined with Bisleri to develop a new approach for helping people with AFib.

The result is a two-part robotic technique using ablations from outside the heart and then going inside using a catheter technique.

“It allows us to not only use the robotic technologies which give us more dexterity, more ability to reach and see the heart, but also to treat broader areas of the heart with the ablation,” Bisleri said.

Using both minimally invasive robotic surgery and catheter technology is a Canadian first, Bisleri said.

Patients interested in the procedure must be referred to Bisleri and Angaran, but the former told Global News while a referral is simple there isn’t enough awareness of their approach.

Patients need to wait a few weeks or months between each procedure, with Angaran noting doctors want patients’ scars on the outside to have healed before they proceed with the internal procedure.

One of their first patients was Davies, who learned about the procedure by searching online.

Davies had the first part of the procedure, the robotic technique, in September and is expected to return to Toronto in the coming weeks for the catheter ablation.

“It’s nice to be able to potentially, you know, take that diagnosis and direct it in a much more human, in a way that, you know, appreciate much more than the alternative,” he said.

Angaran told Global News that in patients with long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation, the long-term success rate through this approach could hit as high as 70 to 80 per cent.

content_blocks.text: AFib is considered the most common arrhythmia and occurs in the upper chambers of the heart.
content_blocks.html: AFib is considered the most common arrhythmia and occurs in the upper chambers of the heart.

content_blocks.text: Affecting one to two per cent of the general population, the irregular heartbeat can cause symptoms such as shortness of breath and fatigue, but can lead to severe consequences such as stroke or heart failure.
Fatigue caused Jon Davies of Edmonton to suspect something was wrong.

“I used to go mountain hiking and played a lot of squash and then that sort of quickly went away as I got into my early 50s,” he told Global News in an interview. “I just figured it was old age and having a desk job and not enough exercise maybe.”
His wife, Nora, said he was often tired and would sleep a lot.
He was eventually diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, but when speaking about treatment options he was left in shock.
“They told me that my heart had enlarged so much that it wouldn’t make sense for them to treat it surgically, so that’s when they said you’re going to stay on blood thinners,” Davies said.

Until this year, he said he’s had to accept the “status quo,” adding he got a second opinion with the same result.
People with AFib often receive treatment either through medication or with what’s known as “catheter ablation.”

“Patients are usually sedated or put to sleep entirely and we put little tubes in the groins and we pass wires into the heart, cross over to the left side of the heart and what we try and do is kill the tissue around the pulmonary veins,” said Dr. Paul Angaran, cardiac arrhythmia director at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto.

The process involves creating tiny scars in an area of the heart, according to the Mayo Clinic. During AFib, faulty signals can tell the heart to beat irregularly. The scars prevent those faulty signals from reaching their target.

“Typically we burn, so we use energy sources that overheat the tissue and sometimes we can use energy sources that freeze the tissue,” said Dr. Gianluigi Bisleri, the director of minimally invasive and robotic cardiac surgery at St. Michael’s Hospital. “But either way, we create these scars that become permanent and stop the irregular heart rate.”
But Angaran said not everyone with AFib will see such a treatment be effective.
Angaran joined with Bisleri to develop a new approach for helping people with AFib.
The result is a two-part robotic technique using ablations from outside the heart and then going inside using a catheter technique.

“It allows us to not only use the robotic technologies which give us more dexterity, more ability to reach and see the heart, but also to treat broader areas of the heart with the ablation,” Bisleri said.
Using both minimally invasive robotic surgery and catheter technology is a Canadian first, Bisleri said.
Patients interested in the procedure must be referred to Bisleri and Angaran, but the former told Global News while a referral is simple there isn’t enough awareness of their approach.
Patients need to wait a few weeks or months between each procedure, with Angaran noting doctors want patients’ scars on the outside to have healed before they proceed with the internal procedure.
One of their first patients was Davies, who learned about the procedure by searching online.
Davies had the first part of the procedure, the robotic technique, in September and is expected to return to Toronto in the coming weeks for the catheter ablation.
“It’s nice to be able to potentially, you know, take that diagnosis and direct it in a much more human, in a way that, you know, appreciate much more than the alternative,” he said.
Angaran told Global News that in patients with long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation, the long-term success rate through this approach could hit as high as 70 to 80 per cent.

stories.title: Drone warfare is evolving faster than armies can adapt, experts warn
stories.summary: Riga - It takes an average of just six weeks for opposing forces to develop a countermeasure to new technology deployed on the battlefield in Ukraine.
stories.author: Stéphane Blais The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Riga - It takes an average of just six weeks for opposing forces to develop a countermeasure to new technology deployed on the battlefield in Ukraine.

That rapid pace of innovation, driven by drones and robotics, is forcing Nato and its member countries to rethink how they acquire military equipment, while raising questions about whether international law can keep up with modern warfare.

The Canadian Press witnessed this technological race firsthand in Latvia, where Canada leads a Nato multinational brigade.

On Aug. 13, in a field near Selija in southwestern Latvia, the country’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, and Defence Minister Raivis Melnis gathered with military officials and representatives from 27 Nato countries, including Canada.

Under cloudy skies, a drone sped overhead before another aircraft suddenly appeared behind it. The second drone, an NS3 interceptor capable of reaching speeds of 350 kilometres per hour, placed an explosive charge on the target drone, destroying it.

The dignitaries applauded. For manufacturer DK Unity, the demonstration was a success.

The company was among dozens of drone manufacturers participating in Baltic Trust, an exercise attended by 375 industry representatives hoping to persuade Nato military officials to purchase their technology.

The exercise took place as Latvia faced repeated drone incursions suspected of originating from Russia and Belarus.

Aleksandrs Stupans, DK Unity’s business development manager, said the company relies on constant feedback from Ukrainian soldiers to improve its products.

“We have all this technology developed with weekly reference from the battlefield because we have our partner company in Kyiv, in Ukraine, and they are working with more than 100 different battle units,” he said.

Some of the company’s drones are already being deployed in Ukraine.

The six-week turnaround was documented in a recent analysis by a French parliamentary committee on foreign affairs and defence.

Janis Kazocins, an expert at the Riga Centre for Geopolitical Studies and former national security adviser to Latvia’s president, said armies that adapt quickly gain an advantage.

The constant need to develop new countermeasures requires close collaboration between soldiers, scientists and private companies.

He recalled how Ukrainian forces developed an effective system to detect Russian drones by sound and shoot them down using heavy machine guns.

“And then the Russians simply started flying them through at 400 metres higher, and the bullets didn’t reach that far,” he said.

The problem, he explained, is that while the hardware is relatively simple, software and communications systems are evolving so quickly that what works today May no longer work in six or eight weeks.

He warned Nato countries against assuming they could simply purchase large quantities of Ukraine’s most effective drones and store them in preparation for a potential Russian attack.

“The most dangerous thing to do is to imagine that we now know how drones or robotics work,” he said.

“We need to buy a service, something which is developing all the time, to which we need to contribute our technology as well.”

At the Ādaži military base in Latvia, Canadian Col. David Brassard, commander of Nato’s multinational brigade, said his unit is modernizing its procurement procedures to become more agile and respond to rapidly evolving technology.

He said innovation no longer comes exclusively from factories but increasingly from soldiers on the front lines.

Ukrainian troops, for example, use computer programming and 3D printers to modify drones directly on the battlefield, adapting them to emerging threats.

Brassard acknowledged that Nato forces in Latvia have not yet reached the same level of adaptability as Ukrainian troops but expressed confidence they would get there.

Kazocins prefers the term “robots” to “drones,” noting that unmanned vehicles increasingly operate on land and at sea, not just in the air.

Ukrainian forces, for example, are deploying autonomous maritime platforms, including the seven-metre-long Magura MV1, which reportedly can operate for seven days at sea and carry a payload of 2,200 kilograms.

“The Ukrainians are now using seaborne autonomous platforms, to bring in drones which fly off from these platforms and attack in Black Sea in the Crimean and the Russian coast,” Kazocins said.

He compared the technological transformation to the shift from cavalry and horse-drawn transport to mechanized vehicles and tanks between the two world wars.

Artificial intelligence is also enabling the development of drone swarms, which the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research describes as systems in which multiple robots coordinate their actions to accomplish a common objective.

Kazocins said such tactics are already being used in Ukraine, where groups of drones carry out different missions, with some serving as decoys, others conducting surveillance and others carrying out attacks.

The operations rely on “very sophisticated software” and “very sophisticated communications technology,” he said.

On April 13, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his forces had captured an enemy position exclusively using unmanned ground vehicles and explosive drones, in what he described as a first in the war. He said the operation was carried out without Ukrainian casualties.

Zelensky also said Ukrainian unmanned ground vehicles had completed more than 22,000 frontline missions in three months, describing each mission as a life saved.

The growing use of autonomous weapons is raising concerns among international organizations.

In a joint appeal published Aug. 25, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres and International Committee of the Red Cross President Mirjana Spoljaric urged countries to establish rules ensuring technological advances do not outpace international humanitarian law.

They warned that the autonomous targeting of human beings by machines risks crossing a moral red line.

The warning came ahead of discussions in Geneva, where countries have been examining ways to regulate lethal autonomous weapons systems.

Over the past three years, the 65 countries participating in the Conference on Disarmament have examined ways to regulate lethal autonomous weapons systems.

A report on the issue is expected at the seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, scheduled for November.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

stories.title: The two young women who could put an unlikely face on B.C. Conservatives' new government
stories.summary: Re-elected MLAs Claire Rattée and Á'a:líya Warbus could very well find themselves ministers in Premier-elect Lorne Doerksen's cabinet.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
When B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerksen considers potential cabinet members in the days ahead, there’s a good chance he will look at two notably tattooed young women with unique lived experience who would put an unexpected face on the government’s conservative policies.

Claire Rattée, a 34-year-old tattoo shop owner and one-time Kitimat city councillor, is a former addict who believes the compassionate approach is to push addicts into treatment.

Á’a:líya Warbus, an Indigenous film-maker and artist in her early 40s, is a proud member of the Stó:lō Nation who is very skeptical of the ousted Ndp’s Undrip legislation that has created immense uncertainty in the province.

Here’s a brief snapshot of the two re-elected MLAs and how they are likely to figure into the new majority Conservative government elected in B.C. on Saturday night and poised to undo years of NDP-created issues throughout the province.

Born in Delta in 1991, Rattée has been open about struggling with addiction to drugs and living on the streets of Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside in her late teens.

She moved to Kitimat and began rebuilding her life in 2011, establishing her own tattoo studio, Arcane Arts Inc. — still operated by co-founder spouse Colton — before entering municipal politics in 2014 at 21 and going on to serve a four-year term.

Rattée pivoted to federal politics in 2019, but failed to win the Skeena—Bulkley Valley seat for the Conservative Party of Canada. She won the provincial Skeena riding in 2024 for former B.C. Conservative leader John Rustad, who quickly appointed her as the party’s shadow cabinet critic for mental health and addictions .

She was one of the MLAs pushed out of the party amid the brief turmoil created by Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s brief leadership, but rejoined after Doerksen took over.

While Saturday’s results are still unofficial, Rattée captured 51.5 per cent of the vote to secure another win over NDP challenger Sarah Zimmerman.

“They are the reason this work matters. And they will remain at the heart of everything I do.”

“This is an issue that is deeply personal to me,” she shared on X when Rustad appointed her critic. “As someone who has faced challenges with addiction, mental health, and homelessness, I understand how critical it is for those struggling to have ready access to the support and services they need to recover and rebuild their lives.”

Rattée has been vocal in her shadow cabinet role, accusing former NDP premier David Eby and his government of having being too focused on “reduction measures” without enough on “harm prevention”

“The narrative that it’s pushing, in my opinion, is almost one of if you’re an addict, you’re always going to be an addict, and so we just need to make sure you can do it in the safest way possible,” she told Northern Beat.

“It’s absolutely disgusting, in my opinion. You’re just feeding people free drugs and trying to keep them high and not giving them a way out, a path out of that life.”

Rattée often uses her own story as an example that the right kind of compassion can help addicts get clean and turn their lives around.

“There were times during my addiction when I was simply not capable of making decisions in my own best interest. I put myself in incredibly dangerous situations, and some of those decisions left me with scars I will carry for the rest of my life,” she said at an October campaign event.

“If my parents had had the ability to get their 17-year-old daughter into treatment when I couldn’t recognize how much danger I was in, they would have taken it in a heartbeat. And I believe that it could have worked.”

Born and raised in Stó:lō Territory to former B.C. Lt.-Gov. Steven Lewis Point and his wife, Gwendolyn, Warbus is a married mother of three children who previously held multiple positions within the Stó:lō Nation tribal council, including chair, and was the Chief Commissioner of the British Columbia Treaty Commission, all before the age of 40.

Like Rattée, she was first elected in 2024, unseating incumbent Kelli Paddon by more than 2,000 ballots, and was soon appointed the Conservatives’ House Leader and caucus chair. She held that position until becoming the seventh-straight MLA to leave the party under Findlay’s rule in September.

At the time, she told Business in Vancouver that the party was more concerned with its internal turmoil than the real issues facing British Columbians — housing affordability, cost-of-living and seniors care.

“We’re devoid of all of that when we’re focused on the drama, the inner workings and the culture wars of pulling people and polarizing them more and more and more,” she said.

“You can only push people to divide so far, and so long, before there’s an exhaustion. People are just craving and looking for a bit of stability and normality. And I have to say that is the complete opposite of what I felt, and what I’ve seen was happening inside of the caucus, inside of the party, and in the direction we were going.”

Warbus followed a handful of defectors in forming the new CentreBC party under MLA Peter Milobar’s leadership, but eventually returned to the reunited Conservatives under Doerksen.

She defeated Paddon again in this election, with just over 60 per cent of the vote, pending final confirmation.

Outside of politics, she is a filmmaker, Indigenous film professor, artist, singer, and cultural communications professional.

Warbus has offered a nuanced position on the province’s Dripa, legislation enacted in 2019 by the former NDP government that attempted to respect Indigenous rights but created uncertainties around property ownership that critics say has chilled development in the province.

It was adopted from the United Nations’ own Dripa, making B.C. the first and only province to do so.

When Rustad and the Conservatives called for it to be repealed last year after a court ruling involving the province’s mineral claim system, she said the law had been implemented in the wrong order.

“Dripa was a layer added on, and it really put the cart before the horse in terms of dealing with the many distinct nations that we have,” Warbus told Global News last December, stressing that the party’s position is not to undermine Indigenous people’s rights.

“Indigenous rights are human rights,” she said.

Her criticism also relates to concerns about legal uncertainties, property rights and economic development, maintaining the province needs more clarity for all communities, Indigenous and otherwise.

Warbus believes in reconciliation, but told Fraser Valley Today during the campaign that the debate needs a range of “authentic” Indigenous voices, including those “willing to ask difficult questions.”

“I also believe any legislation that addresses Title must be practical, transparent, and capable of bringing Indigenous and non-Indigenous British Columbians forward together,” she said. “Division will only serve to distinguish the will and compassion we need to do the work.”

stories.title: More than 1,000 rally in London for publicly funded education
stories.summary: More than 1,000 people gathered at Victoria Park in downtown London on Saturday to rally in support of publicly funded education.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda, Brent Lale
stories.content:
More than 1,000 people gathered at Victoria Park in downtown London on Saturday to rally in support of publicly funded education.

The rally was part of a province-wide series of events called “Together for Publicly Funded Education,” bringing together teachers, education workers, families and community members to call for increased investment in Ontario’s education system.

Similar rallies were held in Toronto, Ottawa, Sudbury and Thunder Bay.

Organizers say the demonstrations come amid concerns about declining per-student funding, staff recruitment and retention, growing class sizes, school safety and access to special education and mental health supports.

The education unions behind the rallies point to a $6.5-billion funding gap and say schools need more resources to meet students’ needs.

“Ontario’s students deserve schools that are fully funded, fully staffed, and equipped to meet their needs,” said Martha Hradowy, president of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation.

The unions also raised concerns about provincial control over school boards and the potential effects of the current round of contract negotiations on students and families.

The rally was organized by leaders from Ontario’s major education unions, including the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association, the Association des enseignantes et des enseignants franco-ontariens, the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario and Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions.

The organizations are calling on the provincial government to invest in classrooms, hire more education workers and provide additional supports for students.

stories.title: Woman dies a day after release from New Brunswick correctional centre
stories.summary: Woman released from remand custody suffered a medical emergency and died a day later, officials say
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The New Brunswick Department of Justice and Public Safety says a woman who was released from remand custody Friday suffered a medical emergency and died a day later.

The department says the emergency happened at the New Brunswick Women’s Correctional Centre in Miramichi on Friday while the woman was waiting for transportation home.

The woman, who was in her 40s, was set to be released following a virtual court appearance.

Staff at the correctional centre called an ambulance and the woman was taken to hospital, where she died Saturday morning.

The department says it is not releasing her name at the request of her family.

It says Coroner Services has been notified and will investigate the death.

stories.title: High-earning couple buy $2-million home in pricey Vancouver after years of holding out
stories.summary: Lifelong renters switch to owning in their late 40s after deciding it was time to stop moving their kids
stories.author: Zahra Khozema
stories.content:
After learning their landlord was selling the house they’d rented for five years, Amina, 48, and Mike, 49, decided they didn’t want to put their two teenagers through another move. It was time to buy.

In May they purchased their first home: a four-bedroom, three-bathroom detached house in East Vancouver for just over $2-million. They put down just over 50 per cent, leaving them with a $1-million mortgage.

It was a decision more than 20 years in the making, although for much of that time, the couple weren’t convinced buying was the right move.

For more than two decades, Amina and Mike watched Vancouver home prices climb higher and higher and wondered whether they had missed their chance to become homeowners. So instead of stretching their finances to buy, they kept renting, investing their savings and enjoying the flexibility that came with not having a mortgage.

The couple, who’ve been married since 2004, worried about getting caught up in bidding wars and overpaying for a property.

“We felt like we had missed the boat,” said Amina.

Their most recent rental, a detached house in East Vancouver, cost them $3,800 a month, well below what they believed it would cost to own a comparable property in the same neighbourhood. Before that, their monthly payments were around $1,800, then $2,400 and then eventually $3,000.

Amina is a lawyer and earns $230,000 annually. She’s held her current job for 17 years. Mike, an engineer, makes $130,000 and has been in his position for 13 years. Both work in the public sector and have workplace pensions.

“We have enjoyed our lives, but we both grew up in immigrant families that had to work super hard,” Amina said.

Both were also financially savvy. By the time they were ready to buy, they’d accumulated enough to put more than a million toward their first home.

For their down payment, they withdrew close to $68,000 from their combined first home savings accounts (FHSAs) and $120,000 through the Home Buyers’ Plan, which allows eligible buyers to withdraw funds from their RRSPs.

The couple also received $250,000 from their families, including $225,000 from Amina’s mother after she sold a property and $25,000 from Mike’s mother. Mike said they had enough investments to cover the down payment without the family assistance, but doing so would have meant dipping further into their savings.

The remainder came from their accumulated cash and investments, including guaranteed investment certificates (GICs). Even after putting down such a large sum, they said they didn’t have to touch their TFSAs or exhaust their retirement savings.

They’d already moved four times before this in 12 years, largely because of property sales or landlords deciding to move back in. With their children getting older, the thought of starting over somewhere else was becoming harder to accept.

Their son, who is not yet 15, has already lived in five homes, Amina said.

When their landlord accepted an offer in February, the couple got serious about house hunting. Within a week, they’d hired a realtor, toured homes and submitted an offer.

Their new home was initially above their preferred budget of $1.7-million, but it had been extensively renovated in 2019 and was close to their son’s high school.

It also includes a ground-floor rental suite with an existing tenant – a perk that made stretching their budget justifiable. The suite generates just over $1,500 a month, and down the road, it could also house their parents or children.

The couple considered buying a cheaper home in the suburbs, but both work in Vancouver and wanted to avoid longer commutes, while their teens were reluctant to leave their neighbourhood. Moving farther out would also likely have meant buying a second car.

With a $1-million mortgage at a three-year fixed rate of 3.84 per cent, they pay $2,333 biweekly. Their mortgage has a 30-year amortization period, although they hope to pay it off sooner through additional lump-sum payments.

The prospect of having debt well into their 70s isn’t ideal, but both qualify for full workplace pensions at 60, which gives them some confidence they can manage the payment, even after they stop working.

After decades of renting, the family is finally getting used to the small freedoms of home ownership. “I can put in (a) hole in the wall versus Command Strips,” said Mike.

The bigger reward is knowing their children won’t have to move again because a landlord decided to sell.

“You can’t put a number on that,” said Amina.

Purchase price: $2,078,000

Down payment: About $1,078,000 (51 per cent)

Legal fees: $1,800

Moving costs: $3,000

Property transfer tax: $40,000

Monthly ongoing costs

Mortgage: $2,333 biweekly

Home insurance: Roughly $290 a month

Repairs: None

Property taxes and utilities: $3,200 for the remainder of 2026

Advice: “Don’t feel pressure to buy before you’re financially ready.”

stories.title: Sunny Sunday for London as mild weather continues into the week
stories.summary: Londoners can expect a sunny Sunday, with temperatures reaching a high of 19 C.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Londoners can expect a sunny Sunday, with temperatures reaching a high of 19 C, according to Environment Canada.

Skies are expected to become partly cloudy overnight, with a low of 7 C. Fog patches May develop overnight.

Monday will bring a mix of sun and cloud, with a high of 16 C. Temperatures will dip to a low of 1 C overnight.

Sunny skies are in the forecast for Tuesday, with a high of 15 C, before cloudy conditions return Wednesday. Temperatures are expected to reach 19 C.

Thursday will bring a mix of sun and cloud, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 19 C. Friday is expected to remain mild, with a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 18 C.

stories.title: Sunday Sports Briefs: Falcons win Ocaa Gold, Western vs Laurier in OUA Playoffs, Knights lose in Owen Sound, Cowgirls earn Ofsaa berth
stories.summary: With an 8-4 win over the Lambton Lions Saturday at Norm Aldridge Field in London, Ont. the Falcons won their second straight Ontario Colleges Athletics Association (Ocaa) title completing a two-game sweep of the Lambton Lions.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
With an 8-4 win over the Lambton Lions Saturday at Norm Aldridge Field in London, Ont. the Falcons won their second straight Ontario Colleges Athletics Association (Ocaa) title completing a two-game sweep of the Lambton Lions.

Neil McComb went the distance on the mound for the champions in the final game.

The Falcons finished the year with a 21-1 record combining the regular season with a pair of two-game sweeps in the playoffs.

Pitcher/third baseman Holden Heipel was named Ocaa Championship MVP.

“This is so exciting man,” said Heipel.

Mustangs ready for rematch with rival golden hawks

Minutes after losing their final regular season game to the Laurier Golden Hawks, the Western Mustangs realized they will face their rival again next Saturday on the exact same field in the opening round of the OUA playoffs.

Laurier (4-4) came to Alumni Field in London, Ont. and pummelled the Mustangs (6-2) 55-39 to win their fourth straight game against Western dating back to when (Mustangs head coach) Michael Faulds was the head coach of the Hawks.

“I said it all week to our guys, if you look at a lot of their losses, they were very close games,” said Faulds.

McIntosh had 200 yards receiving and a touchdown as Western had 614 yards of total offence but it still wasn’t enough.

“I think today was a great wake up call,” said McIntosh.

Knights lose in owen sound for first time since 2023

The London Knights are not used to walking out of the Harry Lumley Bayshore Arena without two points.

The Owen Sound Attack broke a 1-1 tie in the third period with four unanswered goals beating the Knights 5-1 Saturday.

Ranked #2 in the Canadian Hockey League coming into the week, the Knights lost two of their three games to suffer just their second and third regulation losses of the year.

Carson Harmer scored the lone goal for London who went 0-4 on the power play, while surrendering two goals with the Attack man advantage.

After 12 games, the Knights remain one point behind the Guelph Storm for top spot in the Midwest Division.

Medway cowgirls earn ofsaa berth with tvra field hockey title

The Medway Cowgirls are headed back to Ofsaa after a dominant season on the turf in Tvra Girls Field Hockey.

The Cowgirls went a combined 11-0 after a perfect regular season and a 4-0 semifinal win over Parkside Collegiate and a 2-1 win over Saunders S.S. in the Tvra final Thursday.

The defending Ofsaa champions coached by Dana Kajan will have a stiff test in the Wossaa game Wednesday at CityWide Field in London, Ont.

They will face the South Huron Panthers who finished 12-0 in the Huron Perth Athletic Association.

stories.title: Clues to higher incidence of dementia in women May lie in menopause
stories.summary: Women are disproportionately prone to Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers are studying the connection with midlife changes
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
It’s a scientific mystery that puzzles researchers: Why are more Canadian women than men diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias?

That population demographic made up an estimated 62 per cent of people living with dementia in Canada in 2020, according to the Alzheimer Society of Canada.

But new scientific research conducted by Canadian scientists is shedding light on how changes that unfold in menopause could affect the brain later in life. It could also set the stage to uncover why women are disproportionately affected by neurodegenerative disease.

Late last month, research led by scientists at Sunnybrook Research Institute was published in the journal Nature Medicine on how menopause-related biological changes involving the brain are detected in the blood and could be linked to cognitive decline later.

Separately, Natasha Rajah, a researcher at Toronto Metropolitan University, is leading Canada’s only brain-imaging study on how biological sex, menopause and dementia risk factors affect memory-related brain function in midlife.

The study, part of Tmu’s Brain Health Equity in Aging and Memory Lab , has produced papers on memory, brain aging and dementia prevention documenting findings of age-related decline in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women and a link to poor vascular health and memory in the postmenopausal period.

Dr. Rajah hopes, in the long-term, her research will offer insights on what is happening to women in menopause to help identify behaviours or interventions to support them.

Jennifer Rabin, a clinical neuropsychologist and scientist with the Hurvitz Brain Sciences Program at Sunnybrook Research Institute and the Temerty Faculty of Medicine at University of Toronto, said the fact women tend to live longer than men does not explain the disparity.

“All women who live long enough go through menopause, and not all women develop Alzheimer’s disease,” Prof. Rabin said.

“In fact, many more don’t develop Alzheimer’s disease than do. So it can’t just be menopause. But I do think that there is something about menopause that is happening that definitely puts some women on a different trajectory.”

Their research underscores broader questions, such as how menopause affects the brain and how it affects women’s risk for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders later on.

“We know that women are at increased risk for Alzheimer’s disease,” Prof. Rabin said. “We know that the pathology associated with Alzheimer’s disease actually starts developing in midlife.”

Prof. Rabin worked with a postdoctoral candidate that she is supervising, Madeline Wood Alexander, who was the lead author on the research.

Their findings suggest the menopause transition May offer key insights on how biological changes in midlife relate to women’s brain health and dementia risk later.

“We think it’s a really important window to study, to have our best chances of developing preventative strategies and optimizing brain aging for women,” she said.

The scientists used blood to test for hundreds of different molecules in 80 women aged 43 to 58 separated into groups according to their stage of menopause: pre-, peri- and postmenopausal.

The findings found differences in the blood of postmenopausal women, such as higher levels of inflammation, compared to pre- and perimenopausal women.

The researchers also tested their results against data from another study, the UK Biobank, which included 2,814 women age-matched between the pre-to-perimenopausal and postmenopausal periods, between ages of 45 and 60. They found the same menopause-related shifts in blood molecules were also seen in the larger group.

Tmu’s Prof. Rajah, a Canada Research Chair in Sex, Gender, and Diversity in Brain Health, Memory and Aging, said historically, clinical studies did not account for sex-based biological differences.

As a result, she said, little is known about how female sex and sex-specific life experiences influence Alzheimer’s disease risk and symptoms.

She said she began work in this area in 2017 because of her own curiosity about what is going on in midlife, prompting her and a collaborator to closely examine menopause.

Prof. Rajah hopes their research will help identify different risk factors for patients.

Additionally, she said, this could motivate individuals to take their health seriously in midlife through lifestyle changes such as increasing their physical activity, and encourage conversations with health care providers about possible interventions.

She also hopes more women from different backgrounds will participate in ongoing research.

“What we do as scientists is truly connected to what is in the best interest of the public and we need the support of the public to do this work.”

stories.title: Funeral service to be held for Sgt. Morgan Wong, CFB Wainwright fire victim
stories.summary: According to Sgt. Morgan Wong's family, the 26-year-old was training at CFB Wainwright to prepare to deploy on his second tour in Europe.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A funeral service for Sgt. Morgan Wong , one of the four Canadian Armed Forces members killed last week in the deadly CFB Wainwright fire will be held Sunday.

The service is set to start at 10 a.m. local time in Edmonton.

Wong has been described by his family as a man who was there for anyone who needed him, saying they were “extremely proud” of him and that he was proud to serve the CAF.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” they said. “He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family.”

The 26-year-old was born in Edmonton and graduated from the University of Alberta in 2022 with a Bachelor of Commerce degree. He also held certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.

His family said he began to serve as a medical first responder with St. John Ambulance in 2022.

In December 2017, Wong joined the CAF and served on Operation Reassurance in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025.

Last Saturday, he was participating in live-fire exercises as part of training in preparation for potential deployment overseas, including in Latvia and other regions.

According to Wong’s family, he was training in Wainwright to prepare to deploy on his second tour in Europe.

Global News will livestream the funeral service for Wong.

stories.title: Lorne Doerkson leads B.C. Conservatives to power with thumping two-thirds majority
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia has turned blue, electing a B.C. Conservative government with an overwhelming two-thirds majority.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press

Vancouver - British Columbia’s premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s long to-do list includes lowering taxes, while reviewing the provincial finances, working with Alberta and the federal government on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline and repealing Indigenous legislation.

Doerkson laid out his priorities at a news conference Sunday, just hours after his party was elected with about two-thirds of the province’s 93 seats in the legislature.

He said he has spoken to the lieutenant-governor and named Kim Henderson, a former deputy to the premier to previous Liberal governments, to lead his transition team.

“We are going to do this properly, and we are going to do it with obviously some urgency,” he said. “When this government is sworn in, it will be ready on Day 1, and it will hit the ground running.”

Doerkson did not rule out calling a fall legislative session, and if it were to return this year, his government would move to lower taxes.

“Our first priority for the legislature is raising the basic personal exemption to $32,000,” he said. “That is about $1,000 a year back in the pocket of nearly every working British Columbian.”

His government, he said, will also follow through on the election promise to not raise taxes or introduce new ones.

“When I make a promise to British Columbians, I will keep it, and that starts for sure right now.”

The incoming premier said his government will also launch an independent review of the provincial finances.

Current forecasts peg the provincial deficit of $14 billion and B.C. has had eight credit-rating downgrades in three years.

Provincial debt has become a significant challenge, Doerkson said.

“Our interest payment is choking our economy and choking British Columbia,” he said.

The trade conflict with the United States is the biggest economic threat facing the province, he said, and he repeated promises to supercharge the provincial economy through additional resource-projects.

“Among my first calls as premier, will be to the prime minister and to (Alberta) Premier Smith to get the Pacific Link (pipeline project) moving,” he said. “Our resources are the strongest hand that British Columbia hold and we will for sure play them.”

Hamish Telford, associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said Doerkson’s plan to “supercharge” the economy is outside of his control.

He said private companies — not Doerkson — are making the investment decisions.

“They are going to do that based on market demand, and the price that they can offer consumers in other parts of the world,” he said.

Doerkson said that he is still committed to the repeal of the Declaration on the Rights of the Indigenous Peoples Act.

Dripa is “a thick piece of legislation,” that his government wants to repeal as quickly as possible because it has not worked, he said.

“Frankly, it has caused more problems to date than I think potentially anything else,” he said, noting it could be repealed in the spring session.

But Telford said Doerkson’s economic agenda hinges in part on securing Indigenous support for those projects.

“And if he repeals Dripa, he is going to set his government off to a very bad start with First Nations across British Columbia, who are almost universally in favour of maintaining Dripa,” he said.

Doerkson promised a government of respect for all, while speaking directly to his party’s base in rural and northern B.C.

“I know what it means when the mill closes, when the (emergency-room) shuts at night and when there’s fire on the ridge,” he said. “Under this government, you will never be an afterthought.”

He promised that he would use his first 100 days in office to set up an expert commission to keep hospital emergency rooms open and cut down wait times.

Elections BC said Sunday that the Conservatives won 64 seats but results for four of them were extremely close.

In Burnaby South-Metrotown, 66 votes divide the winning New Democrat Paul Choi from the Conservative candidate and there were 58 rejected ballots.

Three ridings that went to the Conservatives; Kelowna Centre, Cowichan Valley and Ladysmith-Oceanside, were all within fewer than 150 votes.

Elections BC says that under the Elections Act, a recount is automatic if the preliminary results show a difference of 100 votes or fewer.

The Conservative’s resounding win even drew the attention of the White House, with U.S. President Donald Trump posting on his social media account that the Conservative Party has won in British Columbia for the first time in almost 100 years.

The post is accompanied by a composite of photos of Trump, Prime Minister Mark Carney, the B.C. legislature and a map of Canada with the province coloured in red.

Doerkson rejected any implications of being aligned with Trump.

“I’m an ally to British Columbia, and we should have taken the opportunity years ago to protect ourselves against these attacks,” he said.

A statement from the B.C. Conservatives released Sunday says Henderson will be chair of the transition team on a volunteer basis and will be taking an unpaid leave from the pipeline firm Trans Mountain Corp. where she took on the post of interim vice-president a year ago.

She spent more than a decade serving the previous Liberal governments of Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell as deputy minister, cabinet secretary and head of the B.C. public service.

Outgoing Premier David Eby announced his resignation as NDP leader, although he won his seat in Vancouver-Point Grey on Saturday.

Manitoba Premier Web Kinew didn’t mention Eby by name, but told reporters in Ottawa Sunday that the election results should be a lesson learned.

“There’s no partisanship in these comments,” Kinew said. “It’s all about reminding people that we have a serious obligation to take our democracy and our duties with the utmost of care.”

Doerkson said he has always started his work the moment after being elected.

“And for me, that isn’t going to change,” he said. “I intend to get to work right away. I intend work for British Columbia hard, because four years come quick.”

Eby’s decision to call a snap election two years early will go down as one of the most disastrous miscalculations in Canadian political history.

The NDP has been reduced to about 27 ridings and the Greens won two, with Leader Emily Lowan securing a seat on Vancouver Island.

Preliminary results show the popular vote went to the Conservatives with about 48 per cent of the vote, while the NDP won about 37 per cent and the Greens 11 per cent.

Doerkson emerged from obscurity when he was named interim leader of the Conservatives just two days before Eby’s fateful election call on Sept. 22.

Voter turnout figures show about 1.8 million cast ballots, representing about 48 per cent of registered voters.

A statement from the office of the clerk of the legislative assembly said Sunday that oath ceremonies for those elected won’t take place until the certified results of the general election are available, which is expected on Nov. 18.

“Arrangements will be made with the three caucuses for oath ceremonies to proceed after that date,” the statement said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.
