stories.title: These Canadian doctors are already wrestling with the dilemmas posed by advance requests for Maid
stories.summary: In Quebec, a person with a “serious and incurable illness leading to incapacity” can request Maid years or months in advance.
stories.author: Raisa Patel
stories.content:
Ottawa — Dr. Laurent Boisvert has fulfilled advance requests for assisted deaths a handful of times. Once, he chose not to follow through.

Dr. Claude Rivard has provided Maid to patients with advance requests on three occasions. He says sometimes he feels like a “trickster” when he helps end the life of a person who can’t consent to the procedure.

Dr. Mathieu Moreau has never drafted or completed an advance request. He isn’t sure if he will.

The Montreal-area physicians work in the only province in Canada where a person with a “serious and incurable illness leading to incapacity,” such as dementia, can request medical assistance in dying months or years before they become incapable of doing so.

All three physicians, who have performed Maid on consenting patients, believe that in the right circumstances and with appropriate safeguards, advance requests are simply the compassionate thing to do.

Access to care should be the focus.

But as Ottawa moves to decriminalize such requests — a plan the Carney Liberals announced earlier this month — jurisdictions across the country will have to look to Quebec as the rest of the country decides whether to follow the province’s lead.

“If they want to do it, they must come to Quebec first. They must question the Quebec ministry on what are the drawbacks and problems they have encountered to not reproduce them,” said Rivard, a family physician who now works in palliative care.

“And if the Quebec ministry tells them that there’s no problem with advance requests for Maid, then they are bullsh—-ing them.”

The province’s advance request law came into effect in the fall of 2024, and the Trudeau government chose not to challenge it. While provinces and territories oversee the administration of Maid, the federal government is responsible for legal considerations under the Criminal Code.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the Carney government will introduce legislation later this fall to allow physicians to draft and honour advance requests under “a set of circumstances” that have yet to be made public.

“We do expect this is going to start a conversation at a provincial level about how they May extend services across Canada, with the full knowledge that the doctors who provide the services will not be treated as criminals for doing so. This will be a conversation I expect that will play out in Canada over the next number of years,” Fraser said.

Since Quebec’s law came into force, 3,463 advance requests have been filed in the province.

Quebec’s Health Ministry told the Star that it was not possible to confirm how many people have actually received Maid through that pathway; those numbers and other findings tied to the practice will be released later this fall in a report from the province’s commission on end-of-life care.

Boisvert estimates that 30 to 40 advance requests have been fulfilled, while Moreau believes the numbers are closer to 20 to 30.

How the process works

A mentally competent patient with an incurable diagnosis initiates an advance request with a medical professional, and files it with the province’s health insurance board.

The patient details the clinical manifestations they must be exhibiting to trigger the procedure.

The most common manifestations, which must be recurring, include no longer recognizing loved ones; needing assistance with hygiene or mobility; becoming aggressive or dangerous to others; and experiencing physical pain that cannot be controlled.

The patient can then select one or two trusted third parties — typically family members — to oversee their case.

Once the patient has significantly declined, Boisvert says, phase two of the process begins.

The trusted parties ask the physician to evaluate the patient and decide whether it is appropriate to provide Maid. The physician and a second medical professional must assess the patient and determine that they are experiencing “enduring and unbearable physical or psychological suffering” that cannot be relieved.

For Boisvert, this is where the weaknesses lie in Quebec’s law.

He recalls the only time that he recommended against carrying out the procedure under an advance request.

“It was a very old woman … and she met some of the manifestations that were in the advance request,” said Boisvert, who is also the president of the Association québécoise pour le droit de mourir dans la dignité, a Quebec right-to-die group.

When he evaluated her, she seemed to be in good spirits and reported no pain, although she didn’t know where she was.

Boisvert told the woman’s trusted party that while she met some of the criteria she had outlined in her request, he felt the patient wasn’t suffering. The third party agreed with his assessment, and decided to re-evaluate the woman at a later point.

A Parliamentary report by MP Marcus Powlowski “is an extremely thoughtful contribution by

But what would Boisvert have done if the third party disagreed with his recommendation? What if two third parties disagreed with each other? And how was he to truly know if his patient was suffering if she was too incapacitated for rational conversation?

“That’s the big conundrum we have,” he told the Star. “Does meeting the clinical manifestations mean I’m suffering, or do I have to demonstrate suffering when I’m incapacitated? That’s the big problem that is not resolved in Quebec.”

Consent for sedation

Moreau, a palliative care doctor, says Canada should also look at the Netherlands, where advance requests have been legally recognized since 2002.

A recent analysis in a French-language Canadian palliative care journal found that between 2017 and 2024, deaths tied to advance requests made by people with neurocognitive disorders who had lost the capacity to consent ranged from only two to eight cases per year.

“I believe that the first numbers we will have will show that in Quebec, there’s more advance requests than in the Netherlands, and because of that, we should think, is this the direction that we want to take? Because the way the law in Quebec is drafted, (it) gives a lot of power to the assessors,” Moreau said.

The analysis found that Dutch physicians are grappling with issues similar to those of their Quebec counterparts: how to objectively evaluate suffering and dealing with family tensions and disagreements.

The researchers also cited a landmark Dutch case in which a physician was cleared of wrongdoing for euthanizing a woman with Alzheimer’s disease, who had indicated her desire for assisted death in a written directive. The doctor had secretly slipped a sedative into the 74-year-old’s coffee to calm her before the procedure, and she needed to be held down after rising from her bed during the final injection.

The case prompted the Netherlands to update its guidance to allow sedation to be provided without consent in severe dementia cases, if there are concerns a patient May become agitated or aggressive.

“Consent for sedation must be included in the advance request for Maid before it’s time, and a lot of the time it’s not there,” Rivard said.

The sedation issue is one of the reasons why Rivard, who initially chose not to provide Maid under advance requests, wound up performing the procedure.

He realized there wasn’t enough clarity when completing the documentation, including clear guidance on requesting sedation. As a doctor with decades of experience, he felt compelled to get involved.

Administrative burdens

Quebec’s Health Ministry says 282 advance request forms have been rejected for “administrative reasons,” and that 51 of those requests were not resubmitted.

“Families are experiencing a lot of frustration,” Rivard said.

Enabling death through a state-funded medical system implicates us all in that decision. And surely the biggest decision of all — literally life

Physicians also have questions about the administrative burdens expanding the practice would place on physicians, with Rivard noting the process is “very, very time consuming” and Moreau pointing out it can sometimes take hours and multiple visits to draft requests.

One year ago, the federal government released its findings from a nationwide public consultation on advance Maid requests.

Included in the feedback were fears that amid an aging population, growing rates of dementia, and an overburdened health care system struggling with current demands, too much strain would be placed on an already limited number of Maid providers.

Some respondents also wanted Ottawa to implement the same standards and processes across the country.

Moreau said his initial reaction to Fraser’s announcement — relief that Quebec physicians will no longer potentially face prosecution — was soon overtaken by concerns about the patchwork of rules that Canada May soon be confronted with.

“This process started, I think, six or seven years ago in Quebec. I’m not sure the provinces right now will have the time to come and put that process into place. It May differ a lot from province to province, and that heterogeneity could mean that people won’t have the same treatment depending on where they are. So from a justice perspective, I’m a bit concerned,” Moreau said.

Advance requests in other provinces

He foresees complications in provinces like Alberta, which banned advance requests for Maid earlier this year, meaning physicians might not be prosecuted for a federal offence but might be sanctioned by a provincial regulatory body.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said last week, however, that she has heard “there’s appetite” to reopen the conversation and that she plans to consult Albertans on the next steps.

The majority of the provinces and territories who responded to the Star’s requests for comment said they want to see the federal government’s bill before charting their next steps. The Ontario government did not respond to requests about what it plans to do.

The range of opinions that could emerge across the country is already playing out in Quebec.

When Rivard offers Maid to people who are not incapacitated, he says, they offer him their arms. But when they can’t consent, “emotionally, it’s not the same thing at all.”

Still, he thinks the practice can be humane. He recently lost his mother, who had dementia and suffered a bad fall.

“My mother didn’t want to end up like her mother,” said Rivard. “Her hip fracture was her way out from years of care … that she didn’t want.”

Boisvert thinks one solution to clarify the law is to focus on clinical manifestations only, rather than getting tangled up in secondary and subjective definitions of suffering.

“I think we need to address suffering because if we don’t address suffering, well, why am I a doctor doing my assessment? I will just become someone doing the administration of Maid,” Moreau said.

“Maid, especially in Quebec, is a form of care … and the goal of care is to relieve suffering. The means to relieve the suffering is through providing death.”

“My mother didn’t want to end up like her mother,” said Rivard. “Her hip fracture was her way out from years of care … that she didn’t want.”
Boisvert thinks one solution to clarify the law is to focus on clinical manifestations only, rather than getting tangled up in secondary and subjective definitions of suffering.

stories.title: 45 years, 100M board games and what the first inside story reveals about the global phenomenon of Trivial Pursuit
stories.summary: John Haney’s new book recounts the unlikely success of Trivial Pursuit. He answers some questions from the Star.
stories.author: Janet Hurley
stories.content:
Inside John Haney’s Caledon farmhouse, under a clock in his “man cave,” hangs a photograph of three siblings on a Spanish street, caught in a moment just before heading to the beach to write questions.

Loads and loads of questions.

It was 1980, and John, the eldest, his brother Chris and their sister Mary were turning the world around them into trivia for a board game idea that Chris and his friend Scott Abbott had sketched on a piece of paper in a Montreal kitchen the previous winter.

Chris and Mary are now gone. The questions, numbering in the thousands, remain.

Trivial Pursuit became a global phenomenon, selling 100 million copies in more than 26 countries and 17 languages. It inspired a memorable “Seinfeld” episode , and the cast of the “Big Chill” played it between takes. Frank Sinatra and Barbra Streisand sent thank-you notes on receiving copies and Princess Margaret reportedly tossed the game into the air after getting an answer wrong. It spawned more than 50 versions, from “Friends” to the Beatles, and proved a windfall for early investors who saw a $1,000 stake grow to $1 million.

That history is etched into Haney’s man cave, where collectible editions share space with photos of family and the game’s four creators: the Haney brothers, Abbott and Ed Werner.

“I’m surrounded by my past here,” says Haney. “It’s almost a shrine, which my wife tolerates.”

At 80, he is a new author and considering his legacy.

Protospiel North, a twice-yearly gathering, brings together designers and players eager to test games in progress.

“It means the world to me they now know the story behind the game and my part in it.”

At the heart of that story is Chris, who called John in 1979 with an idea for a game, setting the whole enterprise in motion. Chris died in 2010 , his ashes scattered on the sixth hole at The Devil’s Pulpit, a nearby golf course he and Abbott built with their Trivial Pursuit earnings.

“Every time I play, I say hello and often drop a bottle of Heineken on his gravestone,” says Haney. “I think I’m jinxed because I can never get it in the fairway where he is; I’m always in the woods.”

Lately, Haney has been thinking about tucking a copy of his new book into his golf cart.

“I should just show it to him, hold it up in the air. Maybe he’s out there. I hope he is.”

What follows is an edited conversation.

What do people constantly get wrong about Trivial Pursuit’s origin story?

Everyone thinks we were American. It drives me crazy. It was an all-Canadian effort, one conceived in Montreal over a game of Scrabble, with Chris and Scott coming up with the lightbulb moment.

How did you turn everyday observations into interesting game questions?

Out of necessity, needing to write 6,000 questions. We’d walk into a bar, which we did quite often, and I would start looking at the liquor labels. I could see a bat on a bottle of Bacardi. So that would be a question, “What mammal is pictured on a bottle of Bacardi?” Then I’d look up bats: Do bats have eyes? It just went from one thing to another. My mind warped into that kind of mindset. Still does.

In the book, you reveal your then sister-in-law ultimately named the game.

Chris came up with Trivia Pursuit. And Sarah was standing there and said, why don’t you put an L on that? It’ll sound much better. That was a second sort of light bulb moment.

Your first sale was two boxes on consignment at a tobacconist in Niagara-on-the-Lake in 1981. When did you know the game was going to be a success?

A store in St. Catharines called Raham’s bought about 24 games, and the guy said, you know, you guys are going to be big man. I said, “Give me a break, we’re just trying to break even.” We went from that to being mentioned by Johnny Carson at the 1984 Academy Awards when he said the winners would be a question in next year’s Trivial Pursuit. That was the ultimate moment we knew we had made it.

Trivial Pursuit is built on the premise that memory and recall is power; it’s how you win the game. At age 80, what does memory mean to you?

Memory is sounds, smells. A lot of times it relates to trivia questions: I can look at a bird and think of a question we wrote about a bird. It’s an odd brain I have now. Chris and I wrote upwards of 30,000 questions in the first five editions. That can blow out a lot of neurons, but it also creates memories stimulated by, sounds, movies, baseball scores.

Is it still fair to play the game with you?

Not really. We play at Christmas. (The kids) scramble to get me on their team, but I can’t get the new questions. I have no idea what’s going on in pop culture anymore. We were sort of experts in pop culture at one time, but now we’ve been passed like a freight train by AI, Google, and time and life.

Smartphones and AI have closed the knowledge gap the game was built on, and yet people are still packing pubs for trivia nights. Is Trivial Pursuit a relic or did it tap into a sense of human curiosity and play that technology can never replace?

I think we’re a relic, but we’re still relevant. Bar trivia is making a huge comeback — you see all kinds of organized events. In our day, none of it was organized: You’d walk into a bar and someone would start shooting sports questions across the table.

Are board games still relevant today? I’d like to think so. Trivial Pursuit has gone through various iterations including computer games, but the board game itself is still being sold, and I’d like to think families are still sitting around the table playing it.

We tapped into (something that was there). We didn’t coin the phrase, but we certainly took pop culture and put it in a box.

You write that when Hasbro bought the game in 2008, your fear was that you’d end up like Lizzie Magie, who invented the precursor to Monopoly but isn’t remembered for it. Was that fear warranted?

When we sold it for $80 million (U.S.), we had already sold upwards of 50 million games so we were doing quite well. We were glad to see our baby leave the nest. Hasbro has all the rights, owns all the parts, pieces, everything. We have zero input. But it’s nice to walk into the Best Buy here in Orangeville and see the latest version. There’s our little baby sitting on the shelf.

We’re not recognized in the street, never were. Young folks haven’t even heard of the game. We’ve transcended the need for our egos to be massaged.

(But) it makes me feel good that I wrote the book and maybe that will twig some interest.

Four of you created the game. Would the others have told a different story?

They have their own version, of course, but they haven’t written it; I have. We sort of live our own lives now: Scott’s up in North Bay; Ed’s down in the St. Catharines area. We don’t really see much of each other anymore, which is kind of sad. I wonder if Chris had lived whether we would have done it together. That would have been neat.

What do you think he would have thought of the book?

He was a very dark person; you couldn’t read him, even as a brother, but I’d like to think he would be thrilled: “Way to go, John, you’re the greatest older brother I’ve ever met. Well, the only one.” Hahaha.

Is there a question from the original edition you’re most proud of? And one you wish you could take back?

The one that always sticks in my mind, and it’s ridiculous, was: Was Humpty Dumpty pushed? The answer we put in was No. He was. Anyone who wants to know or care what the proper answer was can look in the book. We had 120 errors in the first edition. We corrected them in the second but it was inevitable with all the questions we wrote. I wouldn’t take any back.

I do want to tell you my best and latest trivia question: What American university did Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney represent in 1985, when in his only varsity appearance as a hockey goaltender, he stopped five shots in half a period against Colgate University, where Trivial Pursuit co-creator John Haney had starred in goal 15 years earlier?

paragraphs: Inside John Haney’s Caledon farmhouse, under a clock in his “man cave,” hangs a photograph of three siblings on a Spanish street, caught in a moment just before heading to the beach to write questions.
Loads and loads of questions.

It was 1980, and John, the eldest, his brother Chris and their sister Mary were turning the world around them into trivia for a board game idea that Chris and his friend Scott Abbott had sketched on a piece of paper in a Montreal kitchen the previous winter.
Chris and Mary are now gone. The questions, numbering in the thousands, remain.

Trivial Pursuit became a global phenomenon, selling 100 million copies in more than 26 countries and 17 languages. It inspired a memorable “Seinfeld” episode , and the cast of the “Big Chill” played it between takes. Frank Sinatra and Barbra Streisand sent thank-you notes on receiving copies and Princess Margaret reportedly tossed the game into the air after getting an answer wrong. It spawned more than 50 versions, from “Friends” to the Beatles, and proved a windfall for early investors who saw a $1,000 stake grow to $1 million.
That history is etched into Haney’s man cave, where collectible editions share space with photos of family and the game’s four creators: the Haney brothers, Abbott and Ed Werner.
“I’m surrounded by my past here,” says Haney. “It’s almost a shrine, which my wife tolerates.”
At 80, he is a new author and considering his legacy.
Protospiel North, a twice-yearly gathering, brings together designers and players eager to test games in progress.
“It means the world to me they now know the story behind the game and my part in it.”

At the heart of that story is Chris, who called John in 1979 with an idea for a game, setting the whole enterprise in motion. Chris died in 2010 , his ashes scattered on the sixth hole at The Devil’s Pulpit, a nearby golf course he and Abbott built with their Trivial Pursuit earnings.

“Every time I play, I say hello and often drop a bottle of Heineken on his gravestone,” says Haney. “I think I’m jinxed because I can never get it in the fairway where he is; I’m always in the woods.”
Lately, Haney has been thinking about tucking a copy of his new book into his golf cart.
“I should just show it to him, hold it up in the air. Maybe he’s out there. I hope he is.”
What follows is an edited conversation.

In the book, you reveal your then sister-in-law ultimately named the game.

stories.title: Canada once tried to pivot from the U.S. to Europe. Here’s why it didn’t last
stories.summary: It was more than half a century ago, but there are many modern echoes in the twists and turns of this earlier attempt at securing the Canadian economy.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
It wasn’t the threat of annexation that sparked Canada’s first pivot away from the United States and toward Europe.

It was abandon.

“It is time for us to recognize that we have very separate identities, that we have significant differences and that nobody’s interests are furthered when these realities are obscured.”

These were the words of then-U.S. president Richard Nixon, delivered to Canadian lawmakers in the House of Commons on April 14, 1972 .

America’s retreat on the world stage had been dubbed the “Nixon Doctrine.” But it was preceded by the “ Nixon shock ” — a global 10 per cent surcharge on U.S.-bound goods that was calculated to balance trade deficits.

Sound familiar?

It was more than half a century ago, but there are many modern echoes in the twists and turns of this earlier attempt at securing the Canadian economy.

In addition to the tariffs on Canadian goods , there was a hard-driving U.S. treasury secretary who was determined to end the special treatment for Ontario’s automobile industry. The Howard Lutnick of that time was John Connally, a former Texas governor who had been shot in 1963 while riding in the same limousine as John F. Kennedy, who was killed by an assassin’s bullet .

And then, just as now, there was the lure of Canada’s plentiful natural resources for potential new partners across the Atlantic Ocean.

As Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomes European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to Montreal this coming week for the Canada-EU summit, there are expectations of concrete measures to flesh out the offer of “associate” EU membership for Canada , or at least an alliance that deepens and enhances transatlantic ties.

But it won’t be the first time the Old World has shimmered like an oasis for a Canadian prime minister seeking alternatives to the United States.

Ottawa bureau chief Tonda MacCharles and Paris-based reporter Allan Woods took reader questions on “associate” EU membership, Canada’s trade war

In the fall of 1972, Pierre Trudeau’s Liberal government published an article examining what to do about the troubled Canada-U.S. relationship. It was entitled, “Options for the Future.”

There were three choices: suffer the status quo; submit to deeper economic and political integration; or set off on a new and uncertain path.

“The emphasis of the third option is on Canada — on decisions that have to be taken in this country by Canadians — rather than matters to be negotiated with the United States,” said Mitchell Sharp, Trudeau’s external affairs minister. “It means ensuring our continued freedom to develop in our own way through a judicious use of Canadian sovereignty.”

It’s a copy-and-paste version of the preamble to Carney’s every public utterance and press release — that, in a rapidly changing world, “Canada is focused on what we can control.”

The modern-day mantra in Ottawa is building up the economy at home and broadening partnerships abroad with the goal of doubling exports to non-U.S. countries by 2030 .

Back then, there was a different sort of vulnerability.

In the 1970s, large swaths of the Canadian economy, from mining to automobiles to manufacturing, were owned and operated by American investors and multinational corporations.

Unemployment was high and, in branch-plant Canada, there were fears the economic uncertainty south of the border could drive joblessness higher still.

The Trudeau government responded with a heavy dose of economic nationalism.

It created the Foreign Investment Review Agency to examine investments and acquisitions for their potential negative impacts on the Canadian economy and employment. Provincial governments took control of the potash mines in Saskatchewan and partially nationalized asbestos mines in Quebec.

Ottawa cancelled tax credits for companies advertising in American-owned Reader’s Digest and Time magazine, with Trudeau’s secretary of state for culture, J. Hugh Faulkner, proclaiming , “We have to create our own identity … The alternative is to be simply overrun by the American arts and cultures.”

The Trudeau government stepped back onto the world stage by increasing defence spending after a years-long budget freeze. Under pressure from allies, it also boosted Canada’s NATO troop contributions.

And it launched overseas trade missions and support programs for Canadian exporters looking to promote and sell their products and services abroad.

Trudeau’s ultimate gambit was the signing of an agreement, widely known as the “contractual link,” meant to bind Canada a little closer to the nine-country European Economic Community, a rapidly growing precursor to what is now the 27-member European Union.

“We do not know — indeed Europe does not know — how far or how fast its experiment in integration will take it,” Trudeau said in 1975 during a visit to London. But he said the deal would allow Canada and Europe to “consult and confer” going forward.

The eventual treaty , signed in July 1976, pledged in vague terms to offer favourable treatment in international trade and close co-operation on commercial and economic matters.

Canadians were bullish on the possibilities, but not everyone was convinced. A New York Times article cited an unnamed official with the Canadian Manufacturers’ Association who called the deal “a bland bucket of fog.”

It did, however, flash on the Central Intelligence Agency’s radar.

A May 1975 report assessed the impending deal as “more political than economic” and, for Trudeau, “a major public demonstration” of his government’s Third Option policy in action.

Another CIA report after the Canada-Europe agreement was signed predicted it was “likely to have little economic effect on Canada” because the new partners were at cross purposes. Ottawa wanted to export finished goods to Europe, but the Europeans were shopping for Canadian raw materials like energy and minerals.

The skeptical American spies were proven right.

In a 1989 journal article that examined whether Canada’s Third Option pivot away from the U.S. had been “a complete failure,” the academics Gordon Mace and Gérard Hervouet determined that exports to America had remained “well over 65 per cent” since the 1970s while the proportion of exports to other parts of the world had varied only slightly.

Building an economy less dependent on the U.S. is urgent. We need to prioritize not just GDP growth but also our sovereignty, writes Alex Himelfarb.

The problem had not been with Ottawa’s efforts to diversify, but rather with the private sector’s follow-through.

”(Canadian business) did not feel, at that time, that there were enough incentives to balance the costs of expanding economic relations outside the North American markets,” Mace and Hervouet concluded.

If there is a historical warning for the Carney government, it is in the “Field of Dreams” risk that his diversification strategy carries.

In the famous baseball movie, Kevin Costner’s character is convinced that if he constructs a baseball diamond in his cornfield the ghostly greats of the game will come to play.

Carney has similarly doubled down on Canada’s pivot away from the U.S. The Canada-EU partnership-in-the-making is expected to contain initiatives to encourage more research, defence and industrial co-operation as well as measures to ease the administrative burden of companies doing business abroad.

But if the buy-in from Canadian entrepreneurs is tepid, Carney could find himself standing alone in a barren patch of dirt.

A few other historical events contributed to Canada eventually abandoning the Third Option and severing the “contractual link” to Europe.

There was the global recession caused by a stock market crash and the shocks of the 1973 oil embargo and the 1979 Iranian revolution — events that threw governments’ best-laid plans off course around the world.

Another was the U.S. election cycle, which ushered President Jimmy Carter, a Democrat, into the White House in 1977.

Speaking frankly about the challenges of reorienting trade to Europe, then-external affairs minister Don Jamieson said in the House of Commons that Canadian business needed to “revamp its thinking” and take “a more aggressive approach in terms of selling in unfamiliar territory.”

But there was a distinct change of tone when Jamieson, a popular Newfoundland radio and television broadcaster, spoke of Canada’s closest neighbour.

“The United States continues to be not only our best customer, by a very wide margin, but also our closest friend and, in the long run, the country with which we find we can co-operate for a whole range of logical reasons.”

It was in 1982 — only a decade after the declaration of the Third Option pivot — that the Trudeau government struck the Macdonald Commission to conduct a three-year study on Canada’s economic future.

Commission chair Donald Macdonald returned with a final report that urged Ottawa to take a “leap of faith” on a free-trade agreement with the United States.

The report landed on the desk of a new Canadian prime minister, Brian Mulroney. The Progressive Conservative leader was a recent convert to the cause of free trade, but ended up going all-in on the United States, with a bilateral trade deal in 1988 and expanding the agreement to Mexico four years later.

In doing so, he set Canada on a collision course with the current occupant of the White House — one that would take more than three decades for its impact to be felt.

stories.title: This waterfront Ontario town hosts the region’s largest outdoor Christmas market
stories.summary: Christmas On The Bay will run for four days in Meaford, Ontario.
stories.author: Irelyne Lavery
stories.content:
The holiday season has almost reached Ontario and if you’re beginning to fill up your calendar with festivities, this European-style Christmas market in a historic, waterfront town deserves a spot on the agenda.

From Dec. 3 to 6, Christmas On The Bay will run for four days in Meaford, a charming town nestled on the southern shore of Georgian Bay.

Known as the area’s largest outdoor Christmas market, the celebration take place at Meaford Market Square, located at 12 Nelson St. E.

It will run with free admission from 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Dec. 3 and 4, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Dec. 5 and 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Dec. 6.

“Just like the very best Christmas markets, Christmas On The Bay provides all the festive lights, sounds, smells, experiences and ambiance you would expect to put you into the perfect festive spirit,” the team at the market, which consists of local volunteers, said.

At the celebration, visitors can mingle among the wooden kiosks to find the “labours of love of Meaford and South Georgian Bay’s finests artists, offering you a selection of locally produced and crafted foods, beverages and wares just in time for Christmas.”

This year’s vendors include Simply Unique Flowers & Gifts, YF Patissier Chocolatier, Jump 4 Jewels, Gentle Love Soap Company, Eugenia Lake Candle Co. and Meaford Maples.

Plus, there will be live performances from The Meaford Scarecrow Kazoo Band, Enya Dreams, Paige Warner, Drew Wright and more.

If you’ll be stopping by on Dec. 5, the Kinsmens’ Santa Claus Parade will also run as part of the celebration at 5:15 p.m. on Sykes Street.

Before leaving town, head to the Meaford Museum at 111 Bayfield St. to learn more about the area’s history.

Here, you can discover the people, places and events that helped to shape Meaford, from “early settlement and military history to unique local achievements and treasured collections.”

stories.title: Richard Warnica: I went to the last heartland of Alberta separatism. This is what I learned about how my home province has changed
stories.summary: The separatist element has turned the province against immigration — and immigrants.
stories.author: Richard Warnica
stories.content:
Eckville, Alta. — Jerry Andres watched the results roll in Monday night from his usual perch — at his computer, in his living room in Eckville, Alta., windows open to podcasters livestreaming on YouTube and Rumble.

Anders, a retired oilfield worker, wasn’t surprised by the outcome, but he was disappointed. “To be honest with you, I’m more anti-Carney and the Liberals than I am anything,” he said, standing on his porch a day later. “And mostly due to immigration.”

Andres has a bushy white handlebar moustache. A Harley Davidson sat in his driveway. A flag for an Independent Alberta — a snake coiled over the provincial crest — flew from the fence post that frames his green and white bungalow.

“Some people call me a racist,” he said, his wife visible on the couch inside, watching “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” “Maybe. I don’t think I am. I never had any issue with coloured people until the last 10 years.”

Voters in Alberta Monday overwhelmingly rejected the idea of holding a binding referendum on separating from Canada. With 99 per cent of polls reporting, 85 of Alberta’s 87 provincial districts had endorsed the idea that “Alberta should remain a province” of this country.

In total, about 75 per cent of Albertans voted to stay in Canada. But in the Eckville community centre, next to the curling rink, two blocks from Andres’ lawn, 71 per cent voted to leave.

On Tuesday, I drove to Eckville — half an hour west of Red Deer — to find out how some of Alberta’s most ardent sovereigntists were feeling the day after a resounding federalist win.

The town of about 1000 sits in the heart of Alberta oil country near the eastern border of Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, one of the two ridings to vote in favour of a binding referendum. On my two hour drive north from Calgary, I passed through fields thick with cattle, active pumpjacks and flare stacks burning off gas.

Alberta is one of the most urbanized parts of Canada. But when people back east (AKA Ontario) picture my home province, many still imagine places like Eckville, resource towns on the high prairie where the community centres hold cribbage tournaments and the hockey rinks convert every summer into rodeo barns.

Rosita Edwards poses with a Republic of Alberta flag outside her home in Eckville, Alberta, Oct 20, 2026

Rosita Edwards and Drew Daniels live just a few blocks away from the Eckville rink. On Tuesday, their cat, Shady, played on a leash in the front yard. A Republic of Alberta flag hung from two hockey sticks bolted next to the side of their home.

Daniels has spent the last 20 years working in pipelines. When I asked him how most of his colleagues voted, he just laughed.

“We’re oil and gas, man,” he said. “I mean, it’s tough as a man to see more than 40 per cent of your wage going back that way.” (He gestured symbolically toward Ontario.)

Anti-Ottawa sentiment is nothing new for oilfield workers. But separatism at this scale is. I asked Daniels what changed. “Trudeau, man!” he said.

Edwards had a different take: “I think it’s when our youth couldn’t get jobs,” she said. She told me her son dropped out of high school because he couldn’t find part time work. “And now he’s a pipe fitter … because he couldn’t get a job at the local Timmy’s or the local McDonald’s or DQ because it’s predominantly brown people,” she said. “And they wouldn’t hire white kids.”

That’s something I heard repeatedly, not just in Eckville but over and over again in interviews with separatists over the past year: that immigrants brought in by the federal Liberals are stealing opportunities from local youth.

It isn’t true, and certainly not here. Lacombe County, which includes Eckville, is one the whitest places in the entire province. Unemployment in the local economic region is also the lowest in all of Alberta. But the idea — whipped up and stoked by Danielle Smith’s UCP government — that newcomers are a drain, that they are leeching from “real” Albertans has sunk in here nonetheless.

“You go to a hospital, a restaurant, a gas station, fast food, it don’t matter,” Andres told me. “Anywhere you go in public, it’s all run by, or worked by immigrants.”

On Monday night, the riding that includes Eckville voted more than 78 per cent in favour of “Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels.” That’s despite the fact that, according to the most recent tally, the county surrounding Eckville had all of 170 visible minorities out of a population of more than 10,000.

For Bonnie Boisjolie, who lives just outside of Eckville, that just makes sense. “Why would anybody in their right mind vote not to stop immigration?” she said.

Like Andres, Boisjolie, a retired bus driver, gets most of her news from podcasts and online streamers. “I love Jordan Peterson,” she said. “He’s my rock star.”

I was struck, listening to Boisjolie — in her beautiful living room, in her spacious home on the edge of a tree farm, a framed photo of a sea turtle on an ocean beach above her head — that the grievances that drove Alberta separatism were always less about how people are experiencing life in Alberta and more about how they’re seeing it refracted through the media they choose.

On Monday, about 800 people voted in the Eckville Community Centre. Of those, just 234 voted for Alberta to stay. Across the riding, though, the results weren’t nearly so lopsided. Even in the most pro-independence part of all of Alberta, Leave barely broke 50 per cent.

(The riding also contained some of the ardently pro-Canada polls in Alberta, ON the Sunchild First Nation, half an hour west of Eckville, where 98 per cent of voters chose Stay.)

Back in Eckville, Shady the cat skittered across Edwards’ and Daniels’ lawn. On the driveway, Daniels opened the door of his white pickup. He plugged his iPhone into the truck’s audio system and played me a song he wrote with his band. “My life’s been a pipeline … rodeo,” he sang in a baritone twang. “A wild ride. A hell of a show.”

I don’t have any problem with Daniels — a country music singer who works in oil and gas — identifying his culture as Albertan. My issue, with the entire separation movement, is the idea that that’s the only thing an Albertan can be. The province I grew up in has always been more diverse than outsiders, and many of its own politicians, like to pretend. That diversity still stands. I believe it will endure, even after Monday, when a majority of Alberta voted to stay in Canada while also endorsing five referendum questions designed to make Alberta a meaner, less welcoming home.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: B.C. Conservative leader Doerkson retains riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin
stories.summary: The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that interim British Columbia Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson has been re-elected in the riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - British Columbians got their best look so far at Lorne Doerkson on Saturday night, their premier-designate, and self-described “guy from Williams Lake.”

The interim B.C. Conservative leader delivered a rollicking victory speech as he revelled in a sweeping majority win, secured in a snap provincial election called by outgoing Premier David Eby in a disastrous political miscalculation.

Doerkson had emerged from obscurity to unify a fractured Opposition that was a political basket case just six weeks ago. The party had seen waves of defections under former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

The former bronco rider said he knew all about coming back from indignity.

“I have watched a lot of people get thrown at a rodeo and I’ll say I’ve been thrown a few times myself,” Doerkson said.

“But what I’ve learned, what I have learned from that (is) you pick up yourself, dust yourself off and you get back on.”

Doerkson, who has worked as a newspaper publisher and auto dealer, was once little known outside Williams Lake and his home riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin, which he has represented since 2020.

But that all changed on Sept. 20, when he was hurriedly installed as interim leader of the Conservatives — having returned from a trip to Africa — after the resignation of Findlay, whose divisive leadership had been tearing the party asunder.

Two days later, Doerkson was campaigning to become premier after Eby’s early election call.

“I didn’t expect this, I certainly didn’t seek this and I certainly did not plan two years ago to somehow put all of these stars into alignment,” Doerkson said in a campaign interview.

“I mean, the fact is, (in) politics every day is an exciting day and the next one you have no idea what is about to happen.”

His first task was returning Conservative defectors to the fold, including seven who said just days earlier that they were joining the upstart CentreBC party.

He was sometimes being a scarce presence on the campaign trail. But Doerkson and the Conservatives consistently led Eby and the NDP in opinion polls, as the premier faced intense criticism over an early election call that he seemed to struggle justifying.

Before his elevation, Doerkson had stayed mostly out of the culture-war fray, his time in the legislature spent mostly hyper-focused on his riding and region, beset by wildfires and hospital emergency room closures.

Doerkson’s time as publisher of the local newspaper had put him squarely at the heart of the community. As a former rodeo rider, he framed positions on health care from his perspective as a former visitor to emergency rooms.

Scott Tucker, who owns the local Home Hardware in Williams Lake, has been Doerkson’s financial agent since he entered politics, and said in a recent interview that he had known the man for about 15 years or more.

They’re both Rotarians and would encounter each other at community events, where Doerkson was more often than not the master of ceremonies.

Tucker said Doerkson is “not one to go it alone,” describing him as someone who seeks out guidance and input from others, drawing on his experience in business, and volunteering and dealing with different points of view.

Doerkson was certainly gracious in victory.

He thanked Eby for his public service, saying “it asks a lot of a person and a lot of their family.”

“He has given to this province for years, of both of those things. So thank you very much, David Eby,” said Doerkson, who also thanked Green Leader Emily Lowan for “all that she’s done to inspire thousands of young British Columbians.”

His acknowledgment of his political rivals drew warm applause.

But the night belonged to the guy from Williams Lake.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

- With files from Brenna Owen

stories.title: Polls close in B.C. as voters choose next provincial government
stories.summary: Vote count will determine whether Eby’s NDP wins another mandate or whether Doerkson’s Conservatives will form government for the first time in nearly a century
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
British Columbia has elected a Conservative majority government for the first time in nearly a century, delivering a remarkable reversal of fortunes to a party that entered the campaign after months of internal conflict and controversies that threatened to derail its path to power.

David Eby resigned as leader of the NDP, accepting responsibility for the outcome of an election he called two years early. His high-stakes gamble to take advantage of a fractured opposition backfired; with 95 per cent of polls reporting, the results showed 64 Conservatives elected, 27 for the NDP and two for the Greens.

In a sombre concession speech, Mr. Eby reflected on his government’s accomplishments in recruiting family doctors, helping to lower rents and raising the minimum wage.

“This is obviously something I do with a very heavy heart,” he said to supporters at his party’s gathering in Vancouver. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.”

The Conservatives appeared to be on the verge of collapse just weeks ago under the weight of scandal, defections and bitter internal rivalries, but regrouped just as Mr. Eby called the election. The victory ends nine years of NDP rule – four under Mr. Eby – and puts the Conservatives in control of a province facing mounting economic uncertainty, persistent strains in health care services and a continuing trade war with the U.S.

Mr. Eby said in his concession speech that he had spoken with Conservative interim Leader Lorne Doerkson, wishing him the best at a critical time for the province and country.

“The people of British Columbia have asked us to be the official opposition, which is obviously not the result any of us wanted,” he said. “A number of my colleagues, some of the hardest working MLAs I know for their communities, were not elected tonight. It breaks my heart, and I accept full responsibility for that outcome.”

In his victory speech, Mr. Doerkson thanked Mr. Eby and summarized his campaign pledges, which included boosting the economy, cutting red tape and freezing all provincial taxes.

“I want a B.C. where a hard day’s work gets you a family home and a future right here in this beautiful province,” he said.

“And I want to say to those who aren’t in this room: There is a place for you here. Bring your ideas, bring your families, bring your ambitions and somebody will pick up the phone in British Columbia.”

As large sparks shot out of several small cannons behind him, Mr. Doerkson detailed how his government will jump-start the economy by tripling natural gas production over the next nine years and holding an international investment summit in Vancouver.

He repeated his pledge to cut taxes and red tape and to support health care that is “fully and publicly funded.”

Mr. Doerkson has said that repealing the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act would be among his top priorities, arguing it has created needless division. Indigenous leaders have been opposed to any changes to the legislation.

Mr. Doerkson addressed Indigenous people directly in his speech Saturday night.

“To our First Nations: This future is one we will build together as partners with the certainty all of us need,” he said.

“First Nations built lives and nations here for thousands of years.”

But he also told the crowd, to cheers, that he believed “in the protection of private property rights and parks that are open to all British Columbians.”

Recent court rulings in favour of Indigenous groups have made those issues a centrepiece of Conservative commentary in the province.

Green Party Leader Emily Lowan was elected in the Vancouver Island riding of Saanich North and the Islands, while Green MLA Jeremy Valeriote was re-elected in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky.

“We may have a small caucus, but tonight we have inherited an enormous responsibility and that is to hold the majority Conservative government to account,” Ms. Lowan said in her victory speech.

“Over the next four years, our job is to be a voice for the many people who will be harmed by their policies – and that is going to require some serious movement building.”

Mr. Eby had said he called the election early because he wanted the NDP to win a strong mandate to fix a legislature that “wasn’t working.” A one-seat majority had left his government mired in procedural wrangling, he said, and forced some of his MLAs to vote from hospital beds while dying of cancer or hours after giving birth.

The “existential threat” posed by U.S. President Donald Trump ’s trade war made a strong mandate even more important, he said.

“The government’s focus was on just doing whatever we could to make sure the government didn’t fall, because the Conservatives voted 13 times to collapse the government, including just three weeks after the election,” Mr. Eby said on the campaign trail Oct. 16.

Mr. Eby also pointed to a Conservative party whose members were found to have espoused racist , homophobic and otherwise unacceptable views with alarming frequency and said it was never a bad idea for British Columbians to choose their path forward.

Some of the MLAs he named were re-elected on Saturday.

The 2024 election returned 47 New Democrats, 44 Conservatives and two Green MLAs. When the legislature was dissolved last month, the Conservatives were down to 29 seats, officially.

However, Mr. Eby’s early election call was also met with cynicism, seen as an opportunistic move intended to capitalize on an opposition in disarray. After the polarizing Kerry-Lynne Findlay was narrowly won the Conservative leadership in late May, the party was plagued by scandal and bitter infighting; 13 MLAs either quit or were removed, all in clashes with Ms. Findlay. Many went to the nascent CentreBC party – which branded itself as a fiscally conservative, socially progressive alternative – raising questions about vote-splitting on the right that would further increase the likelihood of an NDP re-election.

At the height of caucus conflict, the Conservatives were down to just 24 MLAs – 20 fewer than were elected in 2024.

NDP MLA and cabinet minister Adrian Dix, re-elected in his riding of Vancouver-Kingsway, called Saturday’s result one of the most disappointing nights in the modern history of the BC NDP.

“Clearly, given the results, it was a mistake to call the election,” he told reporters.

NDP MLA and cabinet minister Bowinn Ma, re-elected in North Vancouver-Lonsdale, said she understood and agreed with Mr. Eby’s snap election call.

“The election results tonight are quite different than they were just two years ago, which I would say demonstrates it was a question worth asking British Columbians,” she told reporters.

Ms. Ma noted that Mr. Eby could continue to serve in the legislature, citing the party tradition that saw Carole James and Mr. Dix do so after leading the party to defeat.

North Island-Powell River Conservative MP Aaron Gunn, who had helped to reanimate the moribund Conservative party after the BC Liberals denied him the opportunity to enter their leadership race, said he was in disbelief at the role he played in moving the province further to the right on a host of issues.

“That might have been the spark that lit the flame that made the fire that led to this day, but a lot of people have played a huge role in this,” he said at the Conservatives’ gathering. “It’s been a lot of hard work.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney congratulated Mr. Doerkson on his victory in a social media post .

“I look forward to working with you as Premier to get more homes built, unleash our full potential as an energy superpower, and build a stronger British Columbia and a stronger Canada for all,” Mr. Carney said.

Elections BC reported that less than half of eligible voters in British Columbia – 48 per cent – turned out to vote. It was the lowest voter turnout since 1996, the earliest date listed on the agency’s website.

David Eby resigned as leader of the NDP, accepting responsibility for the outcome of an election he called two years early. His high-stakes gamble to take advantage of a fractured opposition backfired; with 95 per cent of polls reporting, the results showed 64 Conservatives elected, 27 for the NDP and two for the Greens.
In a sombre concession speech, Mr. Eby reflected on his government’s accomplishments in recruiting family doctors, helping to lower rents and raising the minimum wage.
“This is obviously something I do with a very heavy heart,” he said to supporters at his party’s gathering in Vancouver. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.”

The Conservatives appeared to be on the verge of collapse just weeks ago under the weight of scandal, defections and bitter internal rivalries, but regrouped just as Mr. Eby called the election. The victory ends nine years of NDP rule – four under Mr. Eby – and puts the Conservatives in control of a province facing mounting economic uncertainty, persistent strains in health care services and a continuing trade war with the U.S.

“The people of British Columbia have asked us to be the official opposition, which is obviously not the result any of us wanted,” he said. “A number of my colleagues, some of the hardest working MLAs I know for their communities, were not elected tonight. “I want a B.C. where a hard day’s work gets you a family home and a future right here in this beautiful province,” he said.

“And I want to say to those who aren’t in this room: There is a place for you here. Bring your ideas, bring your families, bring your ambitions and somebody will pick up the phone in British Columbia.”

stories.title: B.C. election latest: Voters go to the polls to decide next provincial government
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia is voting on its next government as the snap provincial election called one month ago reaches its culmination.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The British Columbia Conservative Party has won a majority government after NDP Leader David Eby’s decision to call a snap election two years early backfired in spectacular fashion.

Here are the latest developments.

More than three hours after polls closed in B.C., the Conservatives hold a dominant position in the legislature in the latest Canadian Press decision desk projections.

The Conservatives are projected to win in 56 ridings and leading in another eight, while the New Democrats are elected in 24 while leading in three.

The Greens, meanwhile, retained their two seats including Leader Emily Lowan in Saanich North and the Islands.

The mother of B.C. Greens Leader Emily Lowan says she is extremely overwhelmed by her daughter’s victory in Saanich North and the Islands.

Anne MacLaurin says she is very proud of her daughter, who retains the seat for the Greens which the party has held since 2017.

MacLaurin adds her daughter is “a force” and has what it takes to take on a B.C. legislature dominated by the Conservatives.

Hamish Telford, associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, says the British Columbia New Democrats should have called off the snap election when Lorne Doerkson took over the Conservatives.

Telford says the NDP anticipated a campaign against Kerry-Lynne Findlay, and the party should have held off on calling an election citing that governing parties do not call elections when the Official Opposition is leaderless.

“But when they called the snap election, I think that irritated voters who were ready for a change,” the political scientist says.

Former B.C. Conservatives leadership candidate Caroline Elliott says Lorne Doerkson has “earned it” in becoming B.C.‘s next premier.

Elliott was asked how the Conservatives will handle Doerkson’s status as interim leader and says it is “more of a question for the party,” but adds he has earned more votes in the election “than we could ever dream of in a leadership race.”

She had lost a narrow race to be Conservative leader earlier this year to Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who resigned just days before the election was called.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has congratulated B.C. Conservatives premier-designate Lorne Doerkson on his victory in the provincial election.

In a statement on X, Carney says he looks forward to working with Doerkson as premier on housing, energy and other sectors in a bid to “build a stronger British Columbia and a stronger Canada for all.”

Carney also thanked outgoing NDP premier and leader David Eby in the same statement, noting Ottawa and the province had launched major projects and unlocked export markets together during Eby’s tenure.

Former NDP leader and health minister Adrian Dix says tonight’s election represents “one of the most disappointing nights in the modern history” of the BC NDP.

Dix, who was re-elected in Vancouver-Renfrew, says British Columbians had a choice in the election, and they chose Conservatives’ Lorne Doerkson to be their premier.

Dix adds that tonight is not the time to analyze the Ndp’s loss, but rather “the time to commiserate with candidates, who didn’t win” as well as to “recognize the candidates who did win to prepare ourselves for a period of Opposition.”

Green Leader Emily Lowan says there is a “heaviness” in her heart over the Conservative win, at the same time that she and her party feels the joy of victory.

Lowan won in Saanich North and the Islands, and incumbent Green legislator Jeremy Valeriote secured re-election in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky.

But Lowan says she’s “scared of what’s to come” under a B.C. Conservative majority government, adding that Lorne Doerkson’s party “stands against everything” that brought the Green movement together.

Interim B.C. Conservative leader and premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has delivered a rousing speech to supporters after his party was swept into power in a stunning defeat of the incumbent New Democrats.

Doerkson went on stage at an election night event in Vancouver amid fireworks, with crowds of supporters hugging him and shaking his hand.

He promised to follow through on his campaign vow to “supercharge” the provincial economy.

Doerkson says people in B.C. “want a fair shot at building something” in the province, and the Conservatives will “welcome capital back” to the provincial economy.

He also promised to get liquefied natural gas production tripled in the province by 2035.

Doerkson also reiterated his support for full publicly funded health care as well as his campaign promise of no new taxes.

B.C. New Democrat Leader David Eby has conceded the provincial election and says he will resign as party leader.

Eby says his family has “paid a very significant cost” for his work in politics, and he is now keen to spend sometime with his wife and children.

He adds it is time for the provincial NDP to find new leadership within the party.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that Green Leader Emily Lowan has won her seat in Saanich North and the Islands.

The Greens have held the seat since 2017 and Lowan was running in the place of incumbent Rob Botterell, who decided not to seek re-election.

BC Federation of Labour president Sussanne Skidmore says people have heard “lout and clear” that voters “want to see bold changes” with the election results.

Skidmore is attending the NDP election night event as The Canadian Press is projecting a majority Conservative government.

She says labour groups are ready to sit down with “whoever becomes the next premier” and work on being “thoughtful about the decisions they make.”

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that both OneBC interim leader Dallas Brodie and CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko will lose their bids to stay in the legislature.

Sturko is projected to lose in Surrey South, a seat she had held from 2022 to 2024, first as a BC Liberal before she crossed the floor to the Conservatives.

Brodie is projected to lose in Vancouver-Quilchena to B.C. Conservative candidate Carson Binda, who is the former provincial director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that the provincial Conservatives have won a majority government in the B.C. election.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that the B.C. Conservatives have won government in the 2026 provincial election.

The win puts an end to almost a decade of New Democrat rule in the province under John Horgan and David Eby.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that Conservatives interim leader Lorne Doerkson has been re-elected in his riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin.

Doerkson has held the seat since 2020.

The once-obscure legislator became interim Conservative leader two days before Saturday’s provincial election was called on Sept. 22.

The Canadian Press decision desk is calling a victory for Caroline Elliott in the riding of West Vancouver-Capilano.

Elliott finished second in the Conservative leadership race behind Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Findlay resigned had the job about four months but resigned two days before the election was called and Lorne Doerkson took on the job.

The Canadian Press decision desk is projecting that Independent Jordan Kealy has lost his bid for re-election in Peace River North.

Kealy was elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative, but he resigned from the party in 2025, then was charged this June with sexual assault, which he denies.

He has been defeated by Conservative Curtis Whitford.

Former federal Conservative cabinet minister Stockwell Day says the provincial Conservatives took the right strategy in this campaign to win voters.

Day says he believes people “just want back to normal,” and it was correct for Conservatives interim leader Lorne Doerkson to “stand back” and let NDP Leader David Eby “keep talking.”

A former secretary of the BC NDP says interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson was a tougher opponent than expected.

Brian Gardiner says he would have argued for the NDP to wait a couple of weeks before calling the election.

Gardiner says Doerkson’s Conservatives “united in a much stronger way than was expected.”

The Canadian Press decision desk is calling its first result, a B.C. Conservative win in West Kelowna-Peachland.

It’s a safe Conservative riding that’s been retained by Macklin McCall.

Early tallies across B.C. show Conservatives leading in most ridings.

There’s a stark contrast of mood and attendance at the two major parties’ election night events in Vancouver.

There’s a large crowd at the Conservatives’ event at the Rocky Mountaineer Station where supporters are watching election coverage on the big screen in the front of the room.

The NDP event at the Pinnacle Hotel Harbourfront has plenty of reporters but much sparser attendance from supporters.

Polls have closed across British Columbia as voting officially concludes in the provincial election.

Elections BC says advance votes will be tabulated electronically and are being counted first.

Almost 900,000 people, or 24 per cent of registered voters, cast ballots in the advance polls.

Votes that were cast on Saturday will be counted manually due to what the agency called the logistics of the snap election.

Greater Victoria Teachers’ Association president Carolyn Howe says she has felt disappointment with the NDP, despite the party’s history with labour movements.

Howe is running for the Greens in Victoria-Swan Lake and says “it’s time for something better.”

She says people had been waiting on the NDP government to act on issues such as public services but nothing has happened.

Speaking at the Greens election-night event, Howe says she is excited for how the Greens will do in the election and thinks the party will “have so much to celebrate.”

British Columbia Government and Service Employees’ Union president Paul Finch is at the NDP election night event in Vancouver and says he hopes voters had the chance to assess the different platforms between the parties before they cast their ballots.

Finch says he is hopeful that the voters will bring a “strong” and “progressive” government but adds he himself did not get as much information from the platforms as he would have liked.

He adds that the union has planned for all circumstances stemming from the election, but it’s too early to tell on what the group would do in dealing with a possible Conservative government.

A B.C. Conservative candidate arriving at the party’s election night event in Vancouver says the mood is “cautiously optimistic” as polls are set to close.

Carson Binda, the Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Quilchena opposite former party member and current OneBC interim leader Dallas Brodie, says people are “eager for change” and all candidates are “100 per cent” behind interim leader Lorne Doerkson.

Binda says he does not want to “count our chickens before they hatch,” but the local campaign isn’t concerned about Brodie splitting the vote as the Conservatives “had a hard time finding OneBC supporters.”

Supporters have begun arriving at the B.C. Green Party’s election night event in the Greater Victoria area, including outgoing MLA Rob Botterell.

Botterell decided not to seek re-election, clearing the way for Leader Emily Lowan to run.

He says he is proud of Lowan and the party’s campaign after NDP Leader David Eby called a snap election.

The outgoing MLA says people in his riding have told him they are “totally impressed” with Lowan’s poise and advocacy for Green causes, as well as her passion and vision.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.
paragraphs: Vancouver - The British Columbia Conservative Party has won a majority government after NDP Leader David Eby’s decision to call a snap election two years early backfired in spectacular fashion.
Here are the latest developments.
More than three hours after polls closed in B.C., the Conservatives hold a dominant position in the legislature in the latest Canadian Press decision desk projections.
The Conservatives are projected to win in 56 ridings and leading in another eight, while the New Democrats are elected in 24 while leading in three.
The Greens, meanwhile, retained their two seats including Leader Emily Lowan in Saanich North and the Islands.
The mother of B.C. Greens Leader Emily Lowan says she is extremely overwhelmed by her daughter’s victory in Saanich North and the Islands.
Anne MacLaurin says she is very proud of her daughter, who retains the seat for the Greens which the party has held since 2017.
MacLaurin adds her daughter is “a force” and has what it takes to take on a B.C. legislature dominated by the Conservatives.

Hamish Telford, associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, says the British Columbia New Democrats should have called off the snap election when Lorne Doerkson took over the Conservatives.

Telford says the NDP anticipated a campaign against Kerry-Lynne Findlay, and the party should have held off on calling an election citing that governing parties do not call elections when the Official Opposition is leaderless.
“But when they called the snap election, I think that irritated voters who were ready for a change,” the political scientist says.
Former B.C. Conservatives leadership candidate Caroline Elliott says Lorne Doerkson has “earned it” in becoming B.C.‘s next premier.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has congratulated B.C. Conservatives premier-designate Lorne Doerkson on his victory in the provincial election.

stories.title: Riders top Elks 16-9, will face Lions in West semi
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan Roughriders punched their ticket to the West Division semifinal with a 16-9 victory over the Edmonton Elks on Saturday.
stories.author: Jeff DeDekker
stories.content:
Regina – The Saskatchewan Roughriders punched their ticket to the West Division semifinal with a 16-9 victory over the Edmonton Elks on Saturday.

The victory moved Saskatchewan (10-8) into third place in the West Division, meaning the fourth-place Winnipeg Blue Bombers will cross over and face the Toronto Argonauts in the East semifinal on Oct. 31.

The defending Grey Cup champion Riders will visit the B.C. Lions on Oct. 31.

The first-place Elks (13-5) will host the Saskatchewan-B.C. winner in the West final on Nov. 7 in Edmonton.

After allowing a one-yard touchdown run by Edmonton quarterback Cole Snyder early in the first quarter, Saskatchewan responded with 16 unanswered points. Brett Lauther kicked a 32-yard field goal in the second quarter to cut the deficit to 6-3.

Riders quarterback Tommy Stevens then added a pair of one-yard touchdown runs, one in the second quarter and one in the fourth, to give Saskatchewan a 15-6 lead. Stevens now has 17 rushing touchdowns, breaking the CFL record for most rushing touchdowns in a single season. Caleb Evans held the previous record of 16, set with the Ottawa Redblacks in 2022.

Saskatchewan punter Oscar Chapman chipped in a 58-yard single with 3:31 remaining to make the score 16-6.

Vincent Blanchard ended the string of unanswered points with a 24-yard field goal to narrow the Elks deficit to 16-9 with 27 seconds remaining. The Riders recovered the ensuing onside kick by the Elks.

It was an undisciplined first half that saw both teams struggle with penalties. The Elks had seven penalties for 73 yards while the Riders had seven penalties for 70 yards.

The only touchdown of the half came on a penalty-fuelled drive for the Riders. A five-play, 67-yard drive culminated with a one-yard major by Stevens to give the Riders a 9-6 lead with 2:53 left in the half. Of the 67 yards, 62 were from Edmonton penalties, including a 42-yard pass interference call against Elks defensive back Royce Metchie.

Playing in challenging weather conditions — at kickoff the winds were at 46 km/h with gusts to 5 km/h — the teams depended on their running games in the first half. Shunderrick Powell gained 47 yards on six carries for the Elks while Deon Jackson, making his Riders debut, totalled 45 yards on eight carries.

The wind also wreaked havoc with the kicking game. Lauther and Edmonton’s Vincent Lauther missed convert attempts. The Riders also failed on a two-point convert attempt after Stevens’s second touchdown.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.
