stories.title: The Assembly of First Nations prepares for historic meeting with Carney, premiers
stories.summary: The meeting is the first such gathering since 2005, when premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin met with Indigenous leaders in Kelowna, B.C.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak is feeling the weight of the moment as she approaches something her predecessors sought for years: a sit-down meeting with the prime minister and premiers.

“I look at some of our former leaders that had to really push and pull just to open these doors, and I wish they could see that today,” Woodhouse Nepinak said recently between last-minute meetings with chiefs to prepare for the First Nations-First Ministers meeting in Ottawa on Monday.

“It is historic, but at the same time we don’t want it to be one-and-done. We don’t want it to fall flat and not offer hope again.”

The meeting comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney works to speed up major project approvals and development – efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation.

But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario.

The Assembly of First Nations has been preparing for the meeting for months by holding town halls with chiefs to discuss actions they want to see governments take. Gina Wilson, who recently served as deputy minister at Indigenous Services Canada, helped to advise chiefs as they lined up their priorities for the meeting.

The AFN released a handful of position papers last week on economic development, policing and public safety, employment and health.

One of the main goals for First Nations leaders going into the meeting is a First Nations sovereign wealth fund. The fund, proposed by Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, would pool capital to ensure First Nations can build long-term wealth in their communities and invest in projects.

Chippewas of the Thames First Nation Chief Joe Miskokomon has told The Canadian Press the fund would bypass governments and allow major projects to be developed faster by giving communities more authority over investments.

The Monday meeting will be preceded by a day of ceremony on Sunday hosted by the AFN. Woodhouse Nepinak said such First Nations ceremonies were once prohibited under the Indian Act and it’s important for Carney and the premiers to be there.

First Nations will be represented in the closed-door meeting on Monday largely by regional chiefs from the AFN. The Privy Council Office has not said which premiers will attend the gathering.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon confirmed at an unrelated news conference in Montreal on Friday that he would not be attending the meeting.

He explained that he wants to prioritize a different approach with Indigenous peoples and that he has several meetings scheduled in the near future, including one with the chief of the Assembly of First Nations of Quebec and Labrador.

In Alberta, the province’s premier said during an unrelated news conference Saturday that she will be sending representatives from her government to the meeting.

Danielle Smith said she will not be attending because the meeting overlaps with the resumption of question period in her province as well as the aftermath of a historic referendum on separation.

Woodhouse Nepinak said the meeting ought to be broadcast to the public and she continues pushing the Privy Council Office to do so.

The meeting is the first such gathering since 2005, when premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin met with Indigenous leaders in Kelowna, B.C., to work out how to close socioeconomic gaps in their communities.

That gathering of some 1,000 individuals, including representatives from the AFN, Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, the Métis National Council and the Native Women’s Association of Canada, was meant to change policies from prescriptions from Canadian governments to something more collaborative.

The meeting ended with commitments from governments to spend billions of dollars to reduce infant mortality rates, increase education rates and tackle unemployment – the Kelowna Accord. But progress stalled when Martin’s government fell just days after the meetings wrapped.

Stephen Harper succeeded Martin as prime minister and launched an aggressive resource development agenda. That led to more tensions between Ottawa and Indigenous Peoples that culminated in the 2012 Idle No More protest movement.

Jeff Copenace, the chief of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, worked in Martin’s office at the time the Kelowna Accord was being drafted. He said while the agreement itself offered a practical approach to improving the Canadian economy by lifting up its fastest-growing population, the meeting in Kelowna showed many Canadians who Indigenous people really are.

Copenace said a smudging ceremony was conducted at the meeting, giving many Canadians their first glimpse of a traditional practice. He added it was also one of the first times he saw Indigenous people portrayed in the news in relation to something positive.

There’s been some progress in the years since, he said, but not all of the goals set at that meeting have been achieved. He fears a heavy focus on economics in the Monday meeting will further delay action on addictions, homelessness and suicide.

“Unless the prime minister, the premiers and the territories are going to look a little bit deeper than resource development or economic reconciliation, I worry that they’re not going to be successful with their agenda,” Copenace said.

His community is dealing with a suicide and mental health crisis that has taken the lives of nearly 70 people in five years – including a 19-year-old relative whose funeral will held on Monday.

“Things aren’t going to improve if you’re only going to focus on economic development … I plan to look the prime minister in the eye and tell him what’s happening in Onigaming and ask for his help desperately,” said Copenace, who is joining Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s delegation at the meeting. Kinew is a member of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation.

Copenace said he thinks the meeting wouldn’t be happening if Carney’s hadn’t realized his development agenda can’t move forward without First Nations.

“The only way he’s going to get his agenda successfully passed and not locked up in the courts or protests is by speaking directly with First Nations,” he said.

Woodhouse Nepinak said that, in order to avoid another failed attempt like the Kelowna Accord, Canadian politicians need to demonstrate political will and consistency.

“If there’s no political will to work together, then things stay the same,” she said.

Mohawk policy analyst Russ Diabo said he’s also worried the meeting will focus entirely on economics and avoid tougher conversations about First Nations rights. He has helped to organize a counter-meeting of grassroots leaders and advocates and a protest of the meeting itself, saying he does not trust the AFN to act in the best interest of communities.

Diabo said he fears the AFN – which represents chiefs but is not a rights-holding institution – will make agreements with Carney and the premiers.

“It’s totally orchestrated and there’s already a predetermined outcome,” Diabo said. He has accused the AFN of working too closely with the federal government while Ottawa works to negotiate away First Nations rights through cash settlements.

His counter-meeting on Sunday will hear from hereditary leaders, advocates and youth about their opposition to the country’s major projects agenda and what they see as the sidelining of their rights.

“I can’t think of a province in this country where Aboriginal and treaty rights aren’t being violated by provincial law and policy,” Diabo said.

The Truth Before Reconciliation Network is calling on federal and provincial governments to recognize rights-holders as the primary decision makers, to create a First Nation-based decision process that follows traditional governments, and to require community mandates before legislative changes are made.

“No First Nations-related legislation should proceed without documented community engagement and authorization. Consultation should occur before drafting legislation, not after policy decisions have been made,” Diabo wrote in a missive about the counter-meeting.

Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations are at a crossroads and many chiefs see the meeting as a chance to chart a new path forward.

While the meeting itself is seen as a win by some First Nations leaders, others remained concerned about the format and who will be in the room.

The AFN has a rocky relationship with First Nations in Alberta and chiefs in that province do not have a representative on the advocacy body’s executive council.

Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi told The Canadian Press it’s inappropriate for a “third-party organization” to be sitting alongside the country’s decision-makers instead of grassroots leadership.

“This is an unacceptable process,” he said.

His message is echoed by the chief of Onion Lake Cree Nation, who reportedly filed a cease-and-desist notice to the Assembly of First Nations ahead of the meeting to “make clear that the AFN does not, and cannot, represent, negotiate for or presume consent on behalf of the nation” at the meeting.

“We respect the choices of nations that participate through the AFN, and we expect equal respect for our decision to follow our own path,” said Chief Pete Chief. “The Oct. 26 gathering is about ensuring that the voices and authority of independent treaty nations are not overlooked.”

Woodhouse Nepinak said all First Nations should be heard and she’s thankful First Nations leaders, elders and youth will be in Ottawa to witness it – even those opposed to the meeting.

“I want to move to a point where we can have proper discussions and proper debates on finding the path forward,” she said.

“That’s all we can do, try our best every day.”

That gathering of some 1,000 individuals, including representatives from the AFN, Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, the Métis National Council and the Native Women’s Association of Canada, was meant to change policies from prescriptions from Canadian governments to something more collaborative.

The meeting ended with commitments from governments to spend billions of dollars to reduce infant mortality rates, increase education rates and tackle unemployment – the Kelowna Accord. But progress stalled when Martin’s government fell just days after the meetings wrapped.

Stephen Harper succeeded Martin as prime minister and launched an aggressive resource development agenda. That led to more tensions between Ottawa and Indigenous Peoples that culminated in the 2012 Idle No More protest movement.

Jeff Copenace, the chief of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, worked in Martin’s office at the time the Kelowna Accord was being drafted. He said while the agreement itself offered a practical approach to improving the Canadian economy by lifting up its fastest-growing population, the meeting in Kelowna showed many Canadians who Indigenous people really are.

Copenace said a smudging ceremony was conducted at the meeting, giving many Canadians their first glimpse of a traditional practice. He added it was also one of the first times he saw Indigenous people portrayed in the news in relation to something positive.

There’s been some progress in the years since, he said, but not all of the goals set at that meeting have been achieved. He fears a heavy focus on economics in the Monday meeting will further delay action on addictions, homelessness and suicide.

“Unless the prime minister, the premiers and the territories are going to look a little bit deeper than resource development or economic reconciliation, I worry that they’re not going to be successful with their agenda,” Copenace said.
His community is dealing with a suicide and mental health crisis that has taken the lives of nearly 70 people in five years – including a 19-year-old relative whose funeral will held on Monday.

“Things aren’t going to improve if you’re only going to focus on economic development … I plan to look the prime minister in the eye and tell him what’s happening in Onigaming and ask for his help desperately,” said Copenace, who is joining Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s delegation at the meeting. Kinew is a member of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation.
Copenace said he thinks the meeting wouldn’t be happening if Carney’s hadn’t realized his development agenda can’t move forward without First Nations.
“The only way he’s going to get his agenda successfully passed and not locked up in the courts or protests is by speaking directly with First Nations,” he said.
Woodhouse Nepinak said that, in order to avoid another failed attempt like the Kelowna Accord, Canadian politicians need to demonstrate political will and consistency.
“If there’s no political will to work together, then things stay the same,” she said.

Mohawk policy analyst Russ Diabo said he’s also worried the meeting will focus entirely on economics and avoid tougher conversations about First Nations rights. He has helped to organize a counter-meeting of grassroots leaders and advocates and a protest of the meeting itself, saying he does not trust the AFN to act in the best interest of communities.
Diabo said he fears the AFN – which represents chiefs but is not a rights-holding institution – will make agreements with Carney and the premiers.

“It’s totally orchestrated and there’s already a predetermined outcome,” Diabo said. He has accused the AFN of working too closely with the federal government while Ottawa works to negotiate away First Nations rights through cash settlements.
His counter-meeting on Sunday will hear from hereditary leaders, advocates and youth about their opposition to the country’s major projects agenda and what they see as the sidelining of their rights.
“I can’t think of a province in this country where Aboriginal and treaty rights aren’t being violated by provincial law and policy,” Diabo said.

The Truth Before Reconciliation Network is calling on federal and provincial governments to recognize rights-holders as the primary decision makers, to create a First Nation-based decision process that follows traditional governments, and to require community mandates before legislative changes are made.

“No First Nations-related legislation should proceed without documented community engagement and authorization. Consultation should occur before drafting legislation, not after policy decisions have been made,” Diabo wrote in a missive about the counter-meeting.
Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations are at a crossroads and many chiefs see the meeting as a chance to chart a new path forward.
While the meeting itself is seen as a win by some First Nations leaders, others remained concerned about the format and who will be in the room.
The AFN has a rocky relationship with First Nations in Alberta and chiefs in that province do not have a representative on the advocacy body’s executive council.

Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi told The Canadian Press it’s inappropriate for a “third-party organization” to be sitting alongside the country’s decision-makers instead of grassroots leadership.
“This is an unacceptable process,” he said.

His message is echoed by the chief of Onion Lake Cree Nation, who reportedly filed a cease-and-desist notice to the Assembly of First Nations ahead of the meeting to “make clear that the AFN does not, and cannot, represent, negotiate for or presume consent on behalf of the nation” at the meeting.

“We respect the choices of nations that participate through the AFN, and we expect equal respect for our decision to follow our own path,” said Chief Pete Chief. “The Oct. 26 gathering is about ensuring that the voices and authority of independent treaty nations are not overlooked.”
Woodhouse Nepinak said all First Nations should be heard and she’s thankful First Nations leaders, elders and youth will be in Ottawa to witness it – even those opposed to the meeting.
“I want to move to a point where we can have proper discussions and proper debates on finding the path forward,” she said.
“That’s all we can do, try our best every day.”

stories.title: More than 1,000 rally for publicly funded education in Victoria Park
stories.summary: More than 1,000 people gathered at Victoria Park in downtown London on Saturday to rally in support of publicly funded education.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda, Brent Lale
stories.content:
More than 1,000 people gathered at Victoria Park in downtown London on Saturday to rally in support of publicly funded education.

The rally was part of a province-wide series of events called “Together for Publicly Funded Education,” bringing together teachers, education workers, families and community members to call for increased investment in Ontario’s education system.

Similar rallies were held in Toronto, Ottawa, Sudbury and Thunder Bay.

Organizers say the demonstrations come amid concerns about declining per-student funding, staff recruitment and retention, growing class sizes, school safety and access to special education and mental health supports.

The education unions behind the rallies point to a $6.5-billion funding gap and say schools need more resources to meet students’ needs.

“Ontario’s students deserve schools that are fully funded, fully staffed, and equipped to meet their needs,” said Martha Hradowy, president of the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation.

The unions also raised concerns about provincial control over school boards and the potential effects of the current round of contract negotiations on students and families.

The rally was organized by leaders from Ontario’s major education unions, including the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association, the Association des enseignantes et des enseignants franco-ontariens, the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario and Cupe’s Ontario School Board Council of Unions.

The organizations are calling on the provincial government to invest in classrooms, hire more education workers and provide additional supports for students.

stories.title: B.C. election results: Live numbers from the 2026 vote
stories.summary: British Columbians voted in the 2026 provincial election on Oct. 24. Previously, the provincial election was set to take place in 2028, but David Eby called a snap election.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
B.C. voters probably did not expect to be voting in a provincial election until 2028.

However, BC NDP leader David Eby announced on Sept. 22 that he is calling a snap election , which takes place one week after the 2026 municipal election.

In his speech in September, Eby said “for British Columbians and for Canadians, this is an existential moment. The prime minister has called this a rupture, and he is absolutely right.

“Donald Trump is attacking our workers. He’s targeting our businesses, and he is threatening our sovereignty.”

However, Eby changed his messaging shortly after that announcement , moving away from Trump and to the more traditional issue of housing and affordability.

An Ipsos poll, released on Oct. 13, showed that while the BC Conservatives appeared in disarray one month previously, they gained a five-point lead over the BC NDP .

The BC Conservatives appeared to be in disarray when Eby called the snap election.

On Sept. 20, BC Conservative MLA, Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as leader of the party after 13 MLAs either left or were ousted by party leadership.

Lorne Doerkson took over leadership of the party, with most of the MLAs rejoining .

As the election campaign entered the final week, a new poll showed that the BC Conservatives were leading by five points among decided voters .

BC Green Party leader Emily Lowan performed well in the leaders’ debate, according to experts.

Just after the municipal election results were in, Lowan said: “David Eby called this snap election two years early for nobody but himself.”

Vancouver mayor-elect Pete Fry endorsed Lowan in the final week before election day, and many wonder whether the municipal election’s changes could echo in the provincial race .

Voters will decide who will represent their riding during the upcoming B.C. provincial election on Oct. 24, 2026. Visit this page on election night for a complete breakdown of up-to-the-minute results.

See the graphic below for information on the popular vote.

stories.title: Low voter turnout thus far as St. Thomas mayoral candidates make final push
stories.summary: One last campaign push for the mayoral candidates in St. Thomas, Ont.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
One last campaign push for the mayoral candidates in St. Thomas, Ont.

With just hours left until the city’s electronic voting closes, and nearly 80 per cent of eligible votes up for grabs, councillor Jeff Kohler and his supporters were stationed at one of the busiest intersections in the city.

“We completed our door-to-door a couple of weeks ago because we wanted to make sure that everybody was touched on before the voting started,” said Kohler.

Kohler, 58, served on city council for 22 years going back to 2000 when he was appointed to council.

Three years later he was appointed mayor and won the 2004 race before losing his bid in 2006.

He returned as an alderman/councillor in 2010 and has been at city hall ever since.

“For our message we went with local, capable, proven leadership,” added Kohler.

“The next four years are going to be pretty tough in Saint Thomas. We’ve had some exceptional growth opportunities, but it’s how can we get to that to where we start recouping some of that money? We need to have some experience to lead the way through there.”

While Kohler has the experience at City Hall, across the city a newcomer is looking to get his foot in the door.

27-year-old Aidan Frederick was canvassing to let constituents know his vision for St. Thomas.

Frederick is a software engineering graduate from Western University and an accountant.

“That’s really a part of why I was running to get a younger voice,” said Frederick.

“A different perspective that hasn’t been locked into the system for 20 years.”

Frederick would like to focus on the city’s transit system, specially rail transit. While canvassing he’s hearing different concerns from constituents.

“I think there’s a lot of both concern and excitement about the growth that we’re seeing,” said Frederick.

“A lot of people are wondering how it’s going to affect their day to day. But as well, there’s also this kind of excitement of what new opportunities could bring.”

The third candidate in the campaign is Corey Janzen. His platform says he wants accountability and transparency, cutting useless waste, reducing unnecessary expenses, and public safety.

After the retirement of two-term mayor Joe Preston, the city of St. Thomas will have a new man at the helm for the first time since 2018.

During his tenure Preston took pride in reducing homelessness, building affordable and supportive housing units and bringing major industry.

Nearly 20 years after the closure of the Sterling and Ford plants, the city is once again booming.

The new mayor will have big shoes to fill.

As Preston leaves, St. Thomas is entering one of the most important decades in the city’s history.

“That’s why our slogan is ‘Continue to build on the momentum,’” said Kohler.

“We’ve brought things to a certain level right now, and we want to make sure we continue with that. With affordable housing and the social housing, we need to look at expanding that and expanding it over to seniors as well. We need to make sure we’ve done a great job with our homelessness. We’re recognized nationally for that. But now it’s time to make sure that we include everybody and the diverse housing that we’re promoting is helping that out with affordability.”

Frederick credits the current council with getting the city on the right track, and now he wants to be the one to help carry that momentum.

“We’ve got a pretty good path going forward and a strategic plan to still follow to finish some of the great big things we’ve been working on,” said Frederick.

“With the right council, any mayor should be able to say, hey, ‘Let’s take this step next and then this step next.”

As of late Friday, less than 20 per cent of eligible voters had cast their ballots.

For those who struggle with the electronic voting process in St. Thomas the city has set up in-person voter assistance centres.

Voters can receive help Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. at Elgin Centre at 417 Wellington St. and Monday Oct. 26 from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the St. Thomas Public Library at 153 Curtis St.

After the retirement of two-term mayor Joe Preston, the city of St. Thomas will have a new man at the helm for the first time since 2018.
During his tenure Preston took pride in reducing homelessness, building affordable and supportive housing units and bringing major industry.
Nearly 20 years after the closure of the Sterling and Ford plants, the city is once again booming.
The new mayor will have big shoes to fill.
As Preston leaves, St. Thomas is entering one of the most important decades in the city’s history.
“That’s why our slogan is ‘Continue to build on the momentum,’” said Kohler.

“We’ve brought things to a certain level right now, and we want to make sure we continue with that. With affordable housing and the social housing, we need to look at expanding that and expanding it over to seniors as well. We need to make sure we’ve done a great job with our homelessness. We’re recognized nationally for that. But now it’s time to make sure that we include everybody and the diverse housing that we’re promoting is helping that out with affordability.”

“We’ve got a pretty good path going forward and a strategic plan to still follow to finish some of the great big things we’ve been working on,” said Frederick.
“With the right council, any mayor should be able to say, hey, ‘Let’s take this step next and then this step next.”
As of late Friday, less than 20 per cent of eligible voters had cast their ballots.
For those who struggle with the electronic voting process in St. Thomas the city has set up in-person voter assistance centres.
Voters can receive help Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. at Elgin Centre at 417 Wellington St. and Monday Oct. 26 from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the St. Thomas Public Library at 153 Curtis St.

stories.title: London Knights bounce back with win over Sarnia
stories.summary: The London Knights evened up the season series with rival Sarnia Sting Friday night at Canada Life Place.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights evened up the season series with rival Sarnia Sting Friday night at Canada Life Place.

Sarnia would strike first early, just two minutes into the first period, before London came back with two goals in the span off 29 seconds off sticks from Cohen Bidgood and Thomas Zocco. Jack Van Volsen would tie things up for the Sting late in the first.

Juho Piiparinen gave the Knights the lead just 4:19 into the period, and Thomas Zocco would get his second goal of the game just 18 seconds later, to make it a 5-3 game and chasing Sarnia goaltender Ivan Tkach-Tkachenko.

Knights rookie Kane Barch, who hails from Grand Bend, would give the Knights the insurance marker they needed a few minutes later to make it 6-3. That goal ended up being just what they needed as Sarnia’s Tyler Challenger would score with two minutes left in regulation to make it just a two-goal game.

London would hold on, winning the game by a final score of 6-4. The Knights hit the road Saturday to take on the Owen Sound Attack, puck drop is at 7 p.m.

stories.title: PEI legislature reopens after restoration that took nearly 12 years
stories.summary: Neo-classical building in Charlottetown is best known as the site of intense political negotiations that led to Canada’s founding
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The historic provincial legislature in Charlottetown officially reopened today after an extensive restoration that took almost 12 years to complete.

The neo-classical building, known as Province House, was opened for its first legislative session in 1847, making it the second-oldest legislature in Canada.

It is best known as the site of intense political negotiations in September, 1864 that led to the founding of Canada as a country three years later.

In February, 2014, a report from an engineering firm revealed that the legislature’s foundation was crumbling and part of the building could collapse.

At the time, officials confirmed the they were also dealing with a leaky roof, deteriorating masonry and falling plaster.

In 2015, the building was closed for repairs and the legislative chamber was moved to the Honourable George Coles Building on nearby Richmond Street.

The restoration project encountered several challenges over the years, including delays caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, supply-chain issues, inflated material costs and a shortage of skilled tradespeople.

stories.title: Quebec premier to be absent at First Nations meeting
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec’s new premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, will not attend the First Nations-First Ministers’ Meeting in Ottawa on Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The meeting includes Prime Minister Mark Carney, the premiers of Canada’s provinces and territories, the National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, and other leaders.

It is preceded Sunday by a traditional Indigenous ceremony.

At an unrelated news conference in Montreal on Friday, St-Pierre Plamondon confirmed his absence and explained that he wants to prioritize a different approach with Indigenous peoples.

stories.title: B.C. Election Day Live: The latest news, results and reaction
stories.summary: It's election day in B.C. Bookmark our live-blog and follow along for all the updates, results, and reaction from across the province.
stories.author: Stephanie Ip
stories.content:
It’s election day across B.C.

Voters head to the polls today beginning at 8 a.m. to vote on whether the B.C. NDP keeps its majority hold on the province or if a new party will steer for the next four years.

Once polls close at 8 p.m., results will start to trickle in about who’s in and who’s out across B.C.’s 93 electoral districts.

Bookmark this live-blog and check back throughout the day for coverage of the day’s events, results as they come in, and dispatches from reporters covering ridings across Metro Vancouver.

Two years ago, Elections B.C. used electronic machines to count votes for the first time and was happy with it. This year, with the snap election, the agency says there wasn’t enough time to prepare for a repeat.

The 890,000 cast in the 300 advance polling stations were tabulated by machines and are ready to be released when polls close on Saturday at 8 p.m.

Voters wouldn’t have been able to tell the difference in the voting booth because the ballots look the same and were filled out the same.

The difference May be evident by the rate at which results are finalized and released by Elections B.C. to the public.

B.C. Election 2026: 12 hot topics and where each party stands

B.C. Election 2026: A resource guide before you vote

Chief Electoral Officer Shipra Verma explained to Postmedia the “complex operational logistics” cited in an Election B.C. news release for going back to hand-counting.

The polls are open across B.C. While results won’t be available until after 8 p.m., early turnout over six days leaves some room for concern.

Over six days of advance voting from Oct. 16 to 21, 891,348 voters turned out across B.C., representing about 24 per cent of registered voters. That’s compared with 1,001,331 voters in 2024, or about 28 per cent of registered voters. In almost every riding numbers spiked Saturday, the second day of voting, but ultimately fell short of the 2024 turnout over the full six days.

stories.title: Highway 401 closing overnight for interchange work near London
stories.summary: Highway 401 will be closed in both directions overnight this weekend as crews work on interchange improvements near Colonel Talbot Road.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Highway 401 will be closed in both directions overnight this weekend as crews work on interchange improvements near Colonel Talbot Road.

The Ministry of Transportation says the closure will run from 6 p.m. Saturday to 10 a.m. Sunday to accommodate bridge work.

Westbound drivers will be detoured off Highway 401 at Highway 402 and directed along Highway 402 to Colonel Talbot Road.

Eastbound motorists will exit at Colonel Talbot Road and follow Highway 3 to Wellington Road to return to Highway 401.

Drivers are advised to follow posted detour signs and allow extra time for their trips.

The work is part of ongoing improvements to the Colonel Talbot Road interchange, including road and underground infrastructure, paving on Tempo Road and landscaping as weather permits.

Colonel Talbot Road remains closed between Tempo Road and Glanworth Drive until Friday, Nov. 27.

stories.title: First Nations leaders voice priorities ahead of historic meeting in Ottawa
stories.summary: First Nations leaders are preparing for a historic meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and the nation’s premiers, the first of its kind in more than two decades.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
First Nations leaders are preparing to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney and the nation’s premiers, the first gathering of its kind in more than two decades.

Tensions between First Nations leaders and the Government of Canada have risen since Carney was elected in 2025, including over legislation that was passed to streamline development of major projects.

Some Indigenous leaders criticized the legislation over a lack of consultation, saying it posed a threat to reconciliation.

The Assembly of First Nations has been preparing for the meeting for months by hosting town halls with chiefs to discuss the actions they want to see governments take.

The AFN released a series of position papers last week on economic development, policing and public safety, employment, and health.

One of the main goals for First Nations leaders is a First Nations sovereign wealth fund. The fund, proposed by Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, would pool capital to ensure First Nations can build long-term wealth in their communities.

Other leaders worry that if the meeting focuses solely on economics, other concerns like homelessness, addiction and suicide May not get the attention they deserve.

“Unless the prime minister, the premiers and the territories are going to look a little bit deeper than resource development or economic reconciliation, I worry that they’re not going to be successful with their agenda,” Jeff Copenance, the chief of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, said.

Alberta’s recent referendum shed light on the inclusion of First Nations in decision making after First Nations in the province said there were “unnecessary obstacles” to being able to vote.

Siksika Nation said that while it was pleased with the outcome of the referendum, the polling station in its community was understaffed and it did not receive enough ballots from Elections Alberta.

The Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs (AMC) said it will be bringing its priorities to Ottawa on Monday, with a focus on treaty rights, governance and reconciliation.

The AMC said it will be pressing for action on economic sovereignty while making sure that First Nations are consulted in all decisions affecting them.

“Our Treaties and our alliances with the Crown are agreements between Nations. They are not historical arrangements to be set aside when they become inconvenient,” said Grand Chief Kyra Wilson. “We will not accept a relationship defined by promises without action. We expect to be treated as equal partners, and we expect governments to work with us.”

Manitoba First Nations leaders are voicing their priorities Saturday ahead of the meeting in Ottawa Monday.

stories.title: Cuban envoy asks Canada to renew rejection of U.S. blockade
stories.summary: Canada has backed UN motion calling for end of embargo multiple times
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.

“We are confident that Canada will stay with us, as they have done in the past,” Cuban Ambassador to Canada Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz told The Canadian Press.

“The blockade and this intensification is, in practice, killing people.”

The United Nations is set to vote next week on a motion Cuba has put forward nearly every year since 1992. It calls for the termination of “the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba.”

Canada has voted in favour of this motion multiple times.

U.S. President Donald Trump ’s administration has been trying to overthrow Cuba’s Communist government through a de facto oil blockade. Washington cut off Venezuelan shipments in January and has threatened to impose tariffs on countries that sell oil to the island nation.

Washington claims Cuba poses a national security threat to the United States. Malmierca said the Caribbean nation is being collectively punished by an American pressure campaign that is harming the health and education of Cubans.

An economic crisis has gripped Cuba since 2020, triggering critical shortages and severe blackouts that peaked after January’s fuel blockade.

Havana insists its economic struggles stem from six decades of American sanctions, but critics point to the inefficiency of its Communist regime. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say Cuba’s government engages in arbitrary arrests, tortures political prisoners and limits media and political parties.

Cuba produces only 40 per cent of the fuel it needs. Shortages have led to frequent blackouts that have threatened health care systems and crippled the island’s economy. Air Canada and other airlines cancelled flights to Cuba in February because of shortages of aviation fuel.

Ottawa has pledged to distribute $13 million in humanitarian aid for Cubans through international organizations — not the Cuban government. Past Canadian development funding has gone to things like solar panels aimed at making the island less reliant on foreign fuel.

“The people are resisting because we are convinced that the most valuable thing we have is the independence, the sovereignty of Cuba. And we are not going to surrender that,” Malmierca said.

“We would like to have a normal relationship with the U.S. We are ready for dialogue.”

Malmierca said countries that have supported Cuba have told Havana they’re being warned by Washington their access to American trade or aid could be curbed if they continue supporting UN motions to end the blockade.

He said Cuba is “not naive” and knows Canada is facing its own economic pressure from the Trump administration.

“This year is a particular moment because of all this aggressivity of the U.S. government against Cuba,” he said. “They are in a kind of offensive with other countries, trying to exercise influence for them to change their votes. We know they are using threats.”

The Canadian Press asked the U.S. State Department for comment but didn’t receive a response.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz this week urged countries to vote against the motion, dismissing it as a product of “70 years of propaganda” meant to distract from corruption in Havana. He said Washington has been lobbying European countries to vote against the motion.

“Do not let them abuse your vote for their oppression,” he said at a Monday event he hosted. “Do not give in to this lie.”

In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said it is still pondering how it will vote on the UN motion next week.

“As with all UN resolutions, Canada’s voting position is being considered in advance of the vote,” wrote spokesperson Thida Ith.

“Canada continues to call for the Cuban government to implement needed reforms to respect the political and economic rights of the Cuban people, and to release all political prisoners.”

In July, Havana called for a UN debate on the American embargo in the context of the island’s fuel crisis. Washington suggested it was a waste of resources to debate a motion that had already been debated nine months prior, and insisted that the decision to hold a debate be put to a recorded vote.

The vote passed and a debate was held. Canada was among 30 countries that abstained from the motion on holding a debate.

Civil society groups such as the Canadian Network on Cuba said they fear Ottawa May be pulling back from Cuba.

A document The Canadian Press obtained through a freedom-of-information request shows Ottawa had frank exchanges with Cuba about its liquidity crisis before Trump ramped up pressure on the Communist government.

The document — a briefing book prepared by Global Affairs for its deputy minister — shows the deputy minister met with three Canadian firms during a visit to Havana in February 2023 to discuss their Cuban clients’ unpaid bills.

The document says the aim of the meeting was to reassure the three firms that Ottawa “has their back … without unduly encouraging new investors and traders who risk not being paid for their goods/services.”

The companies mentioned in the document are the National Bank, mining firm Sherritt and hotel chain Blue Diamond, now called Royalton. None of the companies responded to The Canadian Press when asked whether they still have accounts in arrears in Cuba.

Sherritt and Royalton have both ceased operations in Cuba. Havana has blamed their withdrawal on American pressure tactics.

The briefing book for the deputy minister reveals some of the nature of Canada’s discussions with Cuba, with Ottawa pushing for details on small and medium-sized enterprises and Havana requesting more aid.

“Canadian firms are facing mounting payment arrears with Cuban buyers. Many Canadian firms in Cuba are SMEs and the situation is threatening their sustainability,” reads the February 2023 document for the deputy minister.

“We sought bilateral meetings for you, that would allow you, for example, to engage on human rights and new economic actors (private sector SMEs and entrepreneurs). The Cuban side wanted rather to talk to you about new tourism initiatives and more Canadian international development projects.”

The briefing book proposed that Canada “leverage Cuba’s desire for increased assistance in our dialogue on other priorities (e.g. human rights)” — but added that the cheapest and most effective things Canada could offer would be technical help with reforming the agriculture sector and rules for smaller businesses.

Malmierca said Cuba is implementing 176 reform measures which came out of parliamentary and public consultations. He said these measures will allow a larger role for the private sector, foreign investment incentives and municipal autonomy.

“In Cuba, we work according to the rule of law,” he said. “Cuba is a society that is continuously trying to improve.”

He said a trade fair in Havana next month is going largely virtual due to the current electricity shortages, and Cuba will hold an event in Toronto ahead of time to drum up interest from Canadian entrepreneurs.

“We can maintain not only the economic relationship, but we can increase it in better conditions in the near future.”

stories.title: B.C. election: How a little-known interim Conservative leader could become premier today
stories.summary: The premier is poised to get unseated in the Oct. 24 election by the relatively unknown Lorne Doerkson following a gaffe-ridden campaign.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
British Columbia voters headed to the polls on Saturday, closing out an unusually turbulent election period that could see the Conservative party take power in a surprising upset, potentially unseating the province’s NDP premier following his highly unpopular snap election call.

Polling just before election day showed Eby’s NDP trailing the British Columbia Conservative Party and its interim leader, Lorne Doerkson, by a narrow margin, with the final result too close to call.

Saturday’s result could see the largely unknown Doerkson, a former rodeo announcer and newspaper publisher, take over the role of premier at a critical juncture in Western Canadian politics. In a recent Leger poll, 44 per cent of decided voters said they would support the Conservatives, while 39 per cent said they would support the NDP. Polling outfit The Writ projected the Conservatives to take 45.7 per cent of the vote, compared with 41.2 per cent for the NDP and 10.8 per cent for the Greens.

stories.title: ‘Always try to buy Canadian’: Retailers see demand for Canadian Halloween products grow
stories.summary: Every time Suzie Wisniewski grocery shops, she looks for Canadian products. For her and many Canadians that sentiment is no different when it comes to buying sweet treats for Halloween.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – Every time Suzie Wisniewski grocery shops, she looks for Canadian products. For her and many Canadians that sentiment is no different when it comes to buying sweet treats for Halloween.

“I always like to try to buy Canadian where I can,” she said, while shopping for candy at Winnipeg’s Food Fare grocery store.

“It’s important for me to support the country.”

A recent online survey conducted by Angus Reid for NextDoor Canada shows a majority of Canadians are on the same page as Wisniewski.

The survey shows 59 per cent of Canadians say it’s a priority to support local or Canadian businesses when shopping for or celebrating Halloween, from pumpkins picked at nearby farms to costumes from neighbourhood shops and treats from local bakeries.

That number is higher in Saskatchewan and Manitoba at 68 per cent, and 69 per cent in Atlantic Canada.

“My neighbours next door are not very nice,” Wisniewski said, referring to the United States. “(They) don’t have very nice leaders, so I choose not to support them if at all possible.”

The push to “buy Canadian” has resurfaced over the last several months, in light of tariff tensions between Canada and the United States.

Food Fare owner, Ramsey Zeid, has placed “Made in Canada” stickers all along his store’s shelves, to help consumers identify which products are Canadian.

Halloween revives buy Canadian sentiment

But he says it’s a little challenging when it comes to Halloween candy and treats.

“I haven’t seen any Canadian-made Halloween candies but certainly see a lot of candies that say prepared in Canada,” he said.

“You’re kind of limited to your choices, right? You got your Coffee Crisps, Aeros, your Oh Henry, your Twizzlers, Nerds, that kind of stuff, and little bags of chips.”

Zeid says sourcing local products and stocking them for Halloween can also be difficult, particularly because the store doesn’t put a significant focus on seasonal candy.

“Halloween comes around once a year. It’s hard for a business to start up and prepare all these candies and invest all this money for one day a year,” he said.

“So, unless you have a consistent supply of other candies for the rest of the year, it’s hard to do it for just the one day of the year.”

Sylvain Charlebois is director of the Agri-Food Analytics Lab at Dalhousie University. He says that while many familiar Halloween treats are manufactured in Canada, their ingredients and ownership May be foreign.

“There are very Canadian options out there, but they’re typically more expensive, but most candies that’ll be given out are manufactured in Canada, but most of them are foreign companies, and many of them are American companies,” Charlebois said.

“If I am a Canadian-focused shopper for Halloween, I would look around because sometimes some of these products are great, even healthy, but they’re not advertised.”

“You need to work a little harder to find them, and sometimes they’re in a pharmacy or in independent stores as well,” he said.

As Canadians fill their bowls for trick-or-treaters, the challenge facing shoppers is finding options that are both Canadian-made and budget-friendly.

The same online survey conducted for NextDoor Canada found that 88 per cent of Canadians plan to spend less than $100 on Halloween this year and about 65 per cent of Canadians set their Halloween budget at less than $50.

stories.title: For Antoni Cimolino, leaving the Stratford Festival is such sweet sorrow
stories.summary: The outgoing artistic director is saying farewell after nearly 40 years. It’s been one heck of a love story, Aisling Murphy reports
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Antoni Cimolino pats his chest for emphasis. Ba-dum. Ba-dum. Ba-dum. The gesture is part and parcel of learning the text of William Shakespeare; actors usually do it to capture the rhythm of iambic pentameter, which, when executed correctly, makes the Bard’s language feel like a heartbeat.

At the top of today’s rehearsal, however, Cimolino is making a point about accents. The cast of Saturday, Sunday, Monday , an Italian family drama set in Naples and the last play Cimolino will helm as the Stratford Festival’s artistic director, will not be using them. But certain words need to be said a certain way, he says with a wry smile: ragù, mamma and papà had better be stressed in the right spot.

A gold wedding band glints on his ring finger as he gesticulates, his decades of research into Italian playwright Eduardo De Filippo spilling into the room.

In the buttery sunlight of the rehearsal hall, it’s not particularly clear if Cimolino, 65, has yet made peace with his decision to leave the Stratford Festival. Saturday, Sunday, Monday will play its final performance at the Avon Theatre on Oct. 24; his official last day will be Nov. 15.

In his preamble to the play’s first table read, his eyes ever-so-subtly glimmer as he speaks. Today marks a difficult milestone: It’s his final first day of rehearsal in the top job. He’s been in the position for 14 years, but the 39 seasons he’s spent working for the festival in different capacities have constituted more than 80 per cent of his adulthood. It’s a tough goodbye to swallow, no matter how long he’s had to get used to it.

But for a blissful afternoon, there is only the work at hand – the play, the actors and the promise of telling an audience a story that will somehow change how they see the world.

After rehearsal, Cimolino slips out a side door, his script tucked under his jacket. His steely dark curls – the same ones that in 1992 made him such a dashing Romeo – bounce as he walks toward Ontario Street. Cimolino officially announced his departure last summer, but he was ready to leave in 2024.

The renovated Tom Patterson Theatre, perhaps Cimolino’s greatest achievement as the festival’s artistic director, was open and operational; the worst impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, for the most part, had come and gone. After 37 years at the Stratford Festival – as an actor, director, administrator and devoted figurehead – he could see a finish line. He was ready to spend more time with his wife and children; he’d missed enough dinners and birthdays.

He agreed to do two more years, emphatic that the contract extension would be his last. There was no pay bump or perk that made delaying his plans any less of a sacrifice. “They wanted me to stay. I stayed,” he recalls.

The intervening years weren’t easy. The company sold fewer tickets in 2024 than in 2023, but then excelled in 2025, with 482,579 tickets distributed across the longest season in festival history. That same year, the company completed a lengthy search process, and landed on Jonathan Church, a highly respected British theatre producer, as Cimolino’s successor.

Church has moved into the office Cimolino once shared with executive director Anita Gaffney. Next year’s season has been announced. For better or worse, the stage is set for Stratford’s next act.

Cimolino’s first act took place in Sudbury, Ont., where he was born in 1961, the second child of working-class Italian parents Gino and Vera Cimolino. His father was a construction foreman; his mother worked in housekeeping at a local hospital.

He didn’t speak a word of English until kindergarten. But in high school, he became a master of public speaking, a debate team captain whose assertive baritone would become his defining hallmark as an actor. For a while, he and his family thought he’d grow up to be a lawyer.

Then came the Stratford Festival.

The first few Stratford shows he saw – Candide in 1978, Richard II in 1979 – didn’t do much for teenage Cimolino. But the 1979 production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the 1,833-seat Festival Theatre stopped him in his tracks. “The theatre itself kind of blew my mind,” he says. “The spatial relationship, the way we were all so focused on the play. There was this connection between them onstage and us in the audience. I’m still in awe of that.”

He was going to be an actor at the Stratford Festival. He’d make sure of it. His parents didn’t quite share his enthusiasm when he told them of his chosen life path – “that was a profoundly unhappy day” in the Cimolino household, he recalls with some amusement – but he was determined to find his way to the festival. He enrolled in the University of Windsor’s acting program, and a few years later graduated from the school with a diploma and the woman who would become his wife, fellow actor Brigit Wilson.

But Stratford didn’t wait for him. His first few auditions for the company were unsuccessful – he wanted it too badly, he recalls. That audition experience coloured how he later hired young actors at the festival. “The theatre doesn’t always take what you have,” he says. “It takes what it needs. That’s hard for a young actor to learn. But you have to learn it.”

In 1988, he finally made it in. Actor Seana McKenna remembers a day they shared on stationary bikes the following year, when he seemed unsure if he’d stay at the festival long term. “We really didn’t have that much to do,” she shares of those early acting years with a laugh.

Obviously, he stuck it out. According to actor Lucy Peacock, he was charming and funny, one of the few young artists who would show up for the festival’s voluntary warm-ups. “He had the commitment and that wish to grow and learn,” she recalls. “He was a fine actor, playful and skilled and willing – he always wanted to know what he could do to help.”

Cimolino’s Romeo in 1992 marked an apex in his acting career – he was recognized for playing the role even when he travelled abroad. He was handsome, hardworking and hungry to improve: If he’d wanted to, he could have played plenty more Romeos.

But according to actor Colm Feore, who played Mercutio alongside Cimolino’s Romeo, the future figurehead wasn’t interested in that. On days off from his own rehearsals, Cimolino snuck into others’, watching how productions came together across the festival. “He wanted to know how the magic happens,” Feore says. “He wanted to look behind the curtain, and when he did, he found that far more attractive than standing in front of it.”

Richard Monette, artistic director of the Stratford Festival from 1994 until 2007, was Cimolino’s professional mentor, but their relationship was deeper than that: Monette was a doting godfather to Cimolino’s children Sophia and Gabriele. At the festival, the men were close to inseparable; Cimolino served as Stratford’s executive director, Monette’s operational counterpart, from 1998 until 2006.

Over cardamom buns and crisp Diet Cokes at Stratford’s Café Bouffon, Cimolino – who admits that the attention around his departure this year has made him squirm – lights up when asked about Monette.

“Many of the directors at that time were autocratic, kind of cruel and humiliating,” Cimolino explains of Monette’s specific breed of leadership. “Richard didn’t do that. He was gentler.” Monette taught Cimolino to be careful with actors’ feelings during curtain calls – where people bow, and when, can carry unintended commentary on their performance, he says. Monette showed him how and when to deal in compassion rather than power.

Monette’s sudden passing in 2008, from a pulmonary embolism, was crushing: “I was a fan, and I really believed in him,” Cimolino says. Monette was generous to a fault – he once surprised company actor Sara Topham, who was honeymooning in Paris with her husband, with a lavish meal at the Eiffel Tower.

Sometimes Cimolino witnessed company members taking advantage of Monette’s kindness, and it made his blood boil, he confides. Those who treated Monette poorly were not invited back under Cimolino’s tenure. “There’s always been that sense of justice in my heart,” he says.

Monette served as artistic director of the Stratford Festival for 14 years – the exact same amount of time as Cimolino.

Owing to a tumultuous string of leadership debacles, the years that followed Monette’s retirement were among the festival’s most chaotic. Cimolino, however, was on an upward trajectory: After his nine-year stint as the company’s executive director, he was named general director in 2006.

The Stratford Festival, looking to shake things up, replaced Monette with a triumvirate structure in which three directors – Des McAnuff, Marti Maraden and Don Shipley – would co-lead the company. It ultimately proved disastrous. Conflicts were regularly reported by the press; programming choices betrayed a lack of unity within the festival’s leadership team. “It wasn’t an easy thing, it wasn’t a happy thing,” Cimolino says. “I failed to keep the group together. Everyone wanted the same thing – these were good people, talented people.”

Things became calmer – sort of – when Maraden and Shipley resigned in 2008. McAnuff, whose splashy approach to Shakespeare and musical theatre divided festival audiences and critics, became the company’s sole artistic director. Cimolino stayed on as general director. “We worked well together,” McAnuff says. “He had a natural talent for administration.”

In 2011, McAnuff announced he’d stay until the end of the 2013 season. From there, the job was Cimolino’s to lose. In 2010, Cimolino had been the founding chair of Culture Days, a nationwide celebration of arts and culture in Canada; for decades, he’d made clear his investment and belief in the arts, with Stratford as an epicentre for them.

A search was done; the requisite hiring protocols were followed. But most everyone knew the Cimolino era was coming. He was the obvious choice, a gifted director who knew where all the company’s bodies were buried. He remained calm in a crisis; to this day, he’s not known to yell. (“There were times he could have been a bit more forceful,” says board chair Larry Stevenson, otherwise praising Cimolino’s composure.)

On March 10, 2012, a new world order was announced. Antoni Cimolino was the Stratford Festival’s next artistic director.

Thirty-nine years is one hell of a love story. But like any great love affair, Cimolino’s has had bumps: He’s keenly aware of the time he missed with his children Gabriele and Sophia, now 33 and 30, when they were growing up. He can list by heart the vacations that became overwhelmed by media interviews, most often following deaths of long-time company members back home.

In 2020, Cimolino drew criticism for how the Stratford Festival had historically treated its Black employees. Black artists, including E.B. Smith, spoke out against “as cast” contracts which, prior to rehearsals, gave actors little insight into how they might be used – or tokenized – in a given production.

In June of that year, the festival released a statement underscoring its “complicity in unjust systems,” and committed to continuously evolving its understanding of anti-racism, but Cimolino knows that response could and should have come sooner. He wishes, too, that he had reached out more intentionally to artists struggling with mental-health issues during the pandemic lockdowns. He wonders often what more the festival could have done to support its most vulnerable employees during such an unspeakably lonely time.

Indeed, the pandemic was awful – it’s not an era Cimolino enjoys remembering. He spent those early months of COVID calling donors, taking walks around the river with friends and quietly fretting about the future of the festival. Prior to March, 2020, he’d never considered even the possibility of cancelling a season outright.

“I watched him go through hell,” says Wilson, his wife and a contracted actor during the season lost to COVID. The day Broadway went dark was a hard one, she says; the evening Cimolino told her she no longer needed to worry about learning her lines for the summer was worse. He and executive director Gaffney were worked to the bone, each toiling around the clock to ensure the festival could someday reopen in full swing.

At home, Cimolino and Wilson snatched moments of lightness where they could find them. “All of a sudden I looked over and there was a man beside me on the couch watching Netflix,” Wilson says. “I said, ‘Who are you?’ He said, ‘I’m your husband.’” Before long, their house was overtaken by recording equipment and ring lights. Cimolino’s hours were somehow even longer than they’d already been. But they could chat between Zoom calls.

“He loves so many things – his family, mainly. He’s made huge sacrifices for the amount of time he’s given to the place, but there has never been any doubt in my mind that his family has come first,” says Donna Feore, a close friend and the festival’s artistic associate for musical theatre development. “Is he hardworking? Yes. But a workaholic? No, I don’t think so.”

Against the odds, the festival muddled through the pandemic, and even launched the digital streaming service Stratfest@Home. Cimolino is widely credited with keeping the festival afloat through his fundraising and advocacy work in 2020. “Stratford is really connected to Antoni,” says Larry McCabe, a restaurateur and Stratford city councillor. “Without him, I don’t think we’d be sitting in such a robust and thriving city.”

For the next year – the first step on the long road to achieving balance – he’ll be travelling in theatre-free bliss. Long visits with his children in Taiwan and Halifax are on the books, plus a big trip to Cyprus. He’s counting down the days to his granddaughter Penelope’s first Christmas. He plans to binge the works of Cormac McCarthy, and, hey, he might even watch Heated Rivalry . He’ll finally have the time.

Just don’t let him hear you say he’s retiring. He’ll likely be back as a guest director at the Stratford Festival, and he and his wife have no plans to move elsewhere. The decimation of theatre education in this country is on his radar; so too is the lack of training available for mid-career artists looking to deepen their practice. The Stratford Festival’s Antoni Cimolino Excellence Fund – a small piece of his legacy which aims to provide cross-training funding for Canadian theatre artists, among other things – will help plug that gap.

But Cimolino knows intimately that the festival will always need more – more money, more time, more staff, more shows. He’ll forever feel a pull to the place, just as he’ll forever treasure his time in rehearsal: Memories such as sharing luxe chocolates with actors and goofing off in the cavernous Festival Theatre are among his favourites.

When we reach the end of our final interview, he brings his hand to his chest before shaking my hand goodbye. He’s not correcting an accent or scanning a passage of Shakespeare’s poetry; there’s something deeper to the gesture. More personal.

Once more, I see evidence of that iambic heartbeat – Cimolino’s, the festival’s, the city’s – its tempo decelerating for the first time in close to four decades.

Today marks a difficult milestone: It’s his final first day of rehearsal in the top job. He’s been in the position for 14 years, but the 39 seasons he’s spent working for the festival in different capacities have constituted more than 80 per cent of his adulthood. It’s a tough goodbye to swallow, no matter how long he’s had to get used to it.

content_blocks.text: But for a blissful afternoon, there is only the work at hand – the play, the actors and the promise of telling an audience a story that will somehow change how they see the world.

content_blocks.text: After rehearsal, Cimolino slips out a side door, his script tucked under his jacket. His steely dark curls – the same ones that in 1992 made him such a dashing Romeo – bounce as he walks toward Ontario Street. For 14 summers, the city’s shops and restaurants have relied on his programming to attract tourists to the 33,000-person town; it’s almost as if the storefronts stand a little straighter when he passes.

content_blocks.text: The renovated Tom Patterson Theatre, perhaps Cimolino’s greatest achievement as the festival’s artistic director, was open and operational; the worst impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, for the most part, had come and gone. After 37 years at the Stratford Festival – as an actor, director, administrator and devoted figurehead – he could see a finish line. He was ready to spend more time with his wife and children; he’d missed enough dinners and birthdays.

content_blocks.text: But the Stratford Festival’s board disagreed. The company was still recovering from the pandemic, and no one but Cimolino could be trusted to steer the ship through whatever came next. He agreed to do two more years, emphatic that the contract extension would be his last. There was no pay bump or perk that made delaying his plans any less of a sacrifice. “They wanted me to stay. I stayed,” he recalls.

content_blocks.text: The intervening years weren’t easy. The company sold fewer tickets in 2024 than in 2023, but then excelled in 2025, with 482,579 tickets distributed across the longest season in festival history. That same year, the company completed a lengthy search process, and landed on Jonathan Church, a highly respected British theatre producer, as Cimolino’s successor.

content_blocks.text: Cimolino’s first act took place in Sudbury, Ont., where he was born in 1961, the second child of working-class Italian parents Gino and Vera Cimolino. His father was a construction foreman; his mother worked in housekeeping at a local hospital.

content_blocks.text: He didn’t speak a word of English until kindergarten. But in high school, he became a master of public speaking, a debate team captain whose assertive baritone would become his defining hallmark as an actor. For a while, he and his family thought he’d grow up to be a lawyer.

content_blocks.text: Then came the Stratford Festival.

content_blocks.text: The first few Stratford shows he saw – Candide in 1978, Richard II in 1979 – didn’t do much for teenage Cimolino. But the 1979 production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the 1,833-seat Festival Theatre stopped him in his tracks. “The theatre itself kind of blew my mind,” he says. “The spatial relationship, the way we were all so focused on the play. There was this connection between them onstage and us in the audience. I’m still in awe of that.”

content_blocks.text: He was going to be an actor at the Stratford Festival. He’d make sure of it. His parents didn’t quite share his enthusiasm when he told them of his chosen life path – “that was a profoundly unhappy day” in the Cimolino household, he recalls with some amusement – but he was determined to find his way to the festival. He enrolled in the University of Windsor’s acting program, and a few years later graduated from the school with a diploma and the woman who would become his wife, fellow actor Brigit Wilson.

content_blocks.text: But Stratford didn’t wait for him. His first few auditions for the company were unsuccessful – he wanted it too badly, he recalls. That audition experience coloured how he later hired young actors at the festival. “The theatre doesn’t always take what you have,” he says. “It takes what it needs. That’s hard for a young actor to learn. But you have to learn it.”

content_blocks.text: In 1988, he finally made it in. Actor Seana McKenna remembers a day they shared on stationary bikes the following year, when he seemed unsure if he’d stay at the festival long term. “We really didn’t have that much to do,” she shares of those early acting years with a laugh.

content_blocks.text: Obviously, he stuck it out. According to actor Lucy Peacock, he was charming and funny, one of the few young artists who would show up for the festival’s voluntary warm-ups. “He had the commitment and that wish to grow and learn,” she recalls. “He was a fine actor, playful and skilled and willing – he always wanted to know what he could do to help.”

content_blocks.text: Cimolino’s Romeo in 1992 marked an apex in his acting career – he was recognized for playing the role even when he travelled abroad. He was handsome, hardworking and hungry to improve: If he’d wanted to, he could have played plenty more Romeos.

content_blocks.text: But according to actor Colm Feore, who played Mercutio alongside Cimolino’s Romeo, the future figurehead wasn’t interested in that. On days off from his own rehearsals, Cimolino snuck into others’, watching how productions came together across the festival. “He wanted to know how the magic happens,” Feore says. “He wanted to look behind the curtain, and when he did, he found that far more attractive than standing in front of it.”

At the festival, the men were close to inseparable; Cimolino served as Stratford’s executive director, Monette’s operational counterpart, from 1998 until 2006.

content_blocks.text: “Many of the directors at that time were autocratic, kind of cruel and humiliating,” Cimolino explains of Monette’s specific breed of leadership. “Richard didn’t do that. He was gentler.” Monette taught Cimolino to be careful with actors’ feelings during curtain calls – where people bow, and when, can carry unintended commentary on their performance, he says. Monette showed him how and when to deal in compassion rather than power.

content_blocks.text: Monette’s sudden passing in 2008, from a pulmonary embolism, was crushing: “I was a fan, and I really believed in him,” Cimolino says. Monette was generous to a fault – he once surprised company actor Sara Topham, who was honeymooning in Paris with her husband, with a lavish meal at the Eiffel Tower.

content_blocks.text: Owing to a tumultuous string of leadership debacles, the years that followed Monette’s retirement were among the festival’s most chaotic. Cimolino, however, was on an upward trajectory: After his nine-year stint as the company’s executive director, he was named general director in 2006.

content_blocks.text: The Stratford Festival, looking to shake things up, replaced Monette with a triumvirate structure in which three directors – Des McAnuff, Marti Maraden and Don Shipley – would co-lead the company. It ultimately proved disastrous. Conflicts were regularly reported by the press; programming choices betrayed a lack of unity within the festival’s leadership team. “It wasn’t an easy thing, it wasn’t a happy thing,” Cimolino says. “I failed to keep the group together. Everyone wanted the same thing – these were good people, talented people.”

content_blocks.text: Things became calmer – sort of – when Maraden and Shipley resigned in 2008. McAnuff, whose splashy approach to Shakespeare and musical theatre divided festival audiences and critics, became the company’s sole artistic director. Cimolino stayed on as general director. “We worked well together,” McAnuff says. “He had a natural talent for administration.”

content_blocks.text: In 2011, McAnuff announced he’d stay until the end of the 2013 season. From there, the job was Cimolino’s to lose. In 2010, Cimolino had been the founding chair of Culture Days, a nationwide celebration of arts and culture in Canada; for decades, he’d made clear his investment and belief in the arts, with Stratford as an epicentre for them.

content_blocks.text: A search was done; the requisite hiring protocols were followed. But most everyone knew the Cimolino era was coming. He was the obvious choice, a gifted director who knew where all the company’s bodies were buried. He remained calm in a crisis; to this day, he’s not known to yell. (“There were times he could have been a bit more forceful,” says board chair Larry Stevenson, otherwise praising Cimolino’s composure.)

content_blocks.text: Thirty-nine years is one hell of a love story. But like any great love affair, Cimolino’s has had bumps: He’s keenly aware of the time he missed with his children Gabriele and Sophia, now 33 and 30, when they were growing up. He can list by heart the vacations that became overwhelmed by media interviews, most often following deaths of long-time company members back home.

Smith, spoke out against “as cast” contracts which, prior to rehearsals, gave actors little insight into how they might be used – or tokenized – in a given production.

content_blocks.text: In June of that year, the festival released a statement underscoring its “complicity in unjust systems,” and committed to continuously evolving its understanding of anti-racism, but Cimolino knows that response could and should have come sooner. He wishes, too, that he had reached out more intentionally to artists struggling with mental-health issues during the pandemic lockdowns. He wonders often what more the festival could have done to support its most vulnerable employees during such an unspeakably lonely time.

content_blocks.text: Indeed, the pandemic was awful – it’s not an era Cimolino enjoys remembering. He spent those early months of COVID calling donors, taking walks around the river with friends and quietly fretting about the future of the festival. Prior to March, 2020, he’d never considered even the possibility of cancelling a season outright.

Long visits with his children in Taiwan and Halifax are on the books, plus a big trip to Cyprus. He’s counting down the days to his granddaughter Penelope’s first Christmas. He plans to binge the works of Cormac McCarthy, and, hey, he might even watch Heated Rivalry . He’ll finally have the time.

content_blocks.text: Just don’t let him hear you say he’s retiring. He’ll likely be back as a guest director at the Stratford Festival, and he and his wife have no plans to move elsewhere. The decimation of theatre education in this country is on his radar; so too is the lack of training available for mid-career artists looking to deepen their practice. The Stratford Festival’s Antoni Cimolino Excellence Fund – a small piece of his legacy which aims to provide cross-training funding for Canadian theatre artists, among other things – will help plug that gap.
