stories.title: Alberta’s vote has softened the rhetoric, but peace and quiet are not guaranteed
stories.summary: Danielle Smith emerges into a fractious fight to keep her position, as Carney seeks ways to move his agenda forward
stories.author: Nathan VanderKlippe, Carrie Tait
stories.content:
For anyone looking, it was right there in bold text: white on blue, a message affixed to the front of the lectern Alberta Premier Danielle Smith used to speak two days after her province overwhelmingly rejected the pursuit of separatism.

“Stronger Alberta within a United Canada,” the text read. It was a new formulation of a familiar refrain for Ms. Smith, who has spent years agitating about Alberta’s place in Canada. Her government passed an “Alberta Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act.” The ranks of her United Conservative Party swelled with separatists. She lowered the signature threshold for citizens to petition lawmakers to consider a proposed referendum question, clearing the way for a campaign that ushered those separatists into a bright international spotlight.

But when Ms. Smith spoke this week, the word “sovereignty” was gone from the lectern, and with it – perhaps, if she can navigate the stormy political waters she herself had a hand in creating – the turmoil of a lengthy chapter in which some in Alberta loudly threatened the breakup of Confederation, until Albertans themselves made clear they had no interest.

“That was quite notable. She was sending a clear signal,” said Monte Solberg, the former Conservative cabinet minister who now leads New West Public Affairs, an influential government relations firm in Calgary. A restive Alberta moment, one in which Ms. Smith had sought to appease both separatists and federalists in her own party, “was over,” he said. “Albertans want to move on. They want some optimism. They want to work with the federal government.”

Out with the strident language, in with co-operative federalism. Out with demands to rip apart and remake the constitution, in with the slow business of talking out change and building new things, Edmonton and Ottawa together with other provinces. Out with “sovereign,” in with “stronger.”

That, at least, is one hope.

But none of this presages peace and quiet. Ms. Smith has found, like generations of Western leaders before her, that stoking anger at Ottawa is a potent political tool. Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, must find a way to calm the political headwinds while showing he is willing to work with Ms. Smith and wrest productive gains from a province where loud voices continue to advocate rupture – all while this country’s largest trading partner continues to inflict economic damage.

Even so, with millions marking ballots this week – in Alberta’s referendum and, on Saturday, in a British Columbia provincial election – the landscape of Western politics could be remade.

Mr. Carney has shown himself eager to spur economic growth, abandoning his predecessor’s desire to cap Alberta’s petroleum production; some Albertans, meanwhile, have taken to calling themselves “Carney conservatives.” British Columbians are choosing a new government, making choices that could alter tensions over the export of energy resources through the province. And three-quarters of Albertans said they wish to remain in Canada, raising a new possibility of snuffing the destructive flame of separatism in the province.

None of this, however, is a foregone conclusion.

Inside Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party, separatist sentiment remains strong. In late November, the party will hold an annual general meeting in which members will elect nearly half the provincial board – and leading independence advocates are gunning for control of the seats.

Ms. Smith said this week that she expects, from this moment on, that party representatives must be committed to Canada. But separatists, beaten in the referendum, are girding to continue their fight for independence by exerting more control over the party, from the provincial executive to its most grassroots level, the constituency associations. If they act in sufficient numbers, they can force a review of Ms. Smith’s leadership.

“It will be a pitched battle,” Mr. Solberg said.

Alberta may have chosen Canada. But it’s no longer clear Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party will continue to choose her. The premier has emerged from the referendum into a fractious fight to hold onto her position.

It is fight for federalism, and for Ms. Smith’s political life. It is a fight for the future of the united conservative movement. And it is a fight to wrestle into submission the fervid forces of separatism as they change course, pursuing a political path to splitting apart the country.

“There’s lots of things that could go wrong,” Mr. Solberg said.

After months of organizing from Edmonton to small-town Alberta, separatists held their referendum night watch party at the Alt Hotel in Calgary. They did not get the result they hoped for. Leah Hennel/The Globe and Mail

Two generations ago, Jacques Parizeau brought the country to within a breath of cracking apart. Mr. Parizeau was a scion of family wealth, an economist who interned at the Bank of Canada, then worked to foment Quebec’s Quiet Revolution from behind the scenes.

As a younger man, though, he “didn’t like politics. He found it difficult, he found it tough,” recalled Jean Royer, who served as Mr. Parizeau’s influential chief of staff.

But the secessionist leader who would rise to become premier came early to a realization that he could not succeed outside the halls of the legislature. To achieve sovereignty, he had to accept “the rules of the game. And the rules of the game are to participate in parliamentary debate,” Mr. Royer said in an interview this week.

It was under Mr. Parizeau that Quebec nearly said yes to secession during its 1995 referendum.

Three decades later, his example has taken on new relevance in Canada’s west.

“In my opinion,” Mr. Royer said, “the best way to demonstrate legitimacy is running in an election with a platform.”

Alberta’s separatists, led by a competing collection of lawyers, podcasters, a farmer and a guns-and-sports shop owner, lost in this week’s referendum, garnering roughly 25 per cent of valid votes. Now some want to capture their province’s governing party, to force it to advance their cause.

To have a shot at getting independence-minded candidates on the ballot under the UCP banner, let alone elected, the separatists have to control the party’s internal machinery. Succeed in that, and they can once again make secession an Alberta priority.

Podcasters Jason Lavigne and Chris Scott hopscotched the province ahead of Monday’s referendum, urging Albertans to vote in favour of instigating the legal process necessary to hold a binding vote on secession.

Now, both intend to compete for seats on the UCP’s provincial board, in races party members will vote on next month at the party’s annual general meeting.

Attendance at the annual convention has swelled in recent years after conservative activists on the party’s right flank recognized they could exert greater control over government if they elected board members who shared their worldview. Ms. Smith last week said roughly 6,900 UCP members already purchased early-bird tickets.

For the Premier, the imperative is to outflank the separatists. She began this week by withdrawing the welcome mat.

“A strong Alberta within a united Canada is the position of our party and our government,” Ms. Smith said in a video released Wednesday, striking the word “sovereign” from her catchphrase to align with the message furnishing her lectern that same day.

UCP candidates, MLAs, provincial board members and constituency association representatives must uphold this position, she said. “If they want to be in a position of representing our party in an official role,” Ms. Smith told reporters, “there has to be a commitment that they also accept the result of the mandate that Albertans gave us.”

Ms. Smith wants to align her party’s values with the outcome of the province-wide referendum, shielding the UCP from being associated with separatism, particularly as it looks toward a provincial election in 2027. The premier refused to say whether she or the party would disqualify those who do not comply. For now, she said she is asking people to use “self-reflection” to determine their future in the party.

Her call for loyalty, if followed, would force out prominent independence advocates with sizable influence in the party. Mitch Sylvestre, who spearheaded a petition to get a separation question on the referendum ballot, is the president of a UCP constituency association in northeast Alberta and one of the party’s most valuable fundraisers. Tanya Clemens co-chaired Let Alberta Decide, a prominent separatist organization, and is one of the party’s local directors in the Highwood constituency, which in September voted in favour of reviewing Ms. Smith’s leadership.

The Premier’s instructions will almost certainly inflame the battle for control of the UCP’s provincial board.

Wrestling separatism into submission, in other words, is unlikely to prove easy.

Mr. Sylvestre, in an online meeting Thursday evening, showed no sign of retreat. He painted Ms. Smith’s loyalty test as a “direct attack” on him and blamed her for the widening the fissures in the already fractured organization.

“She’s telling us to pick between her and Alberta independence,” Mr. Sylvestre said, noting Ms. Smith said there would not be another secession referendum as long as she is Premier. “I am not splitting this party up. Who split this party up? Danielle Smith split this party up. Period. End of conversation.”

He urged followers to flock to the UCP’s annual meeting, support the slate of board candidates he intends to endorse, and agitate to force a review to oust Ms. Smith.

“You have to be in the room with power to address power, and if you want to get your way, there’s no other path here, unless we get into government,” he said.

As Alberta lurches from referendum to an internal party clash, Ms. Smith’s task in enforcing her new federalist decree will also be complicated by something she may not have anticipated.

In this new contest for Alberta, language suddenly matters. Sorting conservative activists into tidy piles will be difficult. Separatists, said Mr. Lavigne, the podcaster, believe secession is the only way to resolve Alberta’s beef with Ottawa, while sovereigntists believe independence is one of many potential solutions. “I really don’t know how you would be able to determine where the line would be between sovereigntist and separatist,” he said.

Sorting friend from foe by preferred labels stands to amplify the UCP’s raging identity crisis, an internal fight with implications for the party, province and rest of the country.

Both Mr. Lavigne and Mr. Scott use the word “sovereignty” the way Ms. Smith once did, to describe a province determining its own future, free from Ottawa’s overreach. “I’m not a separatist. I’m not a federalist,” Mr. Scott said in an interview this week. “I believe in a sovereign Alberta.”

Mr. Scott, who rose to prominence when he refused to shutter his rural café during the COVID-19 pandemic and founded Let’s Talk Alberta, said his preference is for the province to stay in Canada, consistent with Ms. Smith’s vision. However, Mr. Scott thinks independence is the only clear path for Alberta to achieve sovereignty.

He thinks the Premier is making a mistake by trying to dissuade separatists from vying for power inside the party. If she wants party unity, he said, she could get there by returning to her sovereigntist roots, by revving up the effort to extract Alberta from the Canada Pension Plan and taking control over immigration into the province, for example.

“If they block somebody like me because of my views on sovereignty, that would make them disingenuous,” he said. “Because you can’t, out of one side of your mouth, say you believe in Alberta sovereignty, and from the other side say: ‘Hey, you believe in Alberta sovereignty, so you need to get out of our party.’”

Rural communities such as Mossleigh, Airdrie and Okotoks were more likely to see votes for Option 2 than the bigger cities, but over all, the remain side won handily across the province. Todd Korol/Reuters

What, exactly, does 75 per cent mean? Was the Alberta referendum an expression of unalloyed patriotism? A message to Edmonton and Ottawa that Albertans are content?

Or was it something else?

Albertans said yes to Canada. They may not answer the same about Ottawa, warns Gary Mar, a former Alberta Cabinet minister who is now president of the Canada West Foundation, a think tank. “There’s a whole host of issues where Albertans would say, ‘I don’t like the status quo, but I don’t think that separation is the solution, either.’”

In other words: “I don’t think the Prime Minister can rest easy.”

Mr. Carney has the power to bring change without opening messy constitutional debate, like giving provinces greater say in naming judges or rethinking the French language requirement for western civil servants, Mr. Mar said.

In Alberta, meanwhile, this moment represents opportunity for those who have long sought greater autonomy for Alberta. The industrial backbone of Central and Eastern Canada is under acute pressure from the U.S., whose tariffs have hurt the auto sector, steelmakers and others. Alberta’s economy and resources offer a counterweight, and Ottawa has already begun to respond with proposals like a new Pacific pipeline.

“What a great time for us to say, ‘absolutely. We’re here to make a stronger Canada, too. And part of that is to make sure we’re making a stronger Alberta,’” said Michael Binnion, an Alberta energy executive who has sketched proposals for how the province could wrest greater power for itself. Asserting provincial control over pensions and immigration are two areas he advocates. “For Albertans upset by the result, a constructive thing they can do is get involved in building the institutions to responsibly govern ourselves.”

Because, warned Reform Party founder Preston Manning, more trouble for Confederation lies ahead. On Wednesday, Quebec swore in Paul St-Pierre Plamondon as leader of a new government that has pledged another referendum on Quebec independence.

“The West is going to be watching,” Mr. Manning said, adding: “Will there be a double standard on how the federal government treats these two provinces?”

Both Quebec and Alberta, he said, share a desire for a more decentralized federation, Quebec for cultural, social and linguistic reasons, Alberta on economic grounds. If Ottawa were to act on Western priorities, he said, it might mollify at least some of those so frustrated they have agitated to leave.

“The overall high level of support to remain begs a question: remain and do what?”

Still, for a country that has had no shortage of dim self-reflection in recent years, Alberta’s referendum vote was “a refreshing moment,” said Calgary oil and gas pioneer Jim Gray, who spent the past year raising hundreds of thousands of dollars for Forever Canadian, the advocacy group that rallied for federalism. Now 93 years old, he collected signatures for a remain in Canada petition and personally delivered dozens of Forever Canadian lawn signs to people across Calgary.

“I’m glad that we had that referendum. Because it was really a moment to celebrate and to think rather deeply about how lucky we are,” he said this week.

“Canada isn’t perfect. Nobody is perfect,” he added.

But “Canada is not broken.”

At the very least, said former Alberta Lieutenant-Governor Lois Mitchell, the referendum should prompt a change in tone.

“We’re always kind of whining about things. And we shouldn’t be doing that,” she said.

“Ask yourself: Could you actually do something and make it better?”

stories.title: Why thousands of local politicians are winning without a single vote
stories.summary: Norman Beck is still knocking on doors in Brighton, even though he has already won and will return unopposed for a second term on Charlottetown city council.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown - Norman Beck is still knocking on doors in Brighton, P.E.I. even after winning his seat back allowing him to return unopposed for a second term on Charlottetown city council.

It’s part of a pattern playing out across P.E.I., where some communities have struggled to find enough people to run in this year’s municipal election.

Three of the capital city’s 10 wards have just one candidate, similarly in Summerside six out of eight wards only have one. Nominations were extended in 18 Island municipalities after too few people came forward to fill all the available mayoral and council positions.

“The reality of the job is it’s much more public facing than maybe it’s ever been,” said Beck, who represents Ward 3. While social media helps him connect with residents, he added it’s also brought increased public scrutiny and criticism. “I think people May not be ready to accept that or to live with that.”

Uncontested races remain common elsewhere in Canada, although recent totals in some provinces suggest modest improvements .

In Ontario, 400 candidates have been acclaimed in this year’s municipal elections, meaning they won without facing an opponent. There were 548 acclamations in 2022.

Last year, 4,607 mayors and councillors were elected unopposed in Quebec, accounting for more than half of the 7,835 people elected. According to provincial figures, 4,970 won without a contest in 2021.

In Charlottetown’s Ward 4, Spring Park, Rima Rashed is one of five candidates competing in the Nov. 2 municipal election.

She believes distrust in politicians could be discouraging some from running, along with the workload and time commitment of serving on council.

“Maybe people are busy with family and their job, and they don’t have time for this. And it’s not easy,” she said. “They don’t want to be judged, too.”

Although she sees it as a big responsibility, Rashed said she had few hesitations after others encouraged her to put her name forward.

For voters, the competition offers a chance to weigh which candidate they trust to work on their concerns.

“It’s people’s choice now,” she said.

Back in Brighton, Beck also cited the demands on families and work-life balance. He also pointed to the financial commitment of running a campaign.

Fortunately, he said, the job is a good fit at this point in his life. Running uncontested doesn’t change much for him, and he’s excited to continue serving his constituents.

Beck hopes people will get involved in municipal politics - even if they can’t serve on council - by attending public meetings, watching broadcasts, or keeping up with local issues so they understand how decisions are made.

“The more engaged our residents are, I think the better off our city will be.”

content_blocks.text: Charlottetown - Norman Beck is still knocking on doors in Brighton, P.E.I. even after winning his seat back allowing him to return unopposed for a second term on Charlottetown city council.
It’s part of a pattern playing out across P.E.I., where some communities have struggled to find enough people to run in this year’s municipal election.

Three of the capital city’s 10 wards have just one candidate, similarly in Summerside six out of eight wards only have one. Nominations were extended in 18 Island municipalities after too few people came forward to fill all the available mayoral and council positions.

“The reality of the job is it’s much more public facing than maybe it’s ever been,” said Beck, who represents Ward 3. While social media helps him connect with residents, he added it’s also brought increased public scrutiny and criticism. “I think people May not be ready to accept that or to live with that.”
Uncontested races remain common elsewhere in Canada, although recent totals in some provinces suggest modest improvements .
In Ontario, 400 candidates have been acclaimed in this year’s municipal elections, meaning they won without facing an opponent. There were 548 acclamations in 2022.

Last year, 4,607 mayors and councillors were elected unopposed in Quebec, accounting for more than half of the 7,835 people elected. According to provincial figures, 4,970 won without a contest in 2021.
In Charlottetown’s Ward 4, Spring Park, Rima Rashed is one of five candidates competing in the Nov. 2 municipal election.
She believes distrust in politicians could be discouraging some from running, along with the workload and time commitment of serving on council.
“Maybe people are busy with family and their job, and they don’t have time for this. And it’s not easy,” she said. “They don’t want to be judged, too.”
Although she sees it as a big responsibility, Rashed said she had few hesitations after others encouraged her to put her name forward.
For voters, the competition offers a chance to weigh which candidate they trust to work on their concerns.
“It’s people’s choice now,” she said.

stories.title: Tighter immigration rules put nursing homes at risk of losing foreign workers, long-term care providers say
stories.summary: The elder-care sector struggles to find local labour and relies on recruits from abroad to help care for seniors
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Tighter federal immigration rules are putting nursing homes at risk of losing significant numbers of temporary foreign workers, long-term care providers in several provinces say.

The elder-care sector often struggles to find local labour. Nursing homes have to recruit personnel from abroad to supplement the staff looking after seniors who have cognitive problems or dementia and need help for dressing, bathing or feeding.

“There have been changes that the federal government has made to immigration policy that have made a difficult staffing situation in healthcare even worse,” said Lisa Levin, the chief executive officer of AdvantAge Ontario, which represents the province’s municipal and non-profit long-term care homes.

“This is one of those examples of unintended consequences from government decisions,” said Mary Polak, chief executive of the BC Care Providers Association. “They were not maybe aware of the whole scale of impacts that would result from their decisions.”

Ottawa has moved since 2024 to curb the number of international students and temporary foreign workers, following criticisms that their influx created housing problems and made it harder for Canadians to find jobs.

Two measures have had major impacts for long-term care providers, Ms. Levin said.

The first change involved the Labour Market Impact Assessment (Lmia), a document the employer must complete to confirm that no Canadian is available to fill a job. The Lmia enables foreign personnel to apply for a work permit.

LMIAs, which cost a $1,000 processing fee per application, are now only valid for six months, down from a year previously.

The second change Ms. Levin mentioned was the duration of work permits, which was shortened from two years to one.

Gavin McIntosh, operations and finance vice-president for The Care Group, which runs nine facilities in British Columbia, said homes have to pay overtime to compensate for their staffing shortages. “It’s not sustainable,” he said.

Others have turned to temporary staffing agencies, a costly alternative that is also detrimental because vulnerable residents need stable care personnel, Ms. Levin said.

“They’re working with people who have cognitive issues, and then you have to bring someone else in, you have to train them all over again on what the needs are of the residents. Each individual resident has their own care plan and their own needs, and in many cases they can’t communicate it themselves.”

The federal government, however, said that the Temporary Foreign Worker (TFW) Program should only be a last-resort solution for short-term problems. “It is not a substitute for Canadian talent and is conditional on ensuring that measures have been taken to recruit Canadian workers,” Samuelle Carbonneau, a spokesperson for Employment and Social Development Canada, said in an e-mail.

LMIAs are not based on job titles but assessed individually, Ms. Carbonneau said. She noted that there are additional pathways to hire foreign workers.

Quebec employers, for example, have a priority process called “traitement simplifié” that extends to foreign applicants for Personal Support Workers (PSWs), who provide basic care in nursing homes.

However, Jean-François Blanchard, executive director of two long-term care homes west of Montreal, said some of his foreign candidates have been stumped because the Quebec priority stream does not recognize the training they acquired in private establishments.

Mr. Blanchard, who is president of a group representing Quebec private nursing homes, said his members could potentially lose 650 of their 6,000 workers because of immigration issues.

Another option mentioned by Ms. Carbonneau was a temporary extension allowing rural employers to retain their number of foreign workers until next March. However, the measure requires applying for new LMIAs, and two provinces, Ontario and Alberta, aren’t participating in that temporary measure.

Ashley Hoffmeister, the human resources director for the District of Kenora Homes for the Aged, said 28 of the 400 employees in her three facilities in northwest Ontario are facing expiring papers.

She tried to hire foreign staff through another route, the Significant Benefit to Canada permit, commonly known as the Lmia exemption C10.

The C10 work permit only costs $230, but the employer has to explain how the foreign workers will make a contribution so significant that they can be exempted from requiring an Lmia.

Ms. Hoffmeister said some C10 applications have been turned down because bureaucrats didn’t recognize the foreign workers as health care personnel. One rejection letter shared by Ms. Hoffmeister said the PSWs “appear to be highly/mainly specific to individual’s personal care and not health care.”

PSWs, also known in some provinces as healthcare aides, handle the majority of the daily support for elderly residents.

“We literally wouldn’t be able to function without them. They monitor all the health care needs for our residents. If there’s any changes in their cognitive abilities or their physical abilities, they’re the first ones to see it and report it to our nursing staff,” Ms. Hoffmeister said.

The lack of appreciation for PSWs might stem from the fact that nursing homes provide medical care but are also living environments for seniors. “There’s a poor understanding of our sector,” Ms. Polak said. “They think of it as completely aligned with an acute-care setting, a hospital setting, and it absolutely is not. There are so many other things you need to operate.”

Even in areas with high unemployment rates, it is hard to find local labour because of the arduous work required to care for dependent seniors. “It’s a job that’s rather demanding,” Mr. Blanchard said.

Long-term care homes aren’t looking for applicants who “are in it just for the paycheque,” Mr. McIntosh said. “You have to be a fairly well-rounded individual and be willing to help, sometimes in more ways than just doing your job. You have to make people feel loved and supported and cared for and safe.”

Ms. Levin said she hoped Ottawa will enable employers to apply for a single Lmia for each nursing home, rather than for each individual.

stories.title: Kardinal Offishall finds fresh fire after personal loss, career highs and lows
stories.summary: Toronto - Just a few years after helping put Toronto hip-hop on the map, Kardinal Offishall was running out of money, struggling to land gigs and wondering what had gone wrong.
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Just a few years after helping put Toronto hip-hop on the map, Kardinal Offishall was running out of money, struggling to land gigs and wondering what had gone wrong.

In 2001, the trailblazing rapper released his breakthrough album, “Quest for Fire: Firestarter, Vol. 1,” bringing the Caribbean-inflected sounds of his hometown to the world through club-rattling hits such as “BaKardi Slang” and “Ol’ Time Killin’.”

But the industry wasn’t as kind behind the scenes. His American label, MCA Records, was absorbed by Geffen, and plans for a follow-up album featuring Pharrell and Timbaland fell apart. Offishall says the new executives tried to force him into a “cookie-cutter” mould.

Before “Dangerous” became his global smash, Kardinal Offishall says he was running low on money and sleeping on a tour bus. The Toronto rapper reflects on that journey with "Firestarter Vol. 2: Everyday, Sometimes...," a long-awaited sequel that finds him getting candid on grief, relationships and being a 50-year-old family man. (Oct. 24, 2026)

“I was like, oh, you guys really have no idea who I am,” he shares in a recent interview.

After parting ways with the label, Offishall struggled financially.

“Money’s running out and I’m like, yo, we got any tours coming up? They’re like, nah,” the rapper recalls asking his team.

“It was rough, to where them bank accounts were going on E after a few years.”

He eventually toured with Akon and Gwen Stefani, though life on the road was far from glamorous.

“I didn’t even have a room every night. So I was sleeping on the tour bus and I would just go in somebody’s room and use their shower every day.”

For two months, he recorded music in the back of the bus, increasingly uncertain about his future.

“I remember just being like, yo, what is going on with my life?”

Then, ON the final night of the tour, he recorded “Dangerous,” the Akon-assisted smash that would introduce him to a new generation of listeners.

“As soon as we did that, that’s when my life changed again,” he says.

Nearly two decades later, Offishall is looking back on that journey with “Firestarter Vol. 2: Everyday, Sometimes...,” a long-awaited sequel that finds the rapper, born Jason Harrow, trading bombast for candid reflections on grief, relationships and being a 50-year-old family man.

Despite his public profile as a “Canada’s Got Talent” judge and the global A&R lead for Def Jam Records, Offishall says he’s long guarded his personal life. Opening up on the record meant accepting that he’d have to discuss painful subjects with strangers.

“People could ask you about your dad that passed. People could ask about your wife and that relationship,” he says. “I’ve always been a pretty private guy.”

Offishall’s last album was 2015’s “Kardi Gras, Vol. 1: The Clash.” In recent years, a succession of deaths among loved ones left him in no emotional state to make another.

“There was so much death,” he says. “They didn’t warn me about this when I was a kid, that I was going to get to an age where there will be people passing away like flies.”

Nearly a year without another funeral finally gave him room to heal and rediscover the joy of making music.

The 10-track “Firestarter Vol. 2” features some song ideas he’s had for years. The chest-thumping “Top 3” boasts verses from reggae star Buju Banton and British actor Idris Elba.

Singer BJ the Chicago Kid joins title track “Everyday, Sometimes…,” which addresses days when even getting out of bed feels overwhelming. Offishall wanted to show that celebrity offers little protection from ordinary human suffering.

“Money, accolades, fame, those things do not come into play when you have a loved one who is sick,” he says.

Offishall is releasing the album independently, noting streaming and direct-to-consumer distribution allow artists more freedom to chart their own course, without the pressure to make an immediate commercial splash.

“You can kind of do things the way that you want it. It’s not as rigid as it used to be in the industry,” he says.

Meanwhile, his executive role at Def Jam allows him to influence the industry from within, an approach inspired by advice from Stephen Marley: “You can’t change the system from outside of the system.”

That means being in meetings where he can advocate for artists and challenge executives’ assumptions, he says.

Offishall won’t wait another decade to drop more music. He and Elba, a longtime friend, have recorded an entire collaborative project they’re hoping to release in spring or summer 2027.

Most of the vocals were recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but Offishall reworked the production this year, adding orchestral flourishes.

“Strings and orchestras and brass sections and it’s nasty. It’s really nasty,” he says.

Other projects in the works include an EP with Toronto producer Slakah the Beatchild and a possible collaboration with Canadian R&B singer Glenn Lewis.

Offishall is currently on a U.S. press tour, including a stop with radio personality Ebro Darden, who at the height of the Drake-Kendrick Lamar feud sparked debate by suggesting Toronto lacked a distinctive sound.

For a rapper who helped export the city’s diverse music scene, the idea of a singular “Toronto sound” is unnecessarily limiting.

“I’m just glad that the whole Toronto sound thing has died down because I just feel it puts everybody in a box,” Offishall says.

Pointing to the different styles of Drake, the Weeknd and Nav, he adds: “I think the Toronto sound is excellence.”

He says the city’s artists should focus more on setting trends than following them, citing advice from his friend, Toronto Raptors announcer Mark Strong: “You never move with the times, you move the times.”

“We’ve got to continue to create that wave.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

In 2001, the trailblazing rapper released his breakthrough album, “Quest for Fire: Firestarter, Vol. 1,” bringing the Caribbean-inflected sounds of his hometown to the world through club-rattling hits such as “BaKardi Slang” and “Ol’ Time Killin’.”

But the industry wasn’t as kind behind the scenes. His American label, MCA Records, was absorbed by Geffen, and plans for a follow-up album featuring Pharrell and Timbaland fell apart. Offishall says the new executives tried to force him into a “cookie-cutter” mould.

Before “Dangerous” became his global smash, Kardinal Offishall says he was running low on money and sleeping on a tour bus. The Toronto rapper reflects on that journey with "Firestarter Vol. 2: Everyday, Sometimes...," a long-awaited sequel that finds him getting candid on grief, relationships and being a 50-year-old family man. (Oct. 24, 2026)
“I was like, oh, you guys really have no idea who I am,” he shares in a recent interview.
After parting ways with the label, Offishall struggled financially.
“Money’s running out and I’m like, yo, we got any tours coming up? They’re like, nah,” the rapper recalls asking his team.
“It was rough, to where them bank accounts were going on E after a few years.”
He eventually toured with Akon and Gwen Stefani, though life on the road was far from glamorous.
“I didn’t even have a room every night. So I was sleeping on the tour bus and I would just go in somebody’s room and use their shower every day.”
For two months, he recorded music in the back of the bus, increasingly uncertain about his future.
“I remember just being like, yo, what is going on with my life?”
Then, ON the final night of the tour, he recorded “Dangerous,” the Akon-assisted smash that would introduce him to a new generation of listeners.
“As soon as we did that, that’s when my life changed again,” he says.

Nearly two decades later, Offishall is looking back on that journey with “Firestarter Vol. 2: Everyday, Sometimes...,” a long-awaited sequel that finds the rapper, born Jason Harrow, trading bombast for candid reflections on grief, relationships and being a 50-year-old family man.

Despite his public profile as a “Canada’s Got Talent” judge and the global A&R lead for Def Jam Records, Offishall says he’s long guarded his personal life. Opening up on the record meant accepting that he’d have to discuss painful subjects with strangers.
“People could ask you about your dad that passed. People could ask about your wife and that relationship,” he says. “I’ve always been a pretty private guy.”
Offishall’s last album was 2015’s “Kardi Gras, Vol. 1: The Clash.” In recent years, a succession of deaths among loved ones left him in no emotional state to make another.
“There was so much death,” he says. “They didn’t warn me about this when I was a kid, that I was going to get to an age where there will be people passing away like flies.”
Nearly a year without another funeral finally gave him room to heal and rediscover the joy of making music.
The 10-track “Firestarter Vol. 2” features some song ideas he’s had for years. The chest-thumping “Top 3” boasts verses from reggae star Buju Banton and British actor Idris Elba.

Singer BJ the Chicago Kid joins title track “Everyday, Sometimes…,” which addresses days when even getting out of bed feels overwhelming. Offishall wanted to show that celebrity offers little protection from ordinary human suffering.
“Money, accolades, fame, those things do not come into play when you have a loved one who is sick,” he says.

Offishall is releasing the album independently, noting streaming and direct-to-consumer distribution allow artists more freedom to chart their own course, without the pressure to make an immediate commercial splash.
“You can kind of do things the way that you want it. It’s not as rigid as it used to be in the industry,” he says.

Meanwhile, his executive role at Def Jam allows him to influence the industry from within, an approach inspired by advice from Stephen Marley: “You can’t change the system from outside of the system.”
That means being in meetings where he can advocate for artists and challenge executives’ assumptions, he says.
Offishall won’t wait another decade to drop more music. He and Elba, a longtime friend, have recorded an entire collaborative project they’re hoping to release in spring or summer 2027.
Most of the vocals were recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but Offishall reworked the production this year, adding orchestral flourishes.
“Strings and orchestras and brass sections and it’s nasty. It’s really nasty,” he says.
Other projects in the works include an EP with Toronto producer Slakah the Beatchild and a possible collaboration with Canadian R&B singer Glenn Lewis.

Offishall is currently on a U.S. press tour, including a stop with radio personality Ebro Darden, who at the height of the Drake-Kendrick Lamar feud sparked debate by suggesting Toronto lacked a distinctive sound.
For a rapper who helped export the city’s diverse music scene, the idea of a singular “Toronto sound” is unnecessarily limiting.
“I’m just glad that the whole Toronto sound thing has died down because I just feel it puts everybody in a box,” Offishall says.
Pointing to the different styles of Drake, the Weeknd and Nav, he adds: “I think the Toronto sound is excellence.”

He says the city’s artists should focus more on setting trends than following them, citing advice from his friend, Toronto Raptors announcer Mark Strong: “You never move with the times, you move the times.”
“We’ve got to continue to create that wave.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Carney tours Kariye Mosque in Istanbul before departing Turkey
stories.summary: Istanbul - Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up a three-day trip to Turkey today by touring a mosque in Istanbul.
stories.author: Craig Lord The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Istanbul - After three days spent fostering tighter economic and political ties with Turkey, Prime Minister Mark Carney has arrived back in Ottawa.

Carney closed out his trip Saturday morning by visiting one of Istanbul’s many great cultural landmarks, the Kariye Mosque, accompanied by his wife, Diana Fox Carney.

The mosque was once a Byzantine church and is renowned for its historic architecture and its beautiful frescoes and mosaics. The structure itself has evolved through Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman and modern Turkish history.

A backgrounder document from the prime minister’s office said the site was chosen to underscore “Canada’s recognition of the importance of cultural heritage as a bridge between peoples and nations.”

The solemnity of Carney’s visit gave way to an unexpected Canadian moment when a tourist visiting from Canada caught the prime minister on his way out of the mosque.

“Go Oilers!” the man shouted, referring to Carney’s love of the Edmonton Oilers. The prime minister replied, “It looks good this year. Wait until the playoffs.”

The tour marked the end of the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey.

Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan forged a new strategic partnership between Canada and Turkey after meeting in Ankara on Thursday.

That agreement will see the two countries collaborate more closely in areas like defence and energy and set the stage for Canada and Turkey to begin free-trade talks in the coming weeks.

The trip to Turkey came in the context of Carney’s broader efforts to diversify Canada’s trading relationships and reduce reliance on the United States.

“Our goal is not self-sufficiency; it is collective resilience,” Carney said in a joint statement with Erdogan.

“That’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both. And in Turkey, we have an exceptional partner.”

Erdogan called Carney a “dear friend” in his own remarks and signalled that he plans to lead a business delegation to Canada in the future.

Canada and Turkey have not always seen eye-to-eye. Human rights have previously been an irritant in the relationship, and Carney’s efforts to deepen ties with Turkey come as the country faces international scrutiny over a crackdown on Lgbtq+ rights.

The prime minister told reporters that “engagement is not approval” when it comes to doing business with countries that don’t share Canada’s values.

Canada raised human rights during its discussions with Turkish officials, Carney said, though he didn’t confirm whether he raised the topic directly with Erdogan.

Carney met with a number of business leaders and investment firms in Istanbul, including representatives from Turkish Airlines.

During the trip, Canadian and Turkish officials formalized an expanded air transportation agreement that could eventually nearly double the number of direct flights between the nations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 23, 2026) – The London Police Service (LPS) is aware of the cybersecurity incident involving Navigate360, the third-party provider of the P3 tip management platform used by Crime Stoppers programs across Canada. We recognize the seriousness of this incident and community concerns about the security of information provided to Crime Stoppers.

London & Middlesex Crime Stoppers is an independent organization. The P3 platform is operated by a third-party vendor and is not connected to LPS information systems or infrastructure.

The anonymity and safety of individuals who come forward with information are fundamental to public trust and to the integrity of police investigations.

The LPS has received confirmation that London & Middlesex Crime Stoppers has been impacted by this incident and is reviewing available information to assess any potential impact on investigations, as well as the safety and privacy of individuals who provided information in support of LPS investigations.

Effective immediately, the LPS is suspending its participation in the Crime Stoppers program. Participation will not resume until the service is satisfied that the platform is secure and that the risks arising from this breach have been fully assessed.

Members of the public with information about a crime or public safety concern are encouraged to contact the London Police Service directly at 519-661-5670. In an emergency, call 9-1-1. Information provided directly to police does not carry the anonymity associated with Crime Stoppers; however, it ensures that information reaches investigators directly.

Questions regarding the cybersecurity breach, the scope of affected information, or measures taken in response should be directed to the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association or London & Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

For more information about the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association, visit Canadian Crime Stoppers Association .

stories.title: His cancer gave him just months to live. A new early-stage Toronto treatment has been a 'lifesaver' — and could offer hope to other patients
stories.summary: Although most investigational drugs fail to pass clinical trials, experts view invikafusp alfa with cautious optimism.
stories.author: Kevin Jiang; Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
Joe Szostak was in the middle of a family vacation in Florida in February of 2023 when, while getting changed one morning, he noticed a peculiar lump in his right armpit, the size of a ping-pong ball.

Over the next two weeks, Szostak said the lump swelled to the size of an orange. By April, it had grown to the size of a grapefruit: “I couldn’t even hold my arm up properly.”

Szostak’s doctors eventually determined he had squamous cell carcinoma, a common form of skin cancer. But by the time the then-67-year-old noticed the growth, it had metastasized, spreading through his body. Physicians gave him two to three months.

“Then I had to come home and share that with my son,” Szostak told the Star. “I don’t wish that conversation on anyone.”

Today, Szostak’s condition has stabilized. He credits his recovery in large part to a new, investigational immunotherapy he received as part of a Phase 1/2 clinical trial at Uhn’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre.

“I’ve been on this trial for probably well over two years now, with surprisingly no complications, no adverse effects,” Szostak said. “It’s a lifesaver.”

One out of every $10 spent on cancer treatments in Canada goes towards Keytruda. Experts warn that something has to give.

Although it’s still early in the process, and most investigational drugs fail to pass clinical trials, experts are approaching the drug — called invikafusp alfa — with cautious optimism. Only a few dozen patients have received it. But, if successful, it could open the door to new treatment pathways for patients who have run out of options.

Cancer drugs that target the immune system are revolutionizing how some kinds of tumours are treated, but existing immunotherapies still leave too many patients behind. Only about 20 per cent of patients with solid tumours respond to current immune-targeting drugs, which is why experts say research into investigational therapies like the one Szostak took are so important.

“What’s exciting about immunotherapy is that it works even in some patients who have very advanced disease; they still can have a complete response” and be rescued, said Dr. John Bell, senior scientist at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute and scientific director of BioCanRx, Canada’s Immunotherapy Network.

“Cancer is a very complex disease and we’re never going to have one pill or one immunotherapy that’s going to work,” said Bell, who was not involved in the clinical trials. “But combinations of them have a real chance to cure people — and keep them cured.”

Developed by U.S. biopharmaceutical company Marengo Therapeutics, invikafusp alfa is administered via intravenous infusion and is currently in Phase 2 clinical trials. If successful, it could take up to 10 years for this therapy to reach clinics, the Toronto investigators say. Results of the phase 1/2 clinical trial were published Friday in Nature Medicine.

Dr. Lillian SIU, medical oncologist and senior scientist at Uhn’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, said trials of the investigational immunotherapy show promise.

Although Szostak was advised to get his affairs in order following his terminal diagnosis, he refused to give up. In April, over eight hours, a surgeon removed the grapefruit-sized tumour. Over the next year, he underwent immunotherapy, then chemotherapy and radiation treatments.

Szostak lost his hair, feeling in his toes and hands, and suffered a blood clot that made his arm swell up “like the Michelin man.” By the end of 2023, he’d lost 50 pounds and his cancer spread. He developed a lesion under his right arm and a nodule in each lung.

Desperate, Szostak approached a company in the U.S. that offered to sequence the genome of his cancer to identify potential drugs. After shelling out “several thousand dollars,” it produced a 38-page report.

He shared the findings with oncologists at hospitals including Princess Margaret, with low expectations — and was surprised when the Toronto cancer centre called him back about a new trial.

Szostak became one of a few dozen patients around the world with access to invikafusp alfa.

Compared to previous treatments, it was like “night and day,” Szostak said. “When I walk out of my infusion treatments every three weeks, I feel ... I could run around the block.”

Other participants reported side effects: “Some patients had feverish chills the night of the first infusion, and then it gets better over time,” said Dr. Lillian SIU, a co-senior author on the study and a medical oncologist and senior scientist at Princess Margaret. “But it was overall a safe and tolerable drug.”

SIU is also a scientific adviser to Marengo Therapeutics, which developed the drug, and holds equity.

“I feel better than I did in 2022,” before he got diagnosed, said Joe Szostak.

Szostak was one of just 58 patients across 10 cancer centres in Canada, France, Spain and the U.S. to receive the new drug. Only 27 received a dose that could affect their health.

In this select group, roughly 15 per cent saw their tumours shrink enough to meet clinical criteria for a response, while around 44 per cent had less shrinkage.

Importantly, 18 of these patients’ cancers had stopped responding to previous immunotherapies. But after taking invikafusp alfa, two-thirds of this group stabilized or saw their tumours shrink.

“I want to emphasize that this is an investigational drug,” noted SIU. “The identification of anti-cancer activity is not a primary goal — safety is the primary goal” of the trials so far.

The drug, known as a selective dual T cell agonist, is a first-in-class therapy — meaning it functions in a way like no other treatments before it.

It works by activating two specific types of white blood cells that, while relatively rare in the body, are common within tumours. Unlike other immunotherapies that elicit a broader immune response, invikafusp alfa is more selective in its approach, potentially reducing side effects.

Experts warn that too many young people face difficulties in accessing tests and follow-up care

Invikafusp alfa has passed the Phase 1 portion of the trials, meaning it’s been shown to be safe at an optimized dose among a small group of participants. Phase 2, which involves more patients and investigates efficacy and short-term side effects, is underway. A Phase 3 trial will test the drug on a larger pool of patients to evaluate efficacy and test for signs of toxicity.

Only 31 per cent of industry-sponsored pharmaceuticals make it past Phase 2, while about 58 per cent pass Phase 3, explained Christine Williams, an immunologist and executive vice-president of the Ontario Institutes for Cancer Research, who wasn’t involved in this research trial.

Dr. Zhen Su, president and CEO of Marengo Therapeutics, said it will be critical to understand how invikafusp alfa works in different patients, which patients are most likely to respond and whether it’s effective when combined with standard cancer treatments. The company expects to publish further Phase 1/2 results next year.

Clinical trials act as “a bridge between research and changes in clinical care,” Williams said, noting they are an important way for patients to get early access to innovative treatments.

Dr. Erica Tsang, a medical oncologist and clinical investigator at Princess Margaret, is running another clinical trial with invikafusp alfa, testing if it can be used to treat cancers at the earliest possible stage.

It will involve patients whose cancer might come back and who have regular blood tests to look for molecular markers of cancer, with the goal of changing the disease’s trajectory. Tsang called the research “uncharted territory.”

More than two years later, Szostak’s cancer has stabilized; the lesion under his arm is no longer visible on scans, one nodule in his lungs has shrunk by more than half and the other has remained stable.

Szostak has been able to return to much of his regular life. He walks five kilometres a day, cycles on a regular basis and spends time with his wife and adult son.

Szostak feels grateful for the chance to join the trial. “I feel better than I did in 2022 — before my diagnosis — when I was probably feeling some of the early effects of cancer.”

stories.title: Ontario lacks aging strategy as senior population surges, advocates say
stories.summary: Report says province should focus on community programs and supports that help people stay healthier and avoid hospitals or nursing homes.
stories.author: Moira Welsh
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford’s promise to add 58,000 new or renovated nursing home beds has led to just 11,000 completed spaces, while advocates say the province still has no overarching aging plan for cheaper and healthier options in the community.

Instead of focusing primarily on the $6.4-billion construction project, Dr. Samir Sinha says the province needs a strategy for proactive, community-based health and social supports for an aging population that, according to Statistics Canada, will include 1.1 million Ontarians aged 85 and older within 20 years.

While the Progressive Conservative government says it has injected billions of dollars into home care and community services, a recent report by the National Institute on Ageing (NIA) said Ontario is a policy laggard compared with Alberta, British Columbia and Nova Scotia, all of which have “strong and distinct” aging strategies backed by dedicated funding.

“Ontario’s approach remains largely fragmented — relying on a network of locally delivered programs without a formally recognized or resourced system-level co-ordinating or capacity-building structure,” said the report co-authored by Sinha, who is the Nia’s director of health policy research and a Sinai Health geriatrician. He presented the findings at a recent meeting of Canadian health ministers in Winnipeg.

Canada’s “rapidly aging population,” the NIA said, is “placing new demands on the communities in which people live and the services they rely on. In particular, increasing numbers of Canadians are aging alone, living on fixed incomes, and managing multiple chronic conditions.”

An international examination of community programs that help people stay healthier and avoid hospitals or nursing homes shows that comprehensive policies bring “greater clarity and predictability for older persons and their families, caregivers and care providers around what exists to enable both healthy aging and aging in the right place,” the report said.

Advocates such as Sinha have long called for an aging strategy but say time is running out for government action.

In 2026, Ontario became a “super-aged” province , with one in five residents now 65 or older, according to Statistics Canada. And with the massive millennial generation beginning to turn 50 in 2031, the demands of an older society will not fade with the baby boomers, the oldest of whom are now turning 80.

Ontario therefore needs not just an aging strategy, but a plan that supports people at different stages of life, said Laura Tamblyn Watts, CEO of CanAge, a national advocacy group.

“There are actually three distinct generations within that designation, and they have very different needs,” said Tamblyn Watts.

Many in their mid-60s, she noted, are no longer considered “old” and with longevity offering extra decades of life, policymakers “must prepare” for a variety of options to keep people healthy and engaged, avoiding the social isolation that is linked to depression and dementia.

Concerns about housing and health are increasingly part of political discussions at Queen’s Park.

The Green Party’s Aislinn Clancy has questioned the government on plans to help older Ontarians remain at home and Liberal MPP Stephanie Smyth (Toronto—St. Paul’s) is working on a private member’s bill that focuses on aging.

“By expanding community-based programs and making social connections more accessible,” Smyth said, “we can improve quality of life, ease pressure on the health-care system and potentially delay the need for long-term care.”

Cost comparisons show significant savings from government investments in the community with programs that provide transportation, proactive health care and wellness hubs for social connections.

Daily hospital fees range from $700 to $1,200. Nursing homes cost roughly $200 a day. Community programs range from $63 for “supportive care” to $127 in home care, according to Advantage Ontario, which represents long-term care, seniors’ housing, supportive housing, and community service agencies.

Donna Duncan, CEO of the Ontario Long-Term Care Association, which represents nursing homes, said she welcomes the Nia’s focus on community supports.

“Most people want to age at home and in their own communities, and services like meals, transportation, respite and friendly visiting help them do that safely and for longer,” Duncan said.

“We know Ontario needs both. More than 50,000 people are waiting for a long-term-care home, and the residents we care for today have more complex medical needs than ever. For them, 24/7 nursing and personal care is the right care, and the work underway with government to build and redevelop homes needs to continue.”

Financial planners break down what each level of care actually costs — and how to plan for the

Duncan also noted a pilot program operated by the Ministry of Long-Term Care that enables some homes to serve as community hubs where people can access nursing, dementia care, wound care and personal support while still living independently.

In an interview, Sinha said the province’s programs for older adults are siloed under the budgets of the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Long-Term Care and the Ministry for Seniors and Accessibility.

“Who is stepping back and actually saying, ‘What is the overall game plan to create a sustainable health care system?’ ”

The Health Ministry said it is doing just that.

“Our government is taking action to provide more people with the right care, in the right place, at every stage of life,” said Lily Barnes, spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

The ministry has “tripled” funding for home and community care, spending $5.6 billion this year, Barnes said in an email. That money will “strengthen and expand home and community care services, helping thousands more patients access home and community care.”

She also cited “record investments into our home care workforce” that includes better wages for personal support workers and $300 million to “help thousands of people launch their careers as PSWs.”

The $5.6 billion “sounds like a lot,” said Sinha, but is a “tiny” slice of the ministry’s current $91.8-billion health budget.

“We can start to understand why long-term care wait-lists are climbing, and hospitals have a lot of patients occupying beds who don’t want or need to be there — often because we don’t have enough home care or community supports.”

stories.content:
The federal privacy commissioner is examining a large-scale Crime Stoppers data breach that exposed nearly 1.5 million Canadian tips, prompting some local branches to pause the program amid security and safety concerns for tipsters.

Despite the breach falling outside their mandate, Vito Pilieci, spokesperson for the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, said the agency has offered “expertise and guidance” in the aftermath of the breach, and is seeking more information from Navigate360 “before determining next steps.”

Pilieci said he was not in a position to comment further.

As first reported by CBC, the information was stolen last March by a hacking group seeking to disprove the company’s claim that its platform was “anonymous” and “secure.”

All told, more 8.3 million tips were exposed, according to the investigation, 1.5 million of which were submitted by Canadians. In some cases, names of the tipsters or other personal information, like phone numbers or addresses, were included in the data.

The breach, unprecedented in both scope and severity, according to experts who spoke to the Star, could render tipsters vulnerable to offences like identity theft and fraud, and in some cases, risk their public safety. Some local programs, including in Toronto, have opted to pause accepting tips after learning the extent of the leak.

“It could be really dangerous if (this information) got into the wrong hands,” said Lisa Danay Wallace, a lawyer specializing in information technology and privacy. “It takes it a big step further, into physical risk.”

A coalition of hackers, dubbed Internet Yiff Machine, stole data from P3, the tip software used by the charity since 2018, in March. A week later, the organization said Navigate360 informed them that the system was “safe and fully operational.”

Crime Stoppers says it was told by Navigate360 in May that the data — a total of 91GB — had been recovered.

In a statement shared Thursday, Crime Stoppers Toronto said it took months to gain clarity on the extent of the breach. The Guelph Wellington branch shared a similar statement on Thursday.

In that time, a copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists by Distributed Denial of Secrets, an American non-profit that publishes hacked documents, if deemed to be in the public interest.

CBC’s reporting, published on Wednesday, was the first time the Toronto branch was made aware that the leaked information had been accessed by an outside party.

Some of the leaked tips contained personal information, such as full names, addresses and phone numbers, along with allegations they reported to the non-profit. Some of the tips resulted in arrests or charges, with tipsters receiving cash rewards.

“This creates a unique situation where very sensitive, highly sensitive information has been breached,” Danay Wallace said.

But the risk is not only to the tipsters; the leaked tips could harm the reputations of those being reported, particularly if the allegations contained within were unfounded.

“People that are being accused in these tips; they’re still innocent until proven guilty, too,” said Danay Wallace.

Toronto Crime Stoppers saw the most tips of any Canadian city exposed in the breach, a total of 179,891, including more than 14,000 names.

Spokesperson Sean Sportun says the organization has not had the opportunity to review the leaked tips.

“(Navigate360) has not given us the text of the tips, despite repeated requests through our lawyers, so we can’t see what each one says,” Sportun said in a written statement to the Star. The organization says it continues to seek the stolen tips from Navigate360, along with a “full account of what happened.”

Toronto Crime Stoppers announced Thursday it was pausing its tips program and is currently asking the public to direct reports to Toronto police. Sportun says it will not readopt the program until it “can stand behind the system that protects (its tips.)”

“This week’s reporting shows the data has travelled beyond Navigate360, and we don’t know who else May have a copy,” he said. “So we are acting as if it could be misused.”

Along with Toronto police, Hamilton, and Peel, York, Halton and Durham police services have also suspended the intake of tips.

The Crime Stoppers of Canada Association says that the tip program and software has since been secured.

“Navigate360 has advised us that third-party cybersecurity experts have investigated the breach, identified vulnerabilities and completed remediation,” association vice president Craig MacPhail told the Star.

The national tip program remains in operation.

MacPhail says the national association respects the decision of independent branches and continues to work with local programs to implement additional measures and oversights.

“These measures strengthen protections for current and future submissions, said MacPhail. “They cannot undo the exposure of information already taken, which remains a serious concern.”

stories.title: Hate-motivated incident
stories.summary: London, ON (October 24, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service have charged a London man following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident that occurred in the downtown core.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 24, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service have charged a London man following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident that occurred in the downtown core.

On October 22, 2026, police were made aware of an incident that took place in the rear parking lot of a property located in the 0-100 block of St. George Street. It was reported that a male who was completing construction work at the address used equipment, believed to be a pressure washer, to create a symbol resembling a swastika in the gravel surface of the parking lot.

Nearby residents captured video and photographs of the incident and provided the information to police. The property owner was notified and attended the location, removing the symbol.

On October 23, 2026, members of the London Police Service identified and arrested the suspect male.

The investigation was reassigned to members of the London Police Service Hate Crime Unit, and the incident was determined to have been motivated by hatred.

As a result of the investigation, Gordon Botaitis, 56, of London, has been charged with one count of offence motivated by hatred.

The accused was released from custody and is expected to appear in London court on January 18, 2027, in relation to the charge.

Hate has no place in our city. The London Police Service is committed to protecting the safety and well-being of all members of our community and recognizes the significant harm that hate-motivated incidents can cause. Everyone deserves to feel safe and respected in our city. Any incident believed to be motivated by hate will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated. The London Police Service remains committed to working with our community to address hate and ensure London remains a safe and inclusive place for all.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Teachers, support staff rally across province amid stalled contract talks
stories.summary: The rallies come as negotiations between the province and teachers’ unions remain at a standstill.
stories.author: Jake Ross
stories.content:
Thousands of teachers and support staff across the province rallied on Saturday in a show of support for public education, and as their contract talks remain in limbo.

Protests were held in Toronto, Ottawa, London, Sudbury and Thunder Bay to push for better funding, improvements to teacher retention and recruitment, smaller class sizes and plans to address violence in schools, among other issues they want to highlight at the bargaining table.

stories.title: With Osap cut off, can Ontario's private colleges be saved?
stories.summary: The loss of access to Osap grants, and now loans, amid fraud allegations at 8 schools, is sparking fears for the future.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
A clampdown on international students. No new partnerships with public colleges. Then, no access to Ontario Student Assistance Program aid grants. And, for now, no access to Osap loans.

Private colleges have been dealt a number of blows by both the federal and Ontario governments — but it’s the most recent move by the province that could lead to the demise of a number of these mainly for-profit businesses.

Such schools offer quick credentials, typically serving non-traditional students and often in niche programs, but with a much higher tuition price tag, so they rely on student aid funds to keep up enrolment.

Without it, “we are expecting more program pauses and potentially school closures if the Osap freeze continues,” said Taylor Buck, the administration and communications assistant at Career Colleges Ontario.

The government implemented the ban on Osap for all private colleges amid concerns about fraud at a handful, but says it plans to reinstate it under a stringent new process come January. Online programs, however, will remain ineligible.

With at least one private college already suspending programs amid financial uncertainty, the organization that oversees almost 300 such schools worries that’s just the start.

Minister Nolan Quinn asks Ontario Provincial Police to investigate “criminal allegations.”

“We can’t comment on individual institutions or situations not yet made public, but colleges cannot operate indefinitely without the tuition funding their students rely on, and students cannot wait until the new year for certainty,” Buck also said in a statement to the Star.

“There needs to be a path forward now for students at compliant institutions.”

More than eight colleges are now being inspected and targeted by the province amid concerns of misuse — with some allegations already referred to the OPP.

Career colleges sometimes offer programs not easily available elsewhere — trucking or flight schools, for example — and their shorter duration appeals to mature students, lower-income students, those already in the workforce as well as newcomers looking to boost credentials. (International students don’t qualify for Osap.)

About one-third of Ontario’s roughly 600 private colleges qualify to receive Osap funds.

The Canadian Press has reported that in 2024-5, seven private colleges received $385 million in Osap — the same amount that students in all of the province’s public colleges received that same year.

Laurel Schollen, a higher education expert at the University of Toronto’s Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, said that without Osap, students would need to afford such programs; “it will put some into desperate straits.”

While the quality of some has come under fire, critics have blamed the government for poor oversight despite repeated warnings — from provincial auditors, and even Career Colleges Ontario itself.

“It’s a very dramatic move, and it’s one of those situations where I think most of the evidence suggests there’s a small number of players that May be problematic,” said Glen Jones, a higher education expert at Oise, who believes the government doesn’t “have the data to make a distinction” so shut down student aid to all.

Career colleges are regulated by legislation, he noted, but “one of the challenges is the ability of the government to monitor whether all of those regulations are being fulfilled. There are supposed to be regular inspections, and the last study we did, one of the issues that arose was how frequently the government (inspected) institutions.”

Just last week, Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said a sector-wide, third-party audit that recently flagged concerns around misuse continues, and that ministry “investigators began in-person inspections at eight private career colleges,” an investigation that “extends to the sector as a whole.”

He has promised that private college students stuck in limbo will have access to third-party loans, but provided no details.

“To protect against irregularities or fraud, Osap will not resume for private post-secondary institutions until the strengthened validation process is in place” in the new year, he said, and “will include caps on Osap-funded enrolment, the exclusion of predominantly online-only programs, and strengthened student identification and verification controls.”

In 2025-26, some 242 private colleges were eligible for Osap, representing 121,000 students.

Jones also noted that private college graduates have the highest default rates when it comes to Osap repayment, which the government should be paying attention to. In 2023, public universities had a default rate of 1.9 per cent, public colleges 5.5 per cent, and private colleges 7.4 per cent.

Mothercraft, established almost 100 years ago, trains early childhood educators while running daycares and parent support programs. Despite its charitable and non-profit status, it falls under private career college legislation.

The Osap freeze has created “a lot of anxiety and stress for those students that had been counting on loans,” said executive director Michele Lupa, adding the school has deferred tuition payments for about a dozen students for now until the province works out a plan for third-party loans.

“We’re trying to minimize their stress while they’re in the first semester of a very intense program,” she said. She said she worries about the future of the school’s online programming and if it will be permanently excluded.

About half of Mothercraft’s graduating class of 120 will have learned online, but with the requirement for an in-person placement.

While colleges worry about their future, students do, too. Alisson Almeida, who has a bachelor of science in biology from York University, now attends Aaps College for a diploma in pharmaceutical quality control to help “close the gaps on my resume.”

“I wouldn’t have been able to even start the program if I was not approved for Osap,” said the 42-year-old who was approved for $18,000 in Osap this year. The college, he added, “is being very generous to me; they will allow me to complete the program, even though we have no certainty of how this is going to work.”

Alisson Almeida, who has a bachelor of science in biology from York University, now attends Aaps College in Toronto for a diploma in pharmaceutical quality control to help “close the gaps on my resume.”

Some believe this is an opportunity for public colleges, which were also hit hard by the limits to international students — using programs run with private colleges to help boost their budgets — now that some for-profit schools face peril.

What’s needed now is a comprehensive look at the role of the private college sector, says Paul Axelrod, professor emeritus at York University.

“Are students getting their money’s worth? Did they find jobs?” he said, adding while demand is there for shorter courses, the government “will only learn about (effectiveness) if they do a systematic survey of people who have attended them and are attending them, and how have things changed.”

He said the province in the long term should be leaning into public colleges, which have seen programs axed, staff laid off, campuses closed and even school mergers because of budget issues.

Axelrod noted the government’s recent changes to Osap overall, moving to a loan-heavy system instead of nonrepayable grants, was prompted by ballooning costs in the private college sector.

Most experts agree, however, that this latest move by the government has tainted all private career colleges when so far a small number remain under suspicion.

“There’s a difference between treating the entire sector as corrupt rather than taking ownership for the fact that there wasn’t a lot of oversight,” said Elizabeth Buckner of Oise, who has studied the private sector in higher education.

“It allowed certain institutions to take advantage, and that those institutions need to be investigated and punished and closed down. But a niche mom-and-pop school that’s providing (education in a) field for 40 years is not the same.”

stories.title: Ottawa designates B.C. port expansion as project of national interest
stories.summary: Port of Vancouver plans to expand existing facility in Delta, adding capacity at the country’s largest port
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Port of Vancouver’s planned Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion is now officially a project of national interest.

The listing recognizes the project’s critical role in expanding and diversifying Canada’s trade capacity and provides immediate regulatory certainty to move forward.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon says it will add much-needed capacity at the country’s largest port.

It also accelerates the project’s timeline for commercial operations by up to four years, to 2035.

Ottawa says environmental safeguards will be maintained and Indigenous communities consulted.

The Vancouver Fraser Port Authority is the proponent for the project, which Ottawa says is on track to reach a final investment decision by the middle of next year.

More to come

stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The two jurisdictions wrapped up a summit in Montreal on Friday with various agreements, many of which will take months or years to finalize.
