That would build on existing university exchange programs and working-holiday programs Canada operates with multiple European countries.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU wants Canada to fully join Erasmus+, the EU’s student exchange program that offers training and study opportunities in member nations.

Canada is also hoping to become a full member of the Horizon Europe research partnership program by 2028, which would offer new funding for research and innovation projects undertaken with European peers.

Tech workers

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the pact with the EU will give Canadian researchers access to European supercomputers that can cut processing times from six months to a single day.

Canada and the EU have signed a digital trade agreement that looks to fold certain sectors into the trade agreement that has governed how goods are exchanged for a decade.

The European Commission website defines digital trade as “commerce enabled by electronic means.” It cites banks transferring data, agricultural commodity traders using e-signatures and freight companies tracking their machines through the internet.

Canada is also working on joining the EU’s “instant payment systems” to make it easier to send funds. Both jurisdictions are also exploring opening each other’s markets further to Canadian and European banks, insurers and fintech companies.

Mining firms

The European Investment Bank will seek to fund projects to mine critical raw materials in Canada, thanks to negotiations that concluded Friday.

Von der Leyen said Thursday that European “industrial demand, technology and investment” can help get such mineral projects off of the ground.

Canada has signed some sort of updated competition agreement with the EU that looks to crack down on anticompetitive actions by transatlantic businesses, though there were few details provided Friday.

The EU’s border agency is also helping its Canadian counterpart tackle migrant smuggling, human trafficking and identity fraud by exchanging information through the European Border Surveillance System.

Both jurisdictions have also agreed to launch formal discussion groups on the Arctic, foreign information manipulation and interference, climate security and transport.

A joint statement says on misinformation, both sides have agreed to move “from a reactive stance to a proactive one.”

Soldiers in Latvia

In June, Canada became the only non-European partner in the EU’s defence procurement program SAFE.

Just one project had come out of that arrangement until Friday, when Canada announced a contract worth up to $43 million to provide helmets to Latvian troops.

Montreal-based firm Galvion will produce the helmets for Latvia, which has been home to Canada’s largest foreign military presence for years. Canadian soldiers are in Latvia to prevent a Russian invasion.

As Washington pulls back support for Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion, Europe has stepped up with more funding.

Carney announced Friday that Canada will join an EU loan program for Ukraine. Ottawa has pledged an initial contribution of 500 million euros, roughly C$775 million.

“We will continue to provide comprehensive political, financial, economic, energy, humanitarian, military and diplomatic support to Ukraine and its people,” says the joint statement Canada and the EU inked Friday.

stories.title: Why some Canadian police are still promoting Crime Stoppers despite breach
stories.summary: Some Canadian police services continue to promote Crime Stoppers despite a data breach that May have exposed identifying information included in anonymous tips.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Some Canadian police services continue to promote Crime Stoppers despite a data breach that May have exposed identifying information included in anonymous tips.

Meanwhile, other police services have suspended their use of the program over the breach involving Navigate360, the U.S.-based company that manages Crime Stoppers’ P3 tip platform.

Navigate360 said last week that a third party accessed one of its systems and copied data between Nov. 21, 2025, and March 5, 2026.

Names, addresses and other sensitive information May have been affected, though Navigate360 said the data involved varies from person to person.

Despite concerns surrounding the breach, police services such as the Calgary Police Service (CPS) continue to promote Crime Stoppers in news releases.

“We have engaged directly with Crime Stoppers Canada to learn more about how the breach occurred, and we are satisfied that the additional security measures they have put in place provide strong protection for their database,” a CPS spokesperson told Global News in an email.

“We are continuing to accept tips through Crime Stoppers.”

Crime Stoppers tips have “historically been a valuable source of information” that helps investigators advance cases and solve crimes, the spokesperson said.

Jessica Kingsbury, director of media relations for the RCMP, echoed that sentiment.

“Crime Stoppers is an important public safety tool, providing individuals with an alternative to share information that can assist police investigations and help prevent and solve crime,” she said in a statement.

Some RCMP detachments in Nova Scotia, Manitoba and British Columbia promoted Crime Stoppers in news releases this week.

Kingsbury said the RCMP is working with the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association to determine the full scope of the breach.

“We are actively assessing any potential impacts on operations, as are other police services,” she said.

“We will continue to work closely with Crime Stoppers Canada to review the systems and processes used by the program, identify any further security enhancements, and strengthen safeguards.”

Sean Sparling, a former deputy chief of the Sault Ste. Marie Police Service, previously told Global News officers across Canada use Crime Stoppers “on a daily basis.”

He said he relied on Crime Stoppers for many of his own investigations.

“Knowing Crime Stoppers and how well it’s organized, how well it works and its importance to the law enforcement community and the safety of our communities, I fully expect they’re going to recover from this,” Sparling said.

Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said last week people sometimes include identifying details to explain what they saw in their tips.

Before a tip goes to investigators, Crime Stoppers’ practice is to remove those details, Sportun said. However, some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen, he added.

Specifically, 176,859 tips submitted through Toronto Crime Stoppers’ software between January 2022 and November 2025 were affected, including 12,392 that May contain personal information, Sportun said. Navigate360 later supplied a separate list containing 14,973 names.

However, Sportun said the list “lacks detail necessary to measure the risk involved” because it did not identify who the names belonged to.

Toronto Crime Stoppers has paused phone, online and app-based tip intake while seeking more information from Navigate360.

Navigate360, which also provides software to some schools in the U.S., said it has found no evidence the personal information exposed has been used for fraud or identity theft.

The company said it remains dedicated to ensuring the privacy and security of the information under its control.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada is investigating the security safeguards Navigate360 had in place at the time of the breach to determine the organization’s compliance with Canada’s federal private-sector privacy law.

Police services that have suspended their use of Crime Stoppers said members of the public can submit information through regular police-reporting channels, although those methods are not anonymous.

Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 911.

Kingsbury said tipsters using Crime Stoppers should not provide their own name, contact information or other details that could identify them.

The CPS spokesperson said anyone who believes they are being threatened or intimidated, or has concerns for their safety because of the breach, should contact police in their area.

Furthermore, anyone concerned about whether their personal information was affected should contact Crime Stoppers directly, the spokesperson added.

stories.title: Carney says Cleveland-Cliffs making ‘mistake’ by not respecting obligations
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Cleveland-Cliffs' would be making a "mistake" by not respecting its obligations and commitments after it began laying off workers.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Cleveland-Cliffs would be making a “mistake” by not respecting its obligations and commitments, as the U.S.-based owner of Stelco faces potential legal action from the federal government over their laying off of up to 500 Canadian steelworkers.

The comments came at an event in Ottawa when Carney was asked by a reporter if, given what has transpired in recent weeks, the federal government felt it was a mistake to allow Cleveland-Cliffs to acquire Stelco in 2024.

“The mistake here would be Cleveland-Cliffs not respecting the obligations, the commitments that they made in the acquisition,” Carney said in response.

The agreement from 2024, of which only a summary has been shared publicly, includes several legally binding commitments Cleveland-Cliffs and Stelco must maintain, including for employment to be at or above levels measured at the time the agreement was created until 2029.

When pressed for more on Thursday, Carney declined to comment further because there is now a legal process heading before the courts. He added that he would reserve his comments for “some other time.”

This comes just hours after Global News obtained a letter, dated Oct. 29, from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon. In the letter, Joly said she expects a “concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.”

While arguing the company has not broken its agreement with the federal government, Cleveland-Cliffs has also argued they “should not be responsible for impacts of external factors beyond their control,” including U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel.

Speaking to reporters Thursday, Joly reiterated that Cleveland-Cliffs and its CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, have actively supported the U.S. tariffs and must “face the consequences” they have on the Canadian market.

Joly said she reviewed an interim compliance report that was provided by Stelco on Oct. 26 but said the report was “far from satisfactory.”

“It does not alter my belief that Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs are not in compliance with their undertakings under the Investment Canada Act as set out in my October 22 section 39 demand,” she said in the most recent letter.

According to the union representing Stelco’s laid-off workers, about 175 have been let go so far, but an internal memo said that could increase to about 500.

Separately, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves reportedly told The Canadian Press Wednesday that laid off Stelco workers could be recalled by the holidays provided sales of Canadian steel increase.

“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” he said in a statement, adding: “If our plan works, my intention is to call back all the 175 workers before Christmas.”

– with files from Global’s Rachel Morgan, Mackenzie Gray and The Canadian Press

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Defence Minister David McGuinty says the federal government’s planned purchase of 88 F-35 stealth fighters remains under review, even after the military received its first two F-35s in recent days.

McGuinty told reporters today the federal government will take all the time it needs to consider all factors, including industrial benefits and emerging autonomous air systems that can fly alongside fighter craft.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet on hold for investigation: coroner
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police where in her home has been put on hold indefinitely.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home was put on hold indefinitely Thursday just as it reached the final stretch of the proceedings.

“I know everyone has been working extremely hard during this inquest. Unfortunately, I will be adjourning the inquest until further notice,” said Dr. David Cameron, the coroner presiding over the inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet.

“The reason for this is that we have some quite unanticipated investigation that needs to be done before we can continue.”

The coroner gave no details on the nature or focus of the investigation but said jurors and the public would be informed when the inquest was ready to resume.

The inquest finished hearing evidence on Wednesday and was set to reconvene Thursday afternoon so that lawyers for about a dozen parties could make their closing remarks and suggest recommendations to the jury.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old woman of Afro-Indigenous and Ukrainian descent, died on May 27, 2020 after police were called to the west-end apartment she shared with relatives.

Her death closely followed the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, fuelling protests as well as calls to defund the police. It was also one of several cases to draw scrutiny on how police interact with people in crisis.

One of Ontario’s police watchdogs, the Special Investigations Unit, cleared police of wrongdoing in her death, finding that Korchinski-Paquet fell while trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the one next door. Her family disputed the findings.

The SIU did not participate in the inquest, and its investigation is outside the scope of the proceedings.

Last week, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother directed a new allegation at police as she testified about her memories of that day, throwing the inquest temporarily off course.

Claudette Beals alleged officers pushed her daughter toward the balcony, drawing concerns from several lawyers and causing the inquest to go on an extended break so they could figure out a way forward.

Two officers who were in the apartment, Const. Shane Beaudoin and then-Const. Adam Vandenbrink, had previously testified that Korchinski-Paquet was allowed into the apartment to use the bathroom, then introduced to a paramedic.

Korchinski-Paquet moved quickly to the balcony, knocking over an air conditioning unit in the process, they said. When she disappeared from view, they believed she had stepped onto the adjacent balcony, and did not realize she had fallen, the officers testified.

The inquest has focused largely on Korchinski-Paquet’s history of seizures from epilepsy as well as education and training around epilepsy and postictal delirium or psychosis, mental states that can occur after seizures and lead to uncharacteristic behaviour.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures earlier in the day, hours before police were called over a fight involving knives. Korchinski-Paquet, her mother and her brother each called 911 and mentioned her diagnosis and seizures to the call taker, jurors heard.

The jury watched a compilation video combining the recordings of the five calls and two police microphones with CCTV footage from the hallway outside Korchinski-Paquet’s apartment and video from a police cruiser.

Korchinski-Paquet made three of the 911 calls, telling the call taker she was having difficulty breathing after being attacked by her mother and brother. She said she had lost control and thrown two bottles at them in the hallway.

She mentioned her epilepsy after being asked if anyone involved had mental health issues.

In their calls, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother and brother mentioned that she was often agitated after her seizures. Her brother, Reece Korchinski, said she assaulted him with knives after a dispute over the TV volume.

Beals testified she called 911 because she wanted police to take her daughter to Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health.

Six police officers and two paramedics responded to the calls, the inquest heard.

Korchinski told the inquest police assumed an “aggressive” tone toward his sister, treating her like a suspect rather than a citizen. He also felt threatened by what appeared to be a shotgun in one of the officers’ hands, not knowing at the time it was a less-lethal weapon used by police, he said.

Under cross-examination Wednesday, Korchinski said that while he understood police had been called for an assault involving knives, the officers had the chance to assess the situation directly after they arrived at the scene and could see that neither he, his sister or their mother were dangerous.

The officers should have let his sister enter the apartment alone instead of going with her, he said.

“If the police never showed up that day, Regis would still be alive,” Korchinski said.

Beaudoin and Vandenbrink were the first to arrive, the inquest heard. They went up to talk to the family and debriefed each other once some of their colleagues showed up, the jury heard.

Vandenbrink told the inquest it was during that conversation that he first heard about Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures.

Both officers testified that they never stepped out onto the balcony, nor did they know at the time about postictal delirium or psychosis.

A neurologist who reviewed Korchinski-Paquet’s records after her death testified that she had previously shown symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis.

It would be “nearly impossible” to tell whether someone was acting aggressively due to delirium or psychosis after a seizure or for some other reason without knowing their medical history, Dr. Julien Hébert told the inquest.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign blame or legal responsibility, but they may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Canada welcomes EU leaders to Montreal for talks on next steps in relationship
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to welcome European Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen to Montreal today after months of pursuing closer ties with the EU.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Prime Minister Mark Carney now says Canada is working to become an “associate member” of the European Union, after largely avoiding that term.

“We’re here because we share a common mission. We’re in the process of forging a new alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member,” Carney said Thursday.

The prime minister on Thursday welcomed senior officials from Brussels to the two-day Canada-EU Summit in Montreal to negotiate a new partnership — though critics say the outcomes have been unclear.

“We can work on everything from AI and climate, to energy and security, you just name it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

She said the term “associate member” is helpful for deepening policy alignment.

“Canada cannot become a fully fledged member of the European Union because of geography. But we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible, and this is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union,” she said.

Von der Leyen first proposed associate member status for Canada in a September speech to the European Parliament. Canadian and European officials immediately downplayed that terminology, opting instead for “alliance for the future.”

Several EU member nations, including Germany, have rejected the idea of associate membership.

Some have expressed unease with Canada gaining special status while countries such as Ukraine go through arduous reforms to obtain full membership. Others fear a side deal with Canada could encourage countries to leave the EU and seek select benefits while avoiding some of the obligations of full membership.

Prime Minister Carney has said repeatedly the substance of the agreement is more important than the language used to describe it.

“This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter,” he told reporters.

“What matters to Canadians ultimately from this new alliance is going to be affordability, it’s going to be opportunity,” he said, arguing closer economic links will lead to more purchasing power for Canadians.

Von der Leyen’s visit comes after months of Carney pursuing closer ties with the EU. He has argued Europe complements Canada’s economic strengths and shares its values.

Thursday’s agenda included a welcome dinner with elected and business leaders. Canadian and European leaders are expected to get down to talks on Friday.

In his own Thursday afternoon speech, European Council President Antonio Costa endorsed the “bold idea” of associate membership for Canada.

“Regardless of the specific term used, one thing is clear: our partnership will be the closest, deepest and most unique one possible,” he said in French.

“At our summit tomorrow, we will announce an agreement on digital trade that will complement the CETA,” he added, referring to the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement.

“We need to strengthen labour mobility. It’s very important what we are doing with students, but we can do more with labour activity,” he said in English, pointing to how credentials are accepted in both jurisdictions.

“Mutual recognition is good. And also, to use better the digital tools to facilitate air transport on both sides of the Atlantic.”

In her Thursday speech, von der Leyen said the EU wants to work first with Canada and then with other nations to reinforce their sovereignty and interests.

“We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old world order,” she said, adding that nations can work strategically together instead of facing down threats alone.

“We are witnessing a deeper decay in international order. Alliances and assumptions that have enabled our prosperity and security are changing rapidly.”

She cited “choke points” in trade, where one country coerces another by manipulating supply chains. She did not name specific countries.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters Thursday that Canada’s work with the EU seeks to reduce reliance on the U.S. as Washington pursues its trade war.

“The challenge of the era is really to be capable of saving companies that otherwise will fail and will have job losses. So we’re in a hurry,” she said in French.

Von der Leyen said in her speech that a new partnership could see Canada increase its mining of critical minerals, aided by European “industrial demand, technology and investment.”

She said Canadian startups and researchers will soon be able to train their models on the EU’s supercomputers.

“Tomorrow we will finalize our agreement to bring Canada into Europe’s infrastructure for supercomputing,” she said Thursday.

Both sides are also working on joint projects in the Arctic on ocean monitoring, critical raw materials and connectivity as Russia rebuilds its military footprint in the region.

The EU “will deepen Canada’s engagement” in university student exchanges through the Erasmus+ program, von der Leyen said. Both sides are also “working to strengthen Canada’s participation” in the next phase of a scientific research program called Horizon, she added.

She said there also could be cross-Atlantic collaboration between elected officials and judiciaries.

As von der Leyen spoke, the Conservatives dismissed the summit as a “distraction” from deteriorating living standards and the trade war.

“Canadians are faced with another distraction for the next two days, of more meaningless agreements. Meanwhile, they go to food banks and struggle to pay their mortgages,” Conservative trade critic Stephanie Kusie said on Parliament Hill.

Her party colleagues argued Canada should avoid deepening ties with Europe until all EU member states ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada and Brussels stops charging carbon tariffs on Canadian imports.

CETA was signed during the EU-Canada summit 10 years ago and has been applied provisionally since 2017.

Nine EU members have not fully ratified it. Slovenia became the latest country to ratify CETA on Sept. 29. Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy and Poland are the remaining holdouts.

The Conservatives have claimed that any new deal with the EU would see Canada lose control over immigration. Federal officials have insisted repeatedly that any labour mobility agreements would be limited to specific professions or student exchanges.

The Asia-Pacific Foundation argued in a Thursday brief that Carney is focusing on European economies with far slower growth than their Asian counterparts.

“The EU — despite its many strengths — is an occasionally distracted suitor, reckoning with sluggish growth, infighting over budgets and Ukraine (and how to label Canada’s relation to the bloc), and ascendant far-right leaders,” the institute wrote in a Thursday newsletter.

paragraphs: MONTREAL - Prime Minister Mark Carney now says Canada is working to become an “associate member” of the European Union, after largely avoiding that term.
“We’re here because we share a common mission. We’re in the process of forging a new alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member,” Carney said Thursday.
The prime minister on Thursday welcomed senior officials from Brussels to the two-day Canada-EU Summit in Montreal to negotiate a new partnership — though critics say the outcomes have been unclear.
“We can work on everything from AI and climate, to energy and security, you just name it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
She said the term “associate member” is helpful for deepening policy alignment.

“Canada cannot become a fully fledged member of the European Union because of geography. But we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible, and this is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union,” she said.

Von der Leyen first proposed associate member status for Canada in a September speech to the European Parliament. Canadian and European officials immediately downplayed that terminology, opting instead for “alliance for the future.”
Several EU member nations, including Germany, have rejected the idea of associate membership.

Some have expressed unease with Canada gaining special status while countries such as Ukraine go through arduous reforms to obtain full membership. Others fear a side deal with Canada could encourage countries to leave the EU and seek select benefits while avoiding some of the obligations of full membership.
Prime Minister Carney has said repeatedly the substance of the agreement is more important than the language used to describe it.
“This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter,” he told reporters.

“What matters to Canadians ultimately from this new alliance is going to be affordability, it’s going to be opportunity,” he said, arguing closer economic links will lead to more purchasing power for Canadians.
Von der Leyen’s visit comes after months of Carney pursuing closer ties with the EU. He has argued Europe complements Canada’s economic strengths and shares its values.
Thursday’s agenda included a welcome dinner with elected and business leaders. Canadian and European leaders are expected to get down to talks on Friday.
In his own Thursday afternoon speech, European Council President Antonio Costa endorsed the “bold idea” of associate membership for Canada.
“Regardless of the specific term used, one thing is clear: our partnership will be the closest, deepest and most unique one possible,” he said in French.
“At our summit tomorrow, we will announce an agreement on digital trade that will complement the CETA,” he added, referring to the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement.

“We need to strengthen labour mobility. It’s very important what we are doing with students, but we can do more with labour activity,” he said in English, pointing to how credentials are accepted in both jurisdictions.
“Mutual recognition is good. And also, to use better the digital tools to facilitate air transport on both sides of the Atlantic.”
In her Thursday speech, von der Leyen said the EU wants to work first with Canada and then with other nations to reinforce their sovereignty and interests.
“We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old world order,” she said, adding that nations can work strategically together instead of facing down threats alone.
“We are witnessing a deeper decay in international order. Alliances and assumptions that have enabled our prosperity and security are changing rapidly.”
She cited “choke points” in trade, where one country coerces another by manipulating supply chains. She did not name specific countries.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters Thursday that Canada’s work with the EU seeks to reduce reliance on the U.S. as Washington pursues its trade war.
“The challenge of the era is really to be capable of saving companies that otherwise will fail and will have job losses. So we’re in a hurry,” she said in French.
Von der Leyen said in her speech that a new partnership could see Canada increase its mining of critical minerals, aided by European “industrial demand, technology and investment.”
She said Canadian startups and researchers will soon be able to train their models on the EU’s supercomputers.
“Tomorrow we will finalize our agreement to bring Canada into Europe’s infrastructure for supercomputing,” she said Thursday.
Both sides are also working on joint projects in the Arctic on ocean monitoring, critical raw materials and connectivity as Russia rebuilds its military footprint in the region.

The EU “will deepen Canada’s engagement” in university student exchanges through the Erasmus+ program, von der Leyen said. Both sides are also “working to strengthen Canada’s participation” in the next phase of a scientific research program called Horizon, she added.
She said there also could be cross-Atlantic collaboration between elected officials and judiciaries.
As von der Leyen spoke, the Conservatives dismissed the summit as a “distraction” from deteriorating living standards and the trade war.

“Canadians are faced with another distraction for the next two days, of more meaningless agreements. Meanwhile, they go to food banks and struggle to pay their mortgages,” Conservative trade critic Stephanie Kusie said on Parliament Hill.

Her party colleagues argued Canada should avoid deepening ties with Europe until all EU member states ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada and Brussels stops charging carbon tariffs on Canadian imports.
CETA was signed during the EU-Canada summit 10 years ago and has been applied provisionally since 2017.

Nine EU members have not fully ratified it. Slovenia became the latest country to ratify CETA on Sept. 29. Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy and Poland are the remaining holdouts.

The Asia-Pacific Foundation argued in a Thursday brief that Carney is focusing on European economies with far slower growth than their Asian counterparts.

“The EU — despite its many strengths — is an occasionally distracted suitor, reckoning with sluggish growth, infighting over budgets and Ukraine (and how to label Canada’s relation to the bloc), and ascendant far-right leaders,” the institute wrote in a Thursday newsletter.

stories.title: Ontario pauses some skills training funding for unemployed people: career colleges
stories.summary: Toronto - In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private post-secondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private post-secondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.

But the government won’t explicitly say so.

There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the workforce, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.

Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an HVAC program in London, Ont., on Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.

The next intake for the HVAC program is in May 2027.

“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.

“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays ... waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”

Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.

“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.

Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.

“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.

“As with OSAP, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that OSAP payments are paused for students at all private post-secondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Trillium College has suspended classes due to the OSAP pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”

When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.

“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about OSAP usage at private post-secondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

“OSAP payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”

Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.

“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government is ducking accountability.

“This government is terrified of facing the music,” she wrote in a statement.

“They won’t even do the bare minimum of explaining themselves. They’re leaving thousands of people who rely on this program to build a better future and find good jobs without any certainty or support. This is not how you protect Ontario in the face of growing job losses.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

stories.title: Privacy commissioner opens investigation into Crime Stoppers data breach
stories.summary: Canada's privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into a reportedly massive Crime Stoppers data breach as police departments across the country have paused accepting tips through the platform.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada’s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into a reportedly massive Crime Stoppers data breach as police departments across the country have paused accepting tips through the platform.

The office of privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne says the probe will look into the cybersecurity incident involving Navigate360, the third-party company that manages the platform used by Crime Stoppers.

The investigation comes after CBC reported that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed when Navigate360 was hacked in March.

The U.S.-based company confirmed the breach last week, saying it immediately opened its own investigation, took “mitigation measures” and “implemented additional and enhanced safeguards” with the support of another cybersecurity firm after the discovery.

Police forces across Ontario, including several in the Greater Toronto Area, temporarily paused directing public calls to Crime Stoppers following the revelation.

Beyond Ontario, at least two police departments in Manitoba, including Winnipeg, have said that they would stop taking tips through the program as they review and assess the incident.

Saskatchewan Crime Stoppers told the public over the weekend to avoid sending tips through its platform.

“The pause is temporary. We will begin accepting new tips as soon as we are confident it is safe to do so,” it said in a statement.

The privacy commissioner’s office said it has reached out to Crime Stoppers programs to offer “expertise and guidance” in response to the breach.

“The investigation will examine the security safeguards that Navigate360 had in place at the time of the breach to determine the organization’s compliance with Canada’s federal private-sector privacy law,” it said in a statement Tuesday.

The watchdog also said it has contacted Navigate360, though it didn’t say whether the company has responded.

It said its engagement “with both organizations is focused on ensuring that the necessary steps are being taken to address the breach and protect Canadians’ personal information.”

stories.title: After election victory, Chow to face budget pressure and new deal with Ontario
stories.summary: Toronto - Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto's budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow's election victory, as she vowed to be the "mayor for everyone."
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto’s budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow’s election victory on Tuesday, as she vowed to be the “mayor for everyone.”

Chow took her first question from reporters hours after she held off challenger Brad Bradford in Monday’s election and convinced voters to back a second term of her progressive agenda.

“There’s a firm belief that we are stronger together. And the majority of the people of Toronto spoke out so loudly, with such enthusiasm,” she said.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says it doesn't matter who voted for her, she'll be mayor for everyone in Toronto, and will work with the new council and other levels of government to address problems Torontonians face. (Oct. 27, 2026)

“They know that we can take better care of each other.”

Her peacemaking political style earned her approving words from Premier Doug Ford during the campaign, who stopped just short of endorsing her in the contest.

Now, Chow will likely look to summon that goodwill as she looks to negotiations with Ford on a new Toronto-Ontario fiscal deal. The city has projected a 2027 budget hole of around $1.1 billion. Transit ridership continues to lag behind pre-pandemic levels while a softening real estate market is expected to squeeze the municipal land transfer tax.

Chow inherited a $1.8 billion shortfall when she was first elected in 2023. She sought to plug the hole with two sizable property tax increases and a major deal with Ford’s government. Ontario assumed maintenance of the city’s expressways and provided $1.2 billion in operating dollars for transit and shelters, while Chow dropped the city’s opposition to the Ontario Place redevelopment.

That deal is now set to expire at the same time as Chow has campaigned on a promise to keep property taxes at or below the rate of inflation. She reiterated that tax pledge on Tuesday while highlighting that the city had secured its first credit-rating upgrade in more than two decades during her first term.

“I do know the budget very well. I just hope that there is no surprises from outside the City of Toronto, but I don’t expect any,” she said.

Asked on Tuesday how quickly she planned to hash out a new deal with the province, Chow said she had exchanged texts with the premier earlier that morning.

“And no matter which level of government, whether it’s a federal or provincial government, they want to work together and they want do the best they can for the residents of Toronto.”

Chow managed to stave off her challenger on a night where several incumbents were toppled in Ontario’s municipal elections, including Mississauga’s Carolyn Parrish, Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath and Windsor’s Drew Dilkens.

Premier Doug Ford congratulated Chow on the victory and says he will “work with anyone to drive the economy to make sure we protect communities and companies and people” from U.S. tariffs.

Chow will preside over a council with a boosted progressive bloc as she seeks to make good on other campaign promises to cap weekly transit fares, introduce free school lunches and strengthen renter protections.

The departure of rival Bradford from council heralded the political resurrection of former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith, who aligned himself with Chow in his successful run in Beaches East-York after a failed pivot to provincial politics. Chiara Padovani, a tenant organizer, defeated Toronto’s longest-serving councillor Frances Nunziata in York South-Weston.

Voter turnout was around 46 per cent, the highest it’s been since 2014. Chow’s 13 percentage point victory over Bradford would mark the narrowest win by a sitting mayor since the city’s amalgamation.

The dust barely had time to settle on Monday night’s election before Chow, 69, was asked about her long-term political future. As she stood outside city hall, she brushed off a question Tuesday about whether this would be her last run for mayor.

“I’m going to spend every moment of today and the next four years working hard for the people of Toronto,” she said. “As to the future, let us take one day, one week, one month, one year at a time.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec premier accuses Ottawa of censoring him at EU Summit
stories.summary: Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is accusing Ottawa of muzzling him at the upcoming Canada-European Union summit in Montreal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is accusing Ottawa of muzzling him at the upcoming Canada-European Union summit in Montreal.

The federal government has assured the premier that he is invited to dinner with EU representatives, but the premier will not speak at the summit taking place Thursday and Friday.

“He was invited to the dinner and he refused,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday. “It’s his decision to leave the chair empty.”

But the premier wrote on social media that Ottawa is seeking to impose economic decisions on Quebec without allowing the province a seat at the negotiating table.

“The federal government would have us believe that giving the Quebec premier permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence in representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote.

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in Ottawa that geopolitics, including the summit, fall under federal jurisdiction.

The Parti Québécois government also says Ottawa denied Quebec’s request to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, which was submitted by former premier Christine Fréchette in September.

A provincial government spokesperson says the EU routinely holds a forum for economic leaders during such summits, which the province could have hosted or co-hosted.

The spokesperson said that there is precedent to include Quebec at the summit, as provincial representatives participated in negotiations for the Canada-European Union Free Trade Agreement.

Marie-Claude Sarrazin, the new Quebec minister of justice and Canadian intergovernmental affairs, said the federal government’s position serves as a reminder that the province needs “to be fully in charge in our own home.”

“‘When you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,’ Prime Minister Carney once told us,” she said. “The federal government has chosen to prevent Quebec from having a say on its own territory. This is a fundamental lack of respect toward Quebec and a denial of the role of our legislature.”

The tension around the summit comes after St-Pierre Plamondon did not participate in a meeting on Monday between the federal government, provincial premiers and First Nations.

The Quebec premier also spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday.

stories.title: Bazinet winds Goderich mayoral race in a landslide
stories.summary: Central Huron Mayor
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Here’s what you need to know about the candidates running in Central Huron Mayor , Huron East Mayor , Morris-Turnberry Mayor , South Huron Mayor , Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh Mayor , Howick Reeve , North Huron Reeve , Arran-Elderslie Mayor , Brockton Mayor , Kincardine Mayor , Northern Bruce Peninsula Mayor , South Bruce Mayor , Saugeen Shores Mayor , South Bruce Peninsula Mayor , and Huron-Kinloss Mayor

In a landslide victory, capturing nearly 85 per cent of the vote, Trevor Bazinet has been elected mayor of the Town of Goderich.

“Yeah, it is a dream come true. In my high school yearbook, the graduating question was future ambitions, and I wrote I wanted to become the Mayor of the Town of Goderich. So, yeah, you can’t write it any better, right?” said Bazinet.

In front of a crowd of supporters at Steve and Mary’s on the Square in Goderich, Bazinet celebrated the beginning of what is technically his second term as Goderich’s mayor. While this is the first time he has been voted in by Goderich’s electorate, Bazinet has served as the town’s mayor since August 2023, following the death of then-mayor Myles Murdock.

“I’m now elected as the Mayor. Before I was appointed. And, you know, you never want to become the Mayor the way that I became the Mayor, losing a dear mentor and friend of mine in Myles Murdock. But, you know, I can officially say that I have been elected as the Mayor of the Town of Goderich,” he said.

Bazinet received 3,098 votes to runner-up Steve Buchanan’s 587 votes.

“My mom’s no longer with me. And like I said to the people behind me here, it’s a very emotional moment for me, because my mom said several years ago that you would make a great Mayor one day, Trevor. And here I am now, the Mayor of the Town of Goderich, elected Mayor. So I’m very proud. And I think of her often. And I’m thinking of her right now as I talk to you about it,” said Bazinet.

Randy Carroll was acclaimed deputy mayor of Goderich. Liz Petrie, Vanessa McMillan, John Thompson, Jacob Bjerg and Chris Garnier make up the rest of Goderich council. Garnier beat Charles Oliver by just two votes for the final council seat, according to the unofficial results released by the Town of Goderich.

stories.title: ‘Local, capable, proven leadership’: Jeff Kohler elected as St. Thomas mayor
stories.summary: Jeff Kohler elected as St. Thomas mayor
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff, Brent Lale
stories.content:
Here’s what you need to know about the candidates running in Bayham , Central Elgin , Dutton Dunwich , West Elgin , Aylmer , Malahide , and Southwold

St. Thomas, Ont., voters decided to go with a council veteran over a newcomer in the 2026 municipal election.

Jeff Kohler, who has spent 22 years at city hall as a former mayor, alderman and councillor, received nearly 70 per cent of the vote to win.

“Our message of local, capable, proven leadership definitely resonated out there,” said Kohler at his victory party.

“We’re going to start off right away with fiscal responsibility. We need to make sure we put forward some responsible budgets where we’re not impacting the people of today to benefit the people of tomorrow and without cutting services. So that’s going to be a challenge for us. But that’s what we’re looking forward to.”

Kohler, who is succeeding two-term mayor Joe Preston, will also be leading a new council.

Three incumbents, Earl Taylor, Joan Rymal and Jim Herbert, were ousted by three newcomers, Mike Brisson, Joe Docherty Jr. and Kyle Yates, while former mayor Heather Jackson was elected councillor. Gary Clarke, Rose Gibson, Steve Wookey and Lori Baldwin-Sands were also re-elected.

Kohler said some of the new members will quickly realize their campaign promises won’t all happen due to financial restraints.

“At the end of the day, our commitment is going to be to maintain the momentum that they have without cutting services and without impacting the rate they are today with high-impact tax increases,” said Kohler.

As St. Thomas enters one of the most crucial eras in the city’s history, Kohler will be the one to lead the way.

“We are experiencing growth that we haven’t seen for generations,” he said.

“That experience of leading through where we can’t say yes to everything, but what makes it happen? Our transit plan is coming forward. How are we going to improve that? How do we grow that in a responsible way, but not add to the tax impact on taxpayers right now? It’s tough for people, especially seniors on fixed incomes, and we don’t want to add to that pressure.”

stories.title: United Arab Emirates, Canada to share details of strategic partnership today
stories.summary: Mark Carney visited the United Arab Emirates last November, when the UAE pledged to invest around $70 billion in Canada.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a free trade deal on Tuesday they say was reached in a “record” time of 47 days, and have also agreed to start talks on an extradition treaty.

The trade deal was one of a handful of trade and infrastructure agreements signed during the crown prince of Abu Dhabi’s visit to Ottawa on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to Parliament Hill. The crown prince’s motorcade was escorted onto the Hill by four RCMP horses.

It’s just the latest example of the Carney government’s outreach to nations with questionable human rights records as it works to redirect Canada’s trade around an increasingly erratic United States.

Carney was in Turkey last week to discuss deeper economic and social ties with the NATO ally. In recent months, Turkish authorities have targeted multiple LGBTQ+ groups and individuals — detaining dozens of activists, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts.

The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. But the country has been accused of fuelling a militia in Sudan that conducted what Washington has called a genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

Asked Tuesday about human rights concerns linked to the UAE, International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said “human rights never takes a back seat with Canada.”

“It’s important that we continue to engage, being at those tables to make sure that we raise whatever we need to raise in terms of human rights,” he said.

At home, Human Rights Watch says the UAE is responsible for “rampant systemic human rights violations,” particularly with regard to freedom of speech.

Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan.

The letter, signed by the Trade Justice Network, Amnistie internationale Canada francophone and Equality Fund, said as Canada looks to diversify its trade, it needs to assert support for human rights as a core Canadian value.

“Our prosperity cannot be built at the expense of the lives and futures of the Sudanese people,” said the letter.

Ministers from Canada and the UAE have also signed agreements pledging investments in clean power and energy infrastructure and collaboration on diplomatic training.

They’ve signed an agreement on defence co-operation covering military education and training, joint exercises, cybersecurity and information sharing, as well as the creation of a joint military committee.

Stephanie Kusie, Conservative MP and critic for international trade, said in a social media post Tuesday that it’s “tiresome” to see the prime minister holding “yet another flashy meeting with no tangible outcomes for Canadians, as he did today with the UAE.”

“Instead of another fancy ceremony, Canadians deserve clear information about the number of jobs and the names of projects involved, not another vague ‘strategic partnership’ that lacks any real details on how it would improve their lives,” she said.

The Prime Minister’s Office said the trade deal will reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99 per cent of current Canadian exports to the UAE once it’s fully implemented.

The office says the agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including those in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental and engineering sectors.

The Prime Minister’s Office said the trade agreement is expected to take effect next year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan to Parliament Hill. The crown prince’s motorcade was escorted onto the Hill by four RCMP horses.
It’s just the latest example of the Carney government’s outreach to nations with questionable human rights records as it works to redirect Canada’s trade around an increasingly erratic United States.

Carney was in Turkey last week to discuss deeper economic and social ties with the NATO ally. In recent months, Turkish authorities have targeted multiple LGBTQ+ groups and individuals — detaining dozens of activists, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts.

The UAE has taken on increasing importance in global politics and has been praised for work aimed at ending conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. But the country has been accused of fuelling a militia in Sudan that conducted what Washington has called a genocide — a claim Abu Dhabi denies.
Asked Tuesday about human rights concerns linked to the UAE, International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said “human rights never takes a back seat with Canada.”
“It’s important that we continue to engage, being at those tables to make sure that we raise whatever we need to raise in terms of human rights,” he said.
At home, Human Rights Watch says the UAE is responsible for “rampant systemic human rights violations,” particularly with regard to freedom of speech.
Seventeen civil society organizations signed an open letter earlier this year warning Canada against deeper ties to the UAE and arguing the country is perpetuating the war in Sudan.

stories.title: Free labour movement not something Canada and EU considering in new pact: ambassador
stories.summary: Canada and the EU are expected to use the summit to announce a new agreement that could touch on a number of issues including labour, critical minerals and energy.
stories.author: David Baxter and Emilie Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Canada-EU Summit being held this week in Montreal will serve to launch more formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the next year, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday,

Carney will meet with European Union President Ursula von der Leyen and other EU officials on Thursday and Friday in Montreal, where they are expected to announce the next stage of an enhanced alliance.

“This is the launch of further formal discussions, negotiations, over the course of the next year,” Carney said on his way into the weekly cabinet meeting.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says this week's Canada-EU Summit in Montreal offers an opening to expand opportunities for Canadians and Canadian companies in Europe. (Oct. 27, 2026)

The exact nature of the pact between Canada and the EU has been unclear — even to the leaders themselves.

In September, von der Leyen said the new arrangement could make Canada an “associate” member of the 27-member bloc. But “associate membership” does not actually exist in the EU and Canadian officials have downplayed the use of that term.

“It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians, in terms of opportunities to study work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities,” Carney said Tuesday, adding it could open up new research opportunities as well.

Carney used the term “alliance of the future” to describe the deal, which was first made public when he spoke to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France, last month.

Jonathan Wilkinson, who took on the Canadian ambassadorship in Brussels earlier this year after spending more than five years in the Liberal cabinet, told The Canadian Press the labour policy discussions with Europe are focused on “specialized areas” where employers on both sides of the Atlantic could benefit from access to a shared labour pool.

He said any measures that would make it easier for workers and students to move between the two jurisdictions must be approached in a “thoughtful way.”

“We’re not talking about free movement of labour between Europe and Canada. But what we are talking about is, in some specialized areas, it may be actually interesting and useful for both countries to have the ability to tap into labour pools,” Wilkinson said.

The ambassador did not cite specific sectors where labour mobility between Canada and the EU could be eased. The EU and Canada have been discussing increased collaboration on critical minerals, technology, defence and clean energy.

Wilkinson pointed to work already done by Canada and Europe on mutual accreditation for architects and said any future decisions about labour mobility would be focused on areas of “mutual benefit.”

Canada has also discussed joining Erasmus+, the European Union’s student exchange program, which offers study and training opportunities in member nations.

Michelle Rempel Garner, the Conservative immigration critic, has called on the government to explain what these negotiations mean for people coming to Canada.

“Canadians are already struggling with the cost of living due to immigration levels which are too high and have contributed to jobs becoming more scarce and workers getting paid less. Canadians deserve transparency on any EU immigration deal and how it would impact our jobs, homes, and health care,” she said in a statement.

The summit appears to be a source of friction between Carney and the new Parti Québécois government in Quebec.

A spokesperson for Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon St-Pierre Plamondon said in a written statement that Ottawa denied the premier the chance to speak at the summit and refused to allow Quebec to host a reception on the sidelines, following a request submitted by the former government in mid-September.

Following the cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney said in French that St-Pierre Plamondon declined an invitation to join him and the other premiers for a dinner with European officials during the summit. Carney said the federal government has had three consultation sessions with Quebec about the talks with the EU.

Joel Lightbound, Carney’s Quebec lieutenant, said Tuesday that St-Pierre Plamondon is welcome to attend the summit and the dinner but this is still a meeting between Canada and the EU.

This week’s summit will take place on the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Canada-Europe Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA.

Nine EU members — France, Italy, Belgium, Ireland, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece and Hungary — have not yet ratified that trade deal.

Wilkinson said he’s spoken with all 27 of his EU member nation counterparts and there is momentum in Europe to get more countries behind CETA. He did not name specific nations.

One of the EU’s leading nations may have a new government soon. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is the current polling favourite to succeed Emmanuel Macron as president this spring.

Le Pen delivered a nearly hour-long speech to supporters Sunday that focused on her party’s nationalist, anti-immigrant positions.

Wilkinson said politics is always dynamic and Europeans and Canadians will go on sharing values regardless of which party is in power in a particular nation.

“I think in France, it’s a very important debate that they are having. And I think that if in fact the government were to change, people will have to take stock of that,” he said.

“But I do think that the European Union is a much bigger project than any one government in any one country. And I have a lot of confidence that Europeans will find their way through this and be just fine.”

Wilkinson said energy and critical minerals — including natural gas, hydrogen and nuclear power — will play a crucial role in the enhanced partnership between Canada and the EU.

“We’re looking at … how can we, for example, encourage significant additional European investment in Canadian minerals projects. We’re talking about how can we think about things like stockpiling together so that we actually can help to stabilize the market,” Wilkinson said.

The European Investment Bank applied for an exemption from Canadian foreign banking rules earlier this month that would allow the state investor to operate in Canada as part of a critical minerals agreement.

Wilkinson said Canada and the European Union are both looking for ways to build up the infrastructure to refine and ship critical minerals and reduce China’s market dominance.

“That’s not a dependency that’s good for Canada. That’s not a dependency good for the European Union. So we are looking at that,” he said.

— With files from The Associated Press.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

By The Canadian Press

The province says the funding from its Community Economic Development Fund is going to the Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association.

It says the association will use the money to promote local companies at industry trade shows and missions, in trade publications and through online communications and strategic partnerships.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Image 9Image 10Image 11

The Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association was established in 1998 to diversify the industry beyond the domestic fishing boat market.

The province says the investment will help local boatbuilders deliver on national defence priorities and compete internationally for naval contracts.

The executive director of the Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association says the boatbuilding industry maintains small vessels for several of the province’s key industries, including fisheries and defence.

“This investment helps to ensure the ongoing health of our industry, and the rural communities where much of the work takes place, as we navigate an unusually complex trade environment,” said a statement from executive director Jan Fullerton.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Pjhl Recap - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th
stories.summary: The Merchants celebrated two wins, the Braves suffered two losses, and the Trojans had a mixed weekend.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 26 October 2026 at 08:36

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Merchants celebrated two wins, the Braves suffered two losses, and the Trojans had a mixed weekend.

PJHL - It was a great weekend for the Norwich Merchants, but a not so great weekend for the Tavistock Braves.

The Merchants beat the Dorchester Dolphins 4-3 in a shootout on Friday and celebrated a 4-3 overtime victory over the Braves yesterday. Ethan Osborne scored the game winning goal on Friday and Tyler McDole secured the victory for Norwich yesterday.

The Braves were also shutout by the Paris Mounties 5-0 on Friday.

The Thamesford Trojans celebrated a 7-3 victory over the Petrolia Flyers on Friday with Brady Snedden, Owen Eldridge, Ryan Rodney, Andrew Kalantzakos, Nathan Enwright, and Ben Siroen scoring for the home team. However, the Trojans did suffer a 4-3 overtime loss to the North Middlesex Stars on Saturday, with Noah Vandenburg scoring the game winning goal about 30 seconds into overtime.

The Braves still top the Doherty Division standings with 22 points. They're followed by the Wellesley Applejacks with 20 points, the New Hamburg Firebirds with 19 points, and the Merchants with 14 points. The Dolphins are in fifth place with 11 points, the Mounties sit in sixth place with 10 points, and the Hespeler Shamrocks are at the bottom of the standings with six points.

The Trojans are in fifth place in the Yeck Division standings with 12 points, ahead of the sixth place Lucan Irish with nine points and the last place Port Stanley Sailors with seven points.

The Stars top the Yeck Division standings with 18 points and they're followed by the Mount Brydges Bulldogs with 17 points, and the Exeter Hawks and Aylmer Spitfires are tied for third place with 16 points each. The Flyers are in fourth place with 13 points.

Navy Vets Recap - Oct 23rd Oct 25th The Woodstock Navy Vets are in eighth place in the GOHL Western Conference standings.

Woodstock Police Briefs - October 26th, 2026 Woodstock Police briefs include an impaired driver, a shoplifter, and two people wanted by the Waterloo Regional Police Service.

UPDATE: More Assault Charges Laid in Tillsonburg The suspect is facing 13 counts of sexual assault and one count of sexual interference, stemming from five victims.

Municipal Election Day in Oxford County You have until 8:00 p.m. to cast your ballot in the 2026 municipal election.

WITAAR Supports Local Classrooms WITAAR's annual classroom supply drive has helped many classrooms across the County this year.

Ingersoll Pumpkin Fest Returns this Saturday Each family will go home with a free pumpkin, while supplies last.

PJHL Preview - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th The Braves, Trojans and Merchants all have home games tonight.

Navy Vets Preview - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th Tonight's pre-game ceremony will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the Woodstock Navy Vets.

Norfolk OPP Briefs - October 23rd, 2026 Briefs include two incidents in Waterford; a break and enter on Green Street and a stolen vehicle on Concession 8 Townsend.

Wolverines to Face WPS in Friday Night Lights Charity Classic The Woodstock Wolverines will face off against members of the Woodstock Police Service in the first annual Friday Night Lights Charity Classic on October 30th.

Blandford-Blenheim Candidate Profile - Nancy Demarest When the ballots are cast, a current councillor in Blandford-Blenheim is seeking re-election. Nancy Demarest is seeking a third term on council.

OPP Respond to Weapons Call in Tillsonburg The Oxford OPP responded to a weapons call, which turned into a teaching moment for 5 people.

Navy Vets Celebrating 60 Years It is the 60th anniversary of the Woodstock Navy Vets, and the Woodstock Museum has an exhibit to help celebrate.

Woodstock Receives Gaming Revenue Payment from OLG The cheque is worth $416,310 and its for hosting Gateway Casinos.

Schedule Released for CPKC Holiday Train The CPKC Holiday Train will be stopping in Woodstock on Saturday, November 21st.

Local History Speaker Series Returns Two events will be held in November that are part of the Local History Speaker Series.

Woodstock Police Briefs - Oct. 21st, 2026 An impaired driver has been taken off the road, and a suspect in a theft was arrested by the Woodstock Police Service.

Advance Voting Numbers High in Woodstock As election day comes closer, the City of Woodstock has released the number of ballots cast between online and advance polling stations.

Winning Lotto Max Ticket Sold in Oxford A Lotto Max ticket worth $100,000 was sold in Oxford County. The $90 million jackpot was awarded in Alberta.

Voting Opens and Tickets Available for Chamber Awards The Woodstock District Chamber of Commerce will host the 29th annual Business Awards of Excellence on November 4th.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada has received its first pair of new F-35 fighter jets, with Ottawa still deliberating how many of the American planes it will buy.

The Royal Canadian Air Force announced Friday on social media that it received the two Lockheed Martin jets, sharing a photo from Phoenix showing one plane with a maple-leaf roundel.

stories.title: Americans in Canada urge fellow expats to vote in high-stakes midterm elections
stories.summary: Ottawa - American Democrats living in Canada are prepared to shout their political choices from the rooftops ahead of next month's midterm elections — while some of those who back Republican candidates seem leery of speaking out fearing a backlash from their neighbours.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - American Democrats living in Canada are prepared to shout their political choices from the rooftops ahead of next month’s midterm elections — while some of those who back Republican candidates seem leery of speaking out fearing a backlash from their neighbours.

Tammy Wilsker Mermelstein, a Texas voter who moved to the Greater Toronto Area last year, will be voting in a U.S. election from Canada for the first time.

While she used to be a Republican and voted that way until 2016, Wilsker Mermelstein said she has never voted for U.S. President Donald Trump. She said it’s crucial for people to vote this year as “Texas is in play.”

“Texas has not elected a Democrat in high office for at least two decades, probably longer, and this is the first solid chance,” she said. “They say every vote counts. This is really going to be an election where every vote matters, even in states where people aren’t used to having their vote matter if they’re in the minority.”

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections which could see the Democrats seize control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives from the Republicans. Democratic control of one or both chambers could significantly alter the path of Trump’s presidency, including the possibility of new impeachment proceedings against him, and investigations of some of his key allies and agency heads.

Expat participation in U.S. elections is typically low, though the Federal Voting Assistance Program estimates there were more than 430,000 eligible U.S. voters in Canada as of 2024.

The organization estimates turnout among Americans in Canada was about 10 per cent in the 2024 general election, while the domestic voting rate that year was about 76 per cent. The organization estimates the overall turnout among all eligible overseas U.S. citizens at 11 per cent.

Kathryn Sikkink, a professor at the Harvard Kennedy School who has volunteered with the U.S. Vote Foundation, said participation in voting abroad may be low because some citizens find it difficult. Some, she said, don’t even realize they’re eligible to vote.

The U.S. Department of State website says U.S. citizens can get an absentee ballot by mail, email or fax, or by downloading it from the internet, though options vary by state.

Most U.S. citizens can vote absentee for federal office candidates in U.S. primary and general elections. Some states also allow U.S. citizens living abroad to vote for local and state office candidates, and on referendums.

Georganne Burke, the chapter lead for Republicans Overseas in Canada, said it has been a “contentious year” as Americans living in Canada have watched “the back and forth” between the two governments over trade.

“They want to make sure that whatever’s going on in the States stays kind of healthy in case they have to go back home. So people, they are more engaged, I think, than they have in the past,” she said.

A dual citizen, Burke moved back to the U.S. a few months ago after spending 38 years in Toronto and Ottawa.

A Republican and Trump supporter, Burke said she estimates there is a roughly three-to-one Democrat to Republican ratio among American expats living in Canada.

“I know that most Republicans are very motivated to vote,” she said. “They’re very quiet about it. They don’t talk because they’re not received in a very friendly way in Canada, which is kind of unfortunate.

“Democrats are also motivated to vote, especially if they’re in one of those toss-up states, like Michigan.”

When The Canadian Press sought to speak with various American voters via social media pages and message boards, lots of Democrats stepped forward. Not one Republican did.

Burke said it’s a civic duty to vote in elections. She also said while some of the things Trump says and does make her “cringe,” she focuses on his accomplishments.

“A lot of the thing that he has done in the United States have made a huge difference for Americans, including dealing with the border problem in Mexico,” she said. “And I know it drives people crazy, but he is reshoring, as he puts it, American industry to the United States to employ Americans. That’s his job.”

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a leading ballot box issue in some key states ahead of the U.S. midterms.

Trump rapidly escalated his trade war and rhetoric against Canada after trade negotiations fell apart in August. The president signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America and the United States hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs. A few weeks later, Ottawa responded with its own retaliatory duties.

Jessica Matwick, a dual citizen who lives in Ottawa and is involved with Democrats Abroad and Indivisible Ottawa, said every eligible voter should get out and vote “to put a stop to an unhinged administration and a legislative body that has abdicated their responsibility to keep the executive in check.”

“The attacks on Canadian sovereignty and destructive tariff war are actions I cannot remain silent about,” said Matwick, who moved back to Canada in late 2016 and votes in Virginia. “I still have family living in the U.S. and many friends who I am concerned about.

“My heart hurts knowing that the damage that has been done in a relatively short period of time will take years and years to repair.”

Cody Littlefield, who moved to Canada from the U.S. in 2019 and now lives in Calgary, said he tries to vote in every election. A California voter, he said this election presents an opportunity for voters to send a message that what’s happening in the U.S. “is not acceptable.”

“The future of the country really matters to me,” said Littlefield, adding that he and his family may eventually move back to the U.S.

“There are some people who will never go back and maybe they just really don’t care about the domestic stuff, but I would say the foreign policy still does affect them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.
