stories.title: Cuban ambassadors ask Canada to renew its rejection of U.S. embargo and fuel blockade
stories.summary: Ottawa - Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.

“We are confident that Canada will stay with us, as they have done in the past,” Cuban Ambassador to Canada Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz told The Canadian Press.

“The blockade and this intensification is, in practice, killing people.”

The United Nations is set to vote next week on a motion Cuba has put forward nearly every year since 1992. It calls for the termination of “the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba.”

Cuban Ambassador Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz is urging Canada to not change its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo in a United Nations vote next week. The Trump administration has been ramping up pressure on countries supporting Cuba, where Canada has sent aid to respond to a humanitarian crisis stemming from the U.S. fuel blockade. (Oct. 24, 2026)

Canada has voted in favour of this motion multiple times.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has been trying to overthrow Cuba’s Communist government through a de facto oil blockade. Washington cut off Venezuelan shipments in January and has threatened to impose tariffs on countries that sell oil to the island nation.

President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country. (Oct. 23, 2026)

Washington claims Cuba poses a national security threat to the United States. Malmierca said the Caribbean nation is being collectively punished by an American pressure campaign that is harming the health and education of Cubans.

An economic crisis has gripped Cuba since 2020, triggering critical shortages and severe blackouts that peaked after January’s fuel blockade.

Havana insists its economic struggles stem from six decades of American sanctions, but critics point to the inefficiency of its Communist regime. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say Cuba’s government engages in arbitrary arrests, tortures political prisoners and limits media and political parties.

Cuba produces only 40 per cent of the fuel it needs. Shortages have led to frequent blackouts that have threatened health care systems and crippled the island’s economy. Air Canada and other airlines cancelled flights to Cuba in February because of shortages of aviation fuel.

Ottawa has pledged to distribute $13 million in humanitarian aid for Cubans through international organizations — not the Cuban government. Past Canadian development funding has gone to things like solar panels aimed at making the island less reliant on foreign fuel.

“The people are resisting because we are convinced that the most valuable thing we have is the independence, the sovereignty of Cuba. And we are not going to surrender that,” Malmierca said.

“We would like to have a normal relationship with the U.S. We are ready for dialogue.”

Malmierca said countries that have supported Cuba have told Havana they’re being warned by Washington their access to American trade or aid could be curbed if they continue supporting UN motions to end the blockade.

He said Cuba is “not naive” and knows Canada is facing its own economic pressure from the Trump administration.

“This year is a particular moment because of all this aggressivity of the U.S. government against Cuba,” he said. “They are in a kind of offensive with other countries, trying to exercise influence for them to change their votes. We know they are using threats.”

The Canadian Press asked the U.S. State Department for comment but didn’t receive a response.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz this week urged countries to vote against the motion, dismissing it as a product of “70 years of propaganda” meant to distract from corruption in Havana. He said Washington has been lobbying European countries to vote against the motion.

“Do not let them abuse your vote for their oppression,” he said at a Monday event he hosted. “Do not give in to this lie.”

In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said it is still pondering how it will vote on the UN motion next week.

“As with all UN resolutions, Canada’s voting position is being considered in advance of the vote,” wrote spokesperson Thida Ith.

“Canada continues to call for the Cuban government to implement needed reforms to respect the political and economic rights of the Cuban people, and to release all political prisoners.”

In July, Havana called for a UN debate on the American embargo in the context of the island’s fuel crisis. Washington suggested it was a waste of resources to debate a motion that had already been debated nine months prior, and insisted that the decision to hold a debate be put to a recorded vote.

The vote passed and a debate was held. Canada was among 30 countries that abstained from the motion on holding a debate.

Civil society groups such as the Canadian Network on Cuba said they fear Ottawa may be pulling back from Cuba.

A document The Canadian Press obtained through a freedom-of-information request shows Ottawa had frank exchanges with Cuba about its liquidity crisis before Trump ramped up pressure on the Communist government.

The document — a briefing book prepared by Global Affairs for its deputy minister — shows the deputy minister met with three Canadian firms during a visit to Havana in February 2023 to discuss their Cuban clients’ unpaid bills.

The document says the aim of the meeting was to reassure the three firms that Ottawa “has their back … without unduly encouraging new investors and traders who risk not being paid for their goods/services.”

The companies mentioned in the document are the National Bank, mining firm Sherritt and hotel chain Blue Diamond, now called Royalton. None of the companies responded to The Canadian Press when asked whether they still have accounts in arrears in Cuba.

Sherritt and Royalton have both ceased operations in Cuba. Havana has blamed their withdrawal on American pressure tactics.

The briefing book for the deputy minister reveals some of the nature of Canada’s discussions with Cuba, with Ottawa pushing for details on small and medium-sized enterprises and Havana requesting more aid.

“Canadian firms are facing mounting payment arrears with Cuban buyers. Many Canadian firms in Cuba are SMEs and the situation is threatening their sustainability,” reads the February 2023 document for the deputy minister.

“We sought bilateral meetings for you, that would allow you, for example, to engage on human rights and new economic actors (private sector SMEs and entrepreneurs). The Cuban side wanted rather to talk to you about new tourism initiatives and more Canadian international development projects.”

The briefing book proposed that Canada “leverage Cuba’s desire for increased assistance in our dialogue on other priorities (e.g. human rights)” — but added that the cheapest and most effective things Canada could offer would be technical help with reforming the agriculture sector and rules for smaller businesses.

Malmierca said Cuba is implementing 176 reform measures which came out of parliamentary and public consultations. He said these measures will allow a larger role for the private sector, foreign investment incentives and municipal autonomy.

“In Cuba, we work according to the rule of law,” he said. “Cuba is a society that is continuously trying to improve.”

He said a trade fair in Havana next month is going largely virtual due to the current electricity shortages, and Cuba will hold an event in Toronto ahead of time to drum up interest from Canadian entrepreneurs.

“We can maintain not only the economic relationship, but we can increase it in better conditions in the near future.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

stories.title: British Columbians vote in early election, with David Eby's job on the line
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbians go to the polls today in an early election called by NDP Leader David Eby in the biggest gamble of his political life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Just over five weeks ago, Lorne Doerkson was an obscure British Columbia legislator whose party was falling apart at the seams.

He is now set to become premier at the head of a majority government, soundly defeating the New Democrats in Saturday’s snap election that backfired spectacularly on outgoing Premier David Eby, who announced his resignation as NDP leader.

It took a little over an hour after polls closed at 8 p.m. for The Canadian Press decision desk to call the race, underscoring the stunning nature of Doerkson’s win.

Outgoing NDP Leader David Eby told supporters he takes responsibility for losing Saturday's snap election to the Conservatives. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says he'll follow through on campaign promises to supercharge the province's economy. (Oct. 25, 2026)

The Conservatives had won or were leading in about two-thirds of the province’s 93 ridings about three hours after the polls closed.

He said in a victory speech set to fireworks and Fleetwood Mac’s “Don’t Stop” that “B.C. is definitely blue.”

Doerkson emerged from obscurity to unify a fractured Opposition that was a political basket case just six weeks ago.

Doerkson said he would do everything in his power to get the province “back on track.”

“Together our best days are still ahead of us my friends,” he told supporters at a party in Vancouver, adding that he would follow through on a promise to “supercharge” the province, his voice cracking as he said serving as premier would be the honour of his lifetime.

Doerkson, 58, returned from a trip to Africa and assumed the interim leadership of the Conservatives on Sept. 20, Kerry-Lynne Findlay having resigned after a tumultuous four-month reign.

He took over a party that had been losing legislators at a frantic pace, amid concerns about Findlay’s strategies and what one defector, Bruce Banman, called ideological “purity tests.”

After the 2024 election, the party had 44 legislators and was within three ridings of government, but their ranks had dwindled into the 20s by the time Doerkson took charge.

He swiftly wooed disgruntled Conservatives back to the fold, including seven out of the eight legislators who had announced days earlier they were joining the CentreBC party.

Just two days after Doerkson’s elevation, Eby called the snap election that he initially said was needed to tackle the challenge posed by U.S. President Donald Trump; he would later pivot to say the election was needed to overcome the frustrations of governing with a one-seat majority.

Whatever the reason, the election call was the biggest gamble of Eby’s political career, and it would ultimately cut short his premiership of less than four years.

Former federal Conservative cabinet minister Stockwell Day said at the B.C. Conservatives’ election night party in Vancouver that people “just want back to normal” and British Columbians were going to get “a well-deserved break from radical politics.”

“I think the other part of the strategy was just stand back and let Mr. Eby keep talking, and it seems to have worked,” he said.

Eby told his disconsolate supporters in Vancouver that he had called Doerkson to concede and offer his congratulations.

“The people of B.C. have asked us to be the official Opposition, which is obviously not the result that any of us wanted,” Eby said. “It breaks my heart and I accept full responsibly for that outcome.”

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson is wasting no time after his Conservatives swept into power last night in British Columbia.

Doerkson was gracious in victory.

He told his supporters that Eby had “given to the province for years,” a remark that was greeted with warm applause.

Doerkson also congratulated BC Green Leader Emily Lowan, who won her bid for a place in the legislature, and said British Columbians could be “grateful for her passion.”

At a party in Brentwood Bay on Vancouver Island, BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan celebrated her party’s two-seat win, though she told supporters that she was scared of what a Conservative government would mean.

“The Conservative agenda is one of cuts to the programs that we rely on the most. It’s one of culture wars and needless attacks on human rights and the basic tenets of a dignified life. It stands against everything that brought this movement together,” she said.

Doerkson campaigned on his vow to supercharge the economy, pledging to bring down the record deficit with the help of growth his platform forecast to reach 3.2 per cent, a prediction Eby and other critics suggested was optimistic at best.

He promised no tax increases and to raise B.C.’s basic personal income tax exemption from $13,216 to $32,000, resulting in a $1,000 tax cut for most individual workers.

But he said his top priority would be repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, and he also promised to end sexual orientation and gender identity guidelines for schools.

The NDP promised a new tax bracket for those making more than $1 million to help fund health care, price caps on some basic groceries and a training program for international medical graduates already living in B.C.

Eby promised more before- and after-school spaces, but was criticized for having two children in coveted $10-a-day daycare spots. He said he and his wife paid to make up the difference with the previous cost.

Both parties singled out Surrey, B.C.‘s second-largest city, for special attention, pledging new hospitals and a SkyTrain extension for the region.

The Conservatives were the only party to initially field a full slate of 93 candidates this election but tossed two candidates for online remarks, one commenting about Hitler and the other saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest should have “reversed too.”

Doerkson acted quickly to disavow them.

VANCOUVER - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson’s B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do …

But he stood by Conservative campaign director Katy Merrifield, who Eby said should have been removed over social media posts that included describing Islam as an “abhorrent ideology.” Doerkson defended her as a survivor of sexual assault who commented out of anger.

The legislature at dissolution consisted of 47 New Democrats, 29 Conservatives, two Greens, and 13 Independents, with two vacant seats.

But that did not take into account that most of the nominal Independents were Conservatives who returned to the party after Doerkson became interim leader. They may not all have been reflected in the official numbers, but the Conservatives went into the election holding about 37 seats.

The election win caps a remarkable rise not just for Doerkson but for the B.C. Conservatives, whose last premier, Simon Fraser Tolmie, was elected in 1928.

As recently as the 2020 election, the party received less than two per cent of the vote, but the collapse of BC United, formerly known as the B.C. Liberals, paved the way for its rise to official opposition status and now government.

Questions remain about Doerkson’s status as an interim leader, since the Conservative constitution prohibits interim leaders seeking the position permanently, with constitutional changes requiring the support of a two-thirds majority of members.

The party has said it would “pursue the appropriate means under the party’s constitution and bylaws and the Societies Act” to keep Doerkson on as leader.

The Conservative win ends nine years of NDP government that began under the late John Horgan, before he stepped aside and Eby won the NDP leadership in 2022.

His tenure was not smooth.

He inherited a budget surplus from Horgan but the province is now facing a $14 billion projected deficit this year.

Eby eked out a slim win over the Conservatives in the 2024 election, but faced pressure over health care, law and order, a failed drug decriminalization project, and legal challenges related to Indigenous rights.

In the final week of the campaign, his party trailing in opinion polls, Eby appealed to Green supporters, asking them to consider voting NDP to avoid splitting the vote and helping the Conservatives.

He faced criticism over the early election call, with a campaign period that overlapped with the Oct. 17 municipal elections.

“It’s very clear that they just want to do it before the Conservatives get it all together,” said Queena Li, a student voting on Saturday in Eby’s riding of Vancouver-Point Grey.

Eby said on Friday his biggest regret of the campaign was failing to explain to B.C. that he called the election due to the difficulties of working with a bare majority in a “stalled out” legislature.

He must now be regretting that he called it at all.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026

— With files by Nono Shen in Brentwood Bay and Ashley Joannou in Vancouver
